mr president, europe has a unique opportunity and a moral obligation to put an end to the trade in minerals obtained in conditions which violate human rights. we have to get rid of prejudice and ask the companies. the good ones, the responsible ones, the ones that follow the rules are more than willing to join this chain of cleanliness, traceability and corporate social responsibility. it is essential to involve them in this joint endeavour so that they can make their best efforts of transparency and engagement. as elected representatives of the european citizens, it is our duty to act unequivocally and decisively, not only on the treatment of minerals such as coltan, but on the whole chain of production, distribution and supply. dr. mukwege, our sakharov prize, has not stopped claiming it. we owe it to them. if we do not act decisively, europe will be complicit in a true barbarism.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of establishing a mandatory traceability system for minerals extracted from conflict-affected areas, because it is the only way to effectively combat the link between their marketing and the financing of armed violent organisations. so far, only four percent of the companies affected have taken a voluntary certification system to ensure that the minerals they trade in, and that we carry in our phones, computers and many other products that we use every day, are not bloodstained. the european parliament has awarded the sakharov prize to dr mukwege, who has treated some 40,000 women and girls in the congo who have had to 'reconstruct' themselves from the atrocities to which they had been subjected by violent groups, and advocates the mandatory certification system. the rapporteur, from the people's group, nevertheless advocated voluntary regulation because it 'respects and guarantees the functioning of markets and creates a viable framework for businesses'. in the face of this, the socialists stand for 'respect for and guarantee of human rights and a viable framework for the dignity of persons'.
in writing. ‒ the aim of this regulation should be to achieve greater control of certain minerals or metals originating in conflict and high-risk areas, to prevent them from financing destabilisation and violence in areas where, on the contrary, the presence of these materials should serve the sustainable and peaceful development of the local economy. the regulation has huge shortcomings that call into question its usefulness: it unjustifiably restricts the number of materials that must be certified; it leaves import control to the companies themselves, who cannot be expected to declare their activities in conflict zones; it fails to take into account that most of these materials are processed before entering the european market, so most of the traffic is excluded from this legislation. that is why i voted against.

in writing. ‒ one of our foreign policy priorities at european level must be to prevent armed groups in conflict and high-risk areas from accessing funding for their activities through the extraction and trade of minerals. it is our duty to promote legitimate trade channels and to prevent the illegal and immoral trade in these minerals. considerable progress has been made in this area in recent years, but action is still needed at international level to address the problems in resource-rich but vulnerable countries to armed conflict. without underestimating the importance of these minerals to the economy of exporting countries, we must regulate as precisely and rigorously as possible to ensure that any material entering the eu comes from trade in line with european values. that is why i voted in favour of the report.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of establishing a mandatory traceability system for minerals extracted from conflict-affected areas because i believe that the voluntary nature of the commission's proposal was insufficient and would have no effect on the ground. so far, only four percent of the companies affected have taken a voluntary certification system to ensure that the minerals they trade in, and that we carry in our phones, computers and many other products that we use every day, are not bloodstained. mandatory measures are needed to prevent the indirect purchase of minerals extracted from conflict-affected areas and to effectively combat the link between their marketing and the financing of violent organisations.
in writing. ‒ we must ensure from the european parliament that there is a trade in minerals, especially in the areas of the world where there are major conflicts, under safe conditions and that, above all, it is prevented that armed groups can be financed through this activity. that is why i support the bill which establishes mandatory certification for all participants in the supply chain of metals and minerals from conflict and high-risk areas, because we cannot allow the extraction of minerals so necessary to manufacture many of the goods we use so much in our daily lives to be used to maintain illegal and terrorist activities.

in writing. ‒ i have analysed the different elements of this proposal and in the end i also have to listen to my conscience. i believe the right thing to do is to have a mandatory certification for those who purchase metals or minerals for the production of goods such as our mobile phones, washing machines and fridges. this is a just thing to do when we know that, for example, the proceeds of conflict minerals and metals has been linked to the funding of militias in the ongoing congolese conflict which has claimed the lives of 5.4 million people and displaced two million people. of course we must make a clear distinction between legitimate mining and trading in blood-stained minerals globally. as i see it, the commission proposals, which were mostly voluntary measures, did not go far enough. i supported the amendments with mandatory schemes for smelters and refiners, which are the key players in this market and cover most of the global market. i think that this is the right way forward as other sectors such as the diamond industry already have a mandatory labelling system and the united states has also passed mandatory legislation in this field.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report which makes the rules controlling the marketing and manufacture of minerals extracted from conflict zones mandatory. the struggle to exploit these precious minerals has led to massive human resource depletion and in some cases war. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'customs' in the definition of the concept of 'commercial'.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because parliament exercises its power of scrutiny over the regulations by which the european commission tries to impose exceptions to the rule by claiming a political power which it does not have. delegated acts allow parliament to oppose technical legislation developed by the commission and in this particular case the commission has introduced exceptions to the requirements laid down in directive 2011/65/eu on dangerous substances in electrical equipment. the commission has tried to introduce these exceptions to benefit producers at the expense of the safety of european citizens. that is why i have decided to vote in favour of this resolution rejecting the delegated act.
in writing. ‒ when the revisions of the directives on waste electrical and electronic equipment were adopted in 2012, the parliament and the council agreed to allow a transitional exemption from the use of cadmium for certain quantum tv luminaires and displays. that derogation expired last year and the european commission therefore submitted a delegated act to extend the deadline until 2018 which the green group has objected to in view of the high toxicity of cadmium as a substance and the existence of alternatives which they consider that a postponement of the exemption is not justified. the socialists agree that there is no reason to extend the deadline any further and we believe that industry must make an effort to strengthen the existing alternatives.
in writing. i voted in favour of this resolution because parliament exercises its power of scrutiny over the regulations by which the european commission tries to impose exceptions to the rule by claiming a political power which it does not have. delegated acts allow parliament to oppose technical legislation developed by the commission and in this particular case the commission has introduced exceptions to the requirements laid down in directive 2011/65/eu on dangerous substances in electrical equipment. the commission has tried to introduce these exceptions to benefit producers at the expense of the safety of european citizens. that is why i have decided to vote in favour of this resolution rejecting the delegated act.
in writing. ‒ currently, the directive 2011/65/eu on the restriction of the use of certain hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment restricts, among other things, the use of cadmium in such equipment. the usp directive provides for exemptions from the restrictions provided that the inclusion of these substances does not weaken the degree of protection of human health and the environment. furthermore, it does not appear that tv sets with cadmium quantum dots are already on the union market. not only are cadmium-free quantum dots technically available, but a whole line of tvs based on this technology is already widely available on the union market. that is why i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this amendment because the restriction of hazardous substances directive (rohs) adopted in 2011 exempted the use of cadmium in led and display applications until 1 july 2014. in january 2015, the commission proposed a delegated act extending the lifetime of cadmium in televisions until june 2018. the commission is thus effectively reintroducing cadmium on the european market after cadmium tv sets have already been withdrawn from the market with a view to the end of the exemption provided for in the regulation by july 2014.

in writing. ‒ i vote in favour of underlining the importance of the exemption for cadmium in lighting applications. the manufacture of tv sets without cadmium quantum dots on the union market should be taken as a model to allow these technologies to be installed in other cadmium quantum dots lighting products.
in writing. ‒ when the revisions of the directives on waste electrical and electronic equipment were adopted in 2012, the parliament and the council agreed to allow a transitional exemption from the use of cadmium for certain quantum tv luminaires and displays. that derogation expired last year and the european commission therefore submitted a delegated act to extend the deadline until 2018 which the green group has objected to in view of the high toxicity of cadmium as a substance and the existence of alternatives which they consider that a postponement of the exemption is not justified. the socialists agree that there is no reason to extend the deadline any further and we believe that industry must make an effort to strengthen the existing alternatives.
in writing. we voted in favour of this amendment because the restriction of hazardous substances directive (rohs) adopted in 2011 exempted the use of cadmium in led and display applications until 1 july 2014. in january 2015, the commission proposed a delegated act extending the lifetime of cadmium in televisions until june 2018. the commission is thus effectively reintroducing cadmium on the european market after cadmium tv sets have already been withdrawn from the market with a view to the end of the exemption provided for in the regulation by july 2014.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because parliament exercises its power of scrutiny over the regulations by which the european commission tries to impose exceptions to the rule by claiming a political power which it does not have. delegated acts allow parliament to oppose technical legislation developed by the commission and in this particular case the commission has introduced exceptions to the requirements laid down in directive 2011/65/eu on dangerous substances in electrical equipment. the commission has tried to introduce these exceptions to benefit producers at the expense of the safety of european citizens. that is why i have decided to vote in favour of this resolution rejecting the delegated act.

in writing. ‒ this was an objection to a delegated act concerning the import of ethyl alcohol of agricultural origin and the establishment of specific measures relating to the market for this product. we have proposed three amendments to the text because we believe it is important that the problem of access to land and its use for food should be reflected in the text. i have voted in favour of the objection to the delegated act, however, because the existing monitoring of data relating to ethyl alcohol of agricultural origin and its marketing ensures greater transparency and knowledge of market developments than the commission's proposal that these data be collected by eurostat. this would not give such accurate information and would miss data on a controversial market which i am very critical of.
in writing. ‒ the monitoring of data on ethyl alcohol of agricultural origin ensures both transparency and knowledge of the evolution of a market which remains unstable and subject to strong competition, especially in the face of imports from third countries. this information is also extremely useful for the negotiation of international agreements and anti-dumping investigations. since eurostat does not provide such precise information, and there is no alternative for economic operators, member states and eu institutions to gain full knowledge of the market situation, i have considered it necessary to vote in favour of objecting to this commission delegated regulation.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution on maternity leave because i believe that the rights of working mothers cannot be locked in a drawer. the proposal to amend the existing directive extends the protection and safety of pregnant workers and those who have recently given birth, as well as mothers who have adopted a child under one year of age. i find it difficult to understand that the eu is able to agree on many economic measures, and when we are talking about something as relevant as the rights of working mothers, the council is unable to reach an agreement, and the commission is therefore proposing to withdraw the proposal. i also support the need, as expressed in the resolution, for the commission to present a proposal for a directive on paternity leave and a revision of the directive on parental leave, with a view to achieving a better reconciliation of family and working life for mothers and fathers. finally, i also support the call on the commission to submit a new proposal as soon as possible if it finally decides to withdraw the one on the table.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution as it is a four-year-old deadlock in the directive amending directive 92/85/eec on maternity leave. it is an extension and harmonisation of a right of women workers across the eu, extending their right to maternity leave to 20 weeks, and to at least 2 weeks for workers immediately after their birth; at the same time, it also reaffirms directive 2010/18/eu on paternity leave, which guarantees minimum leave to share leave up to four months. the proposal was approved by parliament at first reading but has since been blocked by the council, citing increased labour costs and job security. firstly, we believe it is unfair that it is the workers who are paying the consequences of the financial crisis and that it has a negative impact on their rights; secondly, the commission's withdrawal of this legislative proposal will not help to break with the perpetuation of gender roles associated with women's reproductive capacity in the world of work.

in writing. ‒ the resolution adopted today on the review of the implementation of the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities reiterates the obligations of the eu and its member states to effectively implement the principle of accessibility and non-discrimination for persons with disabilities across the board and not just in access to employment, in order to achieve genuine autonomy and independence. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the protection of the environment from harmful substances. we also welcome the house's support for calling on member states to remove restrictions on the exercise of the right to vote and stand as a candidate for election by persons with disabilities currently in force in 21 of the 28 member states, by a restrictive interpretation of the legal capacity of persons with disabilities and in contravention of article 12 of the crpd on equality before the law.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this resolution because i share its content, the main demand of which is the objective of improving the living conditions of people with disabilities through equal access to services and the labour market. i regret that it is not mentioned that this can only be done through a policy which strengthens public services and sets out concrete policies against discrimination against disabled people, and while it calls for states to cooperate with each other in these matters, it does not set a concrete priority or set a minimum that must be met within the union. i understand that the political will behind this resolution is positive, and i therefore vote in favour, but there are no concrete resources or commitments to end the discrimination (double discrimination in the case of women with disabilities) suffered by these people.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution on the review of the implementation of the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities because it reiterates the obligations of the eu and its member states to effectively implement the principle of accessibility and non-discrimination for people with disabilities in a transversal way and not only in terms of access to employment, in order to achieve genuine autonomy and independence. the resolution calls on the council to adopt without delay a position on the anti-discrimination directive, which has been blocked since parliament's first reading in april 2009, a key demand of the socialists. we have also won the support of the house for the socialists to ask the member states to remove the restrictions on the exercise of the right of active and passive suffrage of disabled people, which are currently in force in 21 of the 28 member states, because of a restrictive interpretation of the legal capacity of disabled people and in contravention of article 12 of the crpd on equality before the law.
in writing. there are 80 million disabled people in the european union, and all too often they face discrimination and barriers in the exercise of their rights and in access to culture, education and employment. the united nations convention on the rights of persons with disabilities entered into force in the european union in january 2011, but three member states (sweden, the netherlands and ireland) have not yet ratified it. parliament called today for the convention to be respected and applied so that people with disabilities can enjoy their rights like any other european citizen. i support this text because there is still a long way to go before there is real equality.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this resolution, which states that the european parliament must be fully involved in monitoring and implementing human rights and in all actions aimed at correcting inequalities in access to them. we believe that the adoption of two key pieces of legislation - the european accessibility act and the general anti-discrimination directive - is essential, both being an essential part of the implementation of the un convention. the resolution also calls on member states to translate into national law the obligations arising from article 12 of the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities and more specifically the right of all persons with disabilities to vote and be elected.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this resolution because it does not reflect the real damage that massive felling of trees can cause to the inhabitants of the puglia region in italy. there is no guarantee that the approved chemical treatments will eradicate this serious disease, while it will bring heavy costs to farmers and no curbs are put on imports from infected regions. our group in the european left has tabled an alternative resolution with the green group and the italian five star movement, which points out the environmental risks of the proposed treatments and the need to help the farmers concerned. in view of the serious risks that this disease may pose to our country, we do not believe that this resolution proposes appropriate measures to control international imports to prevent the spread of the disease and that is why i have decided to vote against it.
in writing. despite the european commission's efforts to contain the outbreak of xylella in olive trees, the disease is still spreading, wreaking havoc in southern italy and raising fears in countries where the sector is key. in this resolution we call, among other things, for the sector to be compensated for losses and for restrictions on the import of plants from affected areas in third countries. we regret that the commission is once again late in implementing preventive measures (as was the case with the black spot from south africa which mainly affected spain) and that it is not determined to review legislation on plant health checks. we hope, however, that the commission will take account of what we have adopted in this parliament.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution calling on the commission to take more effective measures to prevent the spread of xylella fastidiosa in the eu. xylella fastidiosa is a bacterium with a huge pathogenic potential on a large number of plants that can cause serious losses in european agriculture and in the agri-food chain. its appearance in italy with 9 million olive trees affected - apparently from an infected ornamental plant introduced through rotterdam - highlights the malfunctioning of eu plant health protection against imports from third countries and the commission's slowness in reacting to a problem which, if not tackled in time, can be devastating for olive trees in southern europe and whose spread also threatens citrus and vineyards. it is therefore necessary to review the official eu plant health system applicable to imports, to introduce a preventive system for import controls, to launch the mandatory establishment of the olive plant health passport and to use all possible funds and instruments to contribute to the economic recovery of the affected areas.

in writing. ‒ xylella fastidiosa represents an immediate and very dangerous threat to the production of certain crops in southern europe, including olive trees, almonds, peaches and ornamental plants. there is currently no treatment available to cure diseased plants in situ, and affected plants tend to remain infected throughout their lives or die quickly. given the difficulty of stopping the spread of xylella fastidiosa once it has affected a production area, priority should be given to import-oriented prevention measures and outbreak containment, while increasing exchanges in the field of research. that is why i voted in favour.

madam president, the european union's relations with turkey are very important. the european union has longstanding and numerous links with turkey, including a customs union. and it is also a candidate country with which, as we all know, negotiations are under way. accession requires major reforms in turkey. the european standards on the rule of law, the independence of the judiciary and respect for human rights should guide these reforms, which must be advanced. but on the other hand, turkey is experiencing a difficult situation because of its proximity to syria and iraq and the consequent wave of refugees. we must continue to provide them with humanitarian aid. and turkey and several eu member states have neighbouring countries in the southern mediterranean that face serious security and stability challenges. the european union and turkey must therefore cooperate in the field of security and the fight against terrorism, and cooperation on migration is also essential. and so i welcome the recent entry into force of the readmission agreement. we must also cooperate in the energy field. turkey is very much needed to diversify europe's energy supply routes. and it is also appropriate to keep turkey informed of the negotiations we are conducting with the united states on the trade and investment agreement. turkey is a major regional player and has a strategic location. dialogue and cooperation with turkey on foreign and security policy are becoming increasingly necessary in a very difficult regional context. (the speaker agrees to answer a question put under the 'blue card' procedure (rule 162 (8) of the rules of procedure))
the answer is 'blue card'. the customs union. we do not have the other components, which are very numerous, of the european union. i certainly understand that turkey has a legitimate desire to pursue full integration. the customs union is a part, but only a part, of what political union and full membership of the european union is. it's just a part, not the whole thing.
madam president, thank you, mrs piri, for your ability to reach agreements and, even more so, for your patience in the face of various intransigencies. the report contains, firstly, a harsh and necessary criticism of the turkish government's performance in the field of the quality of democracy and respect for the basic rights of its citizens. secondly, an explicit recognition of the lack of leadership by the european union in the recent period and a positive assessment of turkey's strategic role in the economic and geopolitical sphere. thirdly, the need to give new impetus to the discussions on all the outstanding chapters - especially, of course, chapters 23 and 24, but also chapter 15. the opposite, of course, would be precisely to justify the attitudes of victim-oriented nationalism which the majority party wants to turn into an electoral argument. fourthly, the hope restored in a possible agreement with cyprus, in which europe must show serenity without interference and make its full contribution, in a discreet but positive way, to the success of the talks. and finally, there is a certain expectation that the kurds will be able to play a central role in the turkish democratic system in the coming period. so, if the balance is not disturbed, we shall support this resolution. let us work to ensure that the day after the elections turkey will once again be the friendly, positive interlocutor, consistent with the copenhagen criteria, that europe wanted to have when we started the talks ten years ago.
madam president, first of all i would like to thank the rapporteur, kati piri, for the work she has done: a great deal of hard work, and very complex negotiations, to reach an agreement and have the report we have today. the report does two things. it makes a proper and necessary criticism of the deterioration of the rule of law, the quality of democracy, the right to freedom of expression and the independent judiciary that has occurred in recent years in turkey, deep concerns that have also been expressed on several occasions in this parliament. it also reflects the recognition, which is also necessary, of turkey's solidarity with the refugees, of the role it plays in the region in strategic terms or, also, in relation to relations with europe in the energy field. but what we have to be clear about is that the accession process of turkey must be the necessary lever - and the regulation has to go in that direction - for progress to be made in democratic reforms, taking into account the copenhagen criteria and the values which have underpinned the european union for its construction.

i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. i wonder how anyone can propose or say that ethiopia is a model for poverty eradication in the region when we are talking about a government that has made more than ten million hectares of land available to foreign companies, a government that is implementing dam projects such as gibe iii or renaissance - by the way, built by an italian multinational - and, in addition, is setting up large plantations such as in kuraz, which threaten the omo river and lake turkana, which are the livelihood of thousands and thousands of people and the people living on the river and the lake, who are also suffering intimidation and repression so that they will not resist. this, commissioner, will cause more hunger, more poverty and more deaths in a country where 80% of the population already lives on less than two dollars a day. i think this is a model for the interests of the big transnational corporations in the european union, but not for the interests of the people who live in the country. please tell mrs mogherini, on behalf of our group, to put an end to western greed. stopping these projects is the most useful thing we can do to fight terror and save lives.
on behalf of the green group, mr president, mr commissioner, you have left me rather perplexed. you're talking about an ethiopia that has nothing to do with the one i know. everyone knows that the elections in ethiopia are a sham. ethiopia is the fourth largest recipient of development aid from the european union and is also the country where the election observers sent by this parliament are not allowed to enter; the country where swedish journalists are imprisoned on the sole charge of having entered the ogaden area. independent organizations denounce the systematic persecution of political opponents, independent journalists and bloggers who criticize the government and ethnic groups such as oromo, ogaden, or sidama. the ethiopian government does not allow observers or journalists into the ogaden area, where it is estimated that 30% of women have been raped, many of them by government agents. i wonder what the european union is waiting for in order to condemn the ethiopian government and to demand immediate respect for human rights. what are we waiting for to make our aid conditional on the creation of a mission to investigate human rights violations, persecution and torture? the people of ethiopia do not deserve the punishment they suffer at the hands of this government, which is tolerated and aided by the european union. can we be sure that no part of the european union's aid is being used for repression? we have a major responsibility in the suffering of thousands of people and we cannot look the other way. otherwise, we're complicit in the crime. it's time to act now.

president-in-office of the council, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy.– madam president, first of all, please allow me to underline that today, and for this particular debate, i am talking on behalf of the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy/vice-president ms mogherini, so we should take that into account. at the same time, as a presidency i can only underline that several commissioners are already in riga today because, as i mentioned, several side events – for example the first eastern partnership media conference, have started already. so we do appreciate also, as a presidency, the very good cooperation with the commission on preparation of this eastern partnership summit and it is very important to have several commissioners in riga today already. coming back to our debate, please allow me, once again on behalf of the high representative, to underline that we have listened carefully to all that has been said here today during the debate. please rest assured that we will be taking into consideration all the comments and proposals made by members. let me reiterate that the riga summit will demonstrate that the eastern partnership remains our priority and will send a clear political signal that, firstly, the eu is strongly committed to its eastern partnership and determined to pursue closer tailor-made relations with its independent and sovereign eastern european partners. we will therefore continue to give every support to those partners which have taken on mobilisation on the most ambitious reform commitments through all the association agreements. the summit marks a new level in our relations with our partners, the most ambitious: our bilateral association agreements with the three partners. secondly, our partnership involves six partner countries. i cannot stress enough the importance of maintaining the inclusivity of the partnership. the eu will therefore continue to engage strongly with all partners whatever their individual level of relations with the eu. thirdly, we will step up our strategic communication efforts to explain what the relations with our partners are about and what they are not about, and we will certainly argue that they are not directed against any third party. we will therefore continue our dialogue with those who challenge this. several members also raised the question of the european perspective for georgia, moldova and ukraine and the strength of the reflections in the riga declaration. let me first of all stress that the drafting process of the joint declaration of the eastern partnership summit is still ongoing. negotiations are of an inclusive nature between both our member states and partners. negotiations are still ongoing and therefore, at this stage, we still await the final outcome of these negotiations. the agreed consensus will have to reflect each country’s specific needs, priorities and aspirations and the common interests they share with the eu, as well as the euʼs interests, while making a realistic assessment of what can be achieved within the next few years. in this context, riga should highlight first and furthermost that we have moved to a new level in our relations with the three partners with whom we have signed the most ambitious ever bilateral association agreements, but it should also signal our readiness to work for more tailor-made agreements with others to ensure that the partnership remains an inclusive framework. i believe we share the opinion that preparation for the eastern partnership summit in riga is of such utmost importance that we could take much more time to discuss several topics and more details. but respecting your agenda, i will save time and, in concluding, i will just mention that i highly appreciate your commitment and support for the eastern partnership, and that relations with national parliaments and the role of euronest in promoting and consolidating the eastern partnership are highly important. together we must help partners realise their full potential. i thank you very much for all your contributions and your support for the eastern partnership policy and i thank you very much that you do care about the need for us to have a successful riga summit.
zanda kalniņa-lukaševica,president-in-office of the council, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. madam president, honourable members, we have the next topic on our agenda. i am glad to participate in this discussion on the next summit between the eu and the community of latin america and caribbean states (celac), which will take place on 10 and 11 june 2015 in brussels for the first time. it will be the second summit held with celac as a counterpart, but the eighth ever, since our partnership with the region was launched in rio back in 1999. as members are well aware, events all around europe’s neighbourhood keep a good deal of attention focused there. but the eu, as a global player, does not lower its guard in its relations with other regions of the world. in some areas, we find regions which are luckily more stable, sometimes giving the false impression that the international community is less in demand. latin america and the caribbean is such a region, and the upcoming summit of heads of state and government in june will be a critical moment to infuse new dynamism into our relations. we want to create a real partnership for the next generation. under the general heading ‘shaping our common future: working for prosperous, cohesive and sustainable societies for our citizens,’ we intend to highlight the many dimensions of our relations. features such as a common cultural heritage, common values, a strong belief in regionalism and in an effective multilateralism – if combined well – have the capacity to unlock opportunities through our cooperation with the region. the strategic bi-regional partnership that unites the eu and the region has been active for over 15 years. in this time, we have strengthened our relations, making the eu the main investor and a key trading partner, with 26 association or free trade agreements out of 33 countries. however, on the political front, we can still do more to tackle effectively global issues together. this is why part of the summit’s discussion will focus on exploring possible areas of convergence as regards key international processes. negotiations around climate change, the post-2015 development agenda or the international debate on drugs issues, in view of the special session of the united nations general assembly in 2016, will be the object of one of the three working sessions. in order to materialise our common priorities, we also intend to adopt a reviewed and expanded eu-celac action plan, which will include new areas of cooperation such as higher education and citizen security. this shows how much we are linked. citizen security in latin america and the caribbean affects stability in our neighbourhood, through organised crime along the ‘cocaine route’, right into europe. our scientific communities on both sides of the atlantic are working together on similar projects; they will link member of the commission.– madam president, i am speaking here in this plenary debate on growth rates in the eu and the spring 2015 economic forecast on behalf of my dear colleague pierre moscovici. the commission published its spring 2015 european economic forecast on 5 may. its main message is that the near-term outlook for the eu economy has improved. this was confirmed in the first quarter of this year, where real gdp increased by 0.4 % quarter-on-quarter in both the eu and the euro area. the economic recovery therefore continued in both regions and even strengthened somewhat in the euro area. the euro-area economy recorded its highest growth rate in nearly two years. the economy is getting an extra boost in the short term from tailwinds such as low oil prices, a weaker euro and quantitative easing (qe) from the european central bank. the combined strength of these positive factors underpins a slight upward revision for gdp growth this year. according to our forecasts, real gdp growth in the eu is expected to increase from 1.4% last year to 1.8% in the current year, 2015, and 2.1% in 2016. in the euro area, it is now forecast to pick up from 0.9% last year to 1.5% in the current year, 2015 and 1.9% in 2016. however, underlying weaknesses and legacies from the crisis remain and weigh on the medium-term growth outlook. unemployment remains intolerably high. the level of debt, in particular corporate and sovereign, remains very high. the share of non-performing bank loans is elevated and continues to rise in some member states. the shortfall of investment over the past six years has reduced economic growth potential. across eu member states, the recovery is expected to remain uneven. all countries are set to gain from the positive tailwinds, but the extent to which they will benefit will depend on several factors such as the varying responsiveness of individual economies to lower oil prices and the euro depreciation. the ecb’s qe is also likely to have a higher impact in countries with tight financing conditions. the recovery of the labour market in the eu is progressing and is becoming fairly broad-based across sectors. the unemployment rate is projected to decline slowly, reflecting the persistence of high structural unemployment and the large unemployment gaps, as the rise in economic activity is not strong enough for a more marked improvement. inflation is bottoming out. later this year, and more noticeably in 2016, inflation is expected to pick up. it will be underpinned by stronger domestic demand, fading effects of lower commodity prices and higher import prices triggered by the euro depreciation. inflation expectations have recovered, and the risks of deflation have moderated as a result of the ecb’s qe and the stronger growth outlook. the fiscal outlook is improving and the aggregated fiscal policy stance is expected to be broadly neutral in the current year in the european union. in many eu member states, deficit ratios are projected to continue falling in 2015 and 2016, helped by stronger growth and lower interest payments on public debt. following the substantial fiscal adjustment achieved over the last few years, the aggregated fiscal policy stance in 2015 in the eu is expected to be broadly neutral and therefore more supportive to growth. moreover, for the first time since the onset of the crisis, the debt burden is also expected to decrease as of this year. uncertainty remains elevated but risks to our growth outlook are broadly balanced. growth could surprise on the upside if monetary policy and low oil prices have bigger effects than anticipated. also, the investment plan for europe, for which a cautious approach has prevailed in our assessment, could have a stronger than expected impact. downside risks include geopolitical risks, as tensions related to the russia-ukraine conflict remain high. also, if oil prices rebound faster than assumed, this could erase the windfall gains from lower energy prices. in financial markets, the risk of renewed financial market volatility could weigh on economic growth.

in writing. ‒ we voted against as the report calls for a strengthened role for the csdp, with an emphasis on improving cooperation mechanisms and adapting them to security threats and challenges. one of the key ideas in the report is the development of the so-called "military industrial complex", which includes tax incentives as part of the plan (drone development, among other things). the economic crisis is seen as an excuse to modify the athena mechanism, paving the way for its possible financing directly through the budgets. in addition, alignment with nato (as stipulated in the lisbon treaty) is listed as one of the major political challenges in the report.

in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of the report because we believe that in the global context we need more than ever a more integrated defence cooperation, in which resources and capabilities are shared. the report also calls for the athena mechanism to be given a larger budget and regrets that the actual share of common costs covered by the athena mechanism remains very low and that the high share of expenditure and responsibilities for military operations borne by the national level prevents some member states from actively participating in csdp operations. the report calls for more flexibility in csdp missions and operations and for them to be able to be launched more quickly, and stresses the importance of greater cooperation between military operations and civilian missions.
in writing. ‒ the report put to the vote is a clear call for the expansion of the military missions of the common security and defence policy. the text regrets the low investment in missions and calls for increases in military spending. it also raises the possibility of the union having a budget to finance the first stages of the missions. on the other hand, the call for growth and efficiency in spending is not without political orientations. the text makes it clear that the union must be a 'genuine actor in defence in the context of nato' and must be complementary to it. i have therefore voted against this report.

in writing. ‒ the report on the impact of the evolution of the european defence market on security and defence capabilities in europe falls within the remit of both the juri and imco committees. the need for a single defence market is underlined through the reduction of processes and obstacles that avoid duplication, which generates distortions in the market. one of the essential elements in favour of european independence in security and defence is to be able to count on a highly competitive european industry in the r & i-based sector. however, the fragmentation of markets means that collaboration between member states is limited and research is fragmented. it also points to the need for prior planning for strategic investment in equipment purchases and renewals between member states. like the whole of the spanish socialist delegation, i considered it necessary to vote in favour of its adoption.

in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of it because the report: it highlights that directive 2009/81/ec on the procedures for the award of works contracts, supply contracts and service contracts in the fields of defence and security and directive 2009/43/ec on transfers of defence-related products are correctly applied to maximise the available internal market rules. it stresses the need to eliminate all compensation in the security and defence sector for distorting competition in the internal market, ensuring equal conditions for all suppliers in access to public contracts and procurement, with particular attention to smes. it urges the eeas to improve the transparency of public procurement in these areas as a matter of urgency. it called for the tools provided for in the above directives to be used to maximise resources through central purchasing and ensuring that smes have a knowledge of the supply chain. the report also stresses the need for a single defence market through the reduction of processes and obstacles that avoid duplication, which generates distortions in the market.
in writing. ‒ the report on security and defence capabilities in europe has been presented from a perspective that does not contribute to stability on the continent and its surroundings. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover all the activities of the european union. the text also stresses that the eu's work in the framework of nato is important for ensuring security and stability in europe and for increasing the economic efficiency of missions. the report also frequently confuses the european union as an organisation with europe as a continent, projecting it as the only legitimate actor in the geographical space. this is not a secondary aspect, because it involves the negation of the interests of other parties with whom we have to live. good neighbourliness must be our priority. i have therefore voted against this report.

in writing. ‒ we voted against the report proposed by ana gomes. the report begins by stressing that the reduction in defence budgets weakens the defence potential of the member states. it also refers to regional instability to justify the request for coordination and increase in european defence budgets. it explicitly states that the current security threats are common to the eu as a whole and must be tackled in a united and coordinated manner, pooling and sharing both civilian and military resources. we therefore voted against it because we believe that the eu cannot be a force for war but a force for peace.

madam president, in june the g7 will meet in bavaria - the meeting of the 'club of the rich', of those who impoverish the most, exploit the most and pollute the most, and sustain their wealth through war and plunder. a meeting where decisions are going to be made about climate change or how to continue to ravage our planet; about international politics or how to continue bombing; or about energy policy or how to continue stealing natural resources. issues that affect us all, but in this meeting only the chosen have a voice and vote, they usurp the voice of the international community to impose their privileges. the g7 is intended to replace the united nations general assembly, which would be the place where all these decisions are taken. they will also be meeting behind a wall of 2,500 police who will prevent the powerful from hearing the voice of a people who are fed up with those who rule for the elites. but not by killing, as in 2001 they killed carlo giuliani in genoa, they're going to shut us up. carlo, we have not forgotten.
in writing. i would like to start by expressing my surprise at the ways in which the commission is questioning us. it is not normal that we should once again be debating an agenda which the commission is putting before us partially and without prior debate and for the results of which it is not even obliged to give an account to the european parliament. i would like to say a few words about one of the subjects which will undoubtedly be the focus of the debate: the global economic crisis. the difficulties imposed by the difficult access to public and external financing, as in greece and the european periphery, and the negative impact of interstate competition on global social and environmental standards require putting a reform of global trade and financial institutions on the agenda. the g7 must push for reform of the institutions of the imf and the world bank that recovers its original objectives: to provide credit and technical support to those states that implement strategies of social and productive development, instead of reinforcing the permanent blackmail of the markets on the peoples.
mr president, i would first like to congratulate my colleague, mr tarabella, on the great work he has done on this important report. i would like to ask you, since we have the opportunity to be with the commissioner and to be here - i regret that the council is not here - to give your full support to this programme: it is very important to change consumption habits and to promote much healthier consumption. i know you'll support him. i hope the council will change its mind on this. it is very important, in my view, to focus on fresh fruit and vegetables. we want to change lifestyle habits, to make them healthy, in children from six to ten years old. that's why fresh produce is a priority. i would also like to say that i am glad that the educational measures include a product as essential to the mediterranean diet as olive oil or honey. and finally, i would say that i do not think it is appropriate to allocate resources according to historical criteria. so we're done with the historical criteria here and we're going to actually go to the number of children by country. that's my opinion.
mr president, mr tarabella must be congratulated on his work. ladies and gentlemen, the recent crisis, caused by the russian embargo, shows how much we need to strengthen the promotion instruments we have in the european union in order to improve the consumption of our products both inside and outside the union, but above all on the internal market. that is why this initiative is necessary, because the demand for certain products in the european union is, in some cases, declining as a result of much of the change in consumer habits. the programme to promote the consumption of fruit and vegetables and milk in schools, with the aim of encouraging healthy habits among all european citizens, but especially among children, is thus a means of giving a fair start to a part of the production which is sometimes affected by critical market situations, such as the one we are now experiencing with russia. i believe that the new regulation, which merges the two existing schemes, the fruit and vegetable and the milk schemes, gives coherence to the european union's policy in this area and i hope that this merger will be a first step so that in the not too distant future the promotion of the consumption of healthy products will not be limited to specific sectors but will be open to other products whose consumption also has a beneficial effect on health, such as olive oil or nuts. if we are to promote healthy habits, i do not see why we should limit ourselves to two very specific sectors and ignore the nutritional role of other foods as healthy as these. i think it is good news that support has been given for an increase in the funds allocated to these programmes and for the abolition of national co-financing, so as to ensure that the programmes are treated equally in all the member states and thus improve the european dimension of the measures.
on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, eritrea is indeed a forgotten country on a continent that has already been forgotten; it always remains outside the focus of our news, of our debates. we have spoken very little about eritrea, mr commissioner, and we have done very little for eritrea, a country with a high degree of repression - one of the highest in the world - with a bloodthirsty dictator who has been concentrating all the power of the state for more than 20 years and, in effect, an open-air prison. that is eritrea. but if we talk about eritrea today it is not so much because we are concerned about human rights in eritrea, but because we have received the warning, the alert that there are many eritrean citizens who are leaving their country, emigrating or seeking asylum or refuge. that's what makes us talk about eritrea today, that's the truth. with a rather small population -- six million -- last year alone, 300,000 eritreans left their country. many of these who leave their country are children, they are very young children, they are children of 15, 16, 17 years old. the majority of them are living in refugee camps and, as you know, there is a very serious problem of human trafficking and organized torture in the sinai peninsula. the commission has announced a possible aid package: triple the amount so far earmarked. it is good news, but the question, commissioner, is whether we are really going to allocate this aid to the eritreans or whether we are going to succeed in maintaining the status quo of the dictator of eritrea rather than helping the citizens. how do we know that this money will not end up benefiting, as has happened so far, the dictator? we are not talking about asylum and family reunification, which is something that many citizens, those who have been victims of the exodus from eritrea, need. why don't we talk more about that and also open up our space so that these people can come to have a half-decent life? what i would not like is for it to seem, commissioner, that we are like those rich people who throw in the towel so that others can solve their problems.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, commissioner mimica, eritrea is a signatory to the cotonou agreement, in which the parties commit themselves to promote and protect all fundamental freedoms and human rights. this is a country without democratic elections since 1993. a little over a year ago, president afewerki bluntly stated: if anyone in this country thinks that there can be democracy or a multiparty system, let them go to another world to think about such things. we are talking about a government which makes permanent use of the state of emergency and which recruits men, women and children for its army in a forcible and indefinite manner; which arbitrarily arrests and tortures; which restricts freedom of expression, conscience and movement and suppresses religious freedom. a government that provides logistical and financial support to terrorist groups. do we need more reasons to evaluate what we are doing with eritrea? but eritrea is also alganesh fessaha, president of the italian ngo gandhi, the doctor who travels to sudan, ethiopia and sinai to work in the origin, from where more than 5,000 eritreans flee every month to europe, escaping the afewerki regime. alganesh fessaha has managed to rescue hundreds of migrants kidnapped in the sinai. almost half of eritrea's six million people are under 15, and there are thousands of skinny kids with terrible stories behind them in lampedusa, who eat zighini, the dish that reminds them of their land, prepared by the nuns thanks to alganesh's recipe. alganesh fessaha says that the kidnappers call their families in eritrea so they can hear their cries as they torture them: melting plastic into their skin, grinding them with sticks or burning their hair with kerosene, she adds. they demand a ransom that they claim can amount to up to $45,000: "if you don't pay, we will sell one of your corneas or a kidney" the traffickers tell their relatives. so far, alganesh fessaha has managed, yes, to free hundreds of them; but the hope of establishing a path where eritrea not only enters the inclusive governance - which ban ki-moon spoke to us about this afternoon - where europe can be that locomotive that takes it out of that repression and that lack of respect for human rights, is in our hands.

madam president, we do not have only a physical nature in the 21st century, we also have a digital or virtual nature. so every pillar of our lives, security and freedoms has a cyber nature as well. if this is true of our lives as individuals, it is also true of our businesses and our governments. cyberattack is strategic, and in the case of the media, it's key to our democracy because they are, of course, a critical structure, and this applies to both common crimes and crimes of an ideological nature, especially in the case of identity or religious fanatics. it's especially crucial in the face of terrorist strategies -- we've talked about it today. the cyber attack, in any case, is global and the geostrategic board forces us to do the prevention and the persecution work well. but it is essential to maintain proportionality on individual freedoms in the fight against these crimes and attacks. if there is a challenge in the 21st century, it is this. we cannot, with good intentions, go beyond the limits which the public authorities must and can set and which they must set with surgical precision. you, all of us, are going to engage and we're going to engage intelligence experts, engineers, governments, but are we going to engage philosophers, sociologists, historians or jurists as intensely? the broader strategic debate is as key as the short-term reaction or action itself: without it, we are unbalancing an absolutely crucial situation.
member of the commission.– madam president, early or forced marriages constitute a violation of girls and women’s human rights and are a brutal form of discrimination rooted in gender inequalities. protecting children against harmful practices, including child, early and forced marriage, is a priority for the european union. this has been reiterated in various policy documents, including the latest action plan on human rights and democracy. and rest assured: the successor to the eu action plan on gender equality and women’s empowerment in development will foster women and girls’ physical and psychological integrity, with a specific focus on the fight against harmful traditional practices. we all know that addressing child marriage is a very complex issue. it requires a comprehensive strategy that covers the adoption of protective legislation, the enhancement of access to quality education, the promotion of gender equality, and a change in mentalities and social norms. it also requires adequate funding and well-targeted projects. we are committed to ensuring both. at the girl summit in london in july 2014 the european union committed to allocating more than eur 100 million for the next seven years to gender equality and children’s wellbeing under the programme on global public goods and challenges. additional projects are also envisaged under the european instrument for democracy and human rights and under the pan-african programme in order to support the african committee of experts on the rights and welfare of children, which is the only region-focused children’s rights instrument in the world. in order to translate our policy into actions on the ground, the european union has developed a series of projects and actions in the framework of our cooperation with regional organisations. also, through political dialogue the european union regularly engages with countries where early and forced marriages take place. eighty-four eu delegations worldwide have prioritised children’s rights in their human rights country strategies. human rights are at the heart of our partnership with the african continent under the joint africa-eu strategy. at the 4th africa-eu summit in 2014, it was agreed to work together to ensure the full respect of human rights, international law, gender equality, and to fight all forms of discrimination, racism and xenophobia. the european union participated at the casablanca donor meeting on ending child, early and forced marriage last week, following the ‘girls not brides’ conference for a global partnership to end child marriage. all eu framework agreements with third countries – such as association and cooperation agreements concluded since 1995 – include a human rights clause. through it, the parties to the agreement declare their shared commitment to the promotion and protection of human rights. it also gives the eu a clear legal basis on which to raise human rights issues with the respective countries. and we regularly do so. moreover, some eu framework agreements include articles on human rights cooperation and on cooperation related to gender equality. on this basis, specific cooperation initiatives can be agreed to fight against child marriage. the european union welcomed the entry into force in august 2014 of the council of europe convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence. so far 37 countries, of which 23 are eu member states, have signed the convention and 18 countries, of which 11 are eu member states, have ratified it. national ratification processes are progressing well. five member states ratified in 2014 alone. the commission services are also examining the legal, policy and practical implications of a possible eu accession to the convention. as part of its initiatives to tackle violence against women, the commission funds national awareness-raising campaigns by member states, grassroots projects by civil society organisations and european networks in this area. these campaigns, projects and networks play an important role in raising awareness of the convention and in promoting its ratification and proper implementation. to conclude, i would like to praise the work done by the committee on women’s rights and gender equality and the subcommittee on human rights. both use every opportunity to raise awareness and challenge practices contrary to our human rights principles. your work is absolutely essential to the upholding of human rights principles within our partner countries and i am thankful for it.
the european union is a project of the european union, and it is a project of the european union, and it is a project of the european union, and it is a project of the european union. from different ideological positions on many issues, we share today the concern about an issue that tears us all apart when we see how girls, both within the european union and outside the european union, are being forced into marriage. there's a 2014 report that says that this kind of forced marriage is happening within the european union as well. i therefore urge the commission itself to incorporate action in this area into the work it is doing to promote the post-2015 gender equality strategy and, of course, into foreign policy and cooperation policy. it is essential that the gender perspective is incorporated. it is true that on paper most actions incorporate a gender perspective, but then the data tells us that only 28% of projects that have been funded in cooperation incorporate this gender perspective. we are talking about fundamental rights. we are talking about fighting gender violence and we are talking about the rights of children and girls.
on behalf of the alde group. madam president, commissioner, i would like to thank mrs corazza for taking the initiative to bring this oral question to the plenary and for having achieved the consensus of the political groups to discuss something that we often remove from our discussions. we're used to reporting, to prosecuting pedophilia. we were convinced by dr. mukwege when, in his speech, when he received the sakharov prize, he explained to us how rape is a weapon of war that destroys communities. early marriage, forced marriage is a weapon of mass destruction because it destroys girls, removing their ability to be educated: that's the main weapon. forced marriage is not only an attack on human rights, but it is a violation of children's rights and violence against women. the consequences of early marriage are devastating for girls, because it's not just health problems, sexual abuse, domestic violence, but, above all, the destruction of their future because it destroys their ability to empower themselves, to achieve development through education. i would also like to stress the role of the commission and the european union as a whole in getting the european union to sign the istanbul convention, which recognises and specifies forced marriage as something that must be prosecuted and eliminated from our society. i would also like to stress that we are not just talking about rights and violations of rights, but about democratic standards, about our duty as a reference in the world of democracy. i also refer again to what mr ban ki-moon said this afternoon: it is important that inclusive governance, inclusive democracy and our role as the world's engine for human rights should have a special sensitivity and a very clear determination to eliminate forced marriage in all those countries with which we have agreements.
on behalf of the green group, madam president, as mrs garcía pérez has already said, forced marriages continue to occur in the european union. according to the study by the european agency for fundamental rights, carried out last october, it still exists in some groups such as the roma. in a survey focusing on eleven countries where roma are most present, it was found that 2 per cent of girls aged 10 to 15 had been subjected to forced marriage and 16 per cent of teenage girls aged 16 to 17. the internal situation is therefore worrying: how will the european commission ensure that this practice is eradicated in europe? and as far as foreign policy is concerned, our weapons to put pressure on those countries where this terrible practice occurs to fight it are political and commercial support. but the facts show that we have not even fulfilled our commitments to put the gender focus on 75% of the projects funded. are we going to implement the demands of gender equality once and for all in our political and commercial relations? are we going to demand firmly from countries where women are considered second or third class citizens that they respect basic human rights? why do we not pursue a feminist foreign policy with conviction and firmness? in those words: "feminist foreign policy". that's it. i can assure you that women who were forced to marry as children, whom i have met in countries like india, carry with them an infinite sadness for the rest of their lives, a sadness which should be enough for the european union to react with urgency and force.

mr president, promoting the consumption of fruit, vegetables and dairy products is essential to encourage healthier habits in children and adolescents and to encourage local production of these foods. i have abstained from voting on this report because, while supporting its objectives, i lack political commitment to give the european union a comprehensive approach in this area. on the contrary, i regret that agricultural and livestock production is being liberalised in forced marches as seen with the end of milk quotas, allowing large agribusiness and distribution chains to ultimately impose the dietary habits of the population on the basis of their own commercial strategies. we have repeatedly pointed out that the consolidation of a liberalized agri-food system has a very negative impact on the incomes of small farmers and on the traditional ways of life of rural communities, but it also has serious consequences for public health which should not be ignored.
i believe that support for this programme to promote fruit and vegetables and milk in schools is important because it allows us to promote healthy eating habits based on fresh fruit and vegetables and also on the consumption of milk and milk products. i think this has been a good place to promote organic food, to bring schoolchildren closer to production and to get to know the daily activities of farmers. and it's also an important space to promote direct purchasing from schools to local farmers. but i abstained from voting precisely because these latter aspects have little or no place in this programme and, moreover, because i think that this programme should focus solely and exclusively on fresh produce and admit much less processed product.

mr president, firstly i would like to congratulate mr siekierski on the work he has done as rapporteur on this report and secondly i would also like to congratulate the commissioner, as the representative of the european commission, on his proposal, a proposal which maintains the crisis reserve created in the last reform of the common agricultural policy. the objective of the creation of this instrument is to have funds available to deal with the market crisis when it is significant. however, this reserve is set at eur 442 million; it represents an additional effort for european producers, who are thus reduced in their direct aid to cover market contingencies which, in many cases, could be solved by making use of the budgetary margin - as long as we do not continue to scrape funds from that margin to finance projects outside strict agricultural spending. the reserve has not been used up to now and it must be avoided in future to deal with critical situations caused by causes outside the agricultural sector. this is what happened with the embargo imposed by russia, from 7 august last year. the commission's immediate reaction was to use the reserve, but fortunately the majority of the people opposed this measure, which would have made our farmers and livestock farmers the 'turkey's head' of a political decision for which they had no responsibility. i am of the opinion that this crisis should have been financed even with funds entirely outside the agricultural budget. the veto is not over and i would like to ask the commission today what guarantees we have that the agricultural reserve will not be used in the event that the russian embargo is extended beyond the summer. i believe that the reserve should remain, for the time being, untouched and always ready to allow, if necessary, a rapid and effective response by europe to any eventuality that may occur as a result of the intrinsic evolution of agricultural markets - but of agricultural markets. and so i think we should try to make a more effective and efficient management of the resources available.
