member of the commission.– mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur, ms mosca, and the committee on international trade for their valuable work on this report. the report underlines the high importance of protecting and enforcing intellectual property rights around the globe for our stakeholders. it also stresses the need for the commission to not only continue but also go beyond the efforts it has been making in this regard. the commission shares this vision. the commission welcomes the appreciation shown for the approach that the strategy for the protection and enforcement of intellectual property rights in third countries takes in aiming to achieve a balance between divergent interests. it is certainly true that the debate about achieving a fair balance between right-holders’ interests and end-users’ interests is extremely complex, with economic interests on all sides. it is a concern to us all to see infringements of intellectual property rights (ipr) multiplying in recent years and taking away european knowledge and jobs. the commission certainly welcomes the report’s call for further work to tackle this problem. indeed there are many points expressed in the report that the commission fully agrees with, such as, for example, the need for the following: wider informed stakeholder involvement in the debate on ipr; more consumer awareness about the consequences of infringements; and improved coherence between ipr protection and enforcement and other policies. it is also important to reaffirm that the relationship between ipr and universal access to affordable medicines is indeed complex and multi-faceted, a point which is often lost. moreover, we must continue to ensure that appropriate attention is given to chapters on ipr in our free trade agreements. we also agree with the rapporteur that better, appropriately-harmonised, internal ipr-related eu policies could be helpful in the effort to improve the standard of protection and enforcement of ipr globally. further assistance should be considered for developing countries wishing to improve their ipr systems. the commission will be taking careful note of the recommendations made in the report during the implementation of the strategy for the protection and enforcement of intellectual property rights in third countries. we look forward to continuing to work with parliament, and all of its stakeholders, in this exercise. rest assured, furthermore, that i will pass all your comments made tonight to my colleague cecilia malmström, who is the commissioner in charge of this file.
in writing. the report calls for a rigorous extension of intellectual property rights standards in third countries, and even calls for conditionality in this area to establish economic relations with these countries, without taking into account the specific needs of developing countries, where intellectual property rights often undermine their industrial and development policies. the report also addresses the issue of access to medicines from the perspective of large pharmaceutical companies turning their backs on the right of people to access medicines. the report blindly responds to past experiences such as ebola in west africa or hepatitis c in spain. there is evidence that research into new medicines is often driven not by public health requirements but by the economic profit of pharmaceutical companies. the current incentives for research through patents do not raise enough money to develop new drugs that are really needed. it is time for the eu to take the lead in exploring new strategies in biomedical innovation that promote both affordable access to r & d results and knowledge creation as public goods.
member of the commission.– mr president, i would like to thank the house for all the points that have been made and for your work, led by mr svoboda, on this report. the european parliament has made an important contribution to what must be a joint effort to promote and protect creativity and innovation in the eu. along with its action in renovating the legislative framework in some key areas of intellectual property rights (ipr), the commission has decided to take targeted action to enforce these rights in the internal market. we are faced with a very difficult and complex reality: commercial-scale ipr-infringing activities have become more frequent and therefore very harmful to the eu economy, and in particular to the individuals and companies who are supposed to benefit from these rights. commercial-scale ipr-infringing activities are a deterrent to investment in innovation and creativity. they result directly in lost revenue to legitimate businesses, lost tax revenue, lost jobs and high enforcement costs. therefore, it is of the utmost importance to implement adequate measures against activities of this type. the action plan adopted by the commission in july 2014 comprises various non-legislative measures, all of which aim to boost and secure european businesses’ innovation and creativity in order to preserve their competitiveness in trade at global level. as is reflected in mr svoboda’s report, the commission’s efforts in the area of ipr enforcement should remain focused on several important points, such as the protection of consumers against harmful counterfeit goods; stronger support for smes; clarifying the role of intermediaries, especially in the digital environment; promoting the implementation of due diligence mechanisms in global supply chains, and so on. under the leadership of vice-president ansip and commissioner bieńkowska, we are now moving forward and have been working directly with national authorities and industry stakeholders on each of these issues. parliament’s support will be crucial throughout the process. but i also want to bring your attention to the fact that, despite the good faith of various voluntary initiatives envisaged in the 2014 action plan, the enforcement of ipr may also require legislative change. the recently-presented digital single market strategy calls for smarter enforcement for copyright. this does not mean, of course, that less importance should be given to other intellectual property rights, the infringement of which is very harmful to the eu economy. in view of that, over the coming months, the commission will carry out an evaluation of the overall functioning of the current legal framework for ipr enforcement. if the evaluation shows a need for amendment, this will be an important focus of the commission’s work in the future. to conclude, i would like to thank parliament once again for its positive consideration of the action plan, which i recommend to the plenary vote tomorrow. i truly hope that parliament’s cooperation with the commission in the area of ipr enforcement will continue, in the interests of enhancing innovation, creativity and jobs growth for eu businesses and citizens.
in writing. intellectual property rights are one of the driving forces behind innovation and creativity, and make an essential contribution to competitiveness, employment and cultural diversity. infringements of intellectual property rights, including counterfeiting, are detrimental to growth, job creation, innovation and creativity. respect for the law is fundamental to the predictability of legislation, and it is essential to find effective, proportionate and dissuasive means to ensure that intellectual property rights are respected across borders. i believe that civil procedures for the protection of intellectual property should be improved for the benefit of smes and all individual creators, as they play a key role in the creative and cultural sectors. in this regard, i would ask the commission to develop a strategy on intellectual property rights, including a comprehensive legal framework to combat infringements of intellectual property rights, which is adapted to the internet environment, while fully respecting fundamental rights and freedoms, the right to a fair trial, the principle of proportionality and data protection.
mr president, the european union's relations with russia have deteriorated greatly. the cause is russia's behavior with ukraine, including its annexation of crimea. the 21st century requires behavior that respects international law, which russia has ignored. in today's globalised world, there are major global challenges, for example, climate change, terrorism, disarmament. it is true that to meet these serious challenges we need dialogue and cooperation with russia, a major world player and a major military and energy power. however, the european union has lost confidence in the russian authorities. we no longer perceive russia as a strategic partner after what happened. it is essentially up to russia to put an end to this situation of mistrust and to change its course of action. the first is to fully implement the so-called minsk agreements. the recent events in marinka indicate the opposite, and logically the so-called 'blacklist' of eu personalities who are not allowed to enter russia is also a step in the wrong direction.
mr president, i also congratulate the rapporteur on this excellent report. the arbitrary and unjustified measure of the russian authorities to ban european politicians and officials - myself included - from entering their territory is another step in the wrong direction taken by the russian authorities. this growing pressure from putin on the europeans is hampering the efforts of the international community to create a constructive dialogue that will bring about a peaceful and lasting solution to this geopolitical conflict that we are living in our neighborhood. this is what parliament has denounced and what cosac said last week in riga. we must therefore ask ourselves what the russian authorities want: peace or permanent confrontation through the violation of the territorial integrity of their neighbours? inclusion in the european family or isolation? dialogue between equals or punishment of those who dare to think differently? i am finished, mr president. the president has taken the floor. )
madam president, i voted in favour of budgeting for the fund for crisis situations of farmers because i think it is very important, but i will be very attentive to how this fund is used. i think that when the crisis situation comes from wrong decisions taken by the european union, as was the case with the russian veto, for example, the funds must come from elsewhere and this money should not be used to alleviate these crisis situations.
in writing. ‒ article 25 of regulation (eu) no 1306/2013 provides that a reserve is to be created to provide additional support to the agricultural sector in the event of major crises affecting the production or distribution of agricultural products by applying at the beginning of each year a reduction in direct payments through the financial discipline mechanism referred to in article 26 of that regulation. and according to article 26 (1) of regulation (eu) no 1306/2013, in order to ensure compliance with the annual ceilings laid down in regulation (eu, euratom) no 1311/2013, an adjustment percentage for direct payments should be fixed. the report seeks to unlock these provisions and to set the adjustment rate for direct payments for 2015. that is why i voted in favour, although i believe that when the crisis situation comes from incorrect decisions taken by the european union, as was the case, for example, with the russian veto, the funds must come from elsewhere and this money should not be used to alleviate these crisis situations.

we voted in favour of this report on the strategy for equality between men and women because we believe it is moving in the right direction. i would like to take this opportunity, ladies and gentlemen, of voting on this report to recall that in my country - spain - we are far from achieving the objectives of equality and to point out that the austerity policies, sponsored by both the troika and the old parties in our country, have contributed to deepening the differences between men and women. i will say this very clearly: in spain, precariousness has a female face; in spain, poverty wages have a female face; in spain, the care of the elderly and of minors without public assistance has a female face. ladies and gentlemen, the main enemy of equality in europe and in spain is not only machismo, but the destruction of social rights and the gains of workers.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because i believe that the commission should present as soon as possible a new strategy for equality between women and men which is more ambitious than the previous one, setting clear objectives in terms of employment, the wage and pension gap, reconciliation of family and working life, equality in political and economic decision-making, etc., and key priorities such as the fight against gender-based violence, which is the most widespread violation of human rights in europe and the rest of the world and which affects all strata of society, or the defence of women's sexual and reproductive rights, including easy access to contraceptives and abortion under legal and safe health conditions. a strategy that recognises the special needs of the most vulnerable groups of women, the disabled, the elderly, immigrants, minorities, lgbt people, etc., and that takes into account the different types of family that coexist in our society. the report we have adopted today may not be the best, but it is the fruit of negotiations and commitments supported by all the political groups and consultations with all the interested parties.
in writing. ‒ the report sets out guidelines for a new equality strategy 2016-2020, following the failure of the still-existing strategy 2010-2015, which has failed to tackle the problems of inequality between women and men in the eu in any of its areas. although the report finally adopted is particularly unambitious in such areas as the ambiguous distinction between forced and legal prostitution, in the field of reproductive rights and access to safe abortion (leaving it to the discretion of the member states) or by ignoring the fact that the main cause of the aggravation of the feminization of poverty is linked to the severe cuts in public services, the text approves giving a mandate to the european commission to develop a specific directive against gender violence, to include in all policies the gender dimension and to include disabled or lgbti groups among the objectives of the strategy. that is why i voted for it. finally, i would like to express my rejection of the alternative proposal put forward by the ppe not only because of its conservatism but also because it tried to overturn the document voted in the committee on women and gender equality.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because i do not agree with the indiscriminate use of intellectual property rights as a commercial strategy vis-à-vis third countries. the legitimate protection of copyright and the control of the quality of imported products cannot be used as an excuse for the creation of monopolies by the large pharmaceutical and industrial multinationals, nor for the expropriation of the knowledge and resources of third states and communities: they have the same right to health, industrial development and scientific knowledge as the peoples of europe.
in writing. ‒ the last decade has seen significant changes in the area of intellectual property rights: substantial technological changes related to the internet, the increasing importance of emerging economies, challenges in access to medicines and a rising level of ipr infringements, among others. following the rejection of acta in 2012 by this parliament, the commission rectifying and proposing with this strategy a different and updated approach to ipr protection. this report, which i voted for, calls for the need to increase consumer awareness of the harm caused by the acquisition of goods infringing intellectual property, calls for a more transparent and balanced public debate involving all interested parties, and insists on the need to strengthen ipr dialogues with third countries and customs cooperation. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'commercial vehicle' to cover vehicles with a maximum mass exceeding 10 tonnes.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour because i believe that intellectual property rights (ipr) are an essential element for growth and innovation. trade is based on the protection of these rights and therefore adequate protection against counterfeiting on a commercial scale is necessary to improve the eu's competitiveness. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. according to some statistics, about 39% of european gdp and about 26% of employment are derived from sectors with a high idp component. its importance is growing, as is its strategic value as a tool for differentiation and competitiveness in the global economy. we see the importance of ip chapters in eu trade agreements with third countries increasing, and so we believe that an improved, harmonised ipr strategy with broad support in the eu can be very useful in improving ipr protection and enforcement standards globally.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this report because it calls for a rigorous extension of the standards of intellectual property rights in third countries, and even calls for conditionality in this area to establish economic relations with these countries, without taking into account the specific needs of developing countries, where, often, intellectual property rights undermine their industrial and development policies. the report also addresses the issue of access to medicines from the perspective of the big pharmaceutical companies, turning their backs on the right of people to access medicines. the report blindly responds to past experiences, such as ebola in west africa or hepatitis c in spain. there is evidence that research into new medicines is often driven not by public health requirements but by the economic profit of pharmaceutical companies. the current incentives for research through patents do not raise enough money to develop new drugs that are really needed.

madam president, commissioner, it must be admitted that the doha amendment has been a good addition to keeping the kyoto protocol alive. but the hour of truth is urgently knocking at our door. we cannot tell him to come back in a century, as the g7 did in the alps. the most industrialized countries demand 85 more years. there has been more talk about the g7 than there will probably be about this week's bonn meeting, where the 145 parties are still entangled in an 80-page maze, when what the planet needs above all is a figure and a date. let's be practical once and for all. the new paris agreement will not be achieved by a century of moratoriums or by lengthy documents. in paris, it's no longer just about building a better world, but simply keeping it alive by giving kyoto a worthy heir.
madam president, what future are we going to leave for the next generation if we are not able to stop climate change? what planet will be left tomorrow if we are not responsible today? we know very well where the problem is. we just don't dare put a brake on it, that's all. it is the brutal dependence of states - and, consequently, the population - on fossil fuels, due, again and as always, to the interests of large corporations. fossil fuels are double-edged weapons, which end up devastating the health of our people and, of course, the environment. that is why we need the member states to make a real commitment to our earth, and that is where the paris conference plays a key role, which should serve to set the course for the future; a future that will make us move towards an efficient, sustainable and, above all, fair renewable energy model. once again, it's about political will, putting the needs of people and the health of our planet above the interests of markets and big companies. here too we must be courageous and decide which side we want to be on, whether the side of the planet and the people or the side of the polluting corporations.
in writing. we welcome that today's decision on co2 emissions commitments serves to strengthen the european union's negotiating position on its target of reducing emissions by 20% by 2020. but we must not forget that europe as an emitter has a different impact on the global calculation than it does through its consumption patterns or the global organization of production. the growth in global emissions of more than 50% since 1990 is not new to us, although in europe the economic crisis (not permit markets) has stabilised co2 generation. the relocation of european production, the investments of our multinationals and the export of our mode of consumption have all contributed to the growth of global emissions. solving the contradictions of climate change means betting on a different, self-centred and sustainable development model, capable of being exported to all regions of the globe. it means upward harmonization of environmental standards worldwide, provided the technical and financial means for this transition. it is not an easy agreement, but above all it cannot be implemented without abandoning the prevailing neoliberal framework.
madam president, mr cañete, it is not the electricity oligopoly that will solve the problems of energy security: it is the states that must direct resources towards improving energy efficiency and generation from their own resources. we are not just talking about renewables, which were hit hard by the government they were part of in spain. we also talk about coal, a safe alternative which also involves the development of clean combustion technologies, r & d & i - as is the case with elcogas - and not, like fossil fuel imports and the development of energy sources as dangerous as nuclear or fracking. minimum quotas for local coal generation need to be met and the thermal plants need to be prepared for more efficient combustion, and the miner funds and subsidies need to be extended beyond 2018. only in this way can the employment and settlement of the population in the mining areas be guaranteed and, moreover, can the price of energy, which is set for the benefit of the multinationals, be affected.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, europe has sun, wind and tides, so we could clearly say that europe has clean energy, and it would not be understood or it is not understood - at least we do not understand it, a large part of the socialist group - why we should have recourse to energy sources whose extraction is at least controversial. hydraulic fracturing requires huge amounts of water, highly polluting chemicals, and it's not clear that it doesn't produce earthquakes, not least because there are no rigorous environmental impact studies in any case. for these reasons, ladies and gentlemen, i tabled an amendment in committee asking the member states, the governments, not to authorize new prospecting techniques, new prospecting, until it is shown that this technique is safe for health, for the environment and for workers. that is why i am putting this amendment back in. my group is taking this amendment back and putting it back in the house. finally, madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur and the alternative rapporteurs on including the socialist request to the commission to draw up a communication on energy poverty, accompanied by an action plan to combat it in a serious way.
member of the commission.– madam president, first of all i would like to thank you for a further opportunity to reflect with you on smart borders and, in a more general way, the need to modernise eu border management. the commission’s smart borders package of 2013 has already been discussed with parliament and the council. as announced in the agenda on security that we adopted, as you will remember, on 28 april 2015, and in the agenda on migration presented on 13 may, it is now our intention to present, by the beginning of 2016, a revised proposal on smart borders. today’s reality is that member states face difficulties in managing the growing traveller flows at borders and in fulfilling the obligations set by the schengen border code. there were an estimated 200 million border crossings by third country nationals last year, and a 50% increase is expected in the next decade. borders must benefit from technology. the smart borders system will automatically record all incoming and outgoing third country nationals and will support border guards in their tasks. it will also enable the automation or semi-automation of the border controls for travellers already known by the system. this will allow us to face the increases in traveller flows. smart borders will also help us in making our policy against irregular migration more effective. how? by systematically recording all incoming and outgoing third country nationals, the system will automatically identify the travellers who stay longer than the authorised period. smart borders will also help in identifying undocumented persons present in the schengen area. lastly, the system will support an informed visa policy decision-making process, taking into account the actual overstayer figures provided by the system. possible law-enforcement access will be a key issue to be addressed in the impact assessment for the new proposal. the commission has already acknowledged, in the impact assessment for the 2013 proposal, that the data generated at entry/exit could be of use to law-enforcement authorities in the fight against terrorist offences and serious crime in specific cases – both as an identity verification tool and as a criminal intelligence tool. but any decision to allow law-enforcement access from the outset will need to be based on the demonstrated necessity and proportionality of the measure. strict, specific substantive and procedural safeguards would need to be laid down, taking into account, inter alia, the rulings of the european court of justice on data protection. let me now share with you some of the emerging ideas on how we could increase the efficiency and effectiveness of border management. these are, of course, not yet conclusive, as discussions are still ongoing and the testing phase is still under way. these issues will all be covered in depth in the updated impact assessment the commission is undertaking in order to inform its revised proposal. the initial findings of the technical study seem to point to potential advantages of a single piece of legislation. as in 2013, this would be accompanied by a technical modification of the schengen border code. let me give you an idea of the questions which, in my view, need to be answered in the context of our impact assessment, in addition to the already-mentioned issue of law-enforcement access and, of course, the financial implications and efficiency questions. as regards the architecture of the system: should smart borders rely on a single system rather than separate systems for entry/exit recording and registered traveller management? can we further reduce the number of data items about each traveller while still achieving our objectives? how long should the data retention periods be for entry/exit and for registered travellers, in full compliance with data protection rules? can we introduce a ‘lighter’ form of biometric identifiers while maintaining the effectiveness of the system? how can we facilitate border crossings for the very large majority of travellers who do not pose any problem or risk? how can we benefit from the experience and solutions found in the existing large-scale systems, in order to reduce costs? while preparing the revised proposal, the commission will continue to listen carefully to the opinions expressed by the european parliament.
on behalf of the ppe group madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, thank you to mrs fajon for her good work. as has been said, 300 million border crossings are expected to be made by 2025 by approximately 76 million third country nationals, which means that we must improve the management of passenger traffic, given the proven inadequacy of sis ii and the vis. as meps, in the face of a legislative package that is still so vague even though it was born in february 2013, we are determined that parliament's voice is taken into account throughout the legislative process and in the face of the new revised 2016 proposal. as regards the architecture of the system, what we want to know, commissioner, is clearly what your ideas are on this: an input and output system and an rtp? both? one or the other? mixed? because this is an essential question and it is also essential for the budget, of course. the commission must also clarify and commit itself to the main objective and possible secondary objectives. for example, the fight against immigration gangs and other serious crimes such as terrorism. we talk about technology, and technology to add value to this. all that i am saying must, of course, be legally and primarily enshrined, with the maximum guarantees, as far as fundamental rights are concerned, in order to comply with article 77 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. and only after we have this general framework clear can we talk about biometrics, interoperability, accelerators, passenger information systems or the role of transport companies. the technical report and the completion of the pilot projects or test phases sixteen in twelve member states will provide the necessary information for the launch of the new legislative proposal at air, land and sea borders. on the other hand, commissioner, we need to strengthen interinstitutional dialogue to strengthen data protection, access to the system by the security forces and bodies or the consequences of the removal of stamps on passports. i would remind you that all but one of the national parliaments were in favour of access by the security forces and bodies, as you say, taking into account proportionality and necessity.
mr president, they want to sell us the smart border project as a project to speed up and facilitate border inspection procedures, but what is really behind this project is the creation of a police register that makes everyone who enters the european union a suspect; a register with data available to the police authorities. a system which further divides people into three classes: first, those who are citizens of the european union; second, those who consider themselves legitimate, those who do not bother because they come here on business; and third, the poor, who are targeted by the entry and exit system, which once again criminalizes and labels as enemies migrants, treated as criminals simply because their visas have expired. the entry and exit system is intended to further close the borders; an alert system, a search and arrest system for those who have dared to penetrate the 'fortress europe'.
member of the commission.– mr president, first of all i would like to express my thanks to all of you for this very fruitful exchange of views. let me start by telling you that i took note of all your remarks and concerns. they are substantial concerns, and you can be sure that we are not going to repeat past mistakes, as happened with the schengen information system ii. we are going to assess carefully the costs and the architecture, as well as fundamental rights and safeguards, which are very important. and proportionality and necessity will be our compass in any future discussion. the ruling on data retention will also guide us. today’s debate confirms the vital importance of parliament’s input into our joint efforts to create a smart border system that meets its objectives and offers genuine value for money. since we know that traveller flows will continue to grow, we need a better and smarter border management system. if we do nothing, we will either have to face much longer queues at the borders or we shall be obliged to employ more border guards in the near future. neither of these options seems acceptable or feasible. as you understand, we are going to meet many times in the future in order, first of all, to discuss the results of the testing phase and the impact assessment. i want to assure you that the commission is looking forward to working closely with parliament in this very important fight and that it is counting on your support and cooperation in achieving the final balance.
the debate is closed.
the next item is the debate on:- question for oral answer to the commission on the 2014 annual report of the olaf surveillance committee, by petri sarvamaa, on behalf of the european people's party (christian democrats), and by bart staes, on behalf of the group of the greens/european free alliance (o-000060/2015 b8-0553/2015),- question for oral answer to the commission on the 2014 annual report of the olaf surveillance committee, by dennis de jong, on behalf of the confederal group of the european united left/nordic green left (o-000061/2015 b8-0455/2015), and- question for oral answer to the commission on the investigations by olaf, by michael theurer, by libina dlabaj, by martina nováh, by jan-jan gergely, by dita gergely and by chédira aliénz, on behalf of the group of the european democrats and by aliénz ribeira (o-000066/2015 b8-05555).
on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, i welcome those colleagues who for years ignored and persecuted the olaf monitoring committee, when i alone understood that its job, which is to protect the independence of olaf, should be safeguarded and now, in addition, to protect those under investigation. but those were other times. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. that is why my group has considered this debate to be hasty - it deals with only one side of the problem and it was organised even before the annual report of olaf itself, which is the central body we should be talking about, was known - just as we considered the debate on the annual report of the supervisory committee to be hasty at the time, almost before it was made public, without the director-general having been invited. it would be as if the commissioner responsible were not invited to the annual discharge to be given to the court of auditors. well, that's been done. what was the urgency? i said, rush. that is why our resolution concentrates on deploring the fact that parliament, in its committee on budgetary control, instead of offering citizens and colleagues the opportunity to hold a full debate with all the necessary opinions and replies, has preferred, on the part of some groups, to offer a partial debate. olaf is the body to carry out the treaty mandate to fight fraud, and the monitoring committee is the auxiliary body to protect olaf, ensuring its independence, and protecting the rights of those under investigation. there's always been a certain tension between the two of us. if it didn't exist, it would be that they don't do their job well. what we in parliament cannot do is to throw the balance of power off balance maliciously, by deliberately ignoring the answers and explanations of one of the parties, by putting back on the table some of the points which this parliament has already voted for - and voted against - even though some colleague wants us to vote again and again until we get the vote changed. i think that the fact that the monitoring committee is set up as a judge rather than as olaf's protector, and also as a party, since it would not exist without olaf, is not the way it works and is not our role. i therefore ask the commission to undertake as soon as possible the task of ensuring that both are working properly and to clarify whether what some of our colleagues are saying has happened, and in relation to which we have not even been able to verify the answers.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, the report on the activities of olaf in 2014 suggests that the european parliament's supervision of this body leaves much to be desired, in particular in the absence of access to olaf information received from this parliament, which raises many doubts about investigations already carried out or ongoing by that office. i will give you an example: the report on the tindemans refugee camps. it mentions fraud, but it does not give an estimate of it. he says that it was done, but he did not visit the camps at any time and did not consult such basic data as the unhcr's refugee census of october 2000. i would like to make it quite clear that this could lead to a greater humanitarian tragedy than the one the saharawi refugees are already experiencing if their aid is finally cut back.

in writing. ‒ voting in favour of the decision to ratify the commitments of the doha amendment by the eu and iceland is a very positive signal. the european union is telling the world ahead of the paris summit that it wants to continue to lead the fight against climate change, setting an example and inviting the most reluctant and polluting countries to continue investing in the future. doha is a good place to keep the kyoto protocol alive, but paris must be the meeting that will see the birth of a new binding agreement. it is a question of adding up the wills, but also of involving all parties equally in the search for a model that stops damaging the planet and compromising our future generations. the g7 has already sat down to discuss it and the emerging countries are seen as being in a good mood. so the ratification of doha by the eu and iceland makes us proud that, despite the unconstructive criticism from some 'climate skeptics', we are on the right track.
in writing. ‒ the kyoto protocol to the united nations framework convention on climate change was signed in 1997 with the aim of setting an internationally binding emission reduction target. the eu ratified this protocol in 2015. in 2012, the doha climate change conference approved an amendment to the kyoto protocol 1 that establishes a second period (2013 to 2020) with legally binding emission reduction commitments for the parties. the amendment commits the eu member states and iceland to reducing their average annual greenhouse gas emissions. i have supported this report which gives its consent to the doha amendment as a positive step, although i believe that the amended kyoto protocol is still quite far from effectively combating climate change on its own, as it lacks complementary measures, such as climate justice provisions, as well as serious work commitments by the most industrialized countries.

in writing. ‒ the report is merely a procedure to allow the formal entry into force of the doha amendment when the eu, and subsequently the member states, have completed their planned ratification processes by the third quarter of this year at the latest, so that the instruments of acceptance are on the table for the decisive paris climate summit in december. this amendment to the kyoto protocol (decided at the 2012 doha summit) establishes a second commitment period, which started in january 2013 and should run until december 2020. these commitments imply that the eu and the member states commit themselves to ensuring that the average of their emissions over this period is capped at 80% of the emissions in the base year (1990) and always taking as a global the total of the emissions allowed under the emissions trading system (ets). i agree with the aims of this amendment and have therefore voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ this commission recommendation for a council decision is intended to facilitate the accession of croatia to the 1997 convention on the fight against corruption involving officials of the european communities or of member states. this issue arises from the 2011 act of accession for croatia which lists six conventions and protocols in the area of justice and home affairs to which croatia must accede by council decision. the council decision should make the necessary adjustments to the convention required by the accession of croatia. i agree with these considerations and have therefore voted in favour of the report.
in writing. ‒ annex i to the act of accession contains a list of conventions and protocols to which the member states are to accede, including the convention on the fight against corruption. since croatia is acceding to the convention as a sovereign state and in its own right as part of its accession to the european union, i have voted in favour of its decisions being respected in accordance with the principle of selfdetermination.

in writing. ‒ russia is the european union's main neighbour, one of its main trading partners - especially in terms of energy needs - and a country with which all eu countries have closely shared a part of their history. i therefore believe that relations between the eu and russia should be treated with the utmost care and responsibility. in the text put to the vote, however, i have found a disproportionate vocabulary and a lot of condemnation. but above all, there is a double standard which is difficult for anyone with a vague knowledge of european history over the last 25 years to grasp. i voted against this report because, according to the text adopted, russia should not remain a strategic partner for the european union, which is particularly worrying in view of the common interests that exist.
in writing. ‒ russia's involvement in the conflict in ukraine with the annexation of crimea constitutes a serious and deliberate violation of the most fundamental democratic and human principles. if we add to this the restrictions on media freedom, the attacks on lgbt people and the increase in pro-russian propaganda in the member states, the need for a firm and unified response is clear. this translates into certain restrictive measures for certain individuals and companies linked to the russian leadership. however, these sanctions should be lifted when russia has fully implemented the provisions of the minsk agreements, including full control of the border by the ukrainian authorities, unconditional withdrawal of russian troops and their weapons, and an immediate end to support for rebel groups. we need to critically assess relations with russia and to put all the means at our disposal to stop pro-russian disinformation and propaganda within the eu. we must also be vigilant about russia's increasingly frequent support and funding of radical parties in the eu member states. this report does.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because russia's intervention in crimea and georgia violates the principles and values of the eu and international law and has generated political instability in europe. russia cannot therefore be treated as a strategic partner, although in the long term it would be desirable for relations to be constructive and based on mutual trust because of the benefits they bring to both sides. but to do so, it would have to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of ukraine and, in my view, also of crimea, and observe international law. we must also demand respect for human rights and especially for lgbti people who suffer harassment and systematic violence.
in writing. ‒ we socialists believe in constructive relations with russia as one of the eu's most important neighbours, but we hope that russia will do its part to make this possible, starting with the full implementation of the minsk agreements to stop the conflict in ukraine. russia is an important neighbour of the eu; there are interests in practical cooperation and in jointly addressing shared global challenges, such as jihadist terrorism, iran's nuclear programme, destabilisation in the middle east or non-proliferation. russia must change its behavior towards its neighbors. the report sets out clear conditions for the full resumption of cooperation with russia, such as the implementation of the minsk agreements, respect for the security order based on the osce guidelines and principles in europe and full respect for the territorial integrity of ukraine, including crimea. the european parliament has also called for the establishment of a european union-wide network of national and regional authorities responsible for the protection of human rights. i have therefore voted in favour of this report.

in writing. ‒ in this report on eu-russia relations, i voted in favour because i believe that at the moment, and after the role played by russia in the conflict in ukraine and the illegal annexation of crimea, together with the territorial violation of georgia, the eu can only carry out a critical reading of its relations with russia. this critical reading of our relations with russia must be accompanied by a comprehensive contingency plan for future relations with russia and our eastern european partners. eu-russia relations must be based on respect for international law and dialogue. it is also important to resume cooperation in the future on the condition that russia respects the territorial integrity and sovereignty of ukraine, including crimea, fully implements the minsk agreements and stops destabilising military and security activities on the borders of eu member states.
in writing. ‒ the eu should ensure compliance with international law in ukraine, with particular emphasis on russia's compliance with its obligations to maintain peace in eastern ukraine. the eu must also support russian civil society in improving fundamental freedoms and rights and respect for minorities. it is very important for both russia and the eu that relations between the two parties improve in the future, but for this russia must commit itself and work towards the re-establishment of mutual trust. for these reasons, i have voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this report on eu-russia relations, as it does not make any critical assessment of the current eu policy. it also represents a step forward in the escalation of the conflict between the eu and russia, making it possible to develop a policy of confrontation with that country. the report as a whole does not seek a peaceful resolution of the conflict, but rather delves into the existing tension between russia and the eu. those of us who are in favour of a europe which advocates the resolution of conflicts through dialogue and the constant search for peace cannot accept this report.

in writing. ‒ the spanish socialists regret that the saudargas report was not adopted because, thanks to the intensive work in committee, the report was committed to a new energy model for europe, a sustainable and equitable model. during the plenary vote, the socialists had achieved a majority on three key points, two of them at the request of the spanish socialist delegation: 1) a majority in favour of asking the commission to present a communication on energy poverty, accompanied by an action plan to combat it; 2) a majority in favour of asking governments not to authorize any new fracking operations in the eu until it is shown that such operations are safe for the environment, workers and the general population; and 3) a majority in favour of more ambitious targets on renewable energy, energy efficiency and climate change, and that these should also be binding.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because it bases european energy security on two pillars which i oppose. the first is to reinforce the eu's aggressive trade and foreign policy, with its pressures, impositions and attacks on our neighbours to access their energy resources. this is a greedy and short-sighted strategy which only serves to destabilise them and which we oppose, because only a project of mutual development and cooperation can be the basis of trade relations between sovereign states. the second is the boost given to a dangerous energy as nuclear energy in the context of the energy transition. on the contrary, there are indigenous resources, such as coal, which can be developed as a complement to renewable energy and environmental efficiency to reduce our energy dependence. we therefore advocate the maintenance of aid for production and generation from local coal, improvements in its combustion techniques (by investing in the renewal of thermal power stations) and a commitment to the technological development of new techniques of exploitation and capture related to its combustion cycle.
in writing. ‒ it was a pity that this report was not adopted, as europe needs to have a clear strategy for energy security in view of its current dependency. this requires a change of attitude by the 28 eu countries to develop more connected networks and sustainable energy. these conditions will enable us to have cheaper energy, which will favour the industrial sectors and make them more competitive. more efficient use of resources in households with high energy bills will be encouraged and a reduction in oil dependence should be achieved.

in writing. ‒ the european commission has proposed a european energy strategy in the wake of the ukraine crisis. the eu depends on a stable and abundant energy supply to ensure its prosperity and security. energy security problems are often addressed at national level alone without taking full account of the energy interdependencies of the member states. the development of this strategy is therefore crucial for the eu. although the report is generally positive after the adoption of the amendments, it is recommended that certain limits be set in some cases on energy sources and mechanisms which i consider may harm european interests; i therefore abstained from voting on the report.
in writing. ‒ with the political instability in ukraine, the european union is now more aware than ever of the importance of energy security. the eu and its member states are vulnerable in the geopolitical context, and energy policy has become one of the priorities of foreign affairs. although considerable progress has been made in recent years, the eu still faces a number of challenges, such as instability in energy supplying regions and a fragmented internal market. to meet these important challenges, the eu must therefore develop a long-term strategy to address the present and future energy challenges, which are of paramount importance for the well-being of citizens and economic growth. for these reasons i voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ it is sad to see that the european parliament has not been able to agree on what the european energy security strategy should be. i voted in favour of a text which contained many valuable elements for reducing our energy dependence on the outside world, such as improving energy efficiency, developing the infrastructure necessary to achieve a genuine internal energy market which would include the so-called energy islands, diversifying supply or developing indigenous sources. energy is one of the many areas where a european approach can bring added value, but this requires a common policy consensus. we must continue to work together to avoid outcomes like today, where disagreements have prevailed over the ideas we all share.
in writing. ‒ we voted against the text because we consider that it defends a supposed diversification of the energy matrix based on the continuation of the use of conventional hydrocarbons, the exploitation of non-conventional ones by techniques such as fracking, the achievement of gas megaprojects and the maintenance of renewable energies. the text clearly departs from the necessary commitment to a change in the energy model and tries to operate a false transition based on low-carbon technologies whose use perpetuates the current dirty, dependent, unsustainable, asymmetrical, socially unjust and warlike model. the text also does not advocate strongly enough the measures aimed at meeting the objectives of reducing emissions, promoting renewable energy and energy efficiency.
in writing. ‒ although the report had some positive elements and was on the whole in line with the socialist position thanks to the work of the s&d group in the itre committee, the document still raised certain problems with regard to the coal sector which led me not to support it decisively and to opt for abstention. the call for the phasing out of incentives for indigenous coal or the vagueness in differentiation and the lack of more determined support for clean coal are some of the elements i find problematic. since the european commission has accepted that fossil fuels will continue to be part of the energy mix from now until 2050, we should take into account the social and employment impact of the end of subsidies for indigenous coal and propose a decisive conversion action before opting for the cessation of such subsidies. in addition, we should not hesitate to support those forms of clean coal and carbon storage systems (ccs) that, like elcogas in puertollano, offer clean uses of fossil fuels. in this respect, we will continue to work to ensure that future initiatives are more sensitive to this sector.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because it implies a necessary exercise of control by the european parliament of the european anti-fraud office (olaf). the office is an institution that monitors possible fraud against the eu's financial interests. in its field of activity, it conducts investigations into fraud, corruption or malpractice in cases affecting the eu budget. this resolution points out various irregularities in the various disputes between the monitoring committee and olaf itself. the resolution also calls for the commission to take the necessary steps to ensure that the budgetary authority is able to meet its obligations under the treaty. it is in the interest of improving the functioning of this very important institution that i have decided to vote in favour of this resolution.
in writing. ‒ it seems that a poor relationship between olaf and the monitoring committee is causing dysfunctions in the functioning and achievement of the objectives that are to be achieved. i therefore think it is appropriate for the commission to mediate the negotiations between the two so that they can draw up a work plan so that the monitoring committee can fulfil its mandate. i am also pleased that both are working together to improve the content of the procedures and the deadlines for completion. that is why i voted in favour of the resolution by the ppe, gue/ngl and greens/efa groups.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this resolution because it is based on the allegations made by the monitoring committee of the european anti-fraud office (olaf) without the office itself having been able to provide its explanations in the committee on budgetary control of the european parliament and without having waited to analyse the content of the annual report presented on 2 june by olaf. it is regrettable that, for the first time, the committee on budgetary control did not send a formal invitation to the director-general of olaf, despite the importance of the 2014 activity report of the supervisory committee and despite the intense debate between the two bodies, and that it did not give the same importance, or the necessary attention, to the presentation of the olaf annual report. this has prevented parliament from having a full and thorough debate, with all the information on the table.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because it implies a necessary exercise of control by the european parliament of the european anti-fraud office (olaf). the office is an institution that monitors possible fraud against the eu's financial interests. in its field of activity, it conducts investigations into fraud, corruption or malpractice in cases affecting the eu budget. this resolution points out various irregularities in the various disputes between the monitoring committee and olaf itself. the resolution also calls for the commission to take the necessary steps to ensure that the budgetary authority is able to meet its obligations under the treaty. it is in the interest of improving the functioning of this very important institution that i have decided to vote in favour of this resolution.
in writing. ‒ this resolution calls on the commission to take immediate action and present an action plan to ensure the proper functioning of the monitoring committee of the european anti-fraud office. olaf's mission is to protect the eu's financial interests; to investigate fraud and other illegal activities in connection with the performance of professional activities by members and staff of the eu institutions and bodies; and to support the european institutions, and in particular the commission, in the development and implementation of anti-fraud legislation and policies. this role should be carried out in full transparency and in compliance with the legal procedures established by the eu, in particular with regard to the mandate entrusted to the monitoring committee. that is why i support this resolution.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this resolution on the report of the olaf monitoring committee. we agree that there must be verifiable systems to ensure that olaf's performance and its tools are improved, but we believe that any monitoring system that is proposed must be supported by transparent bodies elected with the most democratic tools available, and not by third parties who might be favoured by a monitoring body that is semi-collegiate and operated by institutions that could also require olaf's investigative work.

in writing. ‒ our group does not support this resolution because it is based on the allegations made by the monitoring committee without olaf itself having been able to give explanations in the committee on budgetary control and without having waited to analyse the annual report which was presented only yesterday, on 2 june, and which would have shed light on much of the criticism made. our group believes that both institutions - olaf and the monitoring committee - should be heard, and not just based on the analysis of one of the two parties concerned, in order to have a contrasted view of reality. we also want to be fair and give the same opportunity to the director of olaf to explain himself in the committee on budgetary control before we bring the matter to the house. i therefore voted against the resolution.

in writing. ‒ the european anti-fraud office must have as its fundamental and unshakable pillar independence in relation to the work it carries out. however, we are concerned that in some cases there is a malfunctioning of this office. the committee on budgetary control itself has raised serious doubts as regards the independence of olaf's activities. without a secure, effective and demonstrable independence, we cannot rely on a mechanism, especially when it comes to fighting fraud, one of the major concerns of european citizens. it is a scourge that affects all member states, and our duty of cleanliness and traceability must reach every corner. there are millions of europeans who are having a very difficult time, and the institutions must extend their vigilance, their control and their certainty to all their spheres of action.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because i consider the death penalty to be incompatible with the values of the eu. we socialists strongly condemn the constant statements by prime minister orbán about his possible reinstatement and we make it clear that the european parliament will not tolerate any change in the legal system of any member state which threatens the most fundamental european values. we also denounce the public consultation that the government has launched on migration and its consequent campaign of defamation of immigrants that is being carried out throughout the country. we therefore call for a european mechanism of democracy, the rule of law and the rule of law. we do not want to stigmatise any particular member state or government, but to ensure that a collective obligation of all the eu institutions, and in particular of the commission as guardian of the treaties, to ensure the application and observance of the treaties and the charter throughout the eu is fulfilled. hungary is a key country in the eu and we want to make it clear to its citizens that they have the right to continue to enjoy all their rights in complete freedom.
in writing. ‒ the joint resolution on the situation in hungary sheds light on a recurring problem: the risk to freedoms and human rights in some countries. in this case, it is a country ruled by an authoritarian party in which the extreme right is increasingly influential. in practice, this has involved the adoption of racist policies and the proposal to introduce the death penalty into the country's legal order. i voted in favour of this resolution because, in addition to condemning and censuring the hungarian government, it calls on the council not to have taken action in advance and introduces the possibility that hungary may be deprived of its right to vote in the council if it persists in its attitude.
in writing. ‒ the statements by the hungarian prime minister referring to the debate on the death penalty or the consultations on immigration, as well as the deceptive advertising campaigns, are incomprehensible in the context of the values of respect for human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and human rights. in the face of this behaviour, the council and the member states have shown a lack of reaction and commitment to fully respect the values of the union. it is therefore necessary for the commission to monitor and assess hungary's actions with regard to respect for the rule of law and human rights and to take appropriate action if there is a risk of a breach within the meaning of article 7 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union.
in writing. ‒ the death penalty is incompatible with eu values, the treaties, the charter of fundamental rights, the rule of law and respect for human dignity. in this connection, i condemn the repeated statements by the hungarian prime minister, viktor orbán, which are encouraging a debate on the possible re-establishment of the european union in hungary, thus institutionalising and feeding a concept which is a violation of the values on which the union is founded. its reintroduction would trigger the procedure provided for in article 7 teu. i also condemn the public consultation which is taking place and which tendentiously, maliciously and wrongly links immigration and terrorism, which i call for to be cancelled immediately. the commission should initiate a process of monitoring the situation of democracy, the rule of law and fundamental rights in hungary. in addition, it would be appropriate for it to submit a legislative proposal for the establishment of common indicators on democracy, the rule of law and fundamental rights as a tool for the enforcement and application of the charter and the treaties signed by all member states. i have therefore voted in favour of this resolution.

mr president, three days ago the turkish people sent us a very clear message and gave us an example of how democracy is built, how it recovers, how one must never give up in this area. i voted in favour of the report we have tabled, which we have adopted today. but to some extent this text - which we have adopted today - is an obsolete text, overtaken by events themselves; it is a text still laden with prejudices, with precautions and with obstacles to the process of agreement itself: it does not deny it, but it questions it in a very direct way. i do not know if we are up to the task of what the turkish citizens have been doing this past sunday: the rejection of the authoritarian regime that their president wanted has been achieved; a democratic alternative has been reconstructed - with a very noticeable left foot from the kurdish people's party. and somehow it is now up to us to send a message of hope, of return, in the same sense: we must reopen chapters 23 and 24 now. that would be our best measure in implementing the report we have just adopted.
in writing. ‒ the enlargement policy of the european union has many contradictions. all of these emerge strongly in the case of turkey, which applied for membership in 1987, has been a candidate since 2004 and has only closed one chapter (of 35) in ten years of negotiations with the eu. at the same time, turkey is perpetuating its occupation of part of the territory of the republic of cyprus, an eu member state, violating the human rights of the cypriot population, pursuing a settlement policy and creating tensions in cypriot territorial waters. the proposed resolution makes this clear, which is a good thing. however, i could not vote in favour of the resolution because it contradictorily encourages the continuation of the negotiations. these negotiations cannot continue as long as turkey does not fulfil the basic requirement of recognising the republic of cyprus and ending its occupation. on the other hand, there is the contradiction of positively assessing the possibility of reaching a solution to the situation of the kurds, but not asking for the pkk to be removed from the eu list of terrorist organisations. i therefore decided to abstain.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution and, above all, in favour of the joint amendment by the alde, s&d and epp groups, which recognises the plurality of turkey following the results of the elections ten days ago. i support the opening of negotiations in the various chapters named in this resolution, and not just those referring to chapters 23 and 24.
in writing. ‒ this resolution calls for closer relations between turkey and the eu, and for the commission to rethink the way it has conducted the negotiations so far and how they can be improved and intensified. among other issues, turkey is urged to put the reform process and european legislative values and principles as the benchmarks of that process at the centre of its political agenda. and it is also asked to open a process of reforming its constitution to promote a more pluralistic, inclusive and tolerant society. the peace process with the kurdish community, the reunification of cyprus and cooperation against isis are other issues addressed in the report, as are the prevention of violence against women, anti-discrimination legislation and protection for the lgbti community, respect for religious freedom and the separation of religion and state. the eu should help turkey develop strong democratic institutions and legislation based on respect for fundamental freedoms, human rights and the rule of law, defending and representing all sectors of society. for these and other reasons, i voted in favour of this resolution.

in writing. ‒ we abstained on the resolution on the report on the development of relations with turkey. while we understand that the interest of a general report on this subject may be obvious, at the same time an exercise of responsibility is necessary to ensure that the issues are properly represented and that no injustice is done to any of the parties involved. we believe that the accession process of a country of the size of turkey should be followed with greater interest by the commission and parliament, which should propose texts that do justice to the complex, diverse and, in many cases, difficult to contrast in mere reports, reality of turkey.

in writing. ‒ the enlargement policy of the european union has many contradictions. all of these emerge strongly in the case of turkey, which applied for membership in 1987, has been a candidate since 2004 and has only closed one chapter (of 35) in ten years of negotiations with the eu. at the same time, turkey is perpetuating its occupation of part of the territory of the republic of cyprus, an eu member state, violating the human rights of the cypriot population, pursuing a settlement policy and creating tensions in cypriot territorial waters. the proposed resolution makes this clear, which is a good thing. however, i could not vote in favour of the resolution because it contradictorily encourages the continuation of the negotiations. these negotiations cannot continue as long as turkey does not fulfil the basic requirement of recognising the republic of cyprus and ending its occupation. on the other hand, there is the contradiction of positively assessing the possibility of reaching a solution to the situation of the kurds, but not asking for the pkk to be removed from the eu list of terrorist organisations. i therefore decided to abstain.
member of the commission, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy.– mr president, i am pleased to have the opportunity today to discuss the issues related to the black sea. i will focus on our regional cooperation efforts and perspectives in this area. i welcome the attention that the european parliament is giving to the black sea basin. the eu has interests and responsibilities in the black sea region. we take an active approach to the sea basins that surround us, and the black sea is one of them. there are several reasons – environmental, transport, maritime affairs, civil society – for the eu to play an active role in the black sea region. we welcome the report by mr paşcu, which underlines the significant opportunities and challenges in the black sea area that require coordinated action. as we have mentioned on previous occasions, while there are good reasons to call for a comprehensive eu strategy for the black sea region, we have to make sure it will be well received both within the eu as a whole and among the non-eu black sea states. it must therefore come when the ground has been well prepared. the report before us focuses on the strategic military situation in the black sea basin following the illegal annexation of crimea and sevastopol to russia. the eu stance on this remains clear. we will not recognise the illegal annexation of crimea and sevastopol. we continue to condemn it and to fully implement our non-recognition policy, including a trade and investment ban. the eu is assessing the security risks arising from moscow’s behaviour, for example in the fields of energy security, cyber security, the security of civil aviation and of our banking systems, the stability of our democracies, and ways of countering the kremlin’s propaganda. we remain prepared for the long haul in the crisis with russia and are very conscious of the need to preserve eu unity also in the long term. we must be ready to face moscow’s confrontation as well as its cooperative behaviour. the current eu double-track approach as regards the ukraine conflict should be applied to eu-russia interaction as a whole: resilience and firmness, together with dialogue and engagement. on the one hand, the eu remains steadfast in its support for ukraine’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence. it continues to support all diplomatic efforts and in particular those linked to the implementation of the minsk agreements and those linked to unsc resolution 2202. our current efforts focus on supporting the work of the osce special monitoring mission. the eu has also continued its efforts in the trilateral processes with ukraine and russia on energy and on the implementation of the deep and comprehensive free trade area as part of the eu’s support for the broader comprehensive peace process. there is no doubt that ukraine faces immense challenges in the security, political and economic areas all at the same time. the eu is committed to bolstering ukraine’s ability to deal with these challenges and is therefore delivering unprecedented financial support. the implementation of the eur 11 billion support package is under way and the eu has already committed through loans and grants, including through its banks, the eib and ebrd, around eur 6 billion. in parallel, the eu has adopted consecutive packages of restrictive measures, including those aimed at entities in crimea. the european council in march explicitly linked the duration of sanctions against russia to the complete implementation of the minsk agreements. the eu remains deeply concerned at the continuous military build-up and deterioration of the human rights situation in the crimean peninsula, including the denial of free speech and the persecution of persons belonging to minorities. the eu continues its cooperation initiatives under the black sea synergy as and where possible. as you already know, the eu’s approach to the region is guided by the black sea synergy. this communication, adopted in 2007, sets out goals and tasks across a range of economic sectors and thematic areas based on the notion of the complementarity of various actors and actions. in january 2015, the eeas and commission services reviewed the implementation of the black sea synergy and issued a joint staff working document summarising the lessons learned. this document presents a snapshot of the progress in the main fields of cooperation in the black sea region during the last five years. the lessons learned highlighted in the document will inform the future development of the synergy. stronger partnerships between the eu institutions and member states, increasing stakeholders’ participation, and better coordination with other regional and international organisations are among the lessons that we take on board as we move forward. the results of the black sea synergy to date reveal the practical utility and the potential of this eu regional policy approach. the black sea synergy should remain a bottom-up initiative geared towards strengthening regional cooperation via concrete projects, making the best possible use of the wide range of tools at the eu’s disposal. an important goal is to bring added value to the citizens of the region, while ensuring environmental sustainability. also, we have a substantial programme of cross-border cooperation in the black sea region. there are projects underway to strengthen monitoring capacities of the black sea marine environment as well as in the areas of research, tourism and culture. we do all that while increasingly engaging with the civil society and other regional stakeholders. last but not least, the eu’s recently-adopted maritime security strategy and its associated action plan looks at maritime security in all the sea basins around us, including the black sea, in a cross-sectoral way. as called for by the report, this will help us to address maritime security challenges in an integrated manner, combining civil and military involvement at national and eu level across the numerous policy sectors concerned. the eu needs to remain closely attuned to its interests in the region, including strategic, political and economic interests, and to further discuss how best they can be achieved. on military issues as, very rightly, the report insists upon, we are maintaining and possibly even strengthening close contact with nato at both political and working level. in its conclusions of 18 may, the council welcomed ongoing efforts to strengthen strategic and practical cooperation between the eu and nato, with the overall objective of building a true organisation-to-organisation relationship. in this endeavour, we count on the support of the european parliament, and we look forward to views and ideas from the members of this house.
