first vice-president of the commission.– mr president, exactly 10 years ago in london, 52 people died and hundreds were wounded in a terrible terrorist attack. i remember vividly those days. i remember the outpouring of solidarity in london, in the united kingdom, and across the world, especially in the european union. i want to mention this at the start of my contribution today, because i do believe that we, as europeans – whatever our position may be on european integration, on european cooperation – at that moment had a sense of destiny, of common destiny. whatever else we may do right or wrong, we have a common duty to fight for the security and safety of our citizens. we have a common duty to make sure that these barbarians, these distorted thinkers, these nihilists, are not in a position to wreak havoc in european society. this is one of the main challengers all our nations face. this goes beyond politics. this is about human dignity. this is about our common values. if i look back at the last couple of years, we have seen that europe is facing a number of huge challenges: terrorism, as i just mentioned; the migration crisis; the need to create jobs and to create growth; the need to face the changes in the world’s economy and the place of europe therein; and greece. this is the backdrop against which we are working on our commission work programme for this year and for next year. let me say something briefly about this year’s state of play and the commission work programme 2015. over half of the work programme items are fully or mostly fulfilled. thanks to you, to this parliament, the european fund for strategic investments has been operational since 1 july. we have set out strategic agendas, including for investment, energy union, the digital single market, migration, internal security and a fairer corporate tax system. these agendas and action plans signal a considerable legislative workload for this house in the months and years to come. some of these proposals are already before you, and more are coming – starting with the revision of the energy labelling and emissions trading legislation next week. in total, over 40 proposals for legislation will flow from the strategies we have already presented. that comes on top of the 140 proposals which are pending on the table of the co-legislators. so please let us bust this myth that this commission is not forthcoming enough. where legislation is the right response to address the big things, we will be big on legislation. we are working on ambitious strategies on trade and investment, on the single market for goods and services, on an ambitious package for the circular economy. we will present an action plan for developing a real capital markets union in autumn, and we will accompany it with the first legislative proposals in the most pressing areas. and before the end of the year, we want to put to you a comprehensive – and clearly much-needed –’emu package’. the importance of the social dimension – in emu, obviously, but also more widely – is something president juncker and i are both very attached to. to speed up the youth employment initiative, we proposed making eur 1 billion available this year. we are also actively working on a labour mobility package, to be adopted later this year. the college will have a further orientation debate dedicated to social policy immediately after the summer. before looking ahead towards 2016, i would like to stress that it takes – in this case, oddly enough – three to tango. delivering results where it matters is a shared responsibility of all three institutions. that is why we are now negotiating a revised interinstitutional agreement (iia) on better law making, and i am very much looking forward to my first meeting – on a political level as well – with nicolas schmit, who is representing the presidency, and with guy verhofstadt, who is representing your parliament. our proposal pays particular attention to reinforcing and consolidating the annual and multiannual planning and programming. while respecting the specific arrangements for close cooperation between parliament and commission that are set out in the framework agreement – we respect and will continue to respect that framework agreement – and while respecting each of the three institutions’ roles under the treaties, it is by working better upstream that we believe we can really make sure our combined efforts deliver effective and ambitious results to address the challenges europe faces. let me turn briefly to the preparations for next year. a first orientation debate will be held in college a week from now. in september, we will have an opportunity to take stock of the progress made and of the challenges ahead during president juncker’s state of the union address. we intend to adopt the 2016 work programme on 27 october. in the run-up, the commission will engage actively in dialogue with parliament, in full accordance with the framework agreement. we will also listen to the input of member states in the general affairs council. to launch and guide our discussion, a ‘letter of intent’ will be sent in parallel with the state of the union address here in this house. so that is for september. you can expect another targeted and balanced work programme, focused on 2016 – and 2016 only – grounded in the 10 priorities set out by president juncker and agreed with your parliament. our strategic agendas – those we have already presented and those still to come later this year – will obviously be the main frame, and we will keep a clear focus on delivering what we have announced there. so please remember that those are the pivotal points in our commission work programme. you know this already. this is the basis upon which we will develop our concrete proposals. and then, of course, next year will also be the year of the mff mid-term review, which is also going to be a big challenge for both our institutions. there will be a strong emphasis on refit, because keeping the acquis up to date and pertinent to today’s challenges requires a permanent effort. and if pending proposals need to be repealed or withdrawn to allow the co-legislators to use their energy on files that have a chance of being adopted, we will flag them. we need to be, i believe, pragmatic and result oriented. if others need to be prioritising and speeding up, we will flag them too. i hope that we can work closely together with parliament on this. i strongly believe in this, and i think we need to deliver better results for our citizens. in conclusion, mr president, aligning our political priorities and planning can help make all the difference to whether europeans look at europe as part of the problem or rather as part of the solution to the huge challenges they face. i look forward to the resolution that this house will adopt later this week, which will be very useful in guiding the commission’s ongoing reflections. let us work together, let us work hard. there are so many challenges we face and so many results our citizens expect of us: let us do it together.
on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, mr vice-president of the commission, we are in a double exercise. on the one hand, to check in some way what has happened since the commission presented its investment programme, and on the other hand, to try to provide an opportunity for the european parliament to contribute to the political direction that the commission itself has to set in motion. of course, this is an element of the interinstitutional agreement, but i think it goes beyond an agreement. it goes beyond. the european parliament, because of its high political dimension, must be part of the political leadership of the union. when it comes to reviewing what has happened in this first part of the commission's action, my assessment is frankly positive. the combination of the investment programme, the efsi, with the flexibility of the growth programme has made it possible to turn the union's economic policy around and to orient it towards the elements we have to solve in the context of the economic crisis: growth and job creation. but the commission has also come up with a very substantive proposal on tax policy and with action, as well as a very courageous proposal on immigration. and it has also come with ambitious positions on energy policy and also in other areas in the economic field. i would also like to point out that transparency has been established, has been established in the commission's behaviour and i think that is a positive point. my group has sufficiently identified priorities for 2016 in the social field, in the field of immigration, in the field of fiscal policy and in the field of democracy. in the social field, we want all the union's policies to be cross-cutting social approaches. i know that the vice-president often says that we must be concrete, that it is not enough to say that we are in favour of a social policy. i think we can work together to work out which aspects. for example, in the fight against poverty and exclusion, in respect for collective bargaining, in - as the vice-president has just pointed out - legislation on worker mobility and rights, respect for workers' rights in the context of such mobility. in the field in which you have indicated that you are going to present a package on economic and monetary union, we also want the social dimension to be a basic point of the strengthened economic and monetary union, not only in the document of the presidents but also in the whole of the commission's action. in tax policy, the proposal can be simplified in two respects. we want it to be taxed in those countries where the income is generated and we want there to be a common rate, a common consolidated tax base for corporation tax. and in the field of immigration, what i really want is for the commission to maintain the firm pulse it has maintained so far, asking the member states to meet in solidarity the burdens that are being generated by humanitarian crises, but at the same time, in the longer term, with proposals to seriously organise legal immigration within the union and to deal, also in solidarity, with the issue of asylum. as regards democracy, i would like to conclude by saying that my group wants a proposal to be put forward with objective indicators and a mandatory mechanism to respond to failures and violations of the union's fundamental rights, as enshrined in its treaties. so there is a broad level of agreement and we look forward to working continuously with the commission next year.
on behalf of the green group, the best thing to say about this budget, mr president, mrs georgieva and mr fernandes, is that it will not cause any great damage to anyone. it is correct, it is balanced, it is solvent. we'll negotiate until the last minute, like every year, and i'm sure we'll reach an honorable agreement. let me say, however, that an increase of 2.4% and 1.6% in commitment and payment appropriations is a sign of overall prudence, but it does not mean any appreciable real growth. we are dazzled by a sharp reduction in the volume of outstanding payments, but it is not at all clear what will happen in the following years, when all the 2014-2020 programmes are in full swing. we can mention, in a positive sense, the life programme, a first, provisional and pending attempt to greening the budget. welcome to the club. but we must also mention, in a negative, very negative sense, the support that continues to be given to a project like iter: up to more than 500 million for a project that offers, of course, more doubts than certainties and more concerns than hopes. let's wait for the reports on the approval of the 2013 management and then we will finish judging. but this budget is also a symptom of another much larger problem. like the titanic orchestra, we continue to play our song, our budget, in this case, while everything around us cries out for answers of another order, much more ambitious, urgent and meaningful. the debate on the atci or on greece, which we have in this house today, illustrates this incongruity perfectly. the unequal dialogue europe-us - the us has a budget of over 20% of its gdp and europe, around 1% - speaks to us clearly about this. this budget is safe and sound, but it is also irrelevant. it is not part of the remedies that europe really needs for economic growth and to respond to the inequalities that we have.
mr president, mr fernandes, our group has tabled a number of amendments, many of which have been introduced and which, in our view, improve the document. we are, however, firm in our general criticism of this draft budget. we consider it to be too rigid and insufficient and not up to the challenge of the economic crisis we are experiencing, aggravated by austerity and cutbacks. without truly ambitious public investment policies, stimulating and geared to the creation of quality jobs and the change of the production model not dependent on fossil energy, europe will continue to deepen its problems of cohesion and ignore the need to tackle the real social dramas experienced by a fundamental part of our population. the greek people have just said loud and clear 'enough' to politics and to the europe of austerity. you have a duty to listen to your people.
vice-president of the commission. – mr president, many thanks to all who have contributed to this debate. i will try to be concise and address questions that have been directed to the commission. first, there were a number of comments referring to the difference between commitments and payments in the 2016 budget and some expressing concerns that, a with eur 10 billion difference – with commitments being about eur 10 billion higher than payments – we might not deal with the gap that existed particularly seriously last year. we are confident that this will not be the case, for two reasons. one is that, because of the very specific measures we are taking as part of the payment plan that parliament requested, we can bring down the amount of unpaid bills from eur 24.7 - 20 billion this year to eur 2 billion next year. eur 2 billion is normal, and we would be in normal territory. the other reason is that in 2016 we are out of the pressure of the previous mff, which last year and this year demanded from us significant payments, but we are not yet under the pressure of payments coming from the new mff. so 2016 is a year where it is normal to have commitments being higher and payments being lower, with a difference of eur 10 billion as we have calculated them. i can assure you that we will be monitoring very carefully throughout the implementation of the budget whether or not we are properly managing the payment side in particular. secondly, there was concern on the question of the underlying economic data for the calculation of the amounts to be paid for cohesion. what exactly would be the envelope for cohesion for different countries, given that they are shifting up and down in terms of their relative gdp size? there will be a recalculation in 2016 which would then impact on the envelopes of cohesion. thirdly, a number of speakers brought up very forcefully the point that we want this budget to be different. we want it to be focused more on priorities and we want it to be focused on performance; mr novakov talked about a budget focused on results. we want it to be a budget in which we carefully manage the administrative side and, yes, we are working in that direction. we are, of course, like the queen mary – we take time to shift, but shift we will. you will see over time a results-focused, performance orientation of the budget, also looking into multiple benefits from the euros we invest. that takes me to a very important point: investing in innovation in smes. of course we have to do that. this is where growth in employment is going to come from. this is where we are going to see an increased standard of living, especially for countries where unemployment has been persistently high. that is where the thinking of the budget connects not only with what we spend directly for smes, for example cosme, but also how we are gearing the investment plan for europe – how we are gearing up the juncker plan to be more effective. there was a very specific question on hungary. what would happen to people in hungary as a result of your budget? obviously we need to come back to you with specifics, and i am already running out of time. but what you will see that is somewhat different from previous budgets is this: we are looking at a composition for the hungarian budget which would have a strong cohesion component, from the structural funds; it would have a very strong agricultural component, because the country has a sizeable farming sector; but we would also see the impact, hopefully, of the juncker plan, of taking money to invest in waking up the sleeping liquidity in our financial sector. i would be happy to sit with you and walk you through what would be in it for me if i were a hungarian. mr fernandes, i very much look forward to negotiating with you again, be it day or night – day still being a bit more preferred.

in writing. the greek public debt problem has triggered one of the most serious crises in eu history. it has been emphasized that the single currency is an unfinished project. the monetary union must be supplemented urgently by fiscal, financial and budgetary union and a debt-repayment fund. the eurogroup has shown itself incapable of finding a just and final solution to an economic and financial situation, the causes of which include years of 'austerity-like' policies which put debt before people and whose main consequence is the suffering of thousands of greeks. the eu must resolve crises through its common institutions, including the european parliament. it is now up to the euro summit and the european council to find a balanced agreement, including debt relief, on the basis of the commission's latest proposal of 28 june, and thus prevent the breakdown of monetary union. the integrity of the eurozone must be preserved, otherwise the european construction project will lose its credibility. in the meantime, the ecb must ensure the functioning of the greek banking system by increasing the volume of the emergency liquidity provision.
in writing. we are at a critical moment for greece and for the rest of the european union. let's be rational, sit down and negotiate and resolve this situation once and for all. there are two reasons why we must find an agreement that allows greece to remain in the euro area. the first is solidarity. the greek governments have made many mistakes, but it is the greek people who have suffered the consequences. our greek compatriots have been in adjustment for five years and the unemployment rate has skyrocketed. let us stop resorting to negative stereotypes that could spread to other peoples of the mediterranean and focus on the sacrifices they have already made. in addition to the structural reforms that the eu is demanding of them, they need an investment plan to boost their economy, in the style of the famous juncker plan that has been so well received. the second reason is selfishness. if greece leaves the euro area, the euro will lose much of its credibility and weight as an international currency. in addition, countries in the process of recovery, such as spain, will again see the risk premium soar, which will make it difficult for them to exit the crisis. so let us have a high view.

member of the commission, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy.– mr president, since the beginning of her mandate, improving relations with the latin american continent has been a priority for the vice-president/high representative. the eu-celac summit has underscored once again the strategic nature of our partnership based on shared values and aiming to promote joint solutions to global challenges. enhancing ties with cuba has been a fundamental chapter of this broader strategy. some of the fault lines that have shaped global politics for decades are shifting with impressive speed. sometimes we are so focused on the threats we face that we overlook the positive changes that are also taking place. we should not miss the many opportunities that are arising. furthermore, europe cannot take a back seat whilst someone else makes history. we should be driving the change forward, to make sure too that the outcomes reflect our values and our priorities, from trade to human rights. during these past months, the vice-president/high representative has engaged personally with the cuban side. a first meeting was held with cuban foreign minister rodríguez during the celac summit in january 2015 in costa rica. in march, she travelled to havana and had a series of meetings, including with president castro as well as with the ministers for foreign affairs, the economy, foreign trade and investment. in april, foreign minister rodríguez came to brussels to relaunch the formal political dialogue. finally a bilateral meeting was held with vice-president díaz-canel on the margins of the eu-celac summit. in february 2014 the eu approved the negotiating directives for a political dialogue and cooperation agreement – the so-called pdca – with cuba. this will provide an enabling platform for constructive dialogue and improve cooperation between cuba and the european union. the decision followed a lengthy reflection process in the council. it took into account the incipient domestic reform process under president castro. in parallel, member states also increased their bilateral engagement with cuba. updating our approach in order to promote eu objectives in relation to cuba more effectively was considered: encouraging political and economic reforms, promoting human rights and improving the lives of cuban citizens. the agreement will include chapters on political dialogue and cooperation as well as on trade. negotiations were launched in april 2014 and subsequent rounds took place in august and in march 2015. ms mogherini’s contacts with the cuban side in recent months also served to provide additional impetus to the process. on 15 and 16 june last, negotiators met for a fourth round of talks in brussels. the discussions took place in a good – and may i say constructive – atmosphere. together we managed to achieve substantial progress, mainly on the cooperation and policy dialogue and the trade chapters. these chapters are now at very advanced stages and can hopefully be closed in the next round of talks. there was also progress on the political dialogue chapter, and the negotiators engaged in a productive exchange of views, during which positions were further developed and clarified. this discussion will enable a more in-depth preparation of negotiations on the proposed text in the next round, which means in early september. members will be aware that it was agreed with foreign minister bruno rodríguez to seek to accelerate negotiations and conclude them soon, as both sides agreed that this would be to our mutual benefit. the progress accomplished in this round demonstrates the strong commitment of both sides to enhancing the relationship. progress has also been achieved in an area which is, and will remain, at the core of eu relations with cuba: human rights and fundamental freedoms. in march it was proposed to foreign minister rodríguez that a dedicated and structured dialogue on human rights be set up. during the political dialogue meeting in brussels, an understanding was reached to start consultations on the establishment of a human rights dialogue. a first session led by the eu’s special representative for human rights, stavros lambrinidis, was held in brussels on 25 june, in between a preparatory and a constituting meeting. the purpose was to discuss and agree on the format and objectives of such a dialogue before the pdca negotiations are concluded, to give us a head start. thus the human rights dialogue parameters will be designed in line with the overall terms of the agreement, from where they will derive continuity and formal blessing. the dialogue gives us an opportunity to improve mutual understanding on human rights and exchange experiences and best practices, as well as seek to identify potential areas of cooperation between the eu and cuba. it also provides a platform to address recent developments and, where necessary and appropriate, to address concerns over individual cases. this dedicated dialogue will provide feedback and bolster the formal political dialogue at the political level. in the light of this positive engagement, it was all the more disappointing to learn of the incidents which took place in havana last weekend, including undue violence and a large number of detentions. there is no reason to limit the peaceful expression of opinion, and the use of excessive violence against peaceful protestors is unacceptable. those who overstepped the mark of the legitimate exercise of authority should be disciplined. we expect the cuban authorities to take all necessary measures to remedy this situation, and we call on them to permit all peaceful forms of expression. during the meetings with the cuban authorities, the vice-president/high representative also explored the prospects for cooperation and joint work on a number of foreign policy issues. these include columbia, where cuba plays a positive role in hosting negotiations between the government and farc in the mediation process. other such cases include global cooperation on health issues, in which cuba has a strong role, as we witnessed during the ebola crisis, or, potentially, cooperation on climate change in the run-up to the cop21 conference in paris. obviously, the recent rapprochement between cuba and the united states has also been addressed in these talks. last week, cuba and the us announced the reopening of their embassies in washington and havana. this decision, as agreed between presidents obama and castro, ends a prolonged stalemate and will create new opportunities for cuba, the region and beyond. the isolation of cuba would make no sense at all in today’s world. it is a cold-war relic we should all be happy to dismiss. this is even more true for us europeans, who suffered for decades from the artificial divisions imposed by a conflictual world order. a further normalisation is necessary and should include the end of the us embargo, which is outdated and inconsistent with the context. the eu has always spoken up against this unilateral measure, including its humanitarian impact on many cubans and its territorial effects on eu-cuban economic relations.

madam president, commissioner, this report is of crucial importance to ensure food safety in the event of a nuclear accident or a radiological emergency. i would like to emphasize that the maximum levels of contamination in food listed in the annexes to this proposal for a regulation are not the limits which should be applied automatically in the event of an accident, as the messages we have received 'all orchestrated and managed by a single ngo' seem to imply, but that they should be modulated according to the extent of the accident, since the commission must adjust the reference levels to the actual conditions of contamination through the implementation costs provided for in this proposal for a regulation. i think it is important for us all to bear in mind that these reference levels have been set by the recommendations of the euratom expert group, which i respect, even though i do not know its name or its face. in addition, its recommendations follow the advice provided by the international commission on radiological protection, which is the highest scientific authority worldwide, made up of non-governmental and independent experts. i think it is important to remember this in order to counteract alarmist messages and i also think it is important to stress that the reference levels set in the proposal for a regulation have been established on the basis of the same assumptions as those set out in the codex alimentarius and that these levels are ten times lower than those advocated by the international atomic energy agency for international trade. and finally, as this is a matter of food safety, i also think, as does the rapporteur, that this parliament should have the power of codecision. ladies and gentlemen, this is about multiple targets. the point is that we should take up digital technologies and build on them to review and modernise our existing copyright package at european the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has adopted a number of amendments to the proposal. madam president, during the worst of the crisis, european cultural industries have continued to create jobs. that speaks to his vitality and his strength. and at the core of that strength are the authors, who are the drivers of the cultural industry and who are the drivers of culture, and copyright is also the one that has to guarantee the remuneration for that work that is crucial to our diversity and to our cultural richness. we all want to develop cultural industries in the new digital environment, to harness their potential to generate new jobs, to drive innovative industries. but let no one propose the copyright reform that the commissioner is announcing to us as a confrontation between authors and users, in which some must lose so that others can win. protecting authors is protecting everyone, because it's protecting cultural creation, it's protecting content. if we don't, we all lose. europe needs, as has been said, to revise its legislation, but in order to strengthen its cultural industries, not to weaken them. i believe that content is the new black gold of the internet, and what europe needs to do is to strengthen this role, strengthen the content, strengthen our leadership.
madam president, cultural industries are a significant generator of growth and jobs. copyright is the cornerstone of cultural policy. however, the current regime needs to be better tailored to the digital environment in order to ensure fair remuneration to creators and to conform to consumer expectations. this is the reason why i welcome the commission’s commitment on the modernisation of the copyright directive. the lack of harmonisation of exceptions in the eu creates legal uncertainties. at least a core of exceptions should be made mandatory. restrictions linked to geo-blocking prevent european citizens from enjoying cultural diversity across borders and european companies from fully benefiting from the possibilities offered by the digital environment. we need to find legislative and market—driven solutions so that european citizens can access any work available in a member state from anywhere in the eu. last but not least, i also believe strongly in freedom of panorama.
mr president, i would like to ask that the vote on the commission's work programme be postponed until september, in order to try to reach an agreement with a higher level of consensus and with a greater representation of the shared and balanced priorities of the various political groups.
mr president, i would like to table the following oral amendment to amendment no 2. paragraph 9a would read as follows: 'expresses concern at the intensive arms trade of eu member states with several countries in the region; calls in this regard on the council to verify that the common position of the european union on arms export controls has not been breached and to take measures to ensure that all member states fully respect this common position.'
mr president, i voted against this report on the atci because parliament cannot legitimise a treaty which in its conception, in its elaboration, in its content and in its objectives is an attack on each and every social right, without which there can be no talk of democracy. it is not the time for vagueness, for confusing public opinion with phrases full of good intentions that conceal the political content of this agreement. there is already free trade between the european union and the united states, and the remaining tariff barriers are necessary to keep vital sectors such as agriculture alive. the atci is actually the excuse to institutionalize the primacy of big capital over workers. it is big business that wants to intervene, to express its opinion and even to denounce the recognition of labour rights and environmental and economic standards that could reduce its profits, forcing states to pay fines for defending the common good. democracy cannot be subservient to markets. listen to the people, who have already shouted "no!" to atci.
mr president, we voted against this document which gives legitimacy to the negotiations on the free trade agreement between the european union and the united states, known as the ftaa. we have done so because we do not like the secrecy with which the negotiations are being conducted and because we consider that the treaty is basically a deregulation project. legal deregulation, with the imposition of private arbitration courts that will operate outside the public courts and thus create a parallel justice. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat unemployment, and i am sure that the commission will take them into account. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's energy policy is not disrupted by the introduction of new technologies, such as the new nuclear power stations. at a time when the european union is going through a great economic and social crisis - we were here yesterday discussing the situation in greece - and while the european single market is not yet a reality, the atci is a leap forward in an economic model that is unbridled, unsustainable and socially unacceptable.
i voted against this report, firstly because in a democracy decisions affecting the majority of the people are not opaque, or secret, or their consequences should be hidden, but also because of the content of the treaty itself, which poses enormous risks to employment and working conditions, as many reports by independent experts say; because it opens the door to the privatization of our public services, which are necessary for the well-being of the citizens; because it puts at risk our environmental standards, our countryside, our agriculture; because it is a treaty which opens the door to the interests of multinationals everywhere being put above the interests of citizens. when we talk about trade barriers, when atci talks about trade barriers, for a multinational, a trade barrier is high wages, a trade barrier is collective bargaining, a trade barrier is labor rights and social rights. because we are with social rights we do not want the atci.
i voted against the atci because i think it's a clear attack on democracy. in a democracy, you can't negotiate in secret. the public needs to know what we're playing with this deal. it's vital to put lights and shorthand in atci. i also voted against it because i think it is a clear attack on popular sovereignty. it is a clear attack on our social rights, our labour rights, on public services. it is essential to build a wall against the trojan horse that they are trying to bring into europe with the free trade agreement. and it is also inexcusable that anyone in this house can vote in favour of the just, just creation of extrajudicial tribunals operating in europe against the sovereignty of the people. we'll stop it in the streets and we'll stop it in the parliaments. and, above all, atci, the strategy of dracula: to give it air, to give it light, to let people know it. and it won't pass.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report on the atci to show my rejection of this association, as categorical as the united left's position against the atci, against an agreement that seeks to put democracy, public services and the rights and freedoms of individuals at the service of multinationals. the european parliament, instead of clearly rejecting an agreement designed by and for the benefit of the big corporations, denouncing the obscurantism of the negotiations, demanding transparency and public participation, and defending the sovereignty and interests of the social majority, gives with this report full support to the atci and the current negotiations. the report, which should have been voted on a month ago but was delayed by a unilateral decision by president schulz because of the risk of rejection, also approves the creation of arbitration tribunals (isds), ignoring the majority rejection of these tribunals, which was reflected in the consultation carried out by the european commission, in which 97% of the participants were against this mechanism.
in writing. ‒ there has been significant progress on isds which opens the door to a new improved system (amendment 117), but we abstained in the vote as the expected steps on regulatory cooperation have not been taken. the text does not clearly define those regulations and sectors excluded from any negotiation. we hope that this will be clarified in the coming months, with full guarantees of our political rights and of what is defended by european legislation. we therefore support amendments nos 93, 19 and 72. the us and european standards are very different in the areas listed: pesticides, disruptors, food safety, animal welfare, transparency in clinical trials... we understand that cooperation is necessary to remove barriers to trade, such as excessive bureaucracy, but we must not jeopardise what makes the eu an example and a benchmark. the agricultural and food sectors are key to ensuring food security, but they have also been strategic within the speculative dynamics in stock exchanges and investment funds. its liberalization is evident in the above and in the latest reforms. these sectors and the protection of our standards are red lines for upyd and for the vast majority of eu citizens, and that is why we support them.
in writing. ‒ i have supported this resolution because it clearly sets out the european parliament's position on the att negotiations, including the main demands of the socialist group; because i believe that a market economy is the best way to guarantee progress, growth and employment if it is well regulated and confined to a welfare state that corrects its shortcomings and redistributes fairly; because trade between the eu and the us is already worth almost one trillion euros a year and we need a good treaty to regulate it; because, in addition to the removal of unnecessary trade barriers, which mainly affect smes, the resolution calls for the strengthening of labour rights, with the ratification of the main ilo conventions, and environmental protection; because it abolishes the isds and calls for private arbitration and a new career model, with transparent, independent public hearings and an appeal system. in short, because it demands an agreement that guarantees the standards of protection we enjoy in the eu and serves to promote globally the values and principles we share with the us, making it very clear that we will only support an atci that regulates trade for the benefit of the citizen.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the lange report on the negotiations of the so-called transatlantic trade and investment partnership (ttip) because i am against this partnership on principle. the only recommendation from the european parliament which could be acceptable in this case is to stop immediately negotiations on this text with the united states. the atci encourages the concentration of power and resources in a few hands, makes it inevitable that the standards for labour rights we have in europe will be lowered, and increases the precariousness of work by encouraging competition to the downside. the atci is also a further step in europe's political subordination to the united states. if this partnership is continued, american trade policy will condition european policy to the point where its foreign interests will be totally subordinated to washington's dictates. the atci is an affront to the sovereignty and democracy of the peoples of europe. that is why i voted 'no' and will vote in favour of this in every opportunity to reject this threat.

in writing. - we did not vote for or against the atci today. we have voted today to influence its negotiation, to set out the conditions and the red lines of parliament for the conclusion of an agreement. today i voted for the european commission to demand that the united states ratify the ilo's fundamental conventions and the decent work programme and respect our environmental protection. i also voted for the clear and precise exclusion of public services such as water, health, social services and education from the scope of atci, and for guarantees that eu data protection rules will not be compromised under any circumstances. finally, i have made clear my rejection of isds, calling for a new, transparent model with independent career judges, public hearings and an appeals system. in short, i have sent a clear signal to the negotiating team that i will only support an agreement that guarantees the standards of protection we enjoy in the eu and serves to promote globally the values and principles we share with the us, regulating trade for the benefit of citizens.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this report because it recommends to the european commission lines of action which run counter to the interests of european citizens, their rights, public services, democracy and sovereignty, which are red lines and common sense for podemos. the amendment adopted on isds is also clearly a toast to the sun, because although it advocates, in the long term, the creation of an international and public tribunal for the settlement of differences between investors and states, the us government has publicly stated that it will not accept it. we therefore consider it a deception to the public to claim that the private arbitration system has been abolished. we therefore believe that transnational companies will continue to have a veto over the legislative capacity of the states, which is a frontal attack on democracy.

in writing. ‒ it is known that the explicit objective of the atci is not that of a commercial agreement on use. the aim is not to alleviate the already rather low import or export duties or tax burdens, but to eliminate the different 'situations' and 'regulations' which may exist on both sides and to achieve 'the unification of markets'. while it is true that what was voted on today in the european parliament's plenary session is not the agreement itself, but an opinion of the house for the commission to take into account in the negotiations, eh bildu maintains its position and has given a categorical 'no' to the lange report. public debate and resistance from society has led to the report's wording in relation to isds being modified and improved; the transaction amendment 117 calls for replacing isds and its arbitration systems with judges, but does not specify the nature of these tribunals. eh bildu remains firmly opposed to isds or any other similar formula and, in general, opposed to atci; it has therefore voted against this report.
in writing. ‒ the report includes mandatory labour and environmental objectives specifically, ratification, implementation and enforcement of the main international conventions, such as the eight ilo conventions; exclusion of public services from atci; and full respect for the government's capacity to decide how services of general interest are financed, managed and delivered (regardless of their current financing and management). the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover all the activities of the european union's institutions. i agree with these points and have therefore voted in favour of the report.

in writing. ‒ the stabilisation and association agreement with serbia was approved in 2008 with the aim of developing contractual relations with serbia and the member states of the european union. updating this document to include croatia as a signatory, as the last eu member state following its accession in july 2013, would allow progress to be made in the negotiations towards a future accession of serbia to the union. similarly, customs duties are lifted on agricultural and fishery imports originating in serbia to any eu member state and minimum duties are set on exports from the eu to serbia. pushing for the amendment of the protocol is not just a formality in terms of croatia's accession to the agreement, but it also revitalizes trade with the balkan region, which will generate benefits for both parties. for these reasons, i strongly support the updating of the pact.
in writing. ‒ as in the case of the protocol to the association agreement with macedonia under discussion today, this standard is also of a rather technical nature. nevertheless, it gives us an opportunity to demonstrate once again our support for the rapprochement between serbia and the european union, which is not an easy story, but in my opinion, a story that is now developing successfully. serbia belongs to europe and we must appreciate its steps towards cooperation with europe. i, personally, as an alternate in the delegation with serbia, would like to express my appreciation for today's motion.

in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council amending directive 2007/36/ec as regards the promotion of long-term shareholder involvement and directive 2013/34/eu as regards certain elements of the corporate governance statement because it represents a very important step in the fight against tax evasion and in favour of transparency for listed companies. with this proposal, europe has a great opportunity to create a fairer and more transparent tax system. among the new elements it includes is the requirement for large companies to report "country by country" profits made, taxes paid on profits and subsidies received. this will enable citizens and authorities to know where large companies actually pay their taxes, since they will have to clarify whether they pay taxes in tax havens or where they carry out their economic activities. the directive also provides that shareholders of a listed company may vote on the remuneration of their directors, which should reflect the directors' contributions to the long-term interests and results of the companies.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it means the adoption of a directive which contains important obligations for the shareholders of public limited companies, so that they can be better controlled by the different competent authorities in the member states. this directive represents a major advance in european commercial law, by including for the first time the obligations of shareholders in their long-term relationship with participating undertakings. there are many mechanisms by which this directive will not solve many of the problems of ownership of public limited companies; however, it is an undeniable step forward in imposing obligations on entrepreneurs. for all these reasons, i have decided to vote in favour.

in writing. ‒ the commission's proposal on certain elements of the corporate governance statement was published in april 2014. the review of the shareholder rights directive is part of the initiatives set out in the commission's action plan 'european company law and corporate governance - a modern legal framework for greater shareholder participation and the viability of companies'. the most important provisions proposed are: shareholder identification; facilitation of the transmission of relevant information between the company and shareholders and the exercise of shareholders' rights; transparency provisions for institutional investors, asset managers and voting advisors; new rules on directors' remuneration; new rules on related party transactions (rpt). in this regard, the report should contain some priorities such as the remuneration policy, comply and explain in the identification of shareholders and the abolition of the obligation of long-term incentives.

in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this report. we understand that the outcome is positive and that the possible effects will be positive. the text attempts to deal with tax havens and tax evasion, understanding them as one of the key problems in contemporary capitalism. it also includes a number of positive points, such as the need to justify premiums or the request to introduce compulsory tax reporting by companies. at the present stage, the juri committee is trying to find the legal basis for the possible development of a tax system which meets the needs of the present time. we believe that this report is a step forward in this respect and that further research should be carried out on the question of tax evasion and how it undermines the social economies of the various countries of the union.

in writing. ‒ the report aims to improve stability and encourage long-term investment by encouraging shareholders to be more active and more committed to the results of companies. it also introduces, in order to ensure greater transparency of company grades, the obligation for companies to declare country by country profits made, taxes paid on profits and subsidies received. the proposal is part of a legislative package aimed at strengthening the transparency of companies and shareholder rights. the country-by-country report will enable citizens and authorities to know where large companies actually pay their taxes, as they must clarify whether they pay taxes in tax havens or where they carry out their economic activities. i agree with these considerations and have therefore voted in favour of the report.

in writing. ‒ the proposal for a directive, as originally presented, did not include any mechanism to monitor transparency in relations between european companies and their shareholders. the lack of clarity in the process would inevitably have undermined citizens' confidence in the way business is conducted, in turn damaging the competitiveness of our companies. the final proposal introduces a set of rules to facilitate the identification of shareholders, investors, asset managers and voting advisers involved in the process, thus improving the dissemination of information on the process. it also ensures that the vested rights of the parties involved are respected and that the remuneration of directors is regulated, all with a view to promoting a less opaque system and better adapted to the interests of shareholders. for these reasons, i am voting in favour of the proposal.

in writing. ‒ i welcome very much this report that should help to strengthen the capacity of shareholders to keep the boards of corporates accountable. moreover, the strong position on country-by-country reporting is a step forward in corporate transparency that in my view will help governments to ensure that multinational companies pay taxes in the countries where they make the profits.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report which strongly reinforces the obligation to publish certain information, such as a detailed study of tax burdens in each country, which can make a major contribution to the fight against fraud and unfair tax competition.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council amending directive 2007/36/ec as regards the promotion of long-term shareholder involvement and directive 2013/34/eu as regards certain elements of the corporate governance statement because it represents a very important step in the fight against tax evasion and in favour of transparency for listed companies. with this proposal, europe has a great opportunity to create a fairer and more transparent tax system. among the new elements it includes is the requirement for large companies to report "country by country" profits made, taxes paid on profits and subsidies received. this will enable citizens and authorities to know where large companies actually pay their taxes, since they will have to clarify whether they pay taxes in tax havens or where they carry out their economic activities. the directive also provides that shareholders of a listed company may vote on the remuneration of their directors, which should reflect the directors' contributions to the long-term interests and results of the companies.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it means the adoption of a directive which contains important obligations for the shareholders of public limited companies, so that they can be better controlled by the different competent authorities in the member states. this directive represents a major advance in european commercial law, by including for the first time the obligations of shareholders in their long-term relationship with participating undertakings. there are many mechanisms by which this directive will not solve many of the problems of ownership of public limited companies; however, it is an undeniable step forward in imposing obligations on entrepreneurs. for all these reasons, i have decided to vote in favour.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the creation of the emission allowance market stability reserve because, although the ets is a system that needs to be modified and corrected, i have no doubt that it remains an excellent instrument for combating climate change. the stability reserve is a good solution for better management of emission allowances, but it is true that there are other aspects which must also be improved to make the system more effective. until the european commission presents its proposal to amend the directive, we must hold those who are raising self-interested doubts about the ets to account. our criticism must always be constructive so that we can correct the inadequacy, but remain united against climate change and work towards meeting our goals, both those of the eu and those agreed on at global level. on the other hand, at a time when european innovation, research and science are being punished by cuts, i welcome the fact that the agreement takes into account our idea of allocating funds from the reserve to industrial innovation actions and demonstration projects for low-carbon technologies such as co2 capture and storage.
in writing. ‒ i could not vote in favour of this report because, although it is a modification aimed at making the eu's emissions trading system more efficient, market mechanisms cannot be the only means available to reduce emissions from companies. these market mechanisms are the only proposal for eu action in this area and have proved to be a total failure, allowing the big polluters to increase pollution and even their speculative profits. action on emissions requires the strengthening of public, binding and coercive measures to make the polluter pay.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this report on the creation of a market stability reserve for the eu's greenhouse gas emissions trading system. this emission market was set up by the kyoto protocol in 1997. it was actually interpreted as a "right to pollute" and had the opposite effect of what was intended. again, hell is paved with good intentions. a market for co2 was created out of thin air, based on no reality, on no need, and has therefore experienced a price crisis which makes it ineffective. the decreases in emissions in europe in recent years are mainly due to the economic crisis and the relocation of the most polluting industries to countries that are less concerned about the environment and the health of their people. in the face of the failure of this false carbon market, the measures provided for in this text are only a palliative to an incoherent system that produces elsewhere what we consume here, casting a modest veil over the social and environmental conditions of production. "buy this pollution so i can't see it" is not a responsible attitude.
in writing. ‒ we voted against the ets and the 'trusted price' for carbon, because we believe that carbon is good for the oil and gas industry in the long term. companies that rely on fossil fuels use the existence of the cdec as an argument for the elimination of eu energy efficiency and renewable energy targets. however, the eu emissions trading system is designed to prolong dependence on fossil fuels and to expand and strengthen the role of financial markets in people's daily lives. these fossil energy sources not only generate a considerable volume of unquantified emissions, but also have significant negative impacts on the environment, social aspects and health.

in writing. ‒ i am voting in favour of a reformed and properly functioning emissions trading system (ets) with the aim of further reducing greenhouse gas emissions; this is an important instrument to fight against environmental change and co2 emissions.
in writing. ‒ the eu emissions trading system (ets) aims to prolong dependence on fossil fuels and to expand and strengthen the role of financial markets. the eu ets is not intended to provide a 'price signal' capable of influencing long-term investments, since even the most insignificant price signal will be immediately dampened by the aid. this is the case with the new state aid rules which allow member states to reimburse the most polluting companies for the increase in energy costs resulting from the possibility of buying emission allowances by auction under the ets phase iii. in addition, the new reform proposals allowing new sources of financing for the extractive industries represent another step backwards. instead of spending more time trying to reform the ets, the european parliament should focus on phasing out fossil fuels and adopting effective energy, finance and trade policies that are able to deal with climate change. the eh bildu group therefore abstained from voting in the echr.
in writing. ‒ the commission presented a decision setting up a reserve fund to stabilise the european market for emission allowances by making the supply of emission allowances more flexible in response to changing market conditions, thus protecting the ets from unexpected and sudden disruptions in demand. the report sets out a solidarity clause (possibility to exchange or assign up to 10% of entitlements between member states) until the end of 2025 as a support measure for countries with lower gdps. the basis is laid for the creation, in the new revision of the ets (2021), of an 'innovation fund' through which a limited number of allowances will be allocated to the promotion of low-carbon, ccs, renewable or industrial innovation technologies. the proposed amount is equivalent to 50 million allowances. this should also include enhanced measures to prevent carbon leakage and to promote competitiveness and employment. i agree with these considerations and have therefore voted in favour of the report.

in writing. ‒ the integration of a market stability reserve offers a range of structural reforms to strengthen the existing emissions trading system (ets). to name a few of the changes, a part of the allowances will start to be reinvested in a new innovation fund, through which the transition of industry towards the use of low-carbon technologies will be promoted. a monitoring mechanism for the functioning of the reserve will also be included, which will assess its contribution to job creation, the prevention of carbon leakage and the industrial competitiveness of the union every three years. the reform of the system makes it possible to continue moving towards a less ambiguous and more sustainable system, and that is why i am voting in favour of the proposal.

in writing. ‒ i have decided to vote in favour of this report because it is committed to improving the situation and labour rights of seafarers. the reality of these workers is subject to a high degree of discretion on the part of the member states of the european union because of the exceptions allowed to the application of the conventions. this report seeks to improve their rights, calls for compliance with ilo conventions and refers to agreements reached by the social partners, and calls, inter alia, for improved safety for these workers. all these measures are absolutely necessary to improve the conditions of workers in this sector and that is why i have decided to vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ this report incorporates seafarers into five directives from which they were excluded, in order to protect their rights and ensure equal treatment: directives 2008/94/ec on the protection of employees in the event of the insolvency of their employer, 2009/38/ec on the establishment of a european works council, 2002/14/ec on a general framework for the information and consultation of employees, 98/59/ec on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to collective redundancies and 2001/23/ec on the protection of workers' rights in the event of transfers of undertakings. the result of a difficult balance between european social actors, its aim is to increase the protection of seafarers under the eu charter of fundamental rights and to ensure a level playing field. it also contributes to the objectives of article 151 tfeu of promoting employment, improving living and working conditions, adequate social protection and social dialogue. the current situation creates inequality between the states, since they do not apply the same exceptions. spain, for example, none. minimum requirements are now laid down to allow for more favourable conditions in the various legislations. this is a revision consistent with the treatment of seafarers under spanish law, which is the same as that of other employees.
in writing. ‒ i have decided to vote in favour of this report because it is committed to improving the situation and labour rights of seafarers. the reality of these workers is subject to a high degree of discretion on the part of the member states of the european union because of the exceptions allowed to the application of the conventions. this report seeks to improve their rights, calls for compliance with ilo conventions and refers to agreements reached by the social partners, and calls, inter alia, for improved safety for these workers. all these measures are absolutely necessary to improve the conditions of workers in this sector and that is why i have decided to vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report, which allows a minimum level of social protection for seafarers. there are fewer and fewer eu nationals who are turning to seafaring jobs, because of the harshness of these jobs, but also because of the lower protection they offer than other workers. the employment on european ships is therefore increasingly being occupied by third-country nationals. the main objective of the project is to include all crews in the directive on collective redundancies, provided that the transferred vessel is registered or flies the flag of a member state. all member states which have already chosen to apply the existing directives find that they do not entail any particular additional costs. in addition, the impact on small and micro enterprises is limited, as they were already excluded from most existing directives. in our country, which fully applies the directives in force, seafarers already enjoy a certain level of protection. with the 'seafarers' directive' nothing will change for our country, except that we will be less exposed to social dumping from other member states.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this report because we believe that this new directive represents a step forward in the recognition of labour rights and the promotion of employment in a declining sector, as well as an improvement in the quality of life and work and adequate social protection for seafarers. we welcome this directive, because it avoids an unjustifiable situation of inequality within europe, whereby the same category of seafarers may be treated differently in each member state. this was possible because the states, in certain aspects of labour rights contained in five specific directives, could make exceptions in their application to seafarers. the exceptions in these directives, which cover vital aspects of the protection and recognition of the labour rights of all workers, relate to improving the level of information and consultation of workers, the setting up of a european works council, protection in the event of the insolvency of the employer, the maintenance of rights in the event of transfers of undertakings and the approximation of the laws of the member states in the event of collective redundancies.

in writing. ‒ seafarers are a group excluded from a number of european directives designed to protect workers' rights and which are now being reformed. these amendments formally recognise their work and provide job security applicable to different situations. for example, seafarers are legally and financially protected against the possibility of their employer's insolvency. the same applies if an sre is carried out and they lose their jobs. nor would their position be affected if a transfer of undertakings took place and their situation was endangered in any way. for these reasons, i support these amendments, since this is a basic issue in order to put an end to the inequality of labour rights of seafarers.

in writing. ‒ we voted against the resolution because we consider the iter project to be dangerous, costly and uncertain, with a huge opportunity cost in channelling public investment towards highly polluting energy (iter's nuclear fusion presents the same problems of atomic waste storage as current fission). we believe that what europe urgently needs is a decisive commitment to renewable energy.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this resolution because it supports scientific collaboration with a country which has an influence on the fiscal sovereignty of its neighbouring countries, and it also encourages the mobilisation of resources to finance iter, a project which, beyond the risks it may entail, involves a massive mobilisation of the budget with very little return for european citizens. without going into the project and its implications, the european budget must alleviate the emergencies that are occurring in all countries, which are going through very serious situations that require public resources and are systematically denied. because we believe that the human being must be the first priority, i have decided to vote against this resolution.

mr president, i could not vote in favour of this report because mobility, employability, entrepreneurship, everything is mentioned as if workers were unemployed because of laziness, incapacity or lack of initiative. the figures are not important: in spain almost a third of the workers had jobs below their qualifications; almost two million are now migrants; the number of selfemployed, many of them fake, dependent on large business groups, does not seem to be growing in proportion to the working population. let's get out of the neoliberal framework that clouds these realities. let us talk about public investment, the only one that can guarantee jobs with high added value. let's talk about progressive wages and taxes, which support demand and employment, sunk by austerity policies. let's talk about division of labor, because by working less we all work. finally, let us talk about labour rights, without which work cannot be a dignified activity. employment policies cannot be the social appendage of the neoliberal economic project. on the contrary, work is and must be at the heart of a different and genuinely democratic society.
in writing. ‒ with over 121 million people at risk of poverty and over 7 million jobs lost since the start of the crisis, these guidelines must continue to indicate how to move towards the employment, education and social inclusion objectives to meet the europe 2020 strategy. that is why i voted in favour of this report: because it stresses that we must improve aggregate demand and it clearly calls for the eu to tackle the serious problem of rising inequalities, as well as to invest in quality employment and to guarantee living wages; because it calls on the states to establish minimum standards of social protection with measures such as a guaranteed minimum income. it also sends a clear message to the member states and the union: that we rebalance economic governance towards its social dimension in order to achieve the goals of full employment and social progress. recovery must reach every corner of europe, every citizen. the test of a society's development is not whether it is able to increase the wealth of those who have more, but whether it provides enough for those who have too little.
in writing. ‒ i could not vote in favour of this report because, despite raising important priorities in the field of employment at european union level, it does not propose real political action against neoliberal austerity policies and therefore does not provide a real solution to the problem of unemployment. the report contains many positive points which should be taken into account in the employment policies of the european union, but the main problem is that neoliberal policies are holding back economic activity at a time of global recession. it is necessary to put an end to the austerity of the european commission and to boost the economy through the public sector, since it is the private sector that has sunk the quality of life of europeans.

in writing. ‒ i welcome the agea report which sets out a series of guidelines for member states on employment policy. the negative effect of unemployment on society cannot be overstated. the report covers a wide range of issues, from improving training and mobility of workers to removing red tape for businesses. these are useful guidelines for member states to create job opportunities and to help people find work. according to eurostat, the unemployment rate in the eu was 9,9% at the end of 2014. spain currently suffers from an unemployment rate of 22%. the eu institutions and member state governments must ensure that the europe 2020 objectives are met, which involve the setting of concrete and quantifiable targets for employment, innovation, education, social inclusion and energy. this is a joint effort by all of us and this report is another step in the right direction.
in writing. - we abstained from the vote. while references to 'educational systems adapted to the needs of the labour market', 'promoting entrepreneurship also from school age' as a solution to unemployment', 'encouraging member states to convert unemployment benefits into grants for entrepreneurship' or 'entrepreneurship in the social services sector' make it impossible for us to vote in favour, the rapporteur has made a commendable conciliation effort in her report, which is a substantial improvement on the commission's text. it refers to decent working conditions, adequate wages and collective bargaining; adequate social protection, including a guaranteed minimum income; equality in the labour market, including affordable and quality childcare; reducing labour market segmentation, by addressing precarious employment, subcontracting and undeclared work; fighting poverty and exclusion; and social security support measures. it also dissociates retirement age from life expectancy and mentions labour mobility as a fundamental right and a right of free choice. these are necessary requirements for any employment guidance for the member states and essential guidelines for any employment policy.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because the mobilisation of the european globalisation adjustment fund means an improvement in the situation of workers. the report provides for the provision of eur 1 365 000 for the workers concerned in the finnish telecommunications sector, to invest in their training and re-adaptation following an industrial conversion process. it is a tool to enable telecommunications workers to adapt to the changes affecting the production structure of the european union. the provision of these public funds for training and retraining is clearly not enough to help workers throughout europe, but it is a minimum cushion to improve their situation.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report to approve the mobilisation of eur 1 365 000 from the european globalisation adjustment fund for 568 workers made redundant by broadcom communications and two suppliers or product processors in finland as a result of the major structural changes in world trade patterns brought about by globalisation. during the 2000s, the number of employees in finnish subsidiaries increased on all continents, until in 2004 asia became the largest employer in the electrical and electronics industry. this led to a reduction in staff in europe. this trend affected the entire finnish electronics industry and culminated in nokia's announcement that it would carry out large-scale redundancies in 2011. the personalised services to be financed by the egf include career guidance, training, retraining and job search activities, as well as grants for setting up new businesses and promoting entrepreneurship. although this aid alone cannot alleviate the drama of growing unemployment in the finnish electronics industry, it does constitute good assistance and makes it possible to provide training for the reintegration of the workers concerned.

in writing. ‒ the report gives the green light to the mobilisation of the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) in finland. the request concerns 500 workers made redundant at broadcom communications in finland and two suppliers or product processors. the redundancies have occurred as a consequence of globalisation in trade. the egf contribution of eur 1 365 000 will help to finance the costs of reintegration into the labour market of the 568 workers made redundant. the package includes measures such as employment services, vocational training and retraining, services for new entrepreneurs, etc. i agree with these considerations and therefore i have voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) was set up in 2013 to provide financial compensation to citizens who suffer the consequences of significant structural changes in relation to global trade trends. this has been the case for the employees of the finnish telecommunications company broadcom, which has not been able to survive the competition from its counterparts in other regions of the world. it is estimated that broadcom's former employees need around eur 1.3 million, which will be reinvested mostly in education/training programmes to steer them towards other more viable sectors. the remainder will be used to help those affected find new employment or to set up their own businesses. after the sharp fall of nokia in recent years, it is clear that the finnish market needs a transformation and i therefore think it is appropriate to vote in favour of allocating the funds previously provided for to finland.

in writing. ‒ we abstain in this vote and reaffirm our general criticism of this draft budget. the draft presented by mr fernandes has improved on the unacceptable proposals of the council and the commission and has sought to bring the positions of the groups closer together. our group has tabled a number of amendments which have been introduced and which, in our view, at least partially improve the document: mainly the need to increase funding for cohesion policies and thereby contribute to reducing inequalities between states, regions and localities, and the need to support with special emphasis those countries which are experiencing social, economic and financial difficulties. however, we believe that the budget is clearly too rigid and insufficient, and that it is not up to the challenges that the crisis of the economic model applied by the political currents that have hitherto dominated the economy has left us, and that the policies of austerity, financial and trade deregulation and cuts have only aggravated.
