first vice-president of the commission.– mr president, in this debate on fundamental rights i would like to raise two issues in reaction to the honourable members’ contributions. the first is that of the rule of law which, of course, is the basis upon which we develop our fundamental rights. socrates, when he was convicted on dubious grounds, was approached by friends who said ‘we will help you flee’, and he said ‘i will not’, because if you accept the premise of the rule of law in a consensual society you do not get to pick and choose which laws are applied to you and which are not. that would be my first point. if you accept the premise of the rule of law you cannot, here in parliament, debate by saying ‘well i want this to be applied to me but not to them’, and ‘we have more rights than others’, etcetera. the rule of law applies to every single individual citizen in europe, regardless of their citizenship, when they live in your country – some people are applauding: i think they misunderstood me, but we will see in a moment – so why would you then accept the premise that you could have the rule of law organised also on a level higher than the national one? the answer is part of our european history. we saw in the 20th century, and especially in the 1930s, that you can use democracy as a pretext to undermine the rule of law by saying ‘we have the majority so we decide what the rule of law is.’ of course, that is impossible. if you can change the principles of the rule of law with majority votes, you endanger, especially, individual rights or minority rights, if you are not very careful. that is why one of the greatest politicians of the 20th century thought of the idea that you could have an organisation of fundamental rights and the rule of law going beyond the nation state – an organisation at european level, capable of imposing its rulings on nation states if they did not observe the rights enshrined in the rule of law – and that european nations would subscribe to that principle willingly and democratically by signing conventions. now some of you will be surprised that the politician who thought up this idea was winston churchill, and winston churchill had a high regard for the british system. he had such high regard for the british system, and so much self-confidence, that he did not mind a court in strasbourg having oversight over what the british system produced. he had enough self-confidence to say ‘we are good enough to accept that oversight.’ and this is the basis upon which we work. in effect he said ‘tie me to the mast so i do not succumb to the sirens when they call me.’ and that is the basis upon which our rule-of-law system in the european union, and in the council of europe, was constructed – by member states saying ‘we will be tied to the mast, so that we do not make mistakes, and if we make mistakes our peers will check and correct us.’ (heckling) honourable member, perhaps you should read a bit more, instead of shouting, and you will know that odysseus made a very wise choice. my point is this: any nation with enough self-confidence will accept its peers’ checking on its observance of human rights and the rule of law. we have nothing to fear if we are sufficiently self-confident. do we? my second point concerns diversity. europe is by nature a diverse community, a diverse continent. our societies are by nature diverse, and throughout our history we have been strong when we celebrate our diversity: we are strong when we are welcoming to minorities; we are strong when we are welcoming to those who seek protection because they flee persecution and war. and we are weak when we try and confine ourselves to our own culture; when we see anybody who comes from elsewhere as a threat to our culture; when we believe that we can be overrun – 500 million of us – by a few hundred thousand. that is a testimony of weakness, of a lack of self-confidence, of a lack of trust in the strength of our european culture and our history. i strongly believe that if we claim diversity when we are elsewhere, and if we claim respect for our rights when we are elsewhere, we should also be able to give the same rights to those who come to us. what would europe have looked like if, in 1956, other europeans had said ‘i do not mind where those hungarians go, so long as they do not come to us’? what would have happened then, or in 1968 if people from czechoslovakia fleeing communist oppression had not been allowed, as refugees, into other european nations? (applause)i celebrate the fact that so many hundreds of millions of europeans today are saying to those genuinely fleeing from persecution, ‘you are welcome in my country, you will find protection on these shores, we will not send you back.’ here again i want to come back to the rule of law. it works both ways. the rule of law deserves respect. those who have the right to asylum should get it. those are our values. those are our international treaties. those are our national obligations. but those who claim asylum without having the right to asylum should be refused asylum and should be returned to where they come from. that is also the rule of law. i strongly believe this is the basis upon which we should discuss fundamental rights. fundamental rights apply to everyone on this continent – in this european union – and disregarding respect for the fundamental rights of one individual hurts us all. europe is nothing if it does not protect its minorities. europe is nothing if it does not have an eye for that which is weak. europe is nothing if we close our doors to people who flee persecution and war elsewhere. we will hurt not only the interests of those people: we will hurt our own values, we will do harm to ourselves and we will harm our souls, if that is our attitude. that is the background against which we should be discussing the situation of fundamental rights in the european union.

member of the commission.– mr president, honourable members, first let me thank the two rapporteurs, renate sommer and giulia moi, for the report we have in front of us today. i very much appreciate your hard work and commitment. i am also pleased to see that ms sommer and ms moi fully support the ban on cloning which has been proposed. i also agree that any measures taken now would need to be reviewed at a later stage. these points aside, i am sorry to have to recognise that the amendments would leave little of the initial commission proposals. let me remind you that the commission had proposed to ban the use of the cloning technique in the european union for five species, as well as the import of live clones from third countries. i must reiterate my support for these initial proposals. i am confident that they protect the health and welfare of animals, allow for innovation where desirable and take account of citizens’ concerns. the report that we are discussing today seeks to enlarge significantly this reasonable ban, to include descendants of clones as well as food and feed from descendants of clones. it also seeks to enlarge the ban to include all animal species and their products. mr president, honourable members, last february we discussed all aspects of cloning. i remember that on that occasion i explained that the proposal was shaped in the light of comprehensive analysis of the legal powers available, rigorous impact assessment and consideration of the principle of proportionality. the current commission has upheld these proposals because they are well balanced and respect the legal framework within which we all must operate. unfortunately, i am afraid that many of the amendments in the report which we are discussing are legally impossible or disproportionate. allow me to explain some of the commission’s reservations. the report seeks to enlarge the scope to include descendants of cloned animals. however, descendants of clones are conceived through conventional methods and therefore give rise to neither food safety nor animal welfare concerns. it follows that all measures proposed regarding descendants of clones, and food or feed obtained from such descendants, can be justified only with reference to ethical presumed concerns. to support the view that such extended ethical concerns exist, the report points to the 2008 eurobarometer study. it can, indeed, be inferred from this study that a majority of european union citizens disapprove of cloning. however, if we look closer, it reveals that half of those interviewed thought incorrectly that animal cloning involved genetic modification. if half of the interviewees formed their opinion on incorrect presumptions then the outcome of the study has to be treated with a great deal of caution. indeed, the results have insufficient credibility to justify far-reaching measures with a significant impact for our agriculture. in addition, the line of argument to justify measures on descendants appears to be that even if animal welfare is not compromised in cloned descendants, their very existence is an animal welfare concern for ethical reasons. allow me to express the commission’s doubts as to using this distant link to animal welfare concerns as a justification for such a wide ban. the commission, as guardian of the treaty, has an explicit obligation to respect the legal limits of the treaty. in the case of cloning, the treaties do not provide specific powers to address the ethical concerns that are the motivation for most of the amendments proposed in the report. measures that are motivated essentially by ethical concerns can be proposed only under article 352 of the treaty – the flexibility clause. the flexibility clause allows the union to act beyond the power of action conferred upon it by the treaties if the objective pursued so requires. for that reason, any proposal based on article 352 must be adopted separately under different legislative procedures. mr president, honourable members, i recognise that the idea of manipulating animals as if they were mere objects creates resentment and is perceived as morally wrong. at the same time, however, i firmly believe that the commission has proposed sound and justified measures that represent a balanced workable approach to address the issues of animal cloning and to reconcile science and ethics. therefore we should proceed on this basis.

mr president, i want to say, first of all, that we need a european regulation on cloning. although it is a technique which has so far been little used in europe, it is used in other countries with which we trade: the united states, canada, brazil and argentina. i would point out that the cloning technique is applied to selected animals and that its aim is not to enter the food chain but to produce genetic material, especially to improve livestock production. let us all remember this, because sometimes it seems that there is a large cloning production to enter the food chain and this is not so. the fundamental issue on which this ban is based - on which the socialist group and i personally agree - is animal welfare, because it is not a refined technique. we also take public opinion into account as politicians, of course, but more information should be given. public opinion is overwhelmingly against it, because they believe it's genetic modification. we support the legislative instrument; it is a bad example that we have set with the gmos. we therefore support the regulation in favour of the removal of all species, but i have to say that i do not agree with the extent of the regulation because it affects farmers and researchers.
mr president, we are going to vote in favour of this directive because we are firmly opposed to the cloning of animals for food purposes. besides, we'd like to take this opportunity to go a little further. what we are really concerned about is the spread of highly technological agriculture and livestock farming which are based on large capital investments and which involve energy costs which only mean an irreparable abuse of our land. the use of animal cloning for food or the use of gmos as animal feed is dangerous, especially because it gives greater power to large corporations and leaves helpless the farmers who care for and respect the land. in the face of this, we are committed to a living rural world that is supported by those farmers and livestock farmers who generate decent employment, who are able to give us high-quality products, who understand that what is really important is respect for natural cycles and who, moreover, generate a rich and sustainable economic sector over time.
mr president, i congratulate the two rapporteurs on this report. society does not need animal cloning to feed itself. people who raise livestock also do not need expensive laboratory techniques to provide the food. cloning attacks animal welfare and health. cloning will only serve to create more dependence on agrochemical and pharmaceutical business and patents and will contribute to greater food insecurity. the european institutions often take decisions which are very negative for farmers and food. it is also being reminded of this by the thousands of dairy farmers who are also mobilizing in my country. so we must do the right thing, we must have zero tolerance for cloning, not allowing cloning, not allowing, prohibiting the marketing of reproductive material and also of food.
member of the commission.– madam president, i would like to say that i am pleased to be addressing parliament today on an issue relating to the fight against customs fraud. the commission has always appreciated the strong support from parliament to protect the european economy and european taxpayers’ money from fraud and this is now a shared commitment for both the commission and parliament. customs-related fraud is a cross-border phenomenon which needs to be tackled centrally. therefore, it is important that the relevant customs authorities of the member states be equipped with the right tools to cooperate between themselves and with the commission and to pursue fraudsters effectively at european level. it was against this background that, in 2013, the commission proposed a number of improvements to our basic regulation governing the cooperation of customs authorities in the fight against fraud. this regulation came into being almost 20 years ago and it is important that we keep it up to date with modern technologies. information sharing is a key element in that respect. the lack of available information on, in particular, container movements, can lead to customs fraud detrimental to national and european budgets and cause serious damage to the european economy. our proposals will enable us to curb this fraud and strengthen both the detection and investigation of fraudulent activities in the area of customs. the commission has paid particular attention to striking a careful balance between the necessity to have a fraud-proof system on the one hand and avoiding overburdening businesses on the other. we are grateful for the support from parliament and the member states for the commission’s proposal. i would also like to take this opportunity to commend the diligent work of parliament’s previous and current rapporteurs on tax, especially ms liisa jaakonsaari. the constructive attitude of parliament, but also of the council, has allowed for a swift negotiation and conclusion of the legislative process. i hope that parliament will continue to support our efforts in the field of the fight against customs fraud.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. madam president, detecting and preventing customs fraud is important to avoid losses and further damage to european farmers. but just as important or more important than this is the regulation itself. the decisions to liberalize, to deregulate which this commission, the majority of parliament and the council itself have taken lately are making clear the seriousness of the losses being caused in the agricultural sector in our european union. we must say that the dairy sector is demonstrating this situation today with its mobilizations. that is why we think it is very important to introduce new regulations, a new agricultural and food policy which gives priority to the internal market over exports and to the international market and free trade agreements. that is fundamental and also, of course, to prevent and avoid fraud.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it reinforces international commitments to combat forced labour, which affects 21 million people worldwide. but we must not forget that slave labour has not disappeared in the eu, where the ilo estimates that 880,000 people are in forced labour - many of them women victims of sexual exploitation - and that greater effort is therefore needed by eu states and institutions, including within their own economies.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour because, even in the 21st century, forced labour affects 21 million people who are victims of exploitation, the most vulnerable being women, children and migrants, and generates 150 billion in annual profits for those who organise and control it. we should end this exploitation with concrete actions and the push for legislation and the goal of the 2014 protocol to the international labour organization's forced and compulsory labour convention. that is why i voted in favour of this recommendation.
in writing. ‒ with this recommendation, parliament gives its consent to the opening of negotiations by member states with the international labour organisation, with a view to ratifying the 2014 protocol to the ilo convention on forced or compulsory labour, 1930, which updates the convention by providing it with new tools to combat forced labour and making it legally binding. the protocol thus considers "necessary" preventive and protective measures, and the introduction of legal and reparation actions, such as compensation and reparation for material and physical damage, and calls for the strengthening of the means and cooperation between states in the fight against modern forms of slavery. the parliament's recommendation also points to the need to pay particular attention to immigrants, often the first victims of forced labour, particularly women. i have therefore voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ we have voted in favour of ratifying this protocol on forced or compulsory labour. forced labour contributes to perpetuating poverty and is an obstacle to the achievement of decent work for all. ratifying the protocol is a guarantee that we support continuing the fight against new and traditional forms of forced labour with more modern tools. the new forms of exploitation through forced labour require states to develop new policies and national plans to act more efficiently, and to promote the development of new tools for combating exploitation, and mechanisms for protecting and compensating victims. we are in favour of defending the most vulnerable and this convention allows us to continue along that line. the protocol stresses that in order to protect human beings from forced labour, a focus must be placed on prevention and redress. the protocol calls for the strengthening of labour inspection services to ensure the application of labour legislation. we need more inspections that do not leave employers unpunished and that there is accountability throughout the whole subcontracting chain.

in writing. ‒ regulation (ec) no 1007/2009 establishes a general ban on trade in seal products throughout the union in response to concerns about the presence on the market of products obtained from animals slaughtered by methods that cause excessive pain, distress, fear and other forms of suffering. however, it provided for two exceptions: products of seals hunted by indigenous communities such as the inuit and derivatives of seals hunted not for commercial reasons but for the sustainable management of marine stocks and resources. the amendment to regulation (ec) no 1007/2009 proposed following the trilogue negotiations contains positive aspects such as the need for hunting by indigenous communities to take due account of animal welfare, to contribute to the livelihood of the community or a limitation of the quantity of seal products marketed to prevent it being used for products obtained from hunting mainly for commercial purposes. that is why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ the purpose of this regulation is to implement the 2009 recommendations and resolutions following the actions brought by canada and norway on seal products by removing the so-called orm exemption which allowed the marketing of seal products for the purpose of sustainable management on a small scale and without a profit motive. the proposal preserves the exception which allows the marketing of seal products if it is practised by the inuit and other indigenous peoples, if it has been traditionally practised by that community, if it serves their subsistence and not primarily for commercial reasons and if certain techniques are used. the commission also has the power to take decisions when it sees irregularities.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this revision of the regulation on the prohibition of trade in seal products, in order to bring it into line with the recommendations and resolutions of the wto dispute settlement body. in 2009, the eu adopted the regulation establishing a general ban on trade in seal products in the eu, both for products produced in the eu and for imported products. this prohibition had two exceptions: the inuit exception, which allowed trade in products obtained from seals hunted by the inuit and other indigenous communities, and the marine resource management exception, which allowed trade in products obtained from hunting for the sole purpose of sustainable, small-scale and non-profit-making management of marine resources. however, the wto dispute settlement body (dsb) ruled in june 2014 that the grm exception is discriminatory and should be removed and that the inuit exception should be amended in its wording, which was deemed arbitrary. european legislation should therefore be amended in this respect in order to implement the decision of the dispute settlement body.
in writing. ‒ regulation (ec) no 1007/2009 establishes a general ban on trade in seal products throughout the union in response to concerns about the presence on the market of products obtained from animals slaughtered by methods that cause excessive pain, distress, fear and other forms of suffering. however, it provided for two exceptions: products of seals hunted by indigenous communities such as the inuit and derivatives of seals hunted not for commercial reasons but for the sustainable management of marine stocks and resources. the amendment to regulation (ec) no 1007/2009 proposed following the trilogue negotiations contains positive aspects such as the need for hunting by indigenous communities to take due account of animal welfare, to contribute to the livelihood of the community or a limitation of the quantity of seal products marketed to prevent it being used for products obtained from hunting mainly for commercial purposes. that is why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ i welcome the commission's proposal to bring our european legislation into line with the recommendations issued by the world trade organisation on trade in seal products. the eu should take into account the opinions of international organisations of which it is a member. i therefore vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ the sale of seal products has been prohibited in principle since 2009. but two exceptions would remain: on the one hand, for products from traditional inuit hunting (ci derogation) and on the other hand, for products from sustainable, non-profit and non-commercial hunting (grm derogation). however, canada and norway challenged this prohibition in the wto and in june 2014 the dispute settlement body (dsb) disapproved of the two derogations on the grounds that the derogation in favour of inuit hunting was "discriminatory, arbitrary and unjustifiable" and that non-commercial hunting could not be distinguished from commercial hunting. the new regulation proposes to remove the derogation on hunting for non-commercial purposes, but to allow inuit hunting, limiting the placing on the market of the products of this hunting, in order to prevent fraud. i voted for this report on the trade in seal products because it limits commercial seal hunting while allowing inuit communities to continue their way of life and to provide for their livelihoods.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of the proposed text, as the regulation is intended to ensure that products from seals hunted for commercial purposes can no longer be marketed on the eu market. at the same time it also contains an exception, which defends the rights of the indigenous peoples, the inuit, allowing the hunting of seals by these communities as long as it contributes to the subsistence of the community itself, and that it is practiced with methods that reduce the pain, distress or fear of the animal. the consensus text also follows the recommendations of the wto and the wto dispute settlement body.

in writing. - i vote in favour. i share the need for restrictions on the import of seal products, especially because of the commercial seal hunting.
in writing. ‒ this proposal amends regulation (ec) no 1007/2009 on the prohibition of trade in seal products. the purpose is to bring it into line with the recommendations and resolutions of the wto dispute settlement body (dsb). the regulation ensures that products derived from commercially hunted seals cannot be placed on the eu market and applies to both eu-produced and imported seal products. it provided for two exceptions, the first of which, the inuit, allows trade in products obtained from seals hunted by the inuit population and other indigenous communities. the second exception, marine resource management, allowed trade in products obtained from hunting conducted for the sole purpose of sustainable, small-scale and non-profit-making management of marine resources. this second exception has been removed. i voted in favour because the agreement maintains the total ban on trade in seal products, removes the grm exception and reinforces the inuit exception for inuit communities, as seal hunting is an integral part of the culture and identity of the inuit and other indigenous communities and contributes to their livelihood.
in writing. ‒ regulation (ec) no 1007/2009 establishes a general ban on trade in seal products throughout the union in response to concerns about the presence on the market of products obtained from animals slaughtered by methods that cause excessive pain, distress, fear and other forms of suffering. however, it provided for two exceptions: products of seals hunted by indigenous communities such as the inuit and derivatives of seals hunted not for commercial reasons but for the sustainable management of marine stocks and resources. the amendment to regulation (ec) no 1007/2009 proposed following the trilogue negotiations contains positive aspects such as the need for hunting by indigenous communities to take due account of animal welfare, to contribute to the livelihood of the community or a limitation of the quantity of seal products marketed to prevent it being used for products obtained from hunting mainly for commercial purposes. that is why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this revision of the regulation on the prohibition of trade in seal products, in order to bring it into line with the recommendations and resolutions of the wto dispute settlement body. in 2009, the eu adopted the regulation establishing a general ban on trade in seal products in the eu, both for products produced in the eu and for imported products. this prohibition had two exceptions: the inuit exception, which allowed trade in products obtained from seals hunted by the inuit and other indigenous communities, and the marine resource management exception, which allowed trade in products obtained from hunting for the sole purpose of sustainable, small-scale and non-profit-making management of marine resources. however, the wto dispute settlement body (dsb) ruled in june 2014 that the grm exception is discriminatory and should be removed and that the inuit exception should be amended in its wording, which was deemed arbitrary. european legislation should therefore be amended in this respect in order to implement the decision of the dispute settlement body.

in writing. ‒ i support the ban on the cloning of animals for livestock production proposed by the european commission, which includes animal clones and embryo clones. the european parliament's report has some positive aspects, such as the extension of the ban to all farm species. however, it goes too far in a whole series of demands, which are very difficult to implement, and whose immediate consequence will be the blocking of negotiations with the commission and the council. i have therefore decided that the meaning of my vote in this first reading of the european parliament will be to abstain.
in writing. ‒ at the moment, cloning is not being used for agricultural purposes in the eu. however, it is used in certain third countries, such as the united states, canada, argentina, brazil and australia. the cloning techniques put the welfare of animals at risk. it also raises ethical issues and gives more power to the large breeding industries over conventional animal husbandry. this parliament report strengthens the commission's proposal by taking a broader approach to all aspects of cloning animals for breeding purposes. the aim is to address animal health and welfare concerns and consumer perceptions and ethical considerations in relation to cloning techniques. the proposed amendments are intended to put in place effective and coherent regulation which responds to the legitimate concerns of the agricultural sector and of european citizens in general. that is why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ this proposal for a regulation on the cloning of animals reared and bred for farming purposes aims, among other things, to ensure that the same conditions apply to all those involved in the breeding and distribution of animals and animal products throughout the union. the result of the vote on the amendments prohibits the import of animal clones from third countries, among other restrictions, on the grounds of ethical considerations. although i agree with some of the points in the report, i voted against it because the restrictions are not in keeping with european needs and progress.

in writing. - the subject of cloning is a scientific subject in which i am not an expert. that is why i prefer to trust them to pass legislation based on "ethical" motives that seem more like religious ones. according to the european food safety authority and the european commission, which brings together professionals who are experts in the subjects on which it proposes legislative initiatives, animal cloning raises problems because of the pain inflicted on the animal, but not for reasons of food safety. the liberal group has therefore decided to vote against the parliament's report because we prefer the scientific approach in the commission's original proposal, which leads to a ban on both cloning and the import of cloned animals, but does not extend this ban beyond what is scientifically reasonable, as the report we have voted on today does.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this report because we want to make it clear that we are firmly opposed to the cloning of animals for food purposes. we would also like to take the opportunity of this debate to go a little further and highlight another aspect which is even more important to us. because if there is one thing that we are really concerned about, it is the spread of highly technical agriculture and livestock farming, which is based on large capital investments and which involves energy costs that only mean an irreparable abuse of our land. the use of animal cloning for food or the use of gmos as animal feed is dangerous, especially because it gives greater power to large corporations and leaves helpless the farmers who care for and respect the land. in the face of this, we are committed to a living rural world, which is supported by those farmers and livestock farmers who generate decent employment, who are able to give us high-quality products, who understand that what is really important is respect for natural cycles and who, moreover, generate a rich and sustainable economic sector over time.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the situation of fundamental rights in the eu because, among other things, i consider it positive that it reflects the backward step in the respect of these rights as a result of the austerity policies and the cuts in public spending applied by governments and advocated by the european commission. i am very pleased that the report stresses the need for the european commission to put in place as a matter of urgency a specific strategy to achieve and ensure that fundamental rights are respected so that they are no longer just wet paper. i also share your criticism of the systemic discrimination faced by groups such as immigrants and roma in the eu today, and i also think it is good that you are questioning the current asylum system and the rules on migrants and how they directly and negatively affect the fundamental rights of these people.

in writing. ‒ respect for fundamental rights is the basis of the european project and must be respected, but not always, i have repeatedly complained to the european commission. i therefore support this proposal. i urge the commission and member states to launch investigations into all allegations of violations of fundamental rights guaranteed by the charter and to follow up on such complaints if their accuracy is credited. particularly, i urge the commission to start infringement proceedings where it is suspected that a member state has acted in breach of such rights. i regret, therefore, that the commission alleges lack of competence on numerous responses to petitions alleging possible infringement of fundamental rights; i ask, in this context, the establishment of a mechanism for monitoring, systematic evaluation and issue recommendations to encourage full respect of fundamental values in the member states.

in writing. ‒ the report by mrs ferrara on the situation of fundamental rights in the eu is, as in all years, a report which is controversial. the report you have presented to us today seeks to regulate rights which are not rights and to violate the eu's principle of subsidiarity. a priori, no one would understand why a report on the situation of fundamental rights in the eu is voted against, and in fact this report had very positive aspects. but the introduction of 'new fundamental rights' which are not fundamental rights and the distortion of the principle of subsidiarity have led me to vote against it. it is a pity that these reports are being used to exploit the confrontation in this house.
in writing. ‒ this report concerns the procedure for electing european commissioners following the experience of the election of the last college of commissioners last year. unfortunately, in this case, once again, the european grand coalition (formed by the people's party and the socialists) is imposing its majority in order to cut back more and more on the rights of the other political groups, in order to prevent us from questioning the current european orientation. the change proposed in this report is that it ends the right which each political group had until now to refuse to ratify a commissioner directly after a hearing and to force a vote on a commissioner in the plenary of the parliamentary committee. this mechanism, which has for example led to the rejection of the candidature of the italian rocco buttiglione to the european commission for his homophobic statements, would no longer be applicable, as this report proposes. as a sign of my opposition to the increasingly restrictive democratic rights in the european institutions, i voted against.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the content of the report which analyses the procedures and practices of the necessary hearings of commissioners held in 2014 as well as the improvements proposed for the future. but i would like to stress the need to ensure equality between men and women in the commission, and in this connection i would like to recall the difficulties juncker had because the governments proposed more male candidates. the european institutions must fulfil the treaties and the objectives that have been set and must set an example and be a leader in equality. i therefore consider it necessary to have paragraph 3 which states that in future each member state must put forward at least two candidates, one man and one woman on an equal footing, for the president of the commission.
in writing. ‒ although the procedure for public hearings of commissioners is not provided for in the treaty, it is a practice that has been introduced at the instigation of parliament and increases the transparency and democratic legitimacy of the commission. the report proposes changes to improve the efficiency of this procedure, including the introduction of a deadline for member states to present their candidates, improved control of declarations of economic interest, an increase in the number of questions in the written questionnaire and more interaction during the debate (double question), etc. the report also calls for gender equality to be reflected in the composition of the european commission by the member states submitting at least two candidates - one man and one woman, on an equal footing - for consideration by the president-elect of the commission. i have therefore voted in favour of this report.

in writing. ‒ the public hearings of candidate european commissioners by the european parliament is an exercise that is, in my opinion, very worthwhile. this report had my overall support today as it highlighted making an already good procedure stronger, for example, suggesting a specific section of the parliament’s website where cvs of the commissioners-designate and responses to written questions are published in advance of the public hearings. we must continue to learn from mistakes of the past and this report offers improvements to an example of democratic accountability in the eu.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this report focused on the functioning of the hearings held during 2014. we believe that the report does not finally take up the specific position of the small groups within the parliamentary structure. while the report does contain some points of fundamental importance for our political position, such as the recommendation to promote a gender balance, it fails to bring the small political groups within the logic of constant evaluation required by the commissioners. the reduction of questions also limits the possibilities for small groups to intervene in hearings. we understand that the report sets out certain key criteria and we hope that these criteria will be taken into account in order to promote equality, for example, but the plurality of the plenary must also be reflected.

in writing. ‒ while this resolution calls for respect for human rights, privacy and data protection of individuals in intrusion and surveillance systems in third countries, the text falls far short of what is desirable in this regard in my view, since while it calls for an end to mass spying operations, it does not cite the responsibility of the united states for them and does not criticize the implications of ttip in future cases. it also does not condemn human rights violations committed under the pretext of the 'fight against terrorism' and calls for digital freedom from a free trade approach. despite some good intentions in the text, the elements already mentioned make me feel that the report is clearly insufficient and i could not give it my vote in favour.
in writing. ‒ technological advances and uncensored access to the internet play a fundamental role in ensuring respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, and are an important tool for individuals and social organisations, especially in places with authoritarian regimes. but surveillance of communications through icts can put those rights and freedoms at risk. this requires a commitment from the member states, europol, eurojust and the need to comply with the obligations of the charter of fundamental rights in order to respect international law. all measures are necessary to protect these communications, the development of icts. i have therefore voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this own-initiative report on the impact of intrusion and surveillance systems on human rights in third countries. communications surveillance increasingly interferes with the right to privacy and freedom of expression when an adequate legal framework is not respected. we must demand from the commission that there be consistency between the eu's external action and our internal policies on ict, and that we promote the democratic development and use of security and intelligence services through the political dialogue that the union has with third countries. security measures, particularly those aimed at fighting terrorism, are increasingly being used as an excuse to commit privacy violations and as a tool to repress the legitimate actions of human rights defenders, journalists, bloggers, political activists, as this report underlines. that is why the eu must offer international protection to whistle-blowers, demand the appointment of a un special rapporteur on digital freedom and data protection and recognise internet access as a human right.

in writing. ‒ technological advances and the access to information and knowledge they provide represent an opportunity for the development of democracy, respect for human rights, education and the promotion of peace. however, these same technologies can be a coercive surveillance tool for an authoritarian regime. i therefore supported this text which calls on the european union to fight censorship and to support and train journalists and human rights defenders so that they can protect themselves and their communications from abusive surveillance.
in writing. ‒ the worsening of the terrorist threat over the past 15 years has enabled some states to put in place legislative and technological mechanisms to monitor increasingly intrusive individuals. these devices eventually resulted in increased censorship and surveillance of political activists, media, lawyers and foreign governments. the draft resolution, while appearing to be in favour of protecting digital freedoms, calls for the development of interference in third countries, as the united states is doing. it called for the training and equipping of those whom the european union considers to be human rights defenders or independent journalists. the commission also proposes to include clauses in favour of digital freedoms in all agreements with third countries, even though most eu member states are increasingly restricting these freedoms within their own territories. it is therefore necessary to restore these freedoms in our states, without conditioning them by interference in the affairs of third countries, because such interference constitutes an instrumentalisation of human rights, a factor of tension in international relations.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this report which calls for the need to safeguard human rights in the use and impact of new technologies. in today's times, security should not be a pretext to curtail freedom (including digital freedom). it is therefore essential to regulate ict standards efficiently, especially with third countries which often systematically violate human rights.

in writing. ‒ in an increasingly digital world, information and communication technology (ict) inevitably occupies an increasingly fundamental space. the benefits that have come from it have undoubtedly been impressive, but at the same time they have created new dangers and new challenges in relation to respect for human rights (hrd). there is a delicate balance between respecting ddffs, such as the right to freedom of expression or privacy, and the adoption of icts as intrusion and surveillance systems for the sake of collective security. this situation has been sadly accentuated by the conflicts and dangers that plague most of the globe in one way or another. i am voting in favour of this report because i believe that it seeks to promote in a coherent and responsible way the right balance between the use of certain icts and the safeguarding of related human rights.

mr president, do you know who receives the largest amount of aid from the cap in spain? the mora figueroa family: 6 million euros of aid, paid by all taxpayers, for one of the biggest fortunes in andalusia. it is followed by a number of other large fortunes which, together, share 80% of the money that comes in. in the meantime, the real farmers and ranchers have to make extra efforts to be able to face an increasingly hostile market with the products of our land. that is why we have had to vote against this report, because although we think it is essential that aid should be efficient, there is still one more thing that concerns us. we think it is unacceptable that this aspect, which is probably one of the most serious aspects of the cap, should not be dealt with: the distribution of aid. ladies and gentlemen, it is not possible that the richest receive more public aid than anyone else. what kind of world are we living in? a radical change in the approach to the cap is needed: support for the farmer who respects the climate, who produces wealth and who produces quality products. that is the only way forward and that is the future we must aspire to.
in writing. ‒ this report proposes some necessary aspects, such as more effective and efficient controls through simplification of audit controls, less bureaucracy and performance-based controls. it also distinguishes between unintentional omissions and cases of fraud. the commission is also proposing to create a list of member states with good and bad practices and to reward those member states which achieve the best results in each area by reducing the number of union controls. i have abstained from voting on this report because i do not share a proposal to that effect.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because in the new cap, its implementation, in order to achieve its objectives, is very complex and costly, and has led to a large number of errors and great difficulties for the beneficiaries and the paying agencies. i therefore support the need to simplify the mechanisms for implementing the cap in order to reduce the fees and to create clear instruments to distinguish between error and fraud. and, according to the court of auditors' report, the necessary measures must be taken by the member states to strike the right balance between a reduced administrative burden and effective control.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report which analyses how controls on the implementation of the common agricultural policy have been dealt with and calls for greater simplification and less bureaucracy in the cap, so that it is more easily interpretable and applicable by farmers. the report calls for the rationalization of controls, which cost €4 billion a year. it is also fully in favour of improving the quality and consistency of inspections rather than increasing the number of checks in the agricultural sector by all the member states, the commission and the court of auditors. it also stressed that the beneficiaries themselves bore the consequences of the risk of unintentional errors due to the complexity of the rules and recommended a reasonable, proportionate and effective sanctions policy, which would avoid, for example, double penalisation for the same error in both the payment system and cross-compliance, and that payments would not be interrupted when minor or administrative errors were detected.

in writing. ‒ first of all, i would like to draw attention to the good news we received yesterday from the commission, namely the approval of an emergency package of eur 500 million for european agriculture. we must help our farmers so that they can live off their crops, off their activity. that's all they ask of us. the report by mr sarvamaa goes in this direction, and i would like to stress the need for bureaucratic simplification in the field of agriculture, and in particular that adaptation to greening does not have to be borne by european farmers. i therefore voted in favour of the report on the protection of the european union's financial interests: towards the organisation of performance-based controls in the common agricultural policy.
in writing. ‒ agriculture remains one of the main topics affecting spain today. farmers are surviving in a sector which faces many struggles where high production costs and low prices challenge their livelihoods. i believe that it is in the interest of all to find ways of easing the administration burden on farmers in common agricultural policy policies. therefore, this report had my support today.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this report because although inefficiency or the diversion of funds are something to be taken into account, they are not the main problems of the cap, but are others to which this report does not provide solutions. the majority of cap aid often ends up in the hands of landowners and large agri-food companies, to the detriment of small and medium-sized producers, who face constant economic difficulties and lack the same administrative structures to access cap aid. the current model is profoundly anti-redistributive, contributing to the creation of inefficient oligopolies and undermining the system of equal opportunities. we therefore wholeheartedly support the allocation of resources to small and mediumsized producers in order to increase the efficiency of their production model, and especially to investments in territorial development. increase redistributive criteria to prevent funds from ending up in the hands of those who do not need them, and thus not to harm those who contribute to social and rural development in an efficient and ecological way.

in writing. ‒ the common agricultural policy (cap) has undergone two cycles of reforms, which have resulted in increasingly varied and complex rules governing this area. consequently, the accumulation of these more complex rules leads to a greater number of errors caused by excessive complexity and bureaucratization. it is important to ensure that our cap is organised in the best possible way, ensuring its functionality both at national and supranational level, that there is effective access to it by the actors involved and that the available resources are properly used. the report seeks to tackle these issues by prioritising the need to simplify the functioning and bureaucracy of the cap without undermining or restricting existing instruments. i therefore consider it right to vote in favour.
in writing. ‒ my vote in favour of the report on the organisation of performance-based controls in the common agricultural policy. the rules governing this area are becoming more complex and make it easier to make mistakes. this is why measures must be taken to ensure that checks are effective and fair without imposing a burden on producers. that is why i am in favour of the commission's initiative to simplify the cap by immediately studying measures that can be implemented promptly, while working on simplifying the cap, and all this to ensure that the most efficient use is made of european funds.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report which analyses how the controls on the implementation of the common agricultural policy have been carried out and calls for greater simplification and less bureaucracy in the cap, so that it is more easily interpretable and applicable by farmers. the report calls for the rationalization of controls, which cost €4 billion a year. it is also fully in favour of improving the quality and consistency of inspections rather than increasing the number of checks in the agricultural sector by all the member states, the commission and the court of auditors. it also stressed that the beneficiaries themselves bore the consequences of the risk of unintentional errors due to the complexity of the rules and recommended a policy of reasonable, proportionate and effective penalties, which would avoid, for example, double penalisation for the same error in both the payment system and cross-compliance, and that payments would not be interrupted when minor or administrative errors were detected.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this report because although inefficiency or the diversion of funds are something to be taken into account, they are not the main problems of the cap, but are others to which this report does not provide solutions. the majority of cap aid often ends up in the hands of landowners and large agri-food companies, to the detriment of small and medium-sized producers, who face constant economic difficulties and lack the same administrative structures to access cap aid. the current model is profoundly anti-redistributive, contributing to the creation of inefficient oligopolies and undermining the system of equal opportunities. we therefore wholeheartedly support the allocation of resources to small and mediumsized producers in order to increase the efficiency of their production model, and especially to investments in territorial development. increase redistributive criteria to prevent funds from ending up in the hands of those who do not need them, and thus not to harm those who contribute to social and rural development in an efficient and ecological way.
in writing. ‒ this report proposes some necessary aspects such as more effective and efficient controls through simplification of audit controls, less bureaucracy and performance-based controls. it also distinguishes between unintentional omissions and cases of fraud. the commission is also proposing to create a list of member states with good and bad practices and to reward those member states which achieve the best results in each area by reducing the number of union controls. i have abstained from voting on this report because i do not share a proposal to that effect.

in writing. ‒ the report points to the need to strike a balance between reducing administrative burdens and achieving effective financial control and the implementation of a single audit scheme. we are talking about important matters on which progress is needed, and i therefore think it is necessary to vote in favour of this report.
mr president, we have voted today in favour of a report which is intended to encourage the commission to start paying more attention to family businesses. this is the case for companies representing more than 60% of european enterprises and between 40% and 50% of private sector jobs. we need a common definition that will enable us to collect and compare data at european level. we must tackle the problems which are specific to these companies, such as their more difficult than usual transfer by the application of the inheritance tax. the cooperation between the various national organisations of family businesses must also be strengthened and the exchange of good practice must be further promoted by the european union. finally, we must ensure that measures designed to improve the activity of all enterprises, such as the creation of one-stop shops and the promotion of entrepreneurship, also reach family businesses.
in writing. ‒ i could not vote in favour of this report because, although it represents a necessary boost for small and medium-sized family businesses in europe, it does imply a positioning in favour of large companies with this type of ownership. family businesses account for 85% of european enterprises and generate 60% of private employment. this fundamental importance requires support measures to sustain our production system. it is because of the important support measures proposed in this report that we have not been able to vote against it. however, there is explicit support for making large family businesses the beneficiaries of the support measures currently available to smes. that is why i could not vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ europe has 25 million unemployed. family businesses have an important role to play in overcoming the economic crisis, because of their capacity to create and maintain quality employment, especially in local communities. at present they represent 60% of the union's enterprises, but they are still facing financing problems, problems of internationalisation and administrative problems due to the exodus of workers. it is therefore necessary to improve the existing legislation by analysing its problems in order to solve its difficulties and needs, and to adapt it to european legislation, so that the different states can ensure that it is adapted to them and that it is continued in the future. that is why i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ family businesses account for more than 60% of enterprises in the eu and between 40% and 50% of private sector jobs. however, there is insufficient data and research to understand their specific needs and structures. the absence of a concrete, simple and harmonised definition of a family business legally binding at european level prevents comparable data from being collected in the different member states. as this report calls for, it is necessary to develop a statistically viable definition at european level of the concept of family enterprise, including, in addition to purely quantitative criteria, qualitative criteria such as ownership of the enterprise, control and management, risk and social responsibility or the participation of employees in the management of business activities. it would also be appropriate to set up a permanent working group to deal specifically with the needs and specificities of these companies. the commission and the member states should also promote information and the exchange of expertise and good practice, in particular with regard to business education and training in management and entrepreneurship. i have therefore voted in favour of this report.

in writing. ‒ family businesses account for more than 60% of enterprises in europe and between 40% and 50% of private sector jobs. i agree with the need to put in place measures at european level to tackle the specific problems of family businesses in order to boost their competitiveness. the development of a statistically viable definition of the concept of family enterprise at european level; the extension of the european definition of smes; the creation of a single window at european level for family enterprises and interest groups representing family enterprises; support for their internationalisation or the specific problems that the different tax legislation poses for the succession of ownership of family enterprises are key issues in supporting the successful development of family enterprises in europe.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this own-initiative report on effectively exploiting the potential of research and innovation in the blue economy to create jobs and growth. the report also highlights the importance of the shipping industry, the modernisation and sustainable development of the fishing sector, tourism and underwater heritage, among other issues. the amendments tabled by the spanish socialists also denounce the negative impact, in the short and long term, that cuts in public investment in r & d & i are having on national research systems, call for greater eu support for measures against the degradation of coastal systems and call on researchers to promote open access to data supporting their research results. i would like to emphasize the paragraphs in this report on prospecting activities, which call on the commission to propose and update a non-exhaustive list of maritime activities (marine energy production, mining on the seabed, sand and gravel extraction at sea, etc.) which require prior environmental, but also socioeconomic impact assessments.

in writing. ‒ i abstained on this report which talks about the potential for growth and job creation in the maritime economy. this potential is based on a wide range of activities such as fishing and aquaculture, transport, logistics, tourism, shipbuilding, prospecting and marine energy. if the maritime sector directly or indirectly employs 5.6 million people in europe, it would theoretically be possible to create 1.5 to 2 million additional jobs by 2020. however, care must be taken to ensure that human activities do not damage this environment and biodiversity and that new activities do not harm fishermen, especially small-scale fishermen. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fishermen are not left behind. finally, the development of certain activities, such as marine energy, will only be possible at the cost of substantial investments. at the moment, there are no funds specifically dedicated to the blue economy, although member states can submit projects under the junker plan.

in writing. ‒ the blue economy is one of the eu's big bets for this legislature, and we must exploit the potential of creation and innovation in this sector to create jobs and growth, as we have pointed out from the european parliament in a report that i supported and in which we ask the commission for more ambition and a more comprehensive and integrated approach to tackling this great challenge. we must have a strategic plan for blue economy activities, direct funding modalities, selection of priorities and an action plan to boost this sector before 2020 that includes specific ideas on cooperation mechanisms and investment in infrastructure. as the rapporteur has pointed out, education and training, as well as research and development, are essential elements for the sustainable development of the blue economy. it is important to assess the adequacy of existing programmes and measures (including their level of funding) to the development objectives of the blue economy, as well as the interaction between the various existing structures and programmes, together with their outcomes.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because, once again, it is a report which places the responsibility for youth unemployment on the shoulders of young europeans. this type of action is carried out under the assumption that young europeans are unable to find employment because of their aversion to entrepreneurship, which is completely false, considering that the countries with the highest rates of self-employed workers are those in southern europe, those with the highest youth unemployment. we believe that promoting entrepreneurship in education and training is nothing more than a cynical exercise to encourage the self-exploitation of young people and to avoid taking responsibility for a business system that is incapable of generating enough jobs and wealth for the new generations. it is for all this that i have decided to vote against.

in writing. ‒ based on the fact that young people are not interested in entrepreneurship, the text proposes to remedy this problem by means of an educational approach and measures to encourage the creation of enterprises. the text, however, downplays the fact that what young people who could potentially start a business fear today is the administrative burden, the tax wedge and unfair competition from countries with low labour costs. but even if it is a minimalist response, the intention is commendable. it could help young people to develop an entrepreneurial spirit. for this reason, and without this giving the european union a moral guarantee against its economic policies which are destructive to european smes, i voted in favour of this text.
in writing. ‒ we voted against the report because, while entrepreneurship is a way of development and job creation, it is a very limited way. the orientation and emphasis of the epp group on this proposal reveal how the figure of the entrepreneur is being relied on as if he were a panacea for the dramatic problem of employment in europe, the prognosis of which is not very promising. entrepreneurship is thus used as a wild card to allow governments to evade their responsibility to create the conditions necessary to ensure access to employment or to the resources that will guarantee a life of dignity for all people. it transfers responsibility from the administration to the individual, promoting individual competition (self-help) in a market that tends to deregulation and thus to abuse. the report clearly emphasizes the individual entrepreneurial spirit over the cooperative spirit, which is reduced to a mere statement of fact, despite the suggestions made by the committee on employment and social affairs to give it more relevance in the strategy for job creation. we believe that the neoliberal individualist approach leads to atomization and chronicles precariousness, as opposed to the collective and cooperative resolution of social problems.

in writing. ‒ the high rate of youth unemployment, especially in the canary islands, is a subject that continues to worry us, and a lot, in the european parliament. that is why the report on promoting youth entrepreneurship through education and training which we have supported in the plenary is so important, examining and proposing new measures to help young people find a suitable job through their own projects. it is important to instill an entrepreneurial culture in our children and young people from an early age and to facilitate their path to entrepreneurship through education.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report, which stresses the need for youth entrepreneurship to be part of the current political strategy to support young people, as well as the european objectives of growth, employment, education and social inclusion. the report, thanks to the socialist amendments, has adopted a more social approach, advocating the development of standards in business education linked to social responsibility and its integration into national education plans. it also focuses on the need to equip all young people with computer skills and transversal and entrepreneurial skills to enable them to fully exploit the potential of the digital world, in order to help them create new forms of development, transmission and promotion of entrepreneurship. it also called on the council and the commission to develop tools and methodological support and make them available to national education systems in the field of education and training for entrepreneurship, including social entrepreneurship, and asked the commission to increase the amount of support for young entrepreneurs under the structural and investment funds.
in writing. ‒ we voted against the report because, while entrepreneurship is a way of development and job creation, it is a very limited way. the orientation and emphasis of the epp group on this proposal reveal how the figure of the entrepreneur is being relied on as if he were a panacea for the dramatic problem of employment in europe, the prognosis of which is not very promising. entrepreneurship is thus used as a wild card to allow governments to evade their responsibility to create the conditions necessary to ensure access to employment or to the resources that will guarantee a life of dignity for all people. it transfers responsibility from the administration to the individual, promoting individual competition (self-help) in a market that tends to deregulation and thus to abuse. the report clearly emphasizes the individual entrepreneurial spirit over the cooperative spirit, which is reduced to a mere statement of fact, despite the suggestions made by the committee on employment and social affairs to give it more relevance in the strategy for job creation. we believe that the neoliberal individualist approach leads to atomization and chronicles precariousness, as opposed to the collective and cooperative resolution of social problems.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because, once again, it is a report which places the responsibility for youth unemployment on the shoulders of young europeans. this type of action is carried out under the assumption that young europeans are unable to find employment because of their aversion to entrepreneurship, which is completely false, considering that the countries with the highest rates of self-employed workers are those in southern europe, those with the highest youth unemployment. we believe that promoting entrepreneurship in education and training is nothing more than a cynical exercise to encourage the self-exploitation of young people and to avoid taking responsibility for a business system that is incapable of generating enough jobs and wealth for the new generations. it is for all this that i have decided to vote against.

in writing. ‒ this report follows up on the european commission's communication on an integrated approach to european cultural heritage, which aims to analyse the economic and social impact of cultural heritage and to contribute to the development of a multidisciplinary strategic approach with which the eu can complement national and regional programmes in the member states. as the report points to the importance of europe's cultural heritage and the need to strengthen its conservation by promoting the maintenance and creation of jobs with rights, while calling on the commission to promote new participatory models that include communities in the preservation and conservation of cultural heritage, i have decided to vote in favour.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this own-initiative report in response to the european commission's communication 'towards an integrated approach to european cultural heritage'. as the report points out, the economic and strategic potential of europe's cultural heritage as a source of social innovation for smart, sustainable and inclusive growth is undervalued. it is therefore necessary to develop a comprehensive approach, improving cooperation between the different policy areas, increasing funding for preserving europe's heritage through existing programmes such as creative europe, horizon 2020 or europe for citizens and effectively integrating them into the investment plan for europe. my group calls for the proclamation of a european year of cultural heritage, which would perfectly embody the union's renewed commitment to this heritage. finally, we are once again denouncing in this report the drastic and deplorable cuts in the protection of heritage made by certain governments in the union, among which spain is sadly one.

mr president, we are pleased that the citizens' initiative on water, supported by almost two million europeans, has come to fruition. however, we cannot but express our deep disappointment at the attitude of the epp group in boycotting the success of this initiative. on the other hand, we are not surprised by this attitude either, because their behaviour shows the fear they have of certain cases of alleged corruption that are coming out in certain town halls, some of them in my own region, in asturias. perhaps there are too many vested interests in and behind water management. fortunately, today is not a good day for your lords and it is for those of us who are in favour of defending the common good. today we have taken a first step, but we will not stop here. because we are determined to make institutions transparent, so that citizens have the guarantee and real democratic control over a common good essential for life, such as water.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because i believe that water is not a commercial good but a public good. the right to water and sanitation is a human right, yet in the eu alone over one million people lack access to safe and clean drinking water and 2% of the population do not have access to sanitation either. in the rest of the world, many millions of people are suffering from this inhumane situation. the commission's response to the citizens is disappointing. the commission is not responding to their demands for new action and the presentation of a legislative proposal for the implementation of the human right to water and sanitation as essential public services for all, as recognized by the united nations. the socialists defend the right of all people to water and sanitation, which must be incorporated into the framework directive; we are in favour of a model of public ownership and control of water management, based on water as an indisputable right and not as a commodity; and we are opposed to any attempt to privatise this public good, as well as to cutting off supplies to citizens without economic resources.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report on the european citizens' initiative right2water, whose approval is a step forward to ensure that access to drinking water and sanitation is not a source of speculation and business. this initiative comes to parliament thanks to the intense and important work of social movements across the continent and it includes something that we consider to be a fundamental right: access to water and sanitation. water must always be public and, as a basic resource, be in the hands of the states and public authorities. we cannot allow something so fundamental to life to be traded, and that is why we voted for the european commission to legislate against privatisation, following the example of the social movements in europe.

in writing. ‒ i am enthusiastically in favour of considering access to safe and quality drinking water as a fundamental human right and therefore of taking the product 'water' out of the levels of marketing and speculation. secondly, because i have a lot of sympathy for the first ice that actually gets results. it is true that it has received little support (compared with the european electoral census), but the first steps are always hard and open the first door to this system of participation. but the european citizens' initiative (eci) with its clear and enforceable objective is one thing, and the parliament's initiative that has been voted on is another. the latter touches on other aspects that have nothing to do with the eci and are presented, in an ideological and conminatory way, as being consubstantial to the right to water. for example, it seems that it is mandatory and unassailable that water management and its various facets be public, which deserves much more analysis. some demands go against my convictions. it also introduced an unnecessary chapter on the nature of an eci which is objectively wrong and dangerously changes the concept and operation of the instrument, which will have to be improved. therefore, i have decided to abstain.

in writing. ‒ we all agree that the right to water is a fundamental human right and that much can still be done to improve access to this basic good. for example, water pipe leaks must be reduced, and drinking water and sanitation in developing countries must be improved. the report we have voted on today therefore contains very positive points. however, it also contains very negative and unnecessary references to the role of private enterprise in water management and supply. the public administration should be able to contract a private company for this task, subject to a number of conditions that guarantee affordable prices and supply to families in difficulty. the public undertaking is not the only one ensuring that these conditions are met. that is why i, together with my colleagues in the liberal group, abstained in the final vote.

in writing. ‒ improving drinking water supply and sanitation is an effective way of achieving the objectives of eradicating poverty, as well as promoting social equality, public health, food security and economic growth. yet 748 million people lack access to safe drinking water, and a third of the population lack basic sanitation. ice right2water is the first to reach the minimum requirements: one million signatures and thirteen member states. the organisers' demands were: 1) that the eu institutions and member states be obliged to ensure that all inhabitants enjoy the right to water and sanitation; 2) that water and water management are not subject to 'internal market rules' and that water services are excluded from liberalisation; 3) that the eu step up its efforts to achieve universal access to water and sanitation. the boylan report perfectly captures the demands of the applicants, while making it clear that water must be understood as an ecosocial asset rather than a mere element of production. that is why eh bildu has voted in favour of the report.
