in writing. ‒ my vote was in favour of the report, which is the ep response to the eu urban agenda from july 2014 and focuses on an urban dimension of policies and possible eu instruments to strengthen this approach. it supports the development of an eu urban agenda and further action to be taken to link urban areas closer to european policy making and requests the commission to propose appropriate institutional and procedural tools or to reinforce their application.
in writing. ‒ it is important that cities become increasingly smart, more connected and more open. europe needs cities that promote the use of information and communication technologies, that drive actions to reduce energy dependence and achieve more efficient energy consumption, and transport infrastructure that reduces traffic, improves air quality and makes cities cleaner and safer. this report attempts to make progress in this direction, and i therefore consider it necessary to vote in favour.
mr president, madam high representative, we have once again come to this house to pass a resolution on the situation in the middle east. resolutions which are losing weight because of the union's lack of political weight and capacity to act in foreign affairs; resolutions which all too often end up on wet paper. however, the resolution we are discussing today is a little closer to the reality on the ground. unlike previous resolutions, this house no longer forgets the irrefutable existence of a population dominated by an occupying force, contrary to international law, nor the lack of political will on the part of the parties in the region to accept the existence of the contrary. but we seem to forget - although mrs matias has mentioned it - the undeniable fact that if the blockade of gaza is not lifted, gaza will cease to be habitable in five years. and this is not my opinion: it is the opinion of a recent report by the united nations. we must force a status quo as soon as possible to freeze the conflict and lift the blockade.
mr president, mrs mogherini, we are used to over-acting, being aggressive or double-standards with human rights with certain countries, but we turn a blind eye to others, for example israel. more than 26 un resolutions have been violated, crimes under international law, genocide, war, crimes against humanity, aggression... two hundred children in prison, more than 400 administrative detainees in indefinite detention without trial, legalization of torture or an apartheid state. of course we can do things from the european union! we are israel's biggest partner. we can make the association agreement conditional on compliance with article 2: respect for human rights, prohibition of arms exports and imports between israel and the european union, suspension of cooperation within the framework of the european defence agency or compliance with the prohibition on the sale of products from illegal settlements. everything to achieve peace, a just peace with the borders of '67.
mr president, as we all know, the deterioration on the ground in the middle east is total. we are further and further away from the solution we seek, the only possible solution: two states in the region. and that is why it is essential that the european union and the international community take up this task by doing two things: first, by increasing the price that israel pays for maintaining the status quo, a status quo that is accompanied by an occupation that lasts more than fifty years, illegal settlements, a wall that is a disgrace to all, the blockade of gaza, checkpoints, arbitrary detentions, gross violations of human rights. we have two major tools for this: the association agreement or our trade relations - labelling is one example - and, at the same time, empowerment of the palestinian side, such as the recognition of the state of palestine, which must be accompanied and conditioned by the use of non-violence. in the middle east, either we push history or history will pass over us.
madam president, madam high representative, when a government segregates a section of the population, deprives them of their basic rights, blocks communications between their communities, prevents their access to many places, arbitrarily detains their members and dispossesses them of their lands, it is pursuing a policy that has a well-known name: apartheid. this is what the state of israel is doing to the palestinian people, with a very clear intention: to prevent the two-state solution, which this parliament has supported, from becoming a reality. the european union is a key player in the area and has the capacity to be forceful in order to prevent this policy. it can sanction and it can also curb your investments. and i would do it in a legitimate way, because israel violates international resolutions and continues to establish its colonies in the occupied territories. if we are really committed to a two-state solution as the only guarantor of peace and human rights, we must be courageous and show a strong, unified european voice, unequivocally condemning israel's apartheid policy. mrs mogherini, we are giving you our confidence, but we are also asking you to be firm. thank you, sir.
the question posed by the blue card. i have a question for your colleague. i agree with what he said, but i wonder if he does not see the problem with the agreement in that it gives iran 24 days to prepare itself for possible inspections of its nuclear facilities by the un inspectorate or the international atomic energy agency. is there no danger that iran will have room to hide or that it is violating the agreement? i'm asking for your opinion, sir.
mr president, i too would like to join my voice in support of the agreement reached with iran and congratulate mrs mogherini on the work she has done in the footsteps of her predecessors, mrs ashton and mr solana. the agreement will ensure the civilian character of the iranian nuclear programme through a series of important limitations and restrictions to which the government of iran has agreed and whose compliance will be closely monitored by the international atomic energy agency. i think that the unanimous support of the security council for resolution 2231 - as you have said - is a sign of the positive reception that virtually the entire international community has given to the vienna agreement. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. this verification dimension is, of course, the essential guarantee of the agreement. but i believe that the scope of the agreement goes beyond its very important security dimension. on the one hand, by lifting sanctions and restrictive measures, it will allow for the gradual normalisation of relations with iran - also at the economic and commercial level, with the effect that this is positive for everyone, including the iranian population - and, on the other hand, it will also lead to a normalisation of political relations. with this i hope to create a new climate of cooperation between iran and the international community that i would like to have a positive impact on the region. we are all aware of the activities and role that iran has been playing in the middle east. now, the new climate opened up by the agreement will hopefully allow the iranian attitude to be more constructive and contribute to the stability of a region which so badly needs it. there we have, alongside the stalled middle east peace process, the war in syria, iraq, the terrible rise of daesh and all the death and suffering and displacement of millions of people. i hope that iran, together with other key players in the region, will contribute to bringing much needed stability and security, ending, finding a solution to the war in syria and also eradicating the terror of daesh. and i'm going to finish. when the foreign ministers discussed the vienna agreement with you on 20 july, they invited you to explore ways of promoting a more cooperative regional framework. i wonder if there has been any progress in this study and what role the european union could play or is already playing.
mr president, mrs mogherini, i have enormous respect for you and your work, but i have no diplomatic experience. yes, some, in the field of human rights, and the truth is that the most innocent human things: dancing, laughing, talking, loving are sins in iran and executed for it every day. realpolitik sacrifices our gaze by looking for the least possible evil for international politics. perhaps there is no other chance, no other possibility, and surely time will prove him right. but i want to leave a testimony, with all due respect, of that reality of human rights that today we may not want to see. because it's very hard for free-hearted iranians, free-conscience iranians, activists, to overcome fear every day, whether outside or inside iran. we don't risk our lives like them, so i beg you not to forget human rights.
mr president, first and foremost, the iran agreement is the triumph of diplomacy over war and violence as a method of resolving international conflicts. it ends 36 years of hostility between the west and iran, and prevents iran from becoming a nuclear power. but it also has enormous regional implications. it has implications in the most devastated area of the world, where iran is a regional power that will have the capacity to influence -- or may have the capacity to influence -- to stabilize, especially in the four civil wars that we are seeing happening -- in iraq, unfortunately in libya, in yemen or in syria -- and also has a lot of influence over two important countries, like palestine or libya. this is just the beginning. we are obviously still holding the same criticisms of human rights that we held a few months ago against iran, but the difference is that this agreement will allow us to discuss these criticisms with them, with iran, starting tomorrow.
mr president, mrs mogherini, i would like to ask you about the bloody violations of human rights. since the start of the negotiations on the agreement with iran, when mr rouhani was appointed president, more than 2 000 executions have been carried out in the country, reaching the highest rate in the last 25 years. women have also been condemned for speaking out against political repression. however, this does not seem to be a priority issue for you, because at the press conference, during your visit to tehran, you did not mention the term 'human rights' once, not once. is that part of the deal? perhaps you could give us a few minutes of your position on that subject.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the employment situation in the community is improved. today, there are more than two million social economy enterprises in the european union, employing more than 14 million europeans, and these figures have improved even during the crisis. however, they are recognised at national level only in some member states and in different legal forms. the report i am presenting today underlines the importance of social economy enterprises throughout the european union. these companies are characterised by having as their main objective the realisation of their social purpose rather than maximising their profits. the social purpose is very diverse, such as creating jobs for vulnerable groups or providing services to members of a specific community, but in a generic way it seeks to cause a positive social and environmental impact. in fact, for this latter purpose, social economy enterprises reinvest the surplus that the enterprise itself generates with a long-term view to ensure its sustainability, thus driving greater social innovation. we therefore say that these companies are innovative by nature, and training should be a key pillar to support them. increased encouragement of the spirit of innovation and entrepreneurship from school as well as the values of the social economy, coupled with increased participation. these companies, in the education and training programmes of the member states, will ultimately boost innovation and social entrepreneurship, which will also be helped by the introduction of a european trust mark for social entrepreneurship. the realisation of their social purpose and their strong local roots mean that these companies help to improve the economic, social, territorial and environmental cohesion of the european union, as they know firsthand the specific needs they have to meet and help to integrate the groups furthest away from the labour market. in addition, the organisational model that characterises them allows for an efficient, responsible and transparent management of their resources. however, social economy enterprises need specific support to be able to grow and be sustainable and the first step must be to dispel the false myth that they are not productive or not competitive, as many of them are leaders in their respective fields. this misconception of society in general makes it even more difficult for them than for traditional companies to access finance. to solve this problem, we must not only facilitate access to credit through european funds or other forms such as micro-credit or crowdfunding, but we must also promote them at national and european level, driving greater recognition and visibility in society as a whole. at the same time, we need to improve the environment in which they operate, by encouraging the creation of networks of social economy enterprises and facilitating the exchange of information or good practice. and finally, we also call for the rapid and effective transposition and application of the directives on public procurement and concessions, which will allow for greater participation by companies in the social economy in public procurement procedures, while giving priority to tenders which bring the greatest economic and social value over the criterion of the lowest price.
mr president, work is a basic pillar on which the exercise of social rights is based, and yet the european union does not strive for full employment. it is only trying to shape workers to the demands of the market, which means that the jobs that are created are of poor quality, low wages are received and it is no longer a guarantee to get out of poverty. this has been helped by the imposition of labour reforms, which undermine workers' rights for the benefit of companies. today we are discussing a competitive labour market which is incompatible with a democratic conception of work, since workers are treated as commodities, numbers in the game of supply and demand. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of the employment of young people. it is not a question of individual will, ability or initiative. it is even indecent to suggest that when so many are forced to migrate or work in precarious conditions, while the numbers of poverty and inequality continue to grow. the individualist nature of industrial relations has been encouraged rather than the strengthening of collective bargaining. any change in the model of production structure has been abandoned and, as a measure to promote employment, business contributions are reduced or subsidized, which also undermines a fundamental mechanism for combating poverty, such as pensions. zero-hour contracts, deregulation of part-time work, abuse of trainees are other examples. there are certainly many challenges of work in the 21st century, and all of them involve moving away from the neoliberal framework. this report is a missed opportunity to reflect on employment, from the structural point of view, and to recover the objective of full employment as a source of quality and rights.
mr president, i am very glad that the debate is joint because, at the heart of the matter, the two texts - which i am sure will be adopted tomorrow - are talking about the same thing. i mean, they talk about the future, about adapting to the future, about looking to the future without fear in the world of work, in the world of entrepreneurship, and this is important. i think we've all learned that there's no going back to that old industrial model of big companies with lots of workers, lots of regulation, lots of mechanization. this is gradually changing and it is inevitable and, moreover, beneficial that labour markets adapt to these new technologies, to these new flexibilities, but also to these new potentialities. and then my colleague martina dlabajová's excellent text is very appropriate in speaking about education, which is much more than training in mobility, in the spirit of initiative, in great agility to move from the academic world to the productive world and vice versa, to adapt schools, a new model of social dialogue or a new social dialogue adapted to the circumstances, also participating in training, in the individual projection of the initiative of the workers, which does not mean, in any case, renouncing our social model or the rights they have, even strengthening them. it's not about that. we are drawing up a labour market adapted to the new circumstances.

mr president, today we are talking about one of the phenomena that is happening in our labour market, about the deterioration of our labour market and the precariousness that has been going on for the last few years, something to which we probably do not devote enough time. we talk a lot about the almost 25 million unemployed we have. we also talk a lot, and sometimes, about the emigration that is taking place. mobility is very positive in europe, but when it is voluntary, not when it is a generational obligation, as is happening in some places in europe. and we don't spend enough time looking at what the situation is in our labor market. as regards the labour market, we can say in general terms that where reforms have been made wages have been lower, without a doubt. overtime is getting less and less. it is clear that collective bargaining in many countries has been deteriorating. the temporality has gone up a lot. contract bias, unwanted on many occasions, has been increasing. and above all, within this logic of the internal devaluation that has occurred in recent years within the euro. our debate is about the reforms we need to make. it is clear that structural reforms are needed, something we agree on, changes are needed, it is clear that changes are needed in the labour markets. the problem is that change can be good, bad, positive or disastrous. the question is what changes must be made. either we weaken our labour market, as has been done so far, or we bet on value added, on education, on a more competitive knowledge economy, not on wages, in a world where, because of globalisation, we are not going to be able to compete on low wages.
vice-president of the commission. – mr president, first of all i would like to thank the members of the european parliament for this very interesting debate despite the late hour. i can assure you that from the commission’s point of view we are ready to promote all measures at eu level which may contribute to fostering quality and socially innovative jobs and ensure appropriate protection and skills development for all workers in the eu. it is essential to work hand in hand with the member states and with social partners towards achieving these goals, thus ensuring a sustainable recovery, economic growth and social progress. i wish to thank in particular the rapporteurs ms lope fontagné and ms dlabajová for their important contributions. the commission looks forward to continuing to work with parliament on all those topics.
president of the council. mr president, i would also like to thank you for this very rich debate and all the ideas that have been developed. i shall confine myself to four ideas, since i have already been long in my introduction. firstly, we need real socioeconomic governance which gives a real place to social and employment issues and which is also in line with the treaty objective of a social market economy. secondly, we need to adapt the 2020 strategy with innovative approaches to promote quality employment, to fight poverty and exclusion and to focus on training in all its forms. in this context, i believe that social entrepreneurship also has an important place. i was in madrid, spain, a few months ago, to see the dynamism of the social economy in that country. thirdly, there are major technological changes and i think we have to take very seriously what has been said about digitisation and its impact on the labour market. the presidency will also be looking at the impact on the labour market, qualifications and skills at the latest council meeting on employment, social policy, health and consumers. this point was also raised in the report. fourthly, we must realize that the competition between social systems without a minimum of rules ultimately leads to a social minimum. i would remind you that in this context we have an article 9 in the treaty which may have to be made operational.

vice-president of the commission.– mr president, the commission acknowledges that healthcare systems need to be reformed in order to ensure quality healthcare through efficient structures. furthermore, the commission is addressing sustainability challenges in healthcare systems in the eu by including relevant criteria in various actions – as has been the case, for example, in previous exercises of the european semester – and by using a variety of policy tools. the commission shares the general concern about the affordability of new medical products and the related risks of inequalities arising in access to care, and it is committed to helping member states respond to this challenge. this commitment was highlighted in the commission’s communication of april 2014 on effective and resilient health systems, which, among other things, focuses on increasing the accessibility of health systems. the communication stressed the need for improved cooperation, increased transparency and better coordination to minimise any unintended effects that current national pricing systems may have in terms of accessibility throughout the eu. the commission has no competence to regulate the level of prices of medical treatments: these are determined by member states individually. the commission could, however, explore other avenues, for example by pursuing improved exchanges of information among member states on their pricing policies, with a view to minimising negative effects on the accessibility of medicines in the eu. another way in which the commission could assist would be through further exploring the use of the joint procurement mechanism to encourage more advantageous price offers from the pharmaceutical industry. the transposition deadline for the directive on patients’ rights to cross- border healthcare was 25 october 2013. a number of member states were either late transposing the directive or transposed it incompletely. where necessary, the commission launched infringement proceedings against these member states. as a result, nearly all member states have now transposed the directive in its entirety. there is a small number of cases outstanding, which will be resolved in a near future. the next stage for the commission is to assess whether member states have transposed the directive correctly. the commission and the member states are exploring the possibility of producing a joint eu health technology assessment (hta) report to inform decision makers about clinical outcomes of new health technologies. member states will continue to work under the remit of the upcoming european network for health technology assessment (eunethta) joint action to implement the hta strategy adopted in october 2014, cooperating together on joint assessments of technologies and addressing methodological challenges. joint forces and expertise will help decision-makers to make more informed and faster choices on access to innovative treatments. there is, however, no willingness to harmonise decisions on either the uptake of technologies or pricing and reimbursement. cooperation on hta is complemented by discussions in the commission expert group on safe and timely access to medicines for patients (stamp), which looks at ways to make the best use of existing instruments.

in writing. ‒ i abstained in the final vote on this report because, while it is true that it denounces the unjustifiable delays in the payments of the funds dedicated to cohesion policy (which amount to some eur 25 billion), the low level of absorption (or final receipt thereof), as well as the importance of reindustrialising the european union and the necessary role of these funds in this respect, the final wording of the text includes the congratulation on the new european fund for strategic investments (juncker plan), the promotion of public-private partnerships, or support for the conditionality of state operational programmes to the objectives of the european semester and reform programmes. i therefore believe that, without opposing some of the criticisms highlighted in the report, it is appropriate not to support a text which praises political measures of european economic governance aimed at restricting the political capacity of public investment by administrations, thus having a very negative social and economic impact on the population.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because promoting the economic, social and territorial cohesion of the union is fundamental to europe's growth. austerity plans have left very hard realities in several member states and territorial cohesion via policy development at local and regional level can improve the current situation in some member states.
in writing. ‒ every three years, the commission presents a report on progress in achieving economic, social and territorial cohesion in the eu. in the context of the crisis and austerity policies, when public and private investment at national level ceased/decreased, this report shows that cohesion policy gave stability to the regions, ensuring a flow of funding. the report also points to the importance of investments during the 2014-2020 programming period in areas such as innovation, ict or the low-carbon economy, employment and smes, where the potential for sustainable job creation, especially for young people, is promising. among other issues, the report denounces payment problems and delays in the start of the current cohesion policy cycle, the need to improve the administrative capacity of public authorities, the lack of analysis of crossborder cooperation problems and calls for thinking about cohesion policy post-2020. finally, i would like to say that i think the approach to macroeconomic conditionality contained in it is balanced. i have therefore voted in favour of this report.

in writing. ‒ the demographic challenge of ageing is undoubtedly one of the main challenges facing europe. the objective of the european year of active ageing and solidarity between generations was to raise awareness of the value of active ageing, stimulate the exchange of information, promote active ageing policies and create a framework for concrete actions by the union, its member states and all public and private sector stakeholders. the report adopted insists that demographic change should be seen as an opportunity. in particular, it welcomes the fact that it has become clear that older people are not a burden but, through their experience, productive lives and knowledge, a benefit to society. it regrets, however, that no new networks were established to share resources, projects and ideas between the public, private and civil society sectors and that businesses were not significantly reached. it also called on the commission to carry out a study on demographic decline and to draw up a communication on this problem and on measures that could be taken at all levels to deal with it.

in writing. ‒ we voted against the report because it takes a partial and wholly work-oriented view of active ageing in older people. the report does not include the assertion that the well-being of the older generation does not lie in perpetuating their connection with the labour market, but that this well-being lies in creating the conditions for them to receive fair pensions after a working life, which can only be achieved through the development of countries in an integral way (economic, human, cultural, social, participatory, non-discriminatory, etc.) and with policies that promote stable and secure employment for all generations. because the report implicitly but repeatedly sends contradictory messages about active ageing and the role of older people who are regarded as mere labour force, we do not support it because its content may lead to an increase in the retirement age, precarious employment relationships and the dismantling and privatisation of social security systems. that is why we are opposed to this report.

in writing. ‒ the report assesses the results of the european year of active ageing and solidarity between generations (2012). the objectives of the project include raising social awareness of the value of active ageing and its different dimensions, stimulating debate, information exchange and mutual learning. in the same vein, it is important to combat age discrimination by putting aside existing stereotypes and barriers. the report takes a very positive note, pointing out that there are indications that the effects of the 2012 european year are extending beyond this year and that some will be sustained for a longer period of time. in a context where all the statistics point to a clear global ageing of the population, initiatives and measures such as the european year of active living and intergenerational solidarity are clearly necessary, which is why i am in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ the report on the implementation, results and overall assessment of the european year of active ageing and intergenerational solidarity in 2012 recognises that this occasion provided an important political impetus which helped to open up the debate on the challenges of active ageing and intergenerational solidarity in europe. we are faced with a debate which must always be open and hence my support for this work, which calls on the commission to continue its work in the direction of implementing measures in the eu to deal with this situation.
in writing. ‒ the demographic challenge of ageing is undoubtedly one of the main challenges facing europe. the objective of the european year of active ageing and solidarity between generations was to raise awareness of the value of active ageing, stimulate the exchange of information, promote active ageing policies and create a framework for concrete actions by the union, its member states and all public and private sector stakeholders. the report adopted insists that demographic change should be seen as an opportunity. in particular, it welcomes the fact that it has become clear that older people are not a burden but, through their experience, productive lives and knowledge, a benefit to society. it regrets, however, that no new networks were established to share resources, projects and ideas between the public, private and civil society sectors and that businesses were not significantly reached. it also called on the commission to carry out a study on demographic decline and to draw up a communication on this problem and on measures that could be taken at all levels to deal with it.
in writing. ‒ we voted against the report because it takes a partial and wholly work-oriented view of active ageing in older people. the report does not include the assertion that the well-being of the older generation does not lie in perpetuating their connection with the labour market, but that this well-being lies in creating the conditions for them to receive fair pensions after a working life, which can only be achieved through the development of countries in an integral way (economic, human, cultural, social, participatory, non-discriminatory, etc.) and with policies that promote stable and secure employment for all generations. because the report implicitly but repeatedly sends contradictory messages about active ageing and the role of older people who are regarded as mere labour force, we do not support it because its content may lead to an increase in the retirement age, precarious employment relationships and the dismantling and privatisation of social security systems. that is why we are opposed to this report.
in writing. ‒ the aim of the report is to extend the promotion of active ageing and develop a positive social image of old age, facilitating the social inclusion of older people. while these are objectives with which i agree, their practical consequences are unclear - with one exception: pensions, the main source of income for the older generation. the rapporteur's position is in favour of pension reforms which, under the guise of sustainability, reduce solidarity between generations and even within each cohort by developing private pensions and reducing distributive progressiveness in the calculation and financing of public pensions. that is why i voted against.

in writing. - we are talking about a matter of vital importance. europe is facing the demographic challenge of increasing life expectancy and the changes that this brings. member states should encourage debate on the role of people over 65 in society and fight against any discrimination against these groups. in this sense, the evaluation and the results of the european year of ageing are a positive element to be incorporated into this debate, and i therefore consider it necessary to vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because i believe that its approach does not take sufficient account of the effects of liberalisation of transport on working conditions in the sector, nor does it propose an infrastructure policy linked to a productive model that would underpin and cohesive the european economy, but leaves both to the interests of large companies and private investors. social dumping in air transport, the abuse of the cabotage and displacement directives, the devastating effects of the privatisation of railways and basic infrastructure - these are problems which the commission, with the backing of parliament, refuses to tackle in the context of upward labour harmonization, greater controls on the conditions of self-employed and employed workers and the strengthening of public ownership and management. that is why i voted against.

in writing. ‒ we voted against this report. a report endorsing the commission's decision to carry out a mid-term review of the white paper to assess progress made and proposing further action to achieve its objectives with a view to a more efficient, sustainable, competitive, accessible and user-friendly transport system. however, this report, despite its good technical approach, contains political aspects relating to the opening up of transport markets which make it questionable. it is clearly in line with the commission's pro-market approach and, consequently, the progressive privatisation of transport services. paragraphs refer, without mentioning it, to ttip and other trade agreements: stresses that the creation of a european transport area is an important priority and that it ... remains dependent on international acceptance in the framework of globally negotiated agreements with our trading partners for all modes of transport ... we cannot allow an acceptable technical report to use a back door to pass recommendations that undermine the viability of the public transport system.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report from the committee on women's rights and gender equality, whose main objective is to call on the european commission and the member states to take action to break the so-called 'glass ceiling', i.e. to achieve real equality of access between women and men in higher education and science-related jobs in the european union, where there is clear vertical segregation, as the data in this report show. for this purpose, it would have been useful if several of our amendments as a group on democratizing university institutions, improving the mechanisms for monitoring and publicising vacancies, investing in gender studies chairs or denouncing the fact that austerity measures and cuts in public resources have negatively affected the slight progress in university and scientific posts in recent years had also been included in this resolution. however, by voting in favour i believe i am supporting a report which denounces and calls on the commission and the member states to take measures to promote equality in research, and in academic and scientific careers.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report for equality. there are more women than men in european universities and there is a need to encourage women to pursue careers in science. i also voted in favour of the amendment which referred to the ratification of the istanbul convention on gender-based violence.
in writing. ‒ gender equality is one of the principles on which the eu is founded and must be respected in all areas. however, as this report, which i have supported, shows, despite the progress made in recent years, gender equality in science and academia has not been achieved and the presence of women in academic and decision-making positions of major responsibility in scientific institutions and universities is strikingly low. it is regrettable that women continue to be denied equal access to research positions and to the funding and publication of their research, including the pay gap, despite the provisions on equal treatment and non-discrimination in force in the eu and the member states. the report therefore calls on the commission and the member states to review existing rules to ensure non-discrimination in universities, research centres and funding contracts. it calls for positive actions and institutional changes to encourage women to pursue their scientific and research careers. and she calls for gender equality plans at all levels.

in writing. ‒ gender equality is a basic condition for women to enjoy their rights fully and is fundamental to the achievement of a sustainable and inclusive society. such equality requires that there be free access to all careers and professions. the low presence of women in academic and decision-making positions of greater responsibility in scientific institutions and universities is therefore striking. gender equality must also be respected in the academic and research fields, and all forms of direct or indirect discrimination against women which impede their access to research posts and the funding and publication of their research must be eliminated.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the draft resolution on women's scientific and academic careers. under the guise of respecting and promoting equality, this report aims to apply quotas in the university management bodies, but also in research teams. yet at no point in the report is there any mention of the number of women scientists who have experienced difficulties in their careers because of their gender. on the contrary, women, since marie curie, double nobel prize winner, are increasingly embracing scientific careers. far from valuing women, this quota policy is imposed by law and reduces the possibilities of choice, selection and meritocracy. in the end, this practice is demeaning, with some women suspected of holding their positions only because of their gender. finally, as is the custom in the femm committee, this resolution leaves the lion's share to women from minorities, migrants and lgbti, who must always be more equal than others and favoured in all circumstances. this text is useless. i therefore voted against.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this initiative. this report denounces the under-representation of women at the top levels of scientific and academic fields as a result of discrimination based, among other factors, on prejudice and stereotypes, despite having an equivalent level of professional achievement. it proposes measures to break through this 'glass ceiling' in areas such as: equal treatment provisions, gender violence, non-discrimination in recruitment and project funding, gender balance in budgets in scientific and academic programmes, transparency in selection and promotion processes, specific attention to the lgbti community, awareness-raising and training campaigns on diversity and equality and positive models in science and technology, reconciliation of work and family life, motherhood, changes in european institutions, gender dimension in scientific and technological content.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because i firmly believe that gender equality is a fundamental principle that children should learn from an early age. it is important that member states implement measures to achieve gender equality at all levels of the education system; that they incorporate a higher degree of gender awareness into the training of teachers and other school staff (doctors, nurses, psychologists, social workers, teachers) and that they introduce mechanisms to enable the promotion, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of gender equality in all educational institutions and levels. i also believe it is essential that sex education is tailored to the age and needs of the students, including awareness of lgbt issues. it is also important that states invest in education and awareness-raising campaigns to improve career guidance for girls and boys, addressing gender stereotypes and gender stereotypes in different careers, especially in the field of science and new technologies, in order to reduce gender segregation in the labour market and to strengthen the position of women.

in writing. ‒ education can transform a society and contribute to social, economic and political equality. this requires that all citizens have access to quality education. yet, 30 million girls of primary school age worldwide are excluded from the education system. the european parliament calls on all member states to implement measures to achieve gender equality at all levels of the education system. in addition, we want to underline the potential of education to advocate for gender equality and address the fight against gender-based violence.
in writing. ‒ i opposed the rodrigues report on the empowerment of young girls through education for several reasons: formally, the european institutions are not competent in education, whether school or family. however, the report is full of unacceptable recommendations such as sex education from primary school and awareness of lgbti culture; the report's aim is to favour roma, lgbti and migrant minorities by exposing our children to an anti-family ideology, all under the strict supervision of gender experts. i had tabled an alternative resolution, supported by several family advocacy associations. this amendment recalled the fundamental subsidiarity of the treaties and was supported by all the elected members of the enl. the socialist and republican elected representatives, on the other hand, supported the report, ignoring the concerns of the french people.
in writing. ‒ the vote was in favour of this report. she highlights her impact on free public education for all, lgbt rights and the right to access education, regardless of place of residence. although some issues related to the promotion of self-defence training schemes for women are not incorporated, which would increase their incidence, we still believe that it is a step in the right direction. some interesting measures we support with our vote are: - fighting against gender stereotypes promoted by advertising and the media. -promoting vocational guidance and guidance beyond gender stereotypes. -inculcate the values of equality and human rights. -educate boys and girls in mental health, sexuality and healthy relationships to help them make well-informed decisions. - to reduce maternal and child mortality and prevent the prevalence of sexually transmitted diseases. -to promote the knowledge and control of young girls and girls over their bodies. -to combat physical assaults, discrimination and stigma based on sexual orientation, gender identity and individual expression. fight against bullying.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it emphasises that education is a fundamental right of girls and women, vital for empowerment and respect for their social, cultural, economic and political rights. the text also refers to the prevention of violence against women and girls and proposes concrete actions for all public education systems to promote gender equality and implement various measures to, for example, fight against gender stereotypes or against homophobia/transphobia.
in writing. ‒ the report by mrs rodrigues on empowering young women through education in the eu is a report which, at first sight, if you do not go to the content, you could agree with. what's the matter? that has been used as a weapon of discord between the members of this house, gravely violating the positions of some members. the report goes far beyond what the treaties say. this over-limitation of powers is no longer just about meddling in the internal affairs of the member states. what this report is trying to do is to get into our homes and our schools and tell us how we should educate our children. mr president, i find it intolerable that such a report should be published, and we must put an end to these reports which only go against the house and violate the principle of subsidiarity.
in writing. ‒ this report rightly expresses its concern about the obstacles to labour mobility that switzerland unilaterally imposes on its european neighbours. however, the eu itself denies solidarity to its neighbours, closing its external and internal borders and selectively granting the right of mobility to its own citizens, as the expulsions of spaniards and italians in countries such as belgium have shown. i cannot therefore agree with the interventionist tone of the report, nor with the way in which it equates the rights of workers with the pseudo-freedoms of the single market. i therefore abstained.
in writing. ‒ the resolution considers that the four member states of the european free trade association (iceland, liechtenstein, norway and switzerland) are important trading partners and that the eea agreement is a key element of growth. the resolution welcomes the progress made in the adoption of the relevant acquis in the eea agreement, as well as the recent agreement on the principles for the incorporation of the european regulations establishing the european supervisory authorities. however, it does express some concerns. in relation to liechtenstein, because of its transposition deficit and certain restrictions on the recruitment of eea nationals. for iceland, the transposition deficit is the highest. as for norway, the increase in the transposition deficit and the need to improve energy cooperation. the council also called on the commission to present a report on the implementation of the new rules on the protection of the financial interests of the european union, and to propose that the council adopt a decision on the application of the new rules on the protection of the financial interests of the european union. that is why i voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ the four member states of the european free trade association (iceland, liechtenstein, norway and switzerland) are important trading partners of the european union, with switzerland and norway respectively being the eu's fourth and fifth largest trading partners by trade volume. while relations between the eu and iceland, liechtenstein and norway are based on the european economic area (eea), relations between the eu and non-eea switzerland are currently based on more than 100 sectoral agreements. the benefits of the internal market explain why this report notes with concern the increasing transposition deficit in the eea member states and welcomes the opening of negotiations on an institutional framework agreement with switzerland. it is therefore a report which, in a constructive spirit, seeks to contribute to the deepening of the internal market between these countries and the eu and which deserves my vote in favour.
in writing. ‒ we abstained because the report, despite its criticism of switzerland for its free movement and professional recognition policy, raises doubts about integration into the single european economic area because switzerland is a tax haven. and this report makes no reference to this fact.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report, which seeks to resolve the freedom of access of eu citizens to switzerland, after the referendum that this country held in 2014 under the name of "against mass immigration".
mr president, i was against this report because it is based, in my view, on the wrong philosophy that europe will solve the problem of migrants by allocating them according to quotas agreed by the european commission. he's calculating it by some not-so-clear number. i believe that migrants should go to the country they want, and the country they want to choose as their own should decide under international law whether to accept them or not. and we should support those countries where migrants are flowing, financially and otherwise. but an administrative solution in the form of forced quotas will not solve the problem and will only endanger the future of the schengen area, because i already feel that in my own country, the czech republic, for example, such sentiments are already beginning to rise. as illegal migrants continue to flow through europe, voices and forces against the schengen area will increase, and i would very much like to see that happen. so i think europe should look for a different policy to deal with migrants than the one we agreed on today.
i have decided to support this report, mr president, because at the end it contains an amendment which we tabled on the example that cities of change have begun to set in the spanish state - and which we hope will be an example for the rest of europe - in areas which the states have not usually reached, which our governments have not reached. in the end, it was from below, it was the people, who built the first humanitarian aid cord to address the refugee crisis that we are experiencing right now. it is fundamental. yesterday juncker was making great speeches about refugees, about solidarity, about europe. the problem is that words, if they are not translated into political action and action, are blown away by the wind and in the end all that is left are the fences. and europe cannot continue to build ever higher fences. what we have to do is to implement concrete, real policies, from below, to support acceptance and solidarity, to build a different europe.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because it supports the commission's plan for the emergency relocation of more asylum seekers from italy, greece and hungary to other member states and because it calls for the setting up of a permanent system to amend the dublin regulation, which determines which member state is to process the asylum application. we are in favour of establishing a 'fair and binding' distribution mechanism and taking into account the integration possibilities and the specific situations and needs of asylum seekers. we want member states to take in refugees from third countries through a mandatory resettlement programme, and we consider it a top priority that the eu and its member states create safe and legal pathways for refugees, such as humanitarian corridors and humanitarian visas. in this context, we consider it necessary to amend the visa code to include more specific common provisions on 'humanitarian visas' and we call on countries to make it possible to apply for asylum at their embassies and consular offices.
in writing. ‒ i abstained from voting on this resolution, aware that it is an instrument used by the pp, social democrats and liberal groups to wash their faces while their governments and the european commission maintain their policy of closed borders. the resolution does not go to the root of the problem and leaves the door open to future military interventions which will only aggravate it, as well as tacitly supporting mogherini's plan for the militarization of the mediterranean (eunavfor med) and the commission's insufficient plan to accommodate the small number of 160,000 people, far below the european union's true capacity to host. the resolution also fails to condemn key aspects of the european commission's migration policy, such as the closure of borders and the outsourcing of migration. we reject the continued separation of asylum seekers from migrants fleeing hunger and poverty, and the continued condemnation of the latter group to immediate expulsion. for all these reasons, i cannot support a resolution which is complicit in a criminal policy, but i abstained in recognition of the improvement over previous resolutions which openly criminalized migrants.

in writing. ‒ according to unhcr, 2,800 women, men and children died or disappeared in 2015 while trying to reach safety in europe. in the face of this tragedy, we urge the eu and the member states in this report to do everything possible to prevent further deaths at sea or on land. we also need a longer-term approach to migration and asylum, rather than the current ad hoc decision-making. this means thinking about the causes of the current migration crisis and how they can be tackled.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this resolution, but we also believe that it lacks several key elements, such as a strong condemnation of the policy being pursued with frontex and the successive processes of bunkering of the eurozone. there is also a lack of strong recognition of the responsibility of member states in generating these crises in the states that are the source of migration. the positive elements, on the other hand, are enough to cast a vote in favour; the recognition of the work of civil society or the direct criticism of the efforts of the far right to incite a stance against migration are highlighted. we believe that we must continue to work on a line which, in addition to the positive elements of this resolution, adds those blank spaces which prevent a firm vote in favour.

in writing. ‒ the inclusion and approval by the plenary of the amendment establishing 'effective search and rescue instruments and measures at sea, solidarity and family reunification mechanisms including humanitarian visas and, above all, legal and safe access for migrants and refugees' has been the most progressive report produced by the european parliament to date. while it is true that eh bildu would have liked an explicit rejection of frontex and the externalisation of community borders, as well as the forcible expulsions of migrants and refugees and the interventionist military policies of the western powers, eh bildu sees in the final text the opening of the way or, at least, a clear demand for the reform of the dublin regulation and the establishment of a truly european asylum policy worthy of the name. that is why eh bildu voted in favour of the joint motion for a resolution tabled in the european parliament today.

in writing. ‒ i abstained from voting on this resolution, aware that it is an instrument used by the pp, social democrats and liberal groups to wash their faces while their governments and the european commission maintain their policy of closed borders. the resolution does not go to the root of the problem and leaves the door open to future military interventions which will only aggravate it, as well as tacitly supporting mogherini's plan for the militarization of the mediterranean (eunavfor med) and the commission's insufficient plan to accommodate the small number of 160,000 people, far below the european union's true capacity to host. the resolution also fails to condemn key aspects of the european commission's migration policy, such as the closure of borders and the outsourcing of migration. we reject the continued separation of asylum seekers from migrants fleeing hunger and poverty, and the continued condemnation of the latter group to immediate expulsion. for all these reasons, i cannot support a resolution which is complicit in a criminal policy, but i abstained in recognition of the improvement over previous resolutions which openly criminalized migrants.
in writing. ‒ this summer has once again shown that migration is not a temporary problem and that the wave of refugees continues, all of which highlights the urgent need to do everything possible to save the lives of people fleeing their countries and in danger. persistent conflict, regional instability and human rights violations are leading to an unprecedented number of people seeking protection in the eu. coordination between member states to alleviate and solve this problem is essential. more europe and more solidarity must replace individual measures. it is necessary for all member states to comply with their international obligations, including the obligation to rescue at sea. the number of asylum applications involving children has increased by 75% since last year. i am voting in favour of this resolution in which the european parliament calls on the eu and the member states to do everything possible to prevent further deaths at sea or on land.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because it supports the commission's plan for the emergency relocation of more asylum seekers from italy, greece and hungary to other member states and because it calls for the setting up of a permanent system to amend the dublin regulation, which determines which member state is to process the asylum application. we are in favour of establishing a 'fair and binding' distribution mechanism and taking into account the integration possibilities and the specific situations and needs of asylum seekers. we want member states to take in refugees from third countries through a mandatory resettlement programme, and we consider it a top priority that the eu and its member states create safe and legal pathways for refugees, such as humanitarian corridors and humanitarian visas. in this context, we consider it necessary to amend the visa code to include more specific common provisions on 'humanitarian visas' and we call on countries to make it possible to apply for asylum at their embassies and consular offices.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this resolution, but we also believe that it lacks several key elements, such as a strong condemnation of the policy being pursued with frontex and the successive processes of bunkering of the eurozone. there is also a lack of strong recognition of the responsibility of member states in generating these crises in the states that are the source of migration. the positive elements, on the other hand, are enough to cast a vote in favour; the recognition of the work of civil society or the direct criticism of the efforts of the far right to incite a stance against migration are highlighted. we believe that we must continue to work on a line which, in addition to the positive elements of this resolution, adds those blank spaces which prevent a firm vote in favour.

in writing. ‒ the refugee crisis in europe has shocked every european heart. there has been a tragic loss of lives of people seeking asylum in the eu. this urges the eu and the member states to do everything possible to prevent further loss of life at sea or on land. i am in favour of european solidarity and respect for human dignity.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because amongst many other things it reaffirms the urgent and priority need to create safe channels of entry into the eu for people in need of protection, calls for the creation of humanitarian visas and mentions the need to reform the berlin system, create a binding mechanism for the relocation of refugees and rethink and approach immigration policy more holistically.
in writing. ‒ the european parliament cannot remain passive in the face of the refugee crisis in europe. that is why we are voting in favour of this motion for a resolution, in order to signal the position of the european parliament on this matter and the need for the institutions and governments of the european union to take the necessary action to combat the refugee crisis in europe.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution to support the commission's plan for the emergency relocation of more asylum seekers from italy, greece and hungary to other member states and the setting up of a permanent system to amend the dublin regulation, which determines which member state is to process the asylum application. we are in favour of establishing a 'fair and binding' distribution mechanism and taking into account the integration possibilities and the specific situations and needs of asylum seekers. we want member states to take in refugees from third countries through a mandatory resettlement programme, and we consider it a top priority that the eu and its member states create safe and legal pathways for refugees, such as humanitarian corridors and humanitarian visas. in this context, we consider it necessary to amend the visa code to include more specific common provisions on 'humanitarian visas' and we call on countries to make it possible to apply for asylum at their embassies and consular offices.
in writing. ‒ this resolution focuses mainly on the israeli-palestinian conflict. it reaffirmed parliament's support for the two-state solution along the 1967 lines and stressed the need to ensure the viability of the palestinian state. it condemned the continued expansion of israeli settlements and called on israel to halt them immediately and reverse this policy, and expressed its deep concern at the increasing violence by settlers in the west bank. while the resolution adopted does not at any point criticise the eu's complicity with israel and its actions, it does contain a very positive element in my view, namely the unequivocal and explicit recognition that the eu-israel agreements will not apply to the occupied palestinian territories, as reiterated in the foreign affairs council conclusions of 20 july. in this respect, since the resolution also calls for an end to the israeli blockade of the gaza strip and for its urgent reconstruction, my vote was in favour.
in writing. ‒ i have signed and supported this resolution because the role of the union in the middle east peace process needs to be given a boost. the role the high representative is playing needs the support of parliament. i have also voted against the two amendments by the ecr group because i do not believe that the solution is two states for two peoples, given that 20% of the population of israel are arabs and that would be total discrimination.
in writing. ‒ achieving peace in the middle east remains a key priority for the international community and an indispensable element for regional stability and security. with this resolution, which i voted for, parliament expresses its support for the two-state solution based on the 1967 borders and on jerusalem as the capital of both states. it also expressed its deep concern at the continued stagnation of the middle east peace process and called for credible peace efforts to be resumed without delay. it also condemned the continued expansion of israeli settlements, which violates international humanitarian law, stirs palestinian resentment and undermines the viability and prospects of the two-state solution, and called on the israeli authorities to immediately halt and reverse their settlement policy. it also urged the eu high representative and the eu special representative to make better use of the political relations and institutional expertise of the eu and its member states in order to play a genuine political role in the israeli-palestinian peace process.

in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of the joint resolution on the eu's role in the middle east peace process, as we consider that the achievement of peace remains a key priority for the international community. that said, we reiterate our support for the two-state solution, based on the 1967 borders, with mutually agreed land swaps and jerusalem as the capital of both states. this resolution condemns the persistent israeli expansion, which violates international humanitarian law, stirs up palestinian resentment and undermines the objective viability of the prospects for a two-state solution, and therefore the prospects for peace. the resolution also ensures that all eu-israel agreements state unequivocally and explicitly that they will not apply to the territories occupied by israel since 1967.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because it represents a new attempt to avoid the responsibility of the productive system for the very high levels of unemployment faced by the european states. entrepreneurship and social innovation cannot be the vehicle for the deprivation of the welfare state and social services. furthermore, allowing private investment in these types of instruments will turn them into a speculative bubble. it is the state that should provide these services and try to promote them through public investment. the fight against unemployment must be waged on all fronts, but especially from the reindustrialisation phase, and it must be the large companies that first transform their speculative activity into productive activity in order to create quality jobs. it is for all these reasons that i have decided to vote against this report.
in writing. ‒ i support this report and congratulate the rapporteur on her excellent work. it should not be forgotten that many smes are active in the social economy and generate a very large volume of jobs. that is the case in the basque country where we have a very advanced and well-placed sector. but i did not vote for flexibility in state aid to this sector because it could be discriminatory.
in writing. ‒ europe has 2 million social economy enterprises, 10% of european enterprises, employing more than 14 million people, or 6.5% of the workforce. social economy enterprises have proven to be more resilient to the crisis, as well as providing added value in fostering social cohesion and inclusion through job creation. in this report, which i voted for, parliament calls for the promotion of the sector and for the exchange of best practices both between sectors and between states. it also calls on public authorities and financial service providers to accommodate the financial needs of such enterprises at all stages of their business development, especially at the time of their creation. the committee also called for the promotion of the cooperative model and improved access for cooperatives to public procurement systems, thanks to the contributions of the s&d group.

in writing. – today i voted in favour of this report as social entrepreneurship and social innovation offer mechanisms to soften the social and economic challenges europe faces following the financial crisis. social economy enterprises offer job creation and social well-being, boosting social cohesion and inclusion. the fact that this report is placing the spotlight on this type of entrepreneurship, often non-profit, is beneficial but greater emphasise is required on education and training, improved financing and greater visibility at european and national level to exchange information.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this report, which aims to analyse and propose measures to promote social entrepreneurship and innovation in the fight against unemployment. we share the rapporteur's view and we support social entrepreneurship and innovation as a key area to be developed and supported, and which is particularly relevant for the most vulnerable groups, such as young people, the elderly and women. in the same vein, in a context of crisis, we also see in the social economy a positive outcome which can provide us with solutions to the problems of an ageing and depopulated population in rural areas. however, several positive aspects of the report, which were in line with the recognition of the economy and social innovation as positive solutions to the crisis, were negatively modified by the amendments by considering social economy enterprises as a form of investment for the obtaining of profits through private funds. this completely altered the meaning of the report and led to the withdrawal of our support, because we believe that both issues (social economy and profit in the financial-speculative sector) are incompatible and undesirable.

in writing. ‒ social and solidarity economy enterprises, which do not necessarily have to be non-profit organisations, are enterprises whose main objective is to achieve their social purpose, such as creating jobs for vulnerable groups, providing services to their members or, more generally, making a positive social and environmental impact, and which reinvest their profits primarily to achieve those objectives. studies indicate that the social economy can play a key role in meeting the objectives of strategy 2020 in the area of job creation. it is true that social economy enterprises have proved to be more resilient to economic disruption and have been able to offer innovative solutions for social cohesion and inclusion or job creation. this report, which i voted for, sets out to the responsible bodies the measures to be taken to enhance the role of the social economy in economic growth and employment.
in writing. ‒ in the fight against unemployment, entrepreneurship and social innovation are becoming increasingly important, as my colleague veronica lope fontagne points out in a report we have supported in the european parliament. in the text we stress that social entrepreneurship and social innovation will be fundamental to the further development of the social economy. it is therefore vital to pay particular attention to education and training. the eu needs to instill in its young people that necessary innovative and entrepreneurial spirit from an early age.
in writing. ‒ europe has 2 million social economy enterprises, 10% of european enterprises, employing more than 14 million people, or 6.5% of the workforce. social economy enterprises have proven to be more resilient to the crisis, as well as providing added value in fostering social cohesion and inclusion through job creation. in this report, which i voted for, parliament calls for the promotion of the sector and for the exchange of best practices both between sectors and between states. it also calls on public authorities and financial service providers to accommodate the financial needs of such enterprises at all stages of their business development, especially at the time of their creation. the committee also called for the promotion of the cooperative model and improved access for cooperatives to public procurement systems, thanks to the contributions of the s&d group.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this report, which aims to analyse and propose measures to promote social entrepreneurship and innovation in the fight against unemployment. we share the rapporteur's view and we support social entrepreneurship and innovation as a key area to be developed and supported, and which is particularly relevant for the most vulnerable groups, such as young people, the elderly and women. in the same vein, in a context of crisis, we also see in the social economy a positive outcome which can provide us with solutions to the problems of an ageing and depopulated population in rural areas. however, several positive aspects of the report, which were in line with the recognition of the economy and social innovation as positive solutions to the crisis, were negatively modified by the amendments by considering social economy enterprises as a form of investment for the obtaining of profits through private funds. this completely altered the meaning of the report and led to the withdrawal of our support, because we believe that both issues (social economy and profit in the financial-speculative sector) are incompatible and undesirable.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because it represents a new attempt to avoid the responsibility of the productive system for the very high levels of unemployment faced by the european states. entrepreneurship and social innovation cannot be the vehicle for the deprivation of the welfare state and social services. furthermore, allowing private investment in these types of instruments will turn them into a speculative bubble. it is the state that should provide these services and try to promote them through public investment. the fight against unemployment must be waged on all fronts, but especially from the reindustrialisation phase, and it must be the large companies that first transform their speculative activity into productive activity in order to create quality jobs. it is for all these reasons that i have decided to vote against this report.

in writing. ‒ as a result of the economic and financial crisis in some european countries, levels of poverty and social exclusion have increased, as well as long-term unemployment and social inequalities. the economic and financial crisis should be seen as an opportunity to work for an economic model giving a more sustainable eu, devoting more attention to economic and social cohesion and environmental sustainability. i agree that social investment is investment in people, designed to strengthen their skills and capabilities, and provide support for full participation in employment and social life: that is why i supported this proposal.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because it emphasises the importance and size of the social economy, mentioning that social economy enterprises tend to be stronger in crisis situations. the report also calls for the eu and the member states to be more active in this field and give more support and recognition to this form of economy which is more inclusive, with more democratic structures and is focused towards the general interest.
in writing. ‒ so-called social economy enterprises have shown their ability to provide innovative solutions to stimulate social cohesion and inclusion, while fostering job creation. as the report rightly points out, entrepreneurship and social innovation will be essential to the continued development of our economy. the proposals in this report go in that direction, and i therefore think it necessary to vote in favour of this report.
mr president, i voted against this report because it offers old recipes which we already know do not work, which only generate insecurity, instability, labour poverty and inequality. when we talk about mobility, mobility means emigration, it means that more and more people have to pack up and leave their country forever. is that the answer? can that be the ultimate solution to unemployment? is the solution to unemployment that the regions most affected by the crisis lose that human capital which is so difficult to train? when we talk about flexibility, we are talking about temporary work, part-time work, instability, precariousness. the problem is not that our citizens are not flexible enough, that they are not sufficiently trained, that they are not sufficiently employable. the problem is that we are destroying jobs, we are destroying public investment and we need a radical change in the economic policies of the european union.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because i do not believe that 'competition' can be the remedy for the problems of work in the 21st century. on the contrary, individualism in industrial relations and in the consciousness of workers is the cause of the profound degradation of conquered rights, of the subordination of society to the laws of the market. the limited framework proposed offers opportunities for improvement, for example in active employment policies. but these policies are marginal remedies when the objective of quality full employment is abandoned in public policy.
in writing. ‒ i have supported this report and i would like to thank my colleague martina for her excellent report. unlike my group, i voted in favour of the paragraph which refers to the establishment of a european minimum wage. i hope that in the future a proposal to this effect can be put on the commission's agenda.
in writing. ‒ tackling unemployment is one of the eu's biggest challenges. an unemployment rate of 9.5% (with huge differences between member states: germany, 4.7% versus spain, 22.2%) and a youth unemployment rate that is twice that of the general population, reveal the devastating effects of the crisis on the labour market. unfortunately, this report places a large part of the responsibility for this tragic situation on the unemployed and does not sufficiently emphasise the need to correct serious flaws in labour markets such as the increase in forced temporary work, labour poverty or long-term unemployment. i have therefore voted against.

in writing. ‒ it cannot be denied that unemployment remains one of europe’s most pertinent challenges. at the end of 2014, 24 million europeans were without employment. in spain, the employment rate stands at 22.2%. therefore, i gave my support to this report today as it places the creation of jobs as a complete priority while stresses the ongoing need for labour market reforms, to teach young people the necessary skills to build their future and the encourage needed to foster entrepreneurship.
in writing. ‒ the aim of this report was to better match skills and qualifications to demand and employment prospects as a means of recovering from the crisis. we have voted against it, however, because we believe that the way in which this matching of skills and qualifications is being approached is wrong and will deepen and chronicle unemployment. the main problem with the report is its approach, according to which labour market reforms, especially increasing flexibility and mobility, are the solution and the measures needed to achieve the above mentioned objective. while the report mentions the need to improve existing vocational training and training programmes, taking into account the different experiences of eu countries - as well as the anticipation of future skills - the document treats unemployment as a problem of lack of mobility or motivation of workers. it is with this logic of blaming the worker that the report recommends measures to strengthen the responsibility and "entrepreneurial" education of the unemployed without understanding the problem at a structural and systemic level.
