in writing. i fully agree with the call for unity made here today by such distinguished guests to address the refugee crisis. i would, however, go further and, recalling the spirit of the speech also made today by king felipe vi, stress the need to achieve such unity in order to face all the challenges facing the european union today. as urgent as it is to have a common european response to the refugee crisis, we must not forget that our efforts to create a union with a single voice must extend to all material areas. as mrs merkel has said, we cannot go back to thinking about nationalism, but quite the opposite. hollande has said it even louder: nationalism is war. let us work to ensure that our europe, with its 500 million citizens, its economic and international power and the destination desired by those who yearn for our welfare state, is not disfigured and dismembered by short-term and provincial nationalisms, more concerned with dividing and subtracting than with adding and uniting.
in writing. the speeches by president hollande and chancellor merkel to the european parliament plenary are very significant. i share their view that we must act unitedly in the face of challenges, for as the president of the french republic said, 'nationalism is war'. the european union is the political innovation that has kept peace on the continent and allowed decades of economic prosperity, even if nationalist populism wants to undo the path we have travelled together since 9 may 1950. but it is not enough to say that we do not want to go backwards, because we need more integration, not less, to properly manage the refugee crisis, to achieve full employment, to guarantee the stability of the euro, etc. it is therefore essential to overcome the intergovernmental method, the national vetoes and to put an end to the exclusion of the european parliament from decision-making on such important policies as taxation. in short, the leaders of two member states as important as germany and france must say it clearly: we need a european federation. a union of 28 cannot function under the constant threat of blockade by any of its members.
mr president, this commission has an oil industry representative in charge of the energy portfolio and a former city of london lobbyist in charge of the finance portfolio. given his proposal on capital markets, to say "former lobbyist" is saying too much. since taking office, mr. hill has continued to do what he did until now, only from a much more privileged place: advancing the agenda of the big financial powers, financial deregulation and securitization that triggered the current economic crisis. we cannot bet once again on a casino economy in which the bank always wins. you, mr hill, talk about serving the interests of citizens and small businesses, yet in your consultations you have listened to practically no one but your fellow bankers. if they want to legislate, let them run for office; do not do it for them or, above all, for your own interests.
mr president, mr vice-president, ladies and gentlemen, there is no doubt that smes are the main drivers of growth and, more importantly, of job creation in the european union. no one doubts that small and mediumsized enterprises have had serious financing problems, especially during the crisis in some countries such as my own, spain. it is therefore clear that we must do something to prevent such problems from occurring again in the future. my colleague gunnar hökmark said that there is liquidity. there are still funding problems. it is therefore clear that we must find solutions to this problem, because without funding smes will not be able to hire new people; without funding smes will not be able to launch new projects, and we will therefore be hampering growth and job creation. i therefore welcome, mr vice-president, the initiative of the capital markets union. we must not just welcome this road map, but we must implement it as soon as possible. and a first and fundamental step would certainly be to promote securitisation. quality securitisations, of course, because we cannot repeat the problems of the past, but we do have to solve the problems of the past and the problems of the future, which - i stress - are the lack of funding. so, colleagues, let us get down to business. we need the european citizens to see the results by always ensuring that the financing of small and mediumsized enterprises is improved, because that is how we will be able to boost growth and job creation.
mr president, welcome to the commission. the fact is that my group and i were very happy to see the presentation of this action plan for the development of a single capital market in the european union. i think it's an ambitious proposal but it should be more ambitious and we should try to get it into the ground very quickly. in any case, i had three comments on the initiative. the first of these is based on the difference within the union between those countries which are in the euro area and those which are not in the euro area. within that capital markets union, we are debating the need for an eu-wide insolvency law and we are also debating what we can do to discourage the debt of smes and small businesses to get more capital into companies. but it is true that this debate is directly linked to the discussion on the creation of a fiscal pillar in the euro area and therefore that game between the euro area and the rest of the union should be more present in the project. the second comment is that it is true that we need to harmonize the regulation of financial markets in the european union. we need to standardise the products: securitisations, the whole range of capital market goods and services. but it's true that standardization cannot be accompanied by lax or hyper-lax regulation that somehow takes us back to the problems we experienced in the financial chaos of 2007 and 2008 when the banking sector was poorly regulated. and this brings me to my third comment, which is that if we regulate the capital markets too laxly, we could probably suffer some disintermediation of financial activity from banks - which are currently regulated - to unregulated or poorly regulated activities and therefore, instead of increasing the size, instead of increasing the capital pie in circulation in europe, we could be shifting investment from one place to another and increasing risks. and one last comment: i think this initiative is very good, but we also need to improve the union for households, for consumers, for example, with regard to credit cards, current accounts, commissions. the union still does not have a common market in this area, and we need to tackle this as well.
in writing. the decision to further liberalise financial flows is another example of the commission's return to 'business as usual' following the emergence of the economic crisis. and in doing so, the eu is sowing the seeds of a new recession, fuelling bubbles and speculation in the face of the development of the real economy. if the european economy is more banked than the american economy, that is precisely because the eu has so far maintained a certain harmony between the development of finance and its productive economy - a harmony which is broken by the new proposal. it is a fallacy to claim that the credit shortage can be supplied by the emergence of new funds, for these are only a vehicle for pre-existing savings and only increase the complexity and opacity of financial transactions. on the contrary, the banking sector must be reformed, strengthening its public and industrial pillars and avoiding their excessive concentration, while increasing public spending and wages to reduce economic volatility and pull europe out of recession.
vice-president of the commission.– madam president, i would like to acknowledge the effort and hard work of vice-president tajani in achieving a balanced, fair and forward-looking text that will allow for innovation and greater choice for consumers. i also wish to thank the shadow rapporteurs for their diligent and dedicated work: olle ludvigsson, sophia in ’t veld, ashley fox, eva joly, matt carthy and marco valli. payments, particularly cross-border internet payments, are essential for our single market. what is happening in the field of payments is a striking illustration of digital revolution. the original payments service directive (psd i) was adopted in 2007 and has proved to be an enormous success. it has brought real benefits to all stakeholders, especially consumers, with faster payments and clear refund rights, and it provided the legal basis for the single european payments area. however, financial services have evolved since 2007. when the first psd was adopted it created an opportunity for banks to provide payment services. these new players developed significantly to the extent that they are often the main innovators on the market. now our mobile phone, our banking applications or a third-party provider may well be our favourite way of making payments. digitisation, new players and new processes have brought real benefits to european citizens, but also new risks, notably in terms of security issues that have to be addressed. this is why the revision of the original payment services directive is particularly timely. what does the second payment services directive (psd ii) bring to the european payments market? firstly, it allows for further technological developments and new market entrants while increasing security of payments to prevent fraud. secondly, it introduces enhanced consumer protection, for example in the case of loss or theft of a payment card. thirdly, taken together with the regulation on interchange fees adopted in may 2015, it reduces costs for both retailers and consumers and contributes to the creation of genuine eu-wide payment markets. new, safer and cheaper services have emerged in the area of internet payments. these services have developed massively in some member states, overtaking cards for internet payments, and i trust this will rapidly happen elsewhere. other services known as account information services allow consumers to have a global view of their financial situation and thus help budgeting and financial planning. the creation of a level playing field for newcomers and incumbents alike will ensure that all actors operate to the same standards under the same authorisation and licensing procedures. this directive represents a major step forward for the payments market in europe. high security standards will need to be implemented by all payment services providers for electronic payment transactions. at the same time, security should not unnecessarily impair convenience. some flexibility will be possible, in particular for low-value and low-risk payment situations. it will be the task of the european banking authority (eba) task to prepare draft regulatory technical standards on security and the authentication of customers. the directorate-general for financial stability, financial services and capital markets union (dg fisma) will work with member states to ensure consistent transposition across the european union and will hold transposition workshops starting early next year, 2016. i am very satisfied that the main objectives – competition, innovation and the development of the internal market in payments – are fully met in this text. i hope we have a very fruitful discussion, and once more i want to thank this house for the work done under the leadership of vice-president tajani.
on behalf of the ppe group madam president, vice-president katainen, ladies and gentlemen, as vice-president tajani has rightly said, this directive will complement the work done on the regulation, for which i had the honour of being rapporteur. so let me first of all congratulate the rapporteur, my dear friend antonio, on the great work he has done, and the other rapporteurs. i would also like to thank our former colleague, mr diogo feio, for his work in this area during the last legislature and, of course, as vice-president tajani has said, for the work carried out by commissioner barnier. when i started working on the exchange rate regulation, we set ourselves a number of objectives. first, increase transparency in the entire card payment process. secondly, that european citizens pay less in commissions when they pay with their credit cards. thirdly, we should seek to increase card payments, which would help to combat tax fraud. a fourth objective was undoubtedly to strengthen the single market. and finally, as antonio has rightly said, to encourage and promote innovation in a field such as payment, where we are continually seeing new and innovative payment formulas. we can now say that once this directive is implemented, supplemented by the exchange rate regulation, these objectives will undoubtedly be met. so, ladies and gentlemen, we can be satisfied.

on behalf of the green group, mr president, it is a little sad to see this chamber so empty. i've never seen it so empty. it has happened before that when we have dealt with any equality issue, we always deal with it at the last item on the agenda, when we have fewer people. i hope it's just a coincidence because i think it's a fundamental issue. we welcome this initiative as an urgent need. if we are serious about breaking down the discrimination faced by women in most parts of the world, we must incorporate a gender perspective in our cooperation policies in a decisive way - and not just as a declaration of intent. so, although this initiative is important, we cannot but regret that the text is a working document and does not have the value of an official communication to the commission. we are also not satisfied that it is not clear how this plan will be financed, nor that there is an explicit commitment to increase funding for gender equality policies. without a budget, my dear colleagues, good words are worthless. we've taken a small step, but we still have a long way to go. we will pass the text. we salute your leader, but we won't settle. we want more, more budget, more commitment and more concrete lines of implementation. the fight for real equality must be a commitment of european policy in all its areas.

tackling pay discrimination – tackling the gender pay gap – is an important commitment for the commission. it is a real priority and it has been for a very long time. but, as your report reminds us, we still have work to do. let me highlight at the outset that this is not only about fairness: it is also an economic issue. reduction of the gender pay gap is an investment in the future of the union. there needs to be better use of women’s skills to allow them to contribute more to the economy as a whole. there are clear benefits to this: improved recruitment and retention; reduction of skills mismatches; an increase in motivation and productivity; improvement in a company’s image; and an increased female employment rate. the gender pay gap has numerous complex causes. occupational and vertical segregation, and lower rates of female participation in the labour market are all relevant factors. it is also key to encourage a more balanced sharing of family responsibilities between women and men so as to reduce the persistent gender pay and pension gaps. equal pay legislation is an important part of the solution but the broader mix of law and policy is equally relevant, at both national and eu level. closing the gender pay gap therefore needs a comprehensive approach with both legislative and non-legislative action. it requires the efforts and commitment of all players – decision makers at eu and national level, as well as stakeholders. effective application of the existing eu legal framework on equal pay is crucial for tackling pay inequality. i fully agree with you that this remains one of the biggest challenges. the commission is therefore monitoring constantly whether eu law on equal pay is being correctly applied, and it supports member states and other stakeholders with the proper enforcement of the existing rules. two years ago, the commission published a report reviewing the application of the gender equality directive (recast). this demonstrates to stakeholders what is required for more effective application of the existing legislation, with practical guidance on gender-neutral job classification systems so as to assist member states and employers in bridging the gender pay gap. moreover, last year the commission adopted a recommendation on pay transparency. this provides member states and stakeholders with a toolkit of concrete measures to tackle pay inequality and the gender pay gap. pay transparency and gender-neutral job evaluation, and evaluation systems in companies, are crucial because they reveal gender bias or discrimination in the pay structures of a company or industry. they support employers and social partners in taking concrete action to ensure the effective implementation of the equal pay principle. by the end of this year, member states should notify to the commission the national measures they have taken in accordance with the recommendation. we will closely assess the situation and we will prepare a report on progress made in implementing the recommendation. on that basis, we will assess the potential need for additional measures. we will look specifically at measures to tackle pay discrimination, to ensure equality in occupational pension schemes and to strengthen the implementation and enforcement of the legislation. the core task of national equality bodies is to promote equal treatment, and to provide independent assistance to victims of discrimination. strengthening their role would improve enforcement in general, in particular in relation to equal pay. effective, proportionate and dissuasive sanctions are crucial to provide a strong incentive for compliance with equal pay rules and to guarantee enforcement. let us look at the bigger picture. we have also recently announced our plans for a new initiative in the area of work-life balance. we intend to support working parents and carers across the eu – to strike a better work-life balance, and to encourage more equal sharing of care responsibilities between women and men. this initiative will help women to remain and advance in the labour market and thereby to tackle, over the longer term, the gender pay and pension gaps. as well as legislation, the commission is also undertaking a number of policy and awareness-raising actions to address the gender pay gap. we are currently funding eight multi-national projects, worth around eur 2.5 million, which tackle different aspects of the gender pay gap in a concrete and targeted manner. the commission will mark european equal pay day on 2 november this year, to make the gender pay gap plain and explicit for all europeans and to draw attention to the fact that a pay gap still exists between men and women. this is the day when women symbolically stop earning and work for free for the rest of the year. honourable members, again, thank you for this report. the progress we are making is clearly not fast enough. we need to work together to ensure that everyone steps up their efforts on this issue.
on behalf of the s&d group. i am glad that the commissioner has taken the initiative to put forward a proposal for a directive on equal treatment for men and women in employment and in the workplace. i think it is unacceptable that there is still more than a 15% pay gap between men and women in europe today, which shows that equal pay for equal work is not a reality in our democracies today. that is why we agree and fully support the need to promote - and i look to the commissioner and the commission for that - non-sexist systems of job evaluation and classification, so that through these systems and wage transparency we can develop methodologies for job evaluation to avoid the gender biases that have systematised this wage gap. we are also calling for and supporting the obligation for companies to draw up and implement annual strategic plans on gender equality, and the right for women and men to reconcile work and family life, which is also very difficult today. finally, we believe it is essential that compulsory pay audits be proposed for companies listed on stock exchanges in the member states, with the obvious exception of small and mediumsized enterprises. we also need the social partners, and especially the trade unions, to be supported in all these demands for women, and we certainly need a radical approach in the next commission text. there are good practices - the commissioner told us - in all areas, including at international level, but in our view there is still a gap of more than 15% between men's and women's wages, which is totally unacceptable in our democracy.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this directive, which updates the 2007 payment services directive to take account of the emergence of new players in this market. the text agreed with the council increases consumer protection, thanks to the work of our group, compared with the 2007 text and the commission's initial proposal. in particular, it includes an unconditional right to reimbursement of amounts not due by the payment card holder. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be given the power to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 290 tfeu in order to amend the rules on the application of the principle of proportionality. the tripartite dialogue also included an explicit prohibition on cancelling payment card services for the purpose of transferring the cardholder to another member state, an example of bad banking practice which must be eradicated and which cannot survive in the future single market for capital. in this regard, it is important to ensure that the important capital markets union project does not leave households and users of financial services, including cross-border ones, behind, given the long list of obstacles to capital movements.

in writing. ‒ spanish mortgage legislation, as the ecj has stated in several judgments, is not in line with european legislation (directive 93/13/eec) by allowing the inclusion of unfair clauses in mortgage contracts. the legislative changes carried out by the spanish government are insufficient and do not have the real will to solve the social drama of evictions and family insolvencies, as evidenced by the data (social rent: 0.4%; payment tax: 0.7%; moratoriums: 8%; 35 billion euros still in mortgage contracts with abusive clauses) and the eu advocate general in his report of may 2015. the banking abuses in spain have not only affected mortgage contracts, but some 700 000 savers have had their savings trapped, unable to be recovered, or subjected to deductions of up to 70% due to a misapplication of the right to information by banking institutions, contrary to consumer guarantees. the spanish socialists are calling for the commission to analyse spanish legislation in order to determine the appropriate measures.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because i consider it vital that the european parliament takes a stand and responds to the large number of petitions registered in recent years denouncing the infringements committed by the spanish authorities both in guaranteeing the right to housing and in protecting against the banking abuses suffered by more than 700 000 people, defrauded of their preferences. the text adopted is a step too far, because by voting against all the amendments tabled and by deleting parts of the amendments adopted by the committee on petitions, the social democrats, the conservatives and the liberals have left a resolution totally decaffeinated, relegating the european parliament to a secondary role by preventing the resolution from including calls for the european commission to initiate the process of adopting legislation to promote the introduction of paid rent and to guarantee effectively the right to housing throughout the eu. however, the resolution includes some notable parts such as the call for the government to act to end the intolerable number of evictions occurring in the state or the need for the commission to verify and investigate complaints received for fraud of preferences.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because it is essential to ensure the correct transposition of several european consumer protection directives which, in the case of spain, have been repeatedly violated, as is shown by several national and european judgments. since we cannot rely on the latest legislative reforms of the spanish government, as the advocate general of the court of justice, mr szpunar, points out in his report of may this year, we ask the european commission to carry out the necessary investigations and to prevent fraud and negligence by the spanish government and the banks from ever happening again. we therefore call for an end to abusive behaviour towards customers in the mortgage, sophisticated financial products and credit card sectors, including the imposition of excessive interest rates and arbitrary cancellation of services, and we urge the european commission to 'closely' monitor the implementation of the new measures approved by the spanish government in the banking sector to prevent abuses in banking.

in writing. ‒ the financial crisis and the bursting of the housing bubble left hundreds of thousands of spanish citizens on the streets. this housing crisis was further exacerbated by the sale of abusive products by some banks. the committee on petitions adopted a resolution on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data by the community institutions and bodies and on the free movement of such data. it denounces abuses and fraudulent practices by banks in connection with the sale of toxic financial products, so-called preferential shareholdings. preference shares are highly complex, high-risk financial instruments that should never have been sold to the majority of customers, usually people with no financial knowledge and a strong risk aversion. it is essential to point out that banks not only failed to inform customers adequately, but in some cases they misinformed them: they were given the impression that the instruments were basically fixed-term deposits with full liquidity. for these reasons i have supported this resolution, including the concept of payment for work, and almost all its amendments.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this resolution. our amendments have been rejected by the joint vote of the people's party and the european socialists. the weight of the european socialist group has been decisive in rejecting amendments which sought to tighten the content and tone of the resolution, to make it more executive and to introduce the specific question of payment for services or that of associations of preference holders and those affected by financial fraud being taken into account. the resolution, which, although not incorporating our amendments, was overall positive and meant a warning from the european parliament to rajoy for his breaches in the field of housing and consumer rights, has finally been adopted. we hope that it will serve as a starting point for an in-depth discussion on the risk instruments that banks use without taking into account previous assessments.

in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of the resolution on the death penalty because we share its objective: the total abolition of the death penalty and criticism of all countries where it is practised, from the united states to iran. we also find it relevant that it condemns in particular the death penalty for reasons such as sexual orientation or adultery, which is still carried out in many countries of the world, such as saudi arabia. the resolution also calls on the commission and the european external action service to establish the abolition of the death penalty for drug-related offences as a requirement for aid or support in drug-related policies. we therefore believe that this resolution reiterates the european commitment, which we share, to the fight against this type of state crime and calls on the commission to take this into account in its overall foreign policy.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution on the death penalty, not only because i am one of the co-signatories, but also because of the need to reiterate the condemnation of the use of the death penalty and thus firmly support the introduction of a moratorium as a step towards abolition. it's a 21st century bitch. furthermore, this abolition will contribute to the enhancement of human dignity. the ultimate objective of the union is that this abolition should also be universal.
in writing. ‒ the 13th world day against the death penalty will be celebrated on 10 october. even with substantial progress in several countries, we are far from global abolition. of the 58 countries that still have the death penalty in their legislation, 22 carried out executions in 2014. in several cases, the number of executions remains alarmingly high or has increased over the past few years. this year's world drug day focuses on sentences for drug-related offences. an increasing number of countries have passed laws that impose the death penalty for drug-related crimes. the eu guidelines on the death penalty specify that such crimes cannot be punished by capital punishment. we want to know what concrete measures the eu has put in place to move towards the abolition of the death penalty, especially in its bilateral relations with countries that still have it and particularly with those where there has been a resurgence or a resumption of the practice. i therefore supported this motion for a resolution.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution in the full conviction that the abolition of the death penalty worldwide must be one of the main objectives of the eu's human rights policy. to achieve this, as in the case of the eeas, the commission and the member states need to work in a coordinated manner within the eu and the united nations.
in writing. ‒ the latest figures show that at least 2 466 people in 55 countries were sentenced to death in 2014 and at least 604 executions were carried out worldwide the same year. often used within skewed justice systems, as a political tool against political opponents, or against underprivileged people, the death penalty is – regardless of who is accused – a cruel and inhuman act that simply denies the fundamental right to life. the eu has a crucial role to play to promote the abolition of the death penalty worldwide, and this is one the main objectives of its human rights policy. i therefore strongly supported this resolution that condemns the use of the death penalty worldwide and calls for the introduction of a moratorium as a step towards its abolition.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of the resolution on the death penalty, as we believe that the death penalty should be abolished in all countries of the world. it is true that there is unanimity within the eu on this issue, but despite this we believe that much more effort must be made, especially in foreign policy. the eu must review its trade policy with third countries which do not comply with international law and do not respect human rights, in this case the right to life.

in writing. ‒ this resolution addresses the catastrophe that occurred on 4 october 2010 in hungary, when the rupture of a waste raft released almost one million cubic metres of red mud (a highly alkaline extractive waste) that flooded several villages and left 10 people dead, 150 injured and large areas of land contaminated, including four natura 2000 sites. i voted in favour of the resolution because, among other things, it points to the risk that a similar catastrophe could occur in several member states due to poor enforcement of environmental legislation; calls for more inspections of waste rafts; highlights the existence of serious environmental pollution problems in several member states due to mining activities (e.g. from the use of cyanide in gold mining); calls on the commission, in the context of the current review of the environmental liability directive, to ensure that the proposed review fully applies the polluter-pays principle or involves local authorities, citizens and civil society in the decision-making process on the disposal of hazardous waste and in the planning of risk management measures.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution on the conclusions drawn from the red mud disaster five years after the accident in hungary. it was the worst industrial accident in the history of the country and its victims must not be forgotten. the intervention of the authorities was effective and the immense efforts of civil society were commendable and unprecedented. but we must be careful that similar sites do not exist in other countries of the union.
in writing. ‒ the break-up of a waste raft at a mining company on 4 october 2010 triggered a one million cubic metre red mud tide that caused ten deaths, 150 injuries and flooding of several municipalities and vast areas of land, including four high ecological value areas, and highlighted the lack of implementation of eu legislation and major deficiencies in the inspections framework. i have supported this resolution which criticises the lack of proper implementation of european legislation and international conventions in this area both in hungary and in other member states. as he rightly points out, disaster prevention needs to be strengthened through research, the development of hazardous waste treatment and the implementation of stricter environmental inspections.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution because i considered the serious consequences of the breakdown of a waste raft in hungary which released almost one million cubic metres of highly alkaline red mud, flooding several villages, killing 10 people, injuring nearly 150 and polluting large areas of land. despite the tragedy, similar sites still exist in several member states, and we must ensure that appropriate inspections are carried out and that red sludge is correctly classified as hazardous waste.
in writing. ‒ five years after the environmental disaster in hungary, it is a good time to recall the importance of respecting european environmental legislation. in this resolution we therefore call on the commission and the member states to step up their efforts to ensure the full implementation and proper application of all eu legislation and all international conventions relating to the environmentally sound management of hazardous waste.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this resolution, which seeks to take stock of where we are and where a stricter waste policy should be headed, now that five years have passed since the accident in hungary. here we summarize the question in its expository phase: on 4 october 2010, the breaking of a waste raft in hungary released almost one million cubic metres of highly alkaline red mud. it flooded several villages, killed ten people, injured nearly 150 and contaminated large areas of land, including four sites of the natura 2000 network. the accident exposed the poor implementation of eu legislation, deficiencies in inspections and gaps in relevant eu legislation. we hope that this question and the subsequent resolution will serve as a wake-up call to the commission and that it will focus its efforts on evaluating the methods of evaluating waste bags so that these catastrophes are not repeated. we also expect a policy of sanctions and a policy of subsidies which are equally appropriate in cases where the law is not respected or is respected.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this resolution, which seeks to take stock of where we are and where a stricter waste policy should be headed, now that five years have passed since the accident in hungary. here we summarize the question in its expository phase: on 4 october 2010, the breaking of a waste raft in hungary released almost one million cubic metres of highly alkaline red mud. it flooded several villages, killed ten people, injured nearly 150 and contaminated large areas of land, including four sites of the natura 2000 network. the accident exposed the poor implementation of eu legislation, deficiencies in inspections and gaps in relevant eu legislation. we hope that this question and the subsequent resolution will serve as a wake-up call to the commission and that it will focus its efforts on evaluating the methods of evaluating waste bags so that these catastrophes are not repeated. we also expect a policy of sanctions and a policy of subsidies which are equally appropriate in cases where the law is not respected or is respected.

in writing. ‒ this resolution addresses the catastrophe that occurred on 4 october 2010 in hungary, when the rupture of a waste raft released almost one million cubic metres of red mud (a highly alkaline extractive waste) that flooded several villages and left 10 people dead, 150 injured and large areas of land contaminated, including four natura 2000 sites. i voted in favour of the resolution because, among other things, it points to the risk that a similar catastrophe could occur in several member states due to poor enforcement of environmental legislation; calls for more inspections of waste rafts; highlights the existence of serious environmental pollution problems in several member states due to mining activities (e.g. from the use of cyanide in gold mining); calls on the commission, in the context of the current review of the environmental liability directive, to ensure that the proposed review fully applies the polluter-pays principle or involves local authorities, citizens and civil society in the decision-making process on the disposal of hazardous waste and in the planning of risk management measures.

in writing. ‒ the spanish socialist delegation to the european parliament voted in favour of this resolution, which defends universal access to sexual and reproductive health as a right. we socialists are committed to defending the freedoms, rights and empowerment of women in developing countries. we call for the updating of the eu action plan on gender equality and women's empowerment in development cooperation to address a comprehensive approach to violence against women and girls, as well as increased resources to prevent and eliminate all discriminatory practices against women, such as female genital mutilation, forced sterilisation, forced pregnancy, domestic violence and marital rape, forced and early marriage and gender-based violence in conflict and post-conflict situations. we support the removal of social and legal barriers to women's access to productive goods, as well as actions that contribute to women's economic empowerment and respect for their economic rights, such as ensuring them decent work and equal pay.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution as it broadly recognises the limited progress made on gender equality in cooperation after analysing the results of the action plan on gender equality and women's empowerment in development cooperation (2010-2015); this criticism of eu development policy is necessary as the european commission does not have a reliable and effective strategy in this area. the fact that there is not even a specific section in the annual report of the european commission's directorate-general for international cooperation and development is proof of this. i am also not satisfied that our amendments nos 1 and 2 to the resolution tabled in the plenary were rejected. they called for the provision of humanitarian aid by the eu and its member states not to be subject to restrictions by third states, including access to safe abortion for victims of rape in armed conflict, as well as improved access to health, health education, family planning, etc. we have been astonished to see how these amendments, which are of an eminently humanitarian nature, have been voted against.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution by which parliament calls on the commission to correct the shortcomings of the previous plan and to take a step forward in the new 2016-2020 action plan. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy. it also calls for the physical and psychological integrity of women and girls to be guaranteed and for efforts to be intensified to eliminate all discriminatory practices and to combat and prosecute all forms of violence. efforts are also called for to ensure and strengthen women's access to health, especially sexual and reproductive health, and to enhance women's economic rights and strengthen their voice and participation. the eu is also called upon to put pressure on third country governments and all parties to conflict to end rape as a weapon of war.

in writing. ‒ the european union has always been committed to promoting gender equality and ensuring that the gender dimension is mainstreamed in all its actions. gender equality and the empowerment of women are a precondition for the achievement of the post-2015 sustainable development goals and are also a human rights issue in their own right, as gender-based violence is a serious human rights violation and should never be justified by religion, culture or tradition.the findings of the evaluation of the first action plan show the need for greater focus on eu action, which should define and ensure sufficient human and financial resources to meet its commitments on igcm. this resolution therefore seeks to identify and address possible obstacles in the review of the action plan towards the full implementation of the eu guidelines on violence against women and girls and the elimination of all forms of violence, through a comprehensive approach to violence against women and girls and increased efforts and resources.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour, fully convinced that the eu must promote gender equality and ensure that the gender dimension is mainstreamed in all its actions. it is therefore essential to establish a principle of coherence between development policies and the eu's external policies, as well as between the new action plan and the next action plan on human rights and democracy. women are a particularly disadvantaged and at-risk group in many countries, and we must therefore focus eu development cooperation efforts on ensuring girls' access to education, enabling them to live free from violence and eliminating regulations and practices.

in writing. ‒ this motion for a resolution received my support today, as protecting and empowering women and girls is of vital importance. on a daily basis, we witness reports of women and girls violated in most horrific ways, including in the context of war and conflict – the female sexual enslavement in the democratic republic of congo being one example. we must guarantee that these women and girls are given all the medical care and support necessary to recover their lives. goal 5 of the sustainable development goals, recently signed in new york, emphasises what we are all surely already aware of: the need for education in empowering women and girls. we now need to back up words with action and to re-affirm our commitment to the eu plan of action. therefore, i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this resolution which, taking into account the conclusions of the evaluation of the first action plan on gender equality, underlines the need for a radical change in eu action on gender equality and women's empowerment, while calling for renewed political commitment by the eeas and the commission in this regard. the resolution also stresses the need for the new action plan to focus on all aspects of eu external policy - development cooperation, humanitarian aid, trade, human rights, external relations, migration and asylum - in line with the principle of policy coherence for development. finally, the resolution also calls for measures to ensure access to sexual and reproductive health and rights as a key element for women's empowerment.

in writing. ‒ the spanish socialist delegation to the european parliament voted in favour of this resolution, which defends universal access to sexual and reproductive health as a right. we socialists are committed to defending the freedoms, rights and empowerment of women in developing countries. we call for the updating of the eu action plan on gender equality and women's empowerment in development cooperation to address a comprehensive approach to violence against women and girls, as well as increased resources to prevent and eliminate all discriminatory practices against women, such as female genital mutilation, forced sterilisation, forced pregnancy, domestic violence and marital rape, forced and early marriage and gender-based violence in conflict and post-conflict situations. we support the removal of social and legal barriers to women's access to productive goods, as well as actions that contribute to women's economic empowerment and respect for their economic rights, such as ensuring them decent work and equal pay.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because i believe that equal treatment between women and men in employment is a fundamental principle that must be respected and promoted. unfortunately, there are still wide differences and a review is needed to improve and modernise the employment equality directive. it is unacceptable that there is still a pay gap of more than 16% between men and women in europe today. it is therefore urgent to promote non-sexist systems of job evaluation and classification, which guarantee pay transparency and combat the gender biases that have systematised the pay gap. it is essential that compulsory pay audits be proposed for companies listed on a stock exchange in the member states (except smes). it should also be mandatory for companies to develop and implement annual strategic plans on gender equality and to facilitate the reconciliation of women's and men's working life with family life, which remains very difficult. finally, it is unacceptable that the proportion of women in senior management positions in companies is less than 18%.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it calls on the european commission to review the directive on the implementation of the principle of equal opportunities and equal treatment of men and women in matters of employment and occupation. despite being based on the case law of the european courts, this legislative act has not succeeded in ending the enormous wage gap between men and women in general (16.4% on average), nor between member states, nor with discrimination suffered in workplaces. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environment from harmful substances. however, i think that this report should have included some of our considerations, in particular how the austerity measures to tackle the financial and economic crisis, together with the increasing flexibility of employment contracts, have led to the maintenance of high levels of poverty among women in europe (22 per cent in the spanish state).

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because of the great work done by the committee on women's rights and gender equality on the need to close the current gender pay gap, including support for the imposition of sanctions for non-compliance in the absence of progress in this area, and pushing for mandatory audits of the wages paid by large listed multinationals. it also calls for the prohibition of any discrimination based on gender identity, sexual orientation or sex change, for reconciliation of work and private life by preventing, for example, unjustified dismissals during pregnancy, and for positive measures to accelerate the involvement of women in decision-making processes. i therefore voted in favour of the report.

in writing. ‒ this report is a major work in relation to the implementation of directive 2006/54/ec, which consolidates and modernises the community acquis in the field of equality by merging previous directives. the directive addressed objectives such as equal pay for work of equal value and the reduction of the wage gap, but it has certainly not been taken up in the same way by all member states. a review is therefore needed, a new legislative initiative to replace the existing one, addressing the remaining substantial problems, such as: the correct and uniform assessment of work, the implementation of the provisions on equal treatment in relation to pension schemes, effective monitoring systems and the role of the social partners, as well as the access of victims of discrimination to legal aid.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because i am fully convinced that equal treatment for women and men in matters of employment and occupation is a non-negotiable issue. the eu cannot and will not allow women to be the victims of discrimination at work, either directly or indirectly. the pay gap between men and women for the same work must therefore be pursued and eradicated. similarly, we must continue to work to create the necessary conditions for work-life balance.

in writing. ‒ women in the eu are still paid, on average, 16% less than men and receive 39% less in pensions. there is still a lot to do to ensure that all eu citizens can enjoy sufficient economic independence to exercise control and make free choices in their lives. i welcome this report that calls on the commission to propose concrete action to decrease the gender pay gap, improve labour market accessibility and career progression for women, and fundamentally increase equality in decision-making. however, i do not believe that imposing quotas in enterprises is an adequate answer in terms of preventing gender-based discrimination. i therefore did not support these suggestions.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this report because, despite the benefits of equality between men and women, studies show that eu legislation in this area is still not effectively implemented in the member states. gender discrimination and the failure to achieve equal opportunities and treatment for women and men in employment are a scourge with a very significant cost for individuals, european societies and economies as a whole. generally speaking, member states have not taken the opportunity of directive 2006/54/ec to revise their national systems in depth or to simplify and modernise their legislation on equal treatment. the report calls on the commission to draw up a new legislative proposal to replace the existing directive and to introduce binding measures on the subject of equal treatment and employment. we hope that this will reduce the current gender pay gap of 16% and the pension gap of 39%, which to date place women at a higher risk of poverty than men.

in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this report because, despite the benefits of equality between men and women, studies show that eu legislation in this area is still not effectively implemented in the member states. gender discrimination and the failure to achieve equal opportunities and treatment for women and men in employment are a scourge with a very significant cost for individuals, european societies and economies as a whole. generally speaking, member states have not taken the opportunity of directive 2006/54/ec to revise their national systems in depth or to simplify and modernise their legislation on equal treatment. the report calls on the commission to draw up a new legislative proposal to replace the existing directive and to introduce binding measures on the subject of equal treatment and employment. we hope that this will reduce the current gender pay gap of 16% and the pension gap of 39%, which to date place women at a higher risk of poverty than men.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it calls on the european commission to review the directive on the implementation of the principle of equal opportunities and equal treatment of men and women in matters of employment and occupation. despite being based on the case law of the european courts, this legislative act has not succeeded in ending the enormous wage gap between men and women in general (16.4% on average), nor between member states, nor with discrimination suffered in workplaces. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environment from harmful substances. however, i think that this report should have included some of our considerations, in particular how the austerity measures to tackle the financial and economic crisis, together with the increasing flexibility of employment contracts, have led to the maintenance of high levels of poverty among women in europe (22 per cent in the spanish state).

president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we all agree that the refugee problem will be with europe for years to come. it's not a problem that just came up and will go away on its own. so let us be honest, as some have just said, and let us admit that europe had a difficult start. we haven't taken the real, the right measure of the problem; that's where the procrastination comes from, that's where the hesitation comes from, that's where the fallibility comes from. we can, we must. i do not think that the commission has been able to do so. we have taken a number of important steps in a short time, which may still be insufficient, but the fact is that europe has reacted. of course, we may wonder why we did not anticipate the problem or why we underestimated its magnitude. i think we all, i mean all of us, bear some responsibility for not seeing the forces that were at work behind this phenomenon. today, it is clear that the time for action has come. as i said in my first speech, we have to act on two levels. first, the emergency. we cannot leave the refugees to fend for themselves, especially as winter is upon us, as some have said. nor can we abandon the member states and countries, such as those in the balkans, which are also hosting hundreds of thousands of refugees. we must act with urgency, and above all we must plan for the future, act in the medium and long term. i believe that this is precisely the level at which europe is struggling to move forward. it's like with greece, you said. but the greek crisis has made us grow a little. the refugee crisis poses a similar challenge to us. we have to react to it, we have to build what we have failed to build for years, because we thought that such a crisis could not happen. i would like to make a few corrections on the budgetary questions. at the end of this debate you will adopt budgetary acts on the basis of the commission's proposals. i believe that the council, as the co-budgetary authority, has done its duty and approved these budgetary acts. that's something to be thankful for. as regards the commitments made by the member states, i believe that the message must be reiterated so that the promises are kept, so that all the commitments that have been announced are also followed by effects. but we also know the difficulties that some member states are facing and we know that things do not always happen as quickly as we would like. the same applies to the provision of civil servants. this is extremely important if we want better border controls, if we want hot spots to work better. i was minister for immigration, and i know these situations where, suddenly, the number of asylum seekers increases. take germany, which has to take in hundreds of thousands of newcomers at once. take sweden, which is facing the arrival of tens of thousands of refugees. what can i do? you need officials on the ground. it is not enough to send a few to deal with the hot spots. there is therefore a complex organisational problem, which puts real pressure on the member states. here too, the commitments made must be implemented without delay. as for other subjects, i shall not go back to turkey, which i believe is an essential and fundamental partner. the dialogue we must have with that country must therefore be actively pursued, particularly, but not only, because of the refugees. there is another aspect of the matter that we must not underestimate. it is the report of the five presidents and the deepening of emu. we should not think that because the crisis has calmed down a little, all this can wait, that there is no longer any urgency. are we going to wait for the next crisis? no, i'm not going. when we look around, we see that the situation of the world economy is not very encouraging, not very positive. we heard it in lima at the last meeting of the international monetary fund. it is now urgent to work on deepening the governance of economic and monetary union and improving the governance of emu, extending it to areas where citizens expect us to be. and where are they waiting for us? they expect us to provide them with jobs, they expect us to provide them with social security, they expect us to provide them with living conditions. of course, this is a lot of work for europe, but we cannot choose the news. it is a task that is imposed on us, and it is in these moments of crisis that europe must face up to it and show its capacity to act. i am sure that the next european council will take stock of these problems and the challenges to be faced, and that we will come out with solutions, or at least with the beginnings of solutions, which will better prepare us to face this difficult situation.

in writing. one of the issues to be discussed by the council tomorrow is the reform of economic and monetary union. unfortunately, the direction of the proposed changes is rooted in the shortcomings of the current euro area (and the eu itself): on the one hand, the liberalization and integration of the banking and financial sector into the european economy, without a parallel development of regulation, nor a harmonization of european rules to ensure its control; on the other hand, the primacy of neoliberal and regressive economic objectives, with no more mention of social objectives than to give a veneer of democratic legitimacy to the ordoliberal project. the direction of emu reform should be different: to ensure public funding for states that wish to develop democratically policies other than those imposed by the markets, using the support of the ecb in secondary markets where necessary; to strengthen the separation between credit and speculative activity; and to ensure that the costs of bailouts are borne by shareholders and not by citizens. otherwise, the differences and discontent with emu will increase, and they will be digging their own grave.

madam president, twenty years of summits, ten years of emissions trading and no real solution that addresses the causes of climate change. the buying and selling of emission allowances is a speculative, poorly designed market which has created a huge bubble. in addition, this mechanism has sometimes only benefited the most polluting industries. ladies and gentlemen, we are playing with the health of the planet and the people. the consequences are already disastrous. the loss of biodiversity, the flooding of small island states and the lack of water and food for millions of people are a reality. we therefore call for the exclusion of false solutions for the paris summit such as a price on co2, the red plus system, carbon capture and storage or 'fracking'. ladies and gentlemen, curbing climate change will only be achieved by developing a new production model based on renewable energy. we are facing a historic occasion. please use it for the good of the planet and for the good of humanity.
madam president, commissioner, the european union has demonstrated its commitment to protecting the planet and tackling climate change. we have led successive conferences of the parties and adopted effective policies to reduce emissions over the past years. we have also committed ourselves to meeting emission reduction targets in the coming years. but what we need now is an international agreement with commitments from all sides. that is why it is important to find a balanced solution, so that all the large countries contribute according to their responsibilities and their capacities. the objectives should be binding and ambitious, but they should also be realistic and achievable. we cannot allow our industry to have to relocate or resort to other strategies such as the so-called 'volkswagen case' in order to comply with the rules. in this context, further integration of european climate change and air quality policies is desirable. this resolution has a broad consensus and is a clear endorsement of the commission's work and a call for a good agreement for the environment and also for a level playing field for the competitiveness of companies. finally, i would like to wish the 15 members of the delegation to the paris summit good luck and, of course, to you, commissioner. i'm sure you'll make a major contribution to it on behalf of all of us.
madam president, two ideas for this report on climate change. first, to emphasize the decisive role played by local and regional institutions in this cause. 80% of measures to promote energy saving, sustainable mobility, waste reduction and recycling, or citizen involvement in these efforts, are taken at local or regional level. thinking globally, yeah. supporting action from the front and involving local and regional authorities in decision-making, too. regional alliances such as under 2, which includes california, quebec, baden-württemberg and the basque country, whose minister for the environment, ana oregi, is with us in this debate, are an example of the way forward. secondly, let us promote global agreements to avoid competitive differentials based on production that ignore global climate change objectives. the european industry needs us to be extremely vigilant and to take action against the sale of products which, by their manufacture or characteristics, do not comply with the measures that our companies do comply with to combat climate change.

member of the commission.– madam president, together with first vice-president timmermans, i held our first annual colloquium on fundamental rights last week. i would like to thank the chair of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, claude moraes, and all the other members who were present for their involvement and steady support. the colloquium drew in part on the public hearing on anti-semitism, islamophobia and hate speech which was held in the civil liberties committee in june this year. the colloquium confirmed that anti-semitism and islamophobia, like other forms of hatred, are our common concern. we must not leave the communities targeted, or the groups directly affected by hate, to deal with it alone because only together can we find solutions. and i can promise you that the commission will play its part. the commission has published the conclusions of the colloquium, which include a ‘to do’ list – a roadmap of actions to which we should jointly commit and on which we should work. let me mention some of them. we will monitor rigorously the transposition and implementation of the eu legislation on racist hate speech and crime. where necessary, we will launch infringement proceedings, and we will also assist member states. we will share best practice guidance, reinforce training support and encourage cooperation with civil society so that eu rules are applied correctly. we have also decided to designate two coordinators with specific responsibility for issues relating to anti-semitism and islamophobia, respectively. they will be the contact points within the commission for both communities. furthermore, the commission will convene a high-level eu group on racism, xenophobia and other forms of intolerance. together with member states, civil society and both communities’ representatives, we will evaluate the added value and the feasibility of dedicated national strategies. hate speech currently is the main manifestation of anti-semitic and anti-muslim hatred. it fuels fear, spreads misconceptions and incites violence. i have started to discuss with it companies and civil society how to address the issue of hate speech as a matter of priority, with full respect for freedom of expression. i briefed justice ministers about this at the justice council last friday: they shared our concern and appreciated a coordinated approach to this. we also intend to counter online hate speech through targeted funding, monitoring activities and by identifying the need for further regulatory measures. eur 5 750 000 has been earmarked in 2015 to encourage the monitoring of online hate speech. let me be clear: we are speaking of content which is manifestly illegal under eu rules and european court of human rights jurisprudence. so this is not a move against offensive or disturbing content, but against actual incitement to violent acts and hatred. we also agreed to promote further a pluralistic, inclusive and non-discriminatory society by monitoring the correct application of eu legislation on combating racial discrimination. once again, let me stress the importance of adopting the equal treatment directive. fostering inclusive education, mutual understanding and intercultural dialogue are equally important. we will prioritise eu projects promoting european values and history, including holocaust remembrance, citizenship education and religious and media literacy. we will continue to support youth, student, school and civil-society projects and networks favouring tolerance and intercultural understanding. for example, in 2016 the erasmus+ programme will prioritise projects that promote inclusion in education, training, youth and sport, and prevent marginalisation and the radicalisation of young people i am also committed to making it easier for small grassroots organisations to identify relevant funding and projects related to intolerance and racism. to this end, i will set up an easy-to-access webpage.
on behalf of the ppe group madam president, we are against any kind of discrimination on grounds of belief, profession of faith, race or ethnicity. according to a survey by the european agency for fundamental rights, the jewish population is increasingly afraid of being verbally harassed or physically assaulted: 46% and 33%. the increase in incidents motivated by islamophobia in the union is also unacceptable. in this regard, i want to say that islam is a respectable religion and jihad a pathology of islam. but we cannot ignore the cruel persecution and also the elimination and expulsion of the christian community in more than fifty countries. remember the expulsion of 2,000 christians from the nineveh plain, 21 christians beheaded by daesh in libya in february, hindu extremists attacking churches in nepal, or the total flight of christians in syria and iraq. in addition, daesh is currently holding 230 christians hostage. the expression of hate is a deviation from reason, an aberration. we must guarantee a union and a free and pluralistic world based on tolerance between religions and mutual respect; and the protection of the roma, too. the european agenda on security, madam commissioner, happily deals with these issues, but in all honesty, we are dealing with a declaration of intent. that is why i am supporting, ratifying and congratulating claude moraes' initiative.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. intolerance and anti-semitism are burgeoning across the european union. there's a cause contest and they've been exhibited here over and over again. on the one hand, the poor management of the crisis and the exacerbation of inequalities have led to the radicalisation of a muslim community within the european union prone to clearly anti-semitic attitudes and therefore persecuting jewish identity. but there is also impunity on the net, cowardly disguised as anonymity, which allows the pathogenic transmission of hate speech and hate politics and direct incitement to criminal violence. we therefore have an obligation to deal with this matter, and that is the sense of the public hearing which took place in the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs on 29 june. and above all, to seek a response based on the data produced by the european union agency for fundamental rights in connection with the attacks in paris, brussels and toulouse, but also with the feeling of vulnerability of jewish communities throughout the european union. we therefore need answers. on the one hand, the possibility, promoted by the commission, of appointing a special envoy on anti-semitism who could be part of the commission's own organisational structure, with the participation of this parliament; but above all, the elaboration and implementation of national strategies which take as an example those established in relation to the roma community - with the european gypsies - to deal with the many variations and possibilities of response to this execrable phenomenon. what we must be very aware of is that the commission needs to get involved by taking legislative initiatives to classify hate speech, hate politics and incitement to violence, especially on digital networks, as a serious transnational european crime.
on behalf of the gue/ngl group. madam president, on 9 february 2015, four men assault and burn a homeless person in valencia; on 8 august 2015, a gang assaulted a transgender woman in madrid. these are just two examples of hate crimes in the spanish state. according to the statistical yearbook of the ministry of the interior, which provides figures for 2014, hate crimes in spain increased by 10% in the last year. hate crimes for homophobia or transphobia, for racism, for gypsies, for religious beliefs; attacks on people with disabilities or people in poverty. the movement against intolerance points out that more than four thousand hate crimes still occur every year in spain. in europe, the european union agency for fundamental rights estimates that between 60 and 90 percent of victims do not report. the aggressors are mainly members of neo-nazi and racist groups, groups which enjoy a high degree of impunity. as an example of this impunity, last july seventeen people were acquitted of being members of a neo-nazi ideological group in what is known as operation panzer. among the gang members was the murderer of the young anti-fascist guillem agulló, who was sentenced in 1995 to seventeen years in prison, of which he served only four. the european commission must continue to legislate against hate crimes. a specific and comprehensive directive which also serves to promote comprehensive laws on protection against hatred and discrimination in the member states. (the speaker agrees to answer a question put under the 'blue card' procedure (rule 162 (8) of the rules of procedure))
the answer is 'blue card'. obviously, the fight against hate crimes, against hate speech and against everything that promotes these hate crimes must be carried out in all areas and it is also a fight that has to be carried out in social networks, on the internet. but, of course, the prosecution of this incitement to hate crimes cannot be confused with freedom of expression. i think they are two perfectly compatible things and one should not be confused with the other.
in writing. the annual report of the european commission against racism and intolerance reflects alarming situations within our borders. every day we witness how hatred and fanaticism are sowing chaos and terror in syria, iraq or afghanistan. we cannot allow this hate speech to spread across our borders, we cannot allow fear to dominate european citizens. the conclusions of the commission's report are very significant, there is an increase in attacks and hate speech on religious grounds in all member states. there are even populist politicians who incite these behaviors. social media has been instrumental in this boom as well, but it can also be the solution. as can the politicians themselves and the measures they take. i therefore call on all member states to ratify protocol no 12 to the european convention on human rights, which prohibits discrimination in general. and that appropriate mechanisms are put in place to combat this phenomenon in each member state.
madam president, this week several members of this parliament, members of the western sahara intergroup, visited the saharawi refugee camps. we have experienced the hospitality of the saharawi people on their day of national unity. but above all, we have experienced firsthand a very serious humanitarian crisis. both unhcr and the red crescent informed us of the severe shortage of resources: 25% of refugees suffer from chronic malnutrition. the food budget is practically exhausted and $11 million is needed to cover basic needs until the end of 2016. unfortunately, the propaganda is covering up this humanitarian catastrophe. false allegations of mismanagement and corruption, aired in this very house, have served as a screen to hide the reality. but we have confirmed on the spot the words of the commission and the unhcr: the distribution of food and the management of humanitarian aid is impeccable. it is essential to make an urgent allocation of funds for the saharawi refugees and i appeal to the responsibility of the european union and spain to respond to an unjustly forgotten crisis.
madam president, madam commissioner, the european authorities must remind spain that the basque economic concert and the navarre convention are part of community law. its maintenance is key to avoiding new and irreversible territorial tensions in spain. they help to avoid them by preventing them from using the european union to attack - in a campaign as crude as it is intense and false - institutions that are useful and positive for the citizens. on 11 september 2008, the luxembourg court of justice found both systems to be legal because they were institutionally, procedurally and economically autonomous. they have internal legal backing. they take their tax decisions from independent bodies and the economic effects of these cannot be offset by the state authority. it is the doctrine of the "azores case". we have supported in this parliament the fiscal federalism on which the convention and the convention are based. both are the result of bilateral agreements which update historical rights, are supportive and encourage responsibility. that's why they have massive social support in euskadi and navarre.
in writing. ‒ the european parliament takes a position in this report on a council implementing decision determining the date from which the designated authorities of the member states and europol will have access to the visa information system (vis) in order to facilitate the prevention, detection and investigation of terrorist offences and other serious criminal offences. the question does not raise any problems in terms of content, since it is merely a question of determining the entry into force of a council legal act, and therefore the abbreviated procedure under article 150 has been followed and my vote has been in favour. however, the entry into force of this decision has been delayed as the issue of the failure to take into account the opinion of the european parliament when adopting the decision implementing the measure was raised before the court of justice of the eu. i hope that this vote will resolve these procedural issues and enable the decision to enter into force as soon as possible.
in writing. ‒ i abstained from this vote which fixed the entry into force of decision 2008/633/jha on the exchange of visa information between different member states and authorities. i am opposed to the access of the security forces to any database which contains non-criminal matters, such as a visa register. i understand that this decision criminalizes migrants and foreigners travelling or residing in the union. in any event, as the date from which access to the files is granted is being voted on, i abstained on the grounds that this is a technical matter within a decision which i do not share.
in writing. ‒ this is an agreement to a council proposal on the date on which decision 2008/633/jha regulating access to the visa information system (vis) by competent authorities will enter into force. the objective is to ensure the continuity of access rights for consultation of the vis by the authorities designated by the member states and by europol, for the purposes of the prevention, detection and investigation of terrorist offences and of other serious criminal offences. i am of course not opposed to the prevention of terrorist offences, but i question the order of priorities in the management of migration flows and i reject the harmful effects of such measures. the gue/ngl group has always opposed legal devices that give priority to the mechanisms for identifying migrants, whether through access to the vis or other databases, as it has a stigmatising effect on them. it is also a decision affecting the date of entry into force; the content of this regulation is no longer being assessed. i therefore abstained from voting.
