in writing. ‒ i agree with the exceptional application of article 23 of the common provisions regulation, as i believe that it is the best way to succeed to give priority to transparency and trust within the member states. i believe that the european union should strengthen these two concepts, as i believe they are key to the effective and efficient management of the european structural and investment funds. i also believe that the stability and growth pact contains rules which are sufficiently well founded to enable each member state to monitor the use of the european structural and investment funds, since it consists of fiscal supervision with a system of penalties for non-compliance with its conditions. the simultaneous application of article 23 would therefore, in my view, be an excess of control, with the negative consequences that would follow.
president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let me first of all thank mr moraes and the two rapporteurs, mr diaz de mera and mrs fajon, for this question and, above all, for the efforts they have made to ensure the active participation of parliament in this important european project. in the 2009 stockholm programme, the european council invited the commission i quote 'to submit proposals for an entry and exit system coupled with a fast track traveller registration scheme, with the aim of having such a system operational as soon as possible'. this request has become urgent in the current context - which i do not need to remind you of and describe to you - in fact, the european council of 15 october last called - i quote again - 'for the development of technical solutions to strengthen control of the external borders of the european union with a view to achieving the objectives pursued, both in terms of migration and security, without prejudice to the fluidity of movements'. the creation of a european entry/exit system is a necessary step to preserve the schengen area. currently, there are 12 countries using national entry/exit systems, but the added value is still limited. the commission should also be able to provide information on the progress of the implementation of the smart border and border management system in the member states. such a system should lead to harmonisation and standardisation of border controls and lead to a higher level of security. this system will provide more certainty in the calculation of the period of authorised stay. border guards today spend a lot of time looking at the composting of travel documents and calculating the period of authorized stay. if this system works properly, border guards will have more time to identify passengers posing a migration or security risk. in addition, the fact that composting is no longer necessary will allow the use of automated border control systems to be extended to a part of the travellers, for whom the border crossing will be more smooth. the european entry/exit system will facilitate the identification of persons at the border and within the territory. this could not have been achieved by upgrading sis ii. the technical study presented by the commission a year ago also showed that it would not be realistic to achieve these objectives by redesigning the visa information system, which is still being deployed and applies only to third country nationals who need a visa. a european system would have a deterrent effect on third-country nationals who intend to stay longer than the authorised period of stay. the fact that member states will have a precise view of the number and nationality of these people would also make it possible to provide for more appropriate measures to counter this phenomenon. this information will also be relevant when negotiating visa facilitation agreements, when considering granting a visa waiver to third countries and when examining the application of the visa waiver suspension mechanism. as for the frequent flyer programme, the council has always been in favour of such a programme. at this stage of the discussion, a majority of member states are in favour of such a programme with flexibility in the application of the rules according to the type of border. during the discussions, a majority of the participants were in favour of a lighter rtp, as proposed by the commission in its technical study. as regards the question of law enforcement access to the european entry/exit system, a very large majority of member states have expressed their support for such a possibility from the very beginning of the system's operation. the purpose of such access would be the prevention or detection of, or investigation into, terrorist offences or other serious criminal offences. this was also the wish of a large majority of representatives of national parliaments at the meeting organized by the committee on civil liberties last february. for member states, access to the european system by law enforcement agencies would be introduced on a secondary basis, as in the case of vis and eurodac. such access should be subject to strict conditions and procedures. to this end, the council shall endeavour to identify the elements necessary for future provisions and the list of necessary guarantees in accordance with the case law of the court of justice. as regards architecture, on the basis of the technical study preceding the pilot project, a majority of member states were in favour of implementing the passenger registration scheme and the entry/exit system as a single system. a majority in the council prefers, at this stage, a gradual approach to integrating the i/o system and the rtp into the vis. interoperability between future european systems and existing national systems and the introduction of the possibility to reuse elements already existing in the vis will help to reduce the final cost of this project. as regards the type and number of biometric identifiers, we await the results of the pilot project, which will be decisive for future discussions. as regards data retention periods, a large majority of member states are in favour of a uniform retention period of five years, in order to harmonise all systems and for all the purposes mentioned above: this would be in the interest not only of the authorities but also of travellers, as it would reduce the number of cases where their data would have to be recorded. the council is fully aware of the importance of the judgment of the court of justice of 8 april 2014 annulling the data retention directive. all discussions in the council on the establishment of a smart border system have fully taken into account the principle of doing only what is necessary and proportionate to achieve the objectives pursued. the council also welcomed the commission's proposal to extend the scope of the 'smart border' package to include the european union's external borders, and to extend the scope of the 'smart border' package to include the european union's external borders. the council considers this package of legislation to be vital for the schengen area, and i must congratulate the commission, since yesterday the first vice-president of the commission announced it in the work programme for 2016, which contains three regulations in this area. we all, of course, count on cooperation with parliament to bring this important project to fruition.
member of the commission.– mr president, let me start by wishing the chair of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs a swift recovery. i want you to know, claude, that we need you to be fully operational for months to come. we have a lot of work to do together. (applause) i would like to thank the honourable members for this further opportunity to reflect with you on ‘smart borders’. i know how sensitive the parliament is on this issue. as announced in both the agenda on security and the agenda on migration, and as already mentioned at our previous exchange on 9 june, it is our intention to present a modified proposal on smart borders by the beginning of next year. in our upcoming 2016 proposal we aim to present a solution that is operational and cost effective. we will propose a system that performs well and quickly and that meets the european union’s security and migration policy objectives, improves the traveller’s experience, does not increase the workload for border guards and stands the test of our data protection legislation. the commission will modify the existing proposals in the smart borders package to deliver a single legislative proposal complemented by a targeted modification of the schengen borders code. it will be supported by a new impact assessment in order to incorporate and justify the changes to the original proposals. these changes will be limited to the following issues assessed: the architecture of the system; the biometric identifier to be used; the facilitation of border crossings; the retention time for the storage of data; and access for law-enforcement purposes. the current border control system is neither efficient nor effective given increased travel flows and member states’ financial constraints. the smart borders proposal will, when implemented, lead to a reduction in border guards’ repetitive manual tasks, and release resources where they are urgently needed. it will also facilitate the crossing of eu external borders by third-country nationals through a semi-automated or fully automated system. the modified smart borders proposal will allow for a more effective eu policy against irregular migration and notably the phenomenon of over-stayers. it will help border guards in detecting travellers who did not observe the terms of their stay in the schengen zone and will allow them to undertake appropriate action. this is also expected to have a preventive effect on over-staying. data generated at entry/exit could also be of use to law enforcement authorities in the fight against terrorist offences and other serious criminal offences in specific cases. should access for law enforcement purposes be granted, the necessary substantive and procedural safeguards will obviously be introduced. subject to the results of the new impact assessment, some preliminary conclusions can already be presented. as i have said on previous occasions, it seems preferable to build a single system, with functionalities for both an entry/exit system and registered travellers’ programmes, instead of two different systems. it reduces the development and operating costs, avoids the duplication of travellers’ personal data and reduces the impact on national systems. as for possible synergies with existing systems, the re-use of certain elements from the visa information system, such as the common biometric matching system, seems to be the preferred option. such an approach presents a lower level of risk and will be cheaper than the option of full and immediate integration to a biometric identification and authentication system. the possibility of limited interoperability between the entry/exit system and the visa information system is under assessment: it would prevent registration of the same data concerning the same persons in two different systems. the 2013 proposal was for the use of 10 fingerprints and biometric identifiers. however, the technical study showed that a facial image is sufficient for verification of the identity of a traveller, while the combination of fingerprints and facial image gives the best results for traveller identification. the ongoing test phase will need to compare how these options work out in practice. however, it is clear to me that the biometric identifier used for the entry/exit system has to be as light and non—intrusive as possible. a major challenge for us is to ensure that the introduction of a smart borders system will accelerate the border-control process. to complement the functionalities for a registered travellers’ programme, increased scope for using process accelerators, such as self-service kiosks or mobile device applications, could be promoted. this would facilitate border crossing for a wider group of travellers. the impact assessment will look into the details of this important question. on the subject of data retention, it is clear that if records of previous data are deleted too quickly travellers would have to re-enrol more often. it would also mean that border guards can see only a very short period of the traveller’s history. remember that, in today’s situation with stamped passports, border guards can reconstruct several years of travel history when looking at the passport of the person standing in front of them. in this context i want to underline once again that the court of justice ruling on the data retention directive has no direct effect on other eu legal instruments. however, it is very clear that a strict assessment of the proportionality and necessity of measures that constitute serious restrictions to fundamental rights is needed. these key points raised in the court of justice judgment will be fully addressed in the smart borders proposal.
on behalf of the ppe group mr president, yes, mr moraes's question was very timely and the intervention of the council presidency and mr avramopoulos was very clarifying. i would like to begin by saying that these systems are designed to control, facilitate and speed up the movement of passengers. and to avoid any confusion, we are talking about a type of passenger who normally comes with his passport in hand, not a passenger who arrives in a harsh and terrible way on a beach in turkey or on a beach in greece. that is something which has caused a great deal of confusion here, and that confusion has come from the presidency of the council and the presidency of the commission. it is estimated that there are currently between three and five million people in the schengen area who have exceeded the temporary stay limit set to stay in our territory. it is therefore very important to put an end to these practices and procedures, which are a clear violation of the schengen area. i naturally support the access of the state security forces and bodies to the system as an added value, provided that it is a question of clarifying a few things, such as which authorities would have access; providing those authorities with the necessary guarantees so that access is proportionate and limited to the purposes; and, finally, i am reassured by the fact that the judgment is taken into account and that, although it has no impact on the legislative acts of the european union, it will indeed be taken into account. as you will understand, mr president, after all the work we have been doing, to limit our work to a minute and a half is a real barbarity.
mr president, commissioner, the delays and the change of objective in the smart borders package are making it clear to us that the crisis shaking the european union was not the euro crisis, but the crisis of the free movement of persons, the crisis of confidence between the member states. because what was designed to be an instrument for smarter management of the union's borders is now presented to us as a tool for making them more rigid and, of course, in the service of security. and so we have a right to know what is in this new initiative that is going to affect data retention and data retention safeguards as interpreted by the court of justice in relation to the protection of the fundamental rights of europeans, especially after the safe harbour ruling. we have a right to know what the cost will be, and if possible an alternative that validates the information system provided by dis to avoid an investment that is directed back to the objective of security. in the short term, more fingerprinting and less fingerpointing is needed, but in the medium term we must change the suicidal attitude towards immigration, asylum and the management of the union's borders.

president of the council. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, mr rapporteur, i welcome this opportunity to discuss the european semester with you. we have all just received the commission's proposals for a renewed semester. the council will look at this issue in the coming weeks and draw conclusions for the 2016 financial year. the three institutions share - and i listened carefully to you, mr rapporteur - the analysis of the main challenges facing the european economy, namely the high level of debt, the unacceptable rate of unemployment, overall competitiveness, which is particularly affected by an insufficient level of research and development, and a dangerous investment gap which is weighing on the growth potential of the european economy. we propose similar solutions, more effective and wider implementation of structural reforms, growth-oriented fiscal consolidation, better access to finance for small and medium-sized enterprises, education systems that better meet the needs of labour markets, and above all - and above all - a revival of investment. since the first european semester in 2012, we have made progress, and the 2015 edition is a good example. this year, the number of country-specific recommendations is smaller and more focused on the main macroeconomic problems specific to each country. in addition, while calling for long-term reforms, the recommendations also emphasise short- and medium-term actions. the scope of the recommendations is thus strengthened. the 2015 recommendations are also based on stronger country analyses. the presentation of these analyses in advance of the recommendations, as early as february, enabled the council to examine them in depth, including through the peer review method. the council also had more time to work on the recommendations themselves. we have thus been able to bring the commission's proposals more closely into line with the realities on the ground. this less tight timetable has also allowed member states to involve stakeholders and national parliaments in the process of economic coordination at national level. this contributes to the appropriation of the recommendations and to their more effective implementation. the council discussed this autumn the lessons to be learned from the 2015 semester. and we welcome the progress made in the organisation of this semester. our discussions also highlighted other improvements that could further strengthen the process. this concerns above all the transparency of the macroeconomic imbalances procedure, on which the commission has just presented its ideas, and the link between the european semester and the surveillance provided for in the stability and growth pact. we shall examine the commission's new proposals on these aspects without delay. so what policy should this process of coordination lead to? in what areas have we used this tool? at the macroeconomic level, i would like to focus on investment and access to finance. at the same time last year, the commission presented the investment plan and the co-legislators adopted the proposal on the european fund for strategic investments in record time. second, in reviewing the 2015 country-specific recommendations, member states welcomed the commission's emphasis on growth-friendly fiscal policies, whether in terms of spending efficiency, public investment and stimulating private investment, or more appropriate taxation. this autumn, at ministerial level, work on the commission's action plan for a capital markets union was begun. the council will adopt conclusions on this matter in november. the presidency has committed itself to making progress on the securitisation proposal. we are counting on parliament's cooperation in moving this matter forward. as regards employment and social policy, the council also recognised the realities on the ground when it adopted country-specific recommendations last summer. unemployment and social inclusion continue to pose major challenges in a number of member states. for their citizens, the improvement in economic prospects in europe has not yet been felt in terms of employment or social situation. the increase in poverty remains a major challenge, especially poverty affecting children. the renewed 2020 strategy, which the commission will present in the coming months, should, i believe, include more effective objectives and actions in this area. we need to step up efforts to reduce the still substantially high levels of unemployment in many member states and to improve the functioning of labour markets and social protection systems. progress in these areas is also essential to consolidate growth. the political stakes are high. citizens expect europe to adopt policies that address their problems. progress in the fight against youth unemployment is still insufficient. even if progress is being made, we need to strengthen our instruments, such as the youth guarantee, and go further. we need more economic convergence, we also need more social convergence. and to move social europe forward, certain themes, such as worker mobility, will be the subject of commission proposals later this year. the exchange of good practice and peer review, or the definition of common reference points, such as those we are in the process of establishing for the integration of the longterm unemployed into the labour market, are useful in such an approach. in the field of competitiveness, the council's work confirms that the member states share the same analysis of the main challenges. as regards the country-specific recommendations, the council was very pleased to find the theme of investment, whether it be the opening up of markets for goods and services, the regulatory framework, a better environment for businesses or increased efficiency in public administrations. the council will also continue its work, which includes improving the functioning of the internal market. i consider this a major asset from which we do not always derive full benefits. in this context, the digitisation of the single market is certainly one of our major projects, not to mention smart regulation and support for innovation clusters. strengthening research and development - i recall that we committed ourselves to investing 3% of gdp in research and development - promoting innovation by better linking the public and private sectors, supporting business creation and investing in human capital are essential to a european economy that is renewing itself and positioning itself in relation to its main competitors. before concluding, i would like to briefly review the implementation of the country-specific recommendations. you highlight this problem by recommending that the commission present a detailed report on the progress made by the member states or that it consider introducing an incentive mechanism. i would like to assure you that the implementation of the recommendations remains the council's top priority. we are convinced that the reforms of the european semester introduced last spring are already bringing us closer to this goal. but the most important thing remains to be done, and we shall look at the commission's new proposals for a renewed semester with this in mind.
vice-president of the commission.– madam president, let me start by thanking the rapporteur, mr rosati, as well as the shadow rapporteurs and all members involved in the work for their engagement and dedication. the commission welcomes parliamentʼs constructive contribution by way of its timely reports such as those of mr rosati and the june report by ms berès. today i have an opportunity to present to you the package of measures adopted by the commission last week aiming to make the economic and monetary union more effective, transparent and democratic. our package intends to restart economic and social convergence by implementing key short- to medium-term elements of the five presidents’ report: revamping the european semester, improving the toolbox of economic governance rules, improving the voice of euro area internationally, completing the financial union, and preparing for stage two on more far-reaching measures that could require a treaty change. let me start with the european semester. this is the heart of europeʼs efforts to coordinate economic policies and deliver reforms. nevertheless, as you rightly stated, member states have demonstrated varying degrees of commitment to the process. the commission has constantly been improving the eu semester to strengthen member states’ implementation of reforms. in 2015 we have streamlined it to sharpen its focus, better involve national stakeholders and strengthen its social dimension. we value your support in recognising our efforts. building on these developments, some further adjustments can bring additional benefits. firstly we share your view that many member states, in particular in the euro area, are faced with inter—dependent macroeconomic challenges. therefore we intend to better integrate the euro area and national dimensions. recommendations for the euro area will come out earlier than before, so that common challenges can be reflected in recommendations for individual euro area countries. second, on several occasions parliament also called for the social dimension of the european semester to be strengthened. the commission has already taken steps to do so, on which we will build further. specifically, more attention will be given to employment and social performance in the macro-economic imbalances procedure. moreover, we intend to further improve involvement of eu and national social partners. social fairness will also get more attention in the context of macroeconomic adjustment programmes, and we have already put this into practice for the greek programme, for the first time preparing the social impact assessment of the programme. third, you asked the commission to support member states’ exchange of best practices. we agree that this is a valuable tool to achieve convergence. we will launch new efforts to promote greater use of benchmarking and cross-examination across policy or thematic areas. first, in order to focus eu structural and investment funds on supporting reforms, the commission will enhance their links to key priorities in the csrs. effective reform implementation will also be supported through the progressive roll-out of technical assistance by the commission structural reform support service. last week the commission also presented concrete measures to improve our toolbox of economic governance. the commission is not proposing a legislative reform. more evidence and experience with reform governance structures are necessary before embarking on such a road. but the commission has listened to your calls to improve transparency and to reduce the complexity of available instruments and tools, so we will take action. we will notably increase the documentation on the methodologies we use, publish more information and data backing our decisions under the stability and growth pact and the macroeconomic imbalances procedure, and work to streamline the indicators for assessing compliance with the stability and growth pact. moreover, as you have rightly stated in the report, the foundations of the recovery are fragile owing to the eu’s underlying structural weaknesses, lack of competitiveness and low investment. the capacity to compete and to adjust is essential for economies to deal with shocks and structural changes and to prosper within a monetary union. it is therefore a focus of our economic policy coordination already today; but we suggest that more be done to strengthen national ownership. we are therefore proposing that national competitiveness boards be set up in all euro area member states. they would be independent bodies that provide expertise on competitiveness, performance and reforms. the definition of competitiveness in the commissionʼs proposal is broad, covering both cost and non-cost competitiveness drivers. our objective here is to strengthen and support national processes and the role of social partners – not to hamper them. national traditions are very different. we have therefore considered it better to start with a recommendation to member states and not move straight to legislation. but even so the european parliament must be fully part of this debate from the start, and your views will be important to shape the debate on the competitiveness boards. the commission has also decided to set up an advisory european fiscal board. this board will provide advice on the implementation of fiscal rules, taking into account both national and euro area developments. but let me be clear: any proposals for fiscal decisions under the treaty remain fully with the commission, and we are politically responsible for them to this parliament. we are also taking steps to complete the banking union. we need to implement what was agreed with strong support from this parliament, and we need to finish what we have started. this includes full transposition of the brrd directive and implementation of the deposit guarantee schemes directive; and the agreement on bridge financing for the single resolution fund must be completed swiftly. we plan to present a legislative proposal on first steps towards a european deposit insurance scheme by the end of the year, based on the reinsurance approach. we also plan to set out ways to reduce further risk in the banking sector and ensure a level playing field. a strong emu must go hand in hand with a strong, single voice on the global stage. we therefore propose to gradually develop a unified representation of the euro area in the imf. we propose that the president of the eurogroup should ultimately represent the euro area internationally. finally, the commission considers effective democratic legitimacy and accountability to be an indispensable element of the process to complete emu. steps have been taken towards that in the recent past, and the commission is proposing concrete steps to move further along the lines of the five presidents’ report. we expect the european parliament to take part in shaping the debates to define the economic and social priorities of the eu. this is why we propose to engage in frequent debates throughout the european semester, for instance in the plenary debate after the publication of the ags package and upon presentation of the commissionʼs proposals for country-specific recommendations. the commission and the parliament are in permanent contact, and i am confident we can further refine the details of our cooperation in these matters. to ensure ownership, legitimacy and accountability, we also aim to engage with a broader range of actors. in the lead-up to this european semester, which will start with the annual growth survey next month, we have been consulting social partners, both trade unions and business representatives, on the priorities for the year ahead. during this year, i and my fellow members of the commission have also travelled to many capitals and met national parliament representatives. we want national parliaments to be more deeply involved in the adoption of national reform and stability programmes. this is essential to strengthen the ownership, and thereby implementation, of reforms. the last package should be seen as a first stepping stone towards completing economic and monetary union, but we also need more far-reaching measures – those requiring treaty change. we are talking here about the preparation for stage two of the five presidents’ report. we will need to shape consensus on those more fundamental changes, so we will launch a broad consultation gathering ideas from across europe. next year we will appoint a dedicated expert group to explore legal, economic and political implementation for the long term. all this will feed into the commissionʼs white paper in spring 2017. the european parliamentʼs input will be a crucial contribution to the next stages in the process of completing emu. i am looking forward to hearing your views on the proposed approach.

vice-president of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, i am very pleased to have the chance today to discuss the securities financing transactions regulation (sftr) and to congratulate mr soru and the shadow rapporteurs for the work they have done in taking this proposal forward. this regulation is a central part of our response to the need to increase the safety and transparency of financial markets. it will help us to manage the risks in the shadow banking sector, in line with financial stability board recommendations endorsed by g20. it sits alongside a number of measures we have already taken to regulate the shadow banking sector. for example, the european market infrastructure regulation reduces risks in derivatives markets, and the alternative investment fund managers directive ensures that investment funds are regulated. as those of you who have followed this proposal know well, securities financing transactions are transactions in which securities are used as collateral to borrow cash, or vice versa. they are an important source of funding on europe’s financial markets. they support investment and allow for better risk management. they are integral to european central bank monetary policy operations. during the financial crisis, it became clear that we did not know enough about what was going on in these markets. without reliable data, oversight was more difficult. the european systemic risk board, the european central bank and the financial stability board all argued that transparency in these markets would allow risks to be managed better and would enable better-informed investment decisions. this was also our analysis in the commission. so i am delighted that we are on the verge of reaching a final agreement on legislation that will improve transparency. i am grateful to parliament for its hard work on this issue, and i believe that the political agreement you have reached with the council strikes the right balance. it will enhance transparency in three main ways. firstly, it will introduce the reporting of securities financing transactions to centralised databases known as trade repositories. this will allow supervisors to identify risks better and, if necessary, to take targeted action. secondly, funds will have to become more transparent for investors both in their regular reports and in pre-investment documents. this will give investors the information they need to make sound investment decisions. thirdly, the regulation will improve transparency around the re-use of securities as collateral. this should help reduce domino effects when a default on one transaction can cause other defaults if the same collateral has been used more than once. the legislation builds on the experience of establishing the european market infrastructure regulation. a detailed implementation table will give european markets time to adjust. the proposed reporting system will reduce the burden on small and medium-sized enterprises, and it limits reporting of existing transactions to those strictly necessary for regulatory and supervisory purposes. the proposal enlarges the list of supervisors who can access data in trade repositories, and the european market infrastructure regulation has been modified to ensure consistency. the european securities and markets authority (esma) will prepare draft regulatory technical standards setting out the requirements for reporting. we will work with esma to ensure consistent application of the rules across the european union. the commission is committed to legislating in a proportionate manner in a way that strikes the right balance between managing risk and encouraging growth. transparency is an important part of this agenda. by making the right information available we can help investors make sound decisions; we can encourage responsible behaviour; we can avoid unnecessary burdens; and we can take targeted action, if and when it is needed, on the basis of evidence. the securities financing transactions regulation will be an important step in this direction. i look forward to this debate and to the plenary vote on thursday.
i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr renato soru, for his work over the last few months to get us here in the chamber and to vote tomorrow on this regulation, which i believe is a very important step towards ending opacity and agreements outside regulated markets. the effort made by our group to incorporate new operations into the analysis monitoring system is important. the improvement in the information that market operators will have to provide is also important and i therefore believe that our group, the socialist group, has made important progress on the text with regard to the commission. i would just like to add one final note and that is that, within this great ambitious project of the capital markets union, we need this union not to mean giving new ways of financing to shadow banking, to operations out of control, and it is important that this philosophy of having an organised, transparent market, monitored by the supervisory institutions, be the basis on which we build the capital markets union.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, smes are a source of jobs and growth in europe, but they have a problem with funding. i do not share the commission's diagnosis of the causes of the lack of credit, which serves to guide its financing programmes for smes. we are witnessing a huge concentration of the banking sector in a few private transnational oligopolies. it is a development which favours the commission, as seen in its model of banking union or in the conditions of financial rescues, for example the one established for spain. but without a public bank, without a bank linked to the territory and to industry, what happens is a shift of financial activity towards speculation. the attempt to respond to this problem with greater financial liberalisation, such as the capital markets union, is a false response, because not only does this business remain in the hands of the same large financial groups, but it also strengthens their ability to impose their conditions and transfer their risks to smes, which are the first to suffer the impact of greater volatility and uncertainty. i would like to conclude by adding that the financial suffocation of smes is also due to the stagnation of demand and the lack of prospects for recovery in many countries, especially in the european periphery. i repeat, economic policy must be kept away from financial interests, because otherwise we will continue to suffer from a great deal of macroeconomic instability, a lack of growth which will make it difficult for smes to access credit and, with it, job creation and the growth europe so badly needs.
vice-president of the commission.– mr president, let me first respond to some of the concerns expressed during this evening’s debate. first, capital markets union (cmu) should not be seen as in competition or contradiction with a strong banking system. banks have strong local relationships and knowledge about micro, small and medium—sized enterprises. bank lending will remain the principal source of external finance for smes. the measures provided for in the capital markets union action plan will not interfere with, or detract from, local banking networks. on the contrary, cmu provides for measures that will strengthen the banking system. it seeks to make it easier for banks to refinance their traditional lending business by selling securities and bonds to the capital markets. the larger and more efficient funding market for banks will help them, including the local relationship banks, to focus on their core business, notably lending to micro-businesses and smes. there are, however, member states where bank loans are difficult to obtain. there are also companies – start—ups with limited physical collateral or firms in an expansion phase – whose needs may not always be catered for by the banks. cmu proposes a way to help firms in these situations to raise funding through other channels. cmu will complement, rather than compete with, bank finance by adding to the diversity of funding sources. by promoting more diverse funding channels and reducing europe’s dependency on banks, cmu should increase the resilience of the financial system. nevertheless, we also need to be alert to financial stability risks that may emerge as a result of efforts to further develop europe’s capital markets. recent measures, such as the european market infrastructure regulation (emir), the alternative investment funds managers directive (aifmd), the markets in financial instruments directive (mifid) and the securities financing transactions regulation, will make capital markets more transparent, well-regulated and robust. the european securities and markets authority (esma) will play an important role in ensuring consistent implementation and application of these laws. as markets develop, it will be important to ensure that any risks associated with the deepening of capital-market-based financing are monitored and mitigated. work is underway, within the eu and internationally, to improve understanding and monitoring of systemic risks. the commission will examine the need for changes to the macroprudential framework in the context of the forthcoming review of the european systemic risk board (esrb) and, if it appears necessary, will allow for effective intervention to contain and mitigate risks arising from market—based finance. let me conclude today by saying that it is my pleasure to continue discussions with you on ongoing issues in relation to smes’ access to finance, which are important for all of us. improving access to finance for smes is one of the mainstays of the implementation of the commission’s strategy for growth and jobs. the issues are relatively complex but, through our shared determination, i believe we are moving in the right direction.
in writing. the first results of increased rigour in the eu's economic and budgetary management are already visible, and the european economy is slowly starting to recover. the european commission forecasts that gross domestic product (gdp) will grow by 1.8% in 2015 against 1.1% last year and 2.1% in 2016 against 1.7% last year. europe, however, can aspire to more: we can still make much more of our potential. the important thing is to create a positive investment climate for our businesses and, in general, to improve the entrepreneurial spirit throughout the eu. small and medium-sized enterprises are the backbone of our economy and are creating jobs in the european union; it is essential to continue supporting smes to ensure that they emerge from the crisis.

madam president, i am grateful that the de monte report also focuses on the importance of european cultural tourism and that it asks the european commission to continue to support economically the so-called 'european cultural routes'. these routes are very important, firstly, for the development of a more demanding, selective, thematic tourism and offer a very wide range of offers to satisfy this option of cultural or thematic tourism. i would like to highlight, for example, the camino de santiago, the first european cultural route, which every year breaks records for tourism from all over the world. but there are 32 other cultural routes that are also very relevant. these routes are also useful for understanding the history of europe, european art and the peoples of europe, and they contribute to the preservation of the great historical heritage we have in europe. and these routes also help to highlight - and i will end here - the existence of a common european identity. it is a way for citizens to see that the european project is well-founded, and that is why i am in favour of introducing young people to these european cultural routes.

in writing. ‒ the global financial crisis of 2008 exposed major regulatory loopholes, ineffective supervision, opaque markets and overly complex products in the financial system. that is why i voted in favour of this regulation on the notification and transparency of securities financing operations, as it improves transparency, regulation and supervision, particularly as regards central information and disclosure of these operations, and the minimum requirements for the reuse of securities. these operations encompass the main securities lending and repurchase agreements, which are exchanged for entities and activities outside the regular banking system (i.e. so-called 'shadow banking'). our group has worked to add some improvements to the commission's proposals which we consider particularly important. among them, its scope, so that it covers new financial transactions in its definitions. we have also increased reporting obligations to ensure that all information is provided to the competent authority. in this respect, it is important to ensure that the launch of the capital markets union does not provide an opportunity to deregulate the financial sector.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because it sets the stage for the development of new speculative bubbles which will be sought to be stimulated through the future creation of the capital markets union. the report, which is the result of informal tripartite dialogues, proposes to regulate the notification of securities transactions within the eu by facilitating the mobility of securities. the co-legislators start from the premise that the economic crisis was generated by financial speculation and its lack of financing of the real economy and, to solve it, propose an even greater financialization of the real economy, aspiring to change the bank financing of economic activity by the introduction of securities for the financing of the productive fabric. this will have serious consequences in the transfer of the volatility of the financial markets to the productive fabric, and that is why i voted against it.
in writing. ‒ the global financial crisis that began in 2008 revealed major regulatory gaps in the financial system, supervisory problems, opacity in markets and overly complex products. since then, the eu has been adopting a series of measures aimed at building a stronger and more stable banking system. the regulation on the notification and transparency of securities financing operations is added to these measures. it improves the transparency, regulation and supervision of securities financing operations in relation to central information, the disclosure of such operations and the notification to investors, and the minimum requirements for the reuse of guarantees, which are among the reasons why i have supported it.

in writing. ‒ the global financial crisis that began in 2008 revealed major regulatory gaps in the financial system, supervisory problems, opacity in markets and overly complex products. since then, the eu has been adopting a series of measures aimed at building a stronger and more stable banking system. the regulation on the notification and transparency of securities financing operations is added to these measures. it improves the transparency, regulation and supervision of securities financing operations in relation to central information, the disclosure of such operations and the notification to investors, and the minimum requirements for the reuse of guarantees, which are among the reasons why i have supported it.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this report because, while we share the objective of improving the transparency of financial transactions, we believe that the final result of the text is such a small step forward that, in the end, it means maintaining the situation of opacity that favours shadow banking and financial speculation.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because it sets the stage for the development of new speculative bubbles which will be sought to be stimulated through the future creation of the capital markets union. the report, which is the result of informal tripartite dialogues, proposes to regulate the notification of securities transactions within the eu by facilitating the mobility of securities. the co-legislators start from the premise that the economic crisis was generated by financial speculation and its lack of financing of the real economy and, to solve it, propose an even greater financialization of the real economy, aspiring to change the bank financing of economic activity by the introduction of securities for the financing of the productive fabric. this will have serious consequences in the transfer of the volatility of the financial markets to the productive fabric, and that is why i voted against it.

in writing. ‒ i have voted in favour of this text, because it extends transparency to these instruments which involve borrowing and lending securities or pledging them as collateral.

in writing. ‒ the agreement reached on the regulation enhancing the transparency of securities lending and repurchase transactions will improve financial stability by ensuring that information for such transactions is notified to trade repositories and investors in collective investment undertakings. enhanced transparency will prevent banks and other financial intermediaries from attempting to circumvent regulation by shifting parts of their activities to the less regulated shadow banking sector. securities financing transactions, often carried out by the shadow banking sector, consist of any transaction using assets belonging to the counterparty to generate financing.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this resolution on the mass electronic surveillance of citizens of the european union, as it is a resolution which explicitly condemns the mass spying on european citizens and government structures by the national security agency of the united states. the resolution also regrets the latest measures taken by certain eu countries, such as the united kingdom, which endanger the security of citizens' data. another issue which is important to us and which is reflected in the resolution is the request for the immediate suspension of the safe harbor decision, which allows the transfer of personal data to the united states, and also of the tftp (tracking terrorist financing program), as well as showing concern about the increasing violation of fundamental rights through the limitation of privacy. we would have liked to see more specific reference to the buying and selling of personal data by private companies, which we strongly condemn, and to see the aggravation that the adoption of treaties such as ttip would have on the above issues.

in writing. ‒ i voted against, but always keeping in mind that it is necessary to prohibit widespread mass surveillance activities and the mass processing of personal data of citizens, guaranteeing at all times the fundamental rights of eu citizens.
in writing. ‒ most eu member states and the eu institutions have shown a lack of willingness to prohibit mass surveillance activities since the revelation made by edward snowden. on the contrary, some of them have even adopted laws that extend surveillance capabilities of intelligence bodies, such as france and the uk. i therefore welcome and support this resolution that condemns, once more, the electronic mass surveillance of eu citizens by european and american intelligence and calls for the safeguarding of eu citizens’ fundamental rights.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this text on the follow-up to the 2014 resolution, as it is much more forceful than the original resolution on the mass electronic surveillance of eu citizens. this resolution was adopted following the revelations by edward snowden of the nsa's mass spying on citizens and politicians in europe. important and positive aspects are incorporated in this follow-up text, such as the mention of two ecj judgments on the subject. the mass surveillance legislation of the united kingdom, france and the netherlands is singled out and challenged for opening the door to the legalization of mass surveillance. the text warns the commission that its budget will be frozen if it does not follow the ep's recommendations, thus strengthening the role of parliament as a democratic body. the text also stresses the importance of encryption and calls for the suspension of the tftp (terrorist financing tracking programme) agreement. finally, we are in favour of this text on the follow-up to the resolution as it also calls for legislation to protect whistle blowers, something we in podemos support.

in writing. ‒ in a changing environment, with no security, which is 'difficult and sophisticated' in the words of the commission, it is incredible that we find such ineffectiveness on the part of the institutions. there is not only a lack of knowledge, but also a lack of will to legislate. parliament said so a year ago and the deadlock is still there, even limiting the powers of the national control authorities. fortunately, the court of justice is not part of that immobility and has invalidated the safe harbour. the ruling makes clear that data protection authorities, now national, can review data transfers to the us on a case-by-case basis. it's a step in the defense of free citizens.
in writing. ‒ in the last parliamentary term, a resolution was adopted in which parliament called on the us authorities and member states to prohibit widespread mass surveillance activities. the resolution launched a 'european digital corpus' which included specific actions for the protection of fundamental rights in the digital age. the parliament's civil liberties committee was asked to assess the extent to which the recommendations had been followed up within a year. this resolution shows the widespread unwillingness of the majority of member states and eu institutions to address the issues raised in the resolution, but also points to the progress achieved in certain respects, such as the start of interinstitutional negotiations on the draft general data protection regulation or the judgment of the cjeu of 6 october 2015 declaring the commission's decision on the us safe harbor scheme invalid. this resolution asks the civil liberties committee to continue to monitor the follow-up given to the recommendations made in the 2014 resolution. i therefore support this resolution.

in writing. ‒ one more year, the economic situation remains critical: recovery is slow and fragile, unemployment rates are falling but still excessively high, and poverty is at alarming levels, with one in four people in the eu living in poverty. that is why i did not vote in favour of this report. because i believe that we need a real fiscal responsibility timetable compatible with sustainable growth and the creation of quality jobs. because the gap between the top 10% and the bottom 10% has increased sevenfold in the eu in some countries, and fairer tax policies based on redistributive policies are needed. because the reduction of unemployment has been based on precariousness and wage cuts. the citizens don't need any more words or analysis. they need change, action and, above all, just solutions to the real problems they face every day. the commission and the member states must be given a strong signal in favour of a european minimum wage framework or a european minimum income for integration.
in writing. ‒ the european semester is the annual process by which the commission assesses the budgetary commitments of the member states and assesses their compliance with the principles of economic governance (including deficit and debt limits), proposing, where appropriate, further reforms or cuts to bring them into compliance. in other words, the european semester is a mechanism to legitimize and enable the commission to intervene regularly in the affairs of the member states, always offering the same recipe: social cuts, privatizations, labour reforms and increasingly destructive competition. i voted against because we have repeatedly spoken out against this governance framework and we are strongly opposed to attempts by the rapporteur and the majority groups to strengthen this process by involving representative trade unions and national parliaments or by extending it towards 'social' objectives. this cannot be the justification for a process which, by its very nature, pursues objectives which are far removed from the interests of the working majority.

in writing. ‒ we voted against this report because we are opposed to the european semester mechanism as a whole, even though the final text has incorporated many of the considerations we share (for example, those pointing to the need to improve the quality of employment). the european semester is intended to subject the budgets of governments to scrutiny by the european commission to ensure that certain macroeconomic objectives are met and that the so-called structural reforms are implemented. we don't share the diagnosis or the solution.

in writing. ‒ the coordination of economic and budgetary policies within the european union is a key element of the european semester and forms part of the european union's economic governance framework. it is our responsibility to help ensure convergence and stability in the european union, to help ensure sound public finances, to foster economic growth, to prevent excessive macroeconomic imbalances and to implement the europe 2020 strategy. the way out of the crisis is through a tightening of economic governance and continuing reforms at the national level, this is the only recipe.
in writing. ‒ the resolution following the oral question on longterm unemployment is motivated by a proposal for a commission recommendation which is excessively general, does not provide for new financial resources and does not allow member states to be bound by its implementation. the text of the resolution, for its part, as the socialists had demanded, proposed: (i) a relationship between the unemployed and the employment services within the contract of integration into employment which is more balanced and fair to the worker, respecting his rights and his professional expectations and avoiding forcing him to accept precarious jobs; (ii) that account be taken not only of his needs for retraining but also of his environment and social needs; (iii) that new economic resources be mobilised to combat this problem as was done with the youth employment initiative and that cofinancing instruments be provided to countries with greater financial difficulties to enable it to be implemented rapidly. the resolution also arrives in time for the epsco council in december this year to take it into account before its final decision, as the representative of the luxembourg presidency has said. for these reasons we have decided to support the resolution.
in writing. ‒ the european union's economic policies, its obsession with austerity and its lack of commitment to social and regional cohesion are some of the structural causes of the rapid growth of the longterm unemployment rate and its concentration in the countries of the european periphery. even though the council recommendation will not correct this neoliberal orientation, i do think it is good that funds are being released and policies are being developed to alleviate some of the effects of this high unemployment rate. however, there is a risk that the mistakes of the youth guarantee will now be repeated: the lack of involvement of the social partners in the design, implementation and management of the policies to be developed; the insufficiency of funds (especially in those countries most affected by the cuts); the facilitation of new subsidies to enterprises instead of opting for really effective training and job guidance policies. that is why i abstained.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour, taking into account the serious consequences of long-term unemployment, which has more than doubled since 2007 and represents half of total unemployment, i.e. more than 12 million people. we must therefore continue to work within the eu institutions and in the member states to find solutions for better integration of the longterm unemployed into the labour market.
in writing. the resolution following the oral question on longterm unemployment is motivated by a proposal for a commission recommendation which is excessively general, does not provide for new financial resources and does not allow member states to be bound by its implementation. the text of the resolution, for its part, as the socialists had demanded, proposed: (i) a relationship between the unemployed and the employment services within the contract of integration into employment which is more balanced and fair to the worker, respecting his rights and his professional expectations and avoiding forcing him to accept precarious jobs; (ii) that account be taken not only of his needs for retraining but also of his environment and social needs; (iii) that new economic resources be mobilised to combat this problem as was done with the youth employment initiative and that cofinancing instruments be provided to countries with greater financial difficulties to enable it to be implemented rapidly. the resolution also arrives in time for the epsco council in december this year to take it into account before its final decision, as the representative of the luxembourg presidency has said. for these reasons we have decided to support the resolution.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution as it concerns the integration of the long-term unemployed back into the labour market. it is imperative that a person who experiences long term unemployment is assisted so that he/she could retrain his/her skills. the measure allowing for a ‘job integration agreement’ between a jobseeker and an employment service is to be commended as it assures the best approach for re-integration. given that as europeans we are still experiencing the after-effects of the financial crisis, certainly in spain, i welcome this initiative.
in writing. ‒ i abstained on the motion for a resolution. it analyses the complexity of the situation of the longterm unemployed in a way which is consistent with our views, mentioning shortcomings in statistics and the social, economic, family, occupational, health and integration consequences for the longterm unemployed, among others. the text focuses on three main components: 1) ambitious strengthening of the registration of the unemployed in an employment service for full coverage; 2) assessment of the individual potential and of the employment needs and preferences of the long-term unemployed before they have been unemployed for 18 months; 3) provision of a comprehensive labour integration agreement between employee and employment service before they have been unemployed for 18 months. however, among the negative aspects, there is no mention of economically strengthening public employment services, too much emphasis is placed on aid to employers for the integration of these unemployed without prioritizing the importance of implementing policies that have proven effective. reference is also made to the european semester and to country-specific recommendations, an approach which we reject.

in writing. ‒ of the eu population, 9.6% is unemployed, and of these more than half, 5%, are long-term unemployed. 62% of long-term unemployed have been off work for at least 2 consecutive years. only 24% of long-term unemployed are covered by unemployment benefits. long-term unemployment can lead to poverty and social exclusion. it contributes to passing on poverty down generations in jobless households and lowers rates of academic achievement. i support this vote because addressing long-term unemployment would promote sustainable economic and social growth. additionally, in the long term, it will take financial pressure off the member states’ public spending and finance.

in writing. ‒ currently the european aviation safety agency is the authority that grants the authorisation for the flight of remotely piloted aircraft (rpas) only when the mass of these exceeds 150 kg. in view of this situation, the european commission has put forward a proposal for a european regulatory framework which takes into account the characteristics of rpas (weight, scope of operations, speed) and the nature of their use (recreational or professional). while i support the commission's intention to remove this 150 kg threshold and replace it with a suitable regulatory framework and to create a regular information mechanism between member states where rpas incidents are addressed and good practices are shared, i have abstained in this report. the commission does not provide guarantees for a clear division of civil and military use or for the spying of drones. furthermore, it highlights that the 'very dynamic' israeli manufacturing sector, clearly for military use (used for espionage and extrajudicial and extraterritorial enforcement), facilitates the integration of a civil and military air navigation service into israeli airspace. that is why i did not support this report.

in writing. ‒ tourism is a key activity for europe and, especially for some countries and regions, so there is a need for sufficient funding and a reinforcement of tourism policy to boost this activity under the umbrella of the new eu competences on tourism recognised in the lisbon treaty. the launch of a european commission action plan to develop the eu strategy for coastal and maritime tourism is a key instrument to enhance its growth and job creation potential, as acknowledged in this report on new challenges and strategies to promote tourism in europe. the importance of addressing connectivity and accessibility is fundamental, particularly in island and outermost regions, which are heavily dependent on maritime and air transport. it is also necessary to develop smart and innovative strategies to combat seasonality, adapting to both high and low season periods and taking into account different audiences, and to continue to focus on cruise tourism and ensure that there is a sustainable development of the sector.

in writing. ‒ europe is the world's leading tourist destination, with a market share of 52%. the result is that tourism generates more than 10% of the eu's gdp (if tourism-related sectors are taken into account) and directly employs 13 million workers. we are therefore talking about a fundamental sector. in this report we therefore ask the commission to give this economic sector comprehensive attention and to present a new strategy to meet the challenges facing the sector.
in writing. ‒ in 2010, the commission launched the communication entitled 'europe, the world's number one tourist destination: a new policy framework for european tourism'. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover all the activities of the european union's institutions. the report also proposes a series of actions to develop a common strategy for promoting europe as a preferred tourist destination, taking account of economic, quality, sustainability, responsibility and technological innovation criteria, among others. however, although the report is interesting, it contains a proposal for which we tabled a deletion amendment which was rejected in the vote. the proposal refers to the promotion of health tourism, not health tourism, i.e. in the face of the saturation of public health systems, to promote travel to use private care in other, cheaper countries. we believe that we cannot support a report which includes a measure which goes against one of our basic political principles: the defence of a public and quality health system. we therefore vote against the report.

in writing. ‒ as we know, tourism plays a very important role in promoting europe's rich cultural diversity. it also strengthens european identity and therefore new challenges and strategies need to be set to promote it. it should be noted that in recent years, global competition has increased considerably with the existence of emerging and cheaper countries that attract international tourists. to remedy this situation, we need to exploit our comparative advantages, in particular the diversity of landscapes and the extraordinary cultural wealth. in order to promote tourism in europe, it is essential to implement initiatives that promote responsible management of resources, taking into account a number of constraints affecting the tourism sector, such as climate change. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the new rules and to monitor the implementation of the new rules. the report aims to enable travellers to plan, book and pay for their multimodal journeys 'door to door'. in my view, these measures are more than welcome to exploit our comparative advantages and to strengthen european tourism.

in writing. ‒ this report sets out the range of proposed actions that the eu could develop in the field of tourism. this is a very broad report covering all kinds of initiatives and proposals to promote the tourism sector in the eu, from recommendations on digitalisation, responsible and sustainable tourism, ways to promote the eu as a global tourist destination, etc. the report calls for greater clarity on the actions financed by the structural and cohesion funds in the area of tourism, and in particular for the establishment of a budget line to better identify the different actions carried out by the eu. the report calls for the creation of a brand for europe's destination based on the heterogeneity and multitude of tourist offers available. it stressed the need to promote europe's cultural heritage and the importance of training in ensuring a quality and competitive service. it also affects the sharing economy sector, which is required to comply with the same level of regulation as the traditional sector. i have therefore voted in favour of this report.

in writing. ‒ tourism is a strategic sector for the eu: it accounts for 10% of the eu's gdp and is the world's number one tourist destination. the european union, despite its good tourist figures, is well aware that the trend is changing. we are facing several challenges right now: first, to remain a competitive offer; emerging countries are increasing their market share progressively and are estimated to reach 57% market share in tourist reception by 2030. secondly, a change in the behaviour of tourists. global demographic changes indicate that the number of people over 65 years old in 2020 will be 1/5 of the world's population. this group is a potential target, they have leisure time and in many cases economic capacity. finally, potential tourists in emerging countries. another issue facing the european union is the opening of borders to potential tourists with high purchasing power. the granting of visas and exemption agreements should be made more flexible for those who demonstrate sufficient economic conditions.
in writing. ‒ from 2 to 27 november, the international telecommunications union is holding a world conference on radiocommunications (wcr-15) in geneva. it will address the proposal - currently under consideration and favourably assessed by the international civil aviation organisation - to allocate a specific frequency band in the radio spectrum for the monitoring of flights worldwide. currently only 30% of the world's air traffic is tracked by satellite, making it impossible to locate or rescue an aircraft in the event of an accident. tragedies such as malaysia airlines flight mh370 and air france flight af447 highlight the need for commercial flight tracking systems not to be affected by a disruption of the normal onboard electrical supply and not to be deactivated from the flight. i have therefore voted in favour of this resolution, which calls on the european commission to take the necessary steps to allocate the radio spectrum band needed to support the future development of a global satellite flight tracking system which fulfils these characteristics.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution to support the future development of satellite technology to enable flight tracking systems on a global scale. i support the commission's efforts to develop a world-wide flight tracking system based on results, which will enable air navigation service providers to determine the position of commercial flights at all times.

in writing. ‒ the air france af447 and malaysia airlines mh370 tragedies have proven that the current radar location system has not enabled location of flights in distress, thus seriously hindering rescue operations. i therefore voted in favour of this resolution that calls for the development of satellite-based technology that would enable flight tracking at global level.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this motion for a resolution tabled by the chairman of the committee on transport and tourism. current air navigation systems do not, in many cases, allow aircraft in difficulty to be detected and located in time. flight tracking systems today cover only 30% of global airspace, which significantly impairs the effectiveness of search, rescue and recovery operations. to overcome this limitation, we have technology such as automatic dependent surveillance-broadcast (ads-b) satellites, the use of which would help governments, air navigation service providers and european and global airlines to increase efficiency and capacity in air traffic management, and significantly improve aviation safety, while reducing infrastructure costs. the rapporteur proposes to remove regulatory barriers to satellite flight tracking systems in order to offer eu citizens services that can save lives.

in writing. ‒ recent air tragedies such as malaysia airlines flight mh370 (8 march 2014) and air france flight af447 (1 june 2009) have highlighted the need for new surveillance systems in air traffic management, which are an important tool to increase the efficiency and capacity of air traffic management by significantly improving aviation safety and reducing infrastructure costs. in this respect, ads-b technology based on aircraft-to-satellite communications appears to be very promising; this technology helps to monitor air traffic management outside the most densely populated areas where radar coverage is limited, impossible or very expensive (oceans and uninhabited land areas). the timely allocation of an appropriate band of radio spectrum is of vital importance to ensure the development of this technology. this resolution calls on the commission to adopt the necessary measures in relation to the allocation of this radio spectrum band at the next world radiocommunication conference to be held in geneva in november 2015. i have therefore supported the resolution.

mr president, the european semester is used more as an observer-commentator than as a useful corrector and common governance. we watch the chess game; we tell each player what he does right or wrong; we punish some behaviors but not others; we make predictions that are not always confirmed and recommendations that are not always followed. the real deficit we are suffering from is european, global, democratic, responsible economic governance. everything seems to be the same here: we have moderate growth, they say. we have some new problems - like the refugee problem - but we must continue with the policy of the past: jobs and growth, structural reforms and fiscal balance. we want to believe - it seems - that just repeating the mantra of austerity will solve everything. we insist on the mistaken idea that the problems lie exclusively in the countries where the specific symptoms appear: the imbalances, the imbalances - mainly the deficits and unemployment - and on the mistaken idea that it is these countries which must and can solve them. there is no deficit without a symmetric surplus and no debt without equivalent credit. an excess of debt implies an equivalent excess of credit. insisting on payment for what should not have been borrowed ends up drowning the debtor and dragging the creditor along. that is why the united nations just approved in september the basic principles for the restructuring of sovereign debt as the only way to break the pernicious loops of 'debt, austerity, more debt, more austerity'. we have issued recommendations for individual countries and none for the government as a whole: for countries, the european union is to blame; for the european union, the countries are to blame. isn't it time we all acknowledged that we are equally guilty and responsible? without addressing the disparities, an increase in demand would increase the deficits and debt of the less competitive countries. if we maintain austerity globally to contain these imbalances, aggregate demand falls and unemployment soars. we will not get out of this loop without a european fiscal policy, both on the revenue side, which is now being reduced by fiscal dumping between countries, and on the expenditure side, which is being diligently designed to increase supply where there is unemployment. i therefore conclude with three requests: to democratize european governance so that it serves the citizens, to move rapidly towards fiscal union and to apply it in the service of full employment as a common and shared objective.
