president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would first like to thank the european parliament for its essential contribution throughout the legislative process on the open internet and the end of roaming, and in particular for its vote on 27 october. the vote removed the internal market barrier of roaming charges and confirmed non-discriminatory access to all internet services. it has taken time, but together we have put into practice, for the benefit of consumers, a common vision which also opens the door to innovative services which we want to see increasingly developed in europe. the zero rate issue, which you wanted to discuss today, is indeed worth discussing in the context of the open internet. it is true that leading experts, including mr tim berners-lee, called on the honourable members of parliament on 26 october to adopt amendments which would allow member states to create their own rules to regulate the practice of zero rate. in our discussions, both in the council and in parliament, the zero rate was indeed considered. why then have we not chosen to include these elements in the agreement or indeed to propose amendments? i think it was important for parliament and the council to achieve real european coherence in order to continue to develop the single telecommunications market. we wanted to avoid the proliferation of divergent national legislation that could create so many new barriers to the digital single market. in this respect, the adoption of a european regulation would of course be ideal. in addition, when we studied the question of zero rates, we listened to the opinions and took into account the experiences of countries which had banned the practice and those which accept it within certain limits. we have seen that the practice, while it has risks, also has a number of tangible benefits, particularly for the consumer. the main risk is related to the power of operators to favour their own services or to choose services to be preferred over the consumer. we recognize that if there is insufficient competition between operators or between services, this practice poses real risks to the open internet. in the light of these benefits and risks, we did not want to abolish this practice, but we wanted to introduce a safety system in the regulation based, in particular, on the control carried out by the national regulators or the competent national authorities. in concrete terms, the regulation obliges the competent entities to supervise and ensure that the end-users' rights as defined in the regulation are not infringed. in this context, the competent entities are empowered to intervene against agreements or practices that are detrimental to the rights of end-users and, if necessary, to impose sanctions. i believe that after discussions within the institutions and between the co-legislators, we have reached a balanced compromise with this regulation which guarantees an open internet and protects the interests of consumers and internet users, which excludes abusive conduct, but leaves open the possibilities for innovation, both for new companies and for established operators, and which encourages investment by both parties. i would also like to remind you of the context in which we find ourselves: the council, parliament and the commission are constantly working to improve the internal market, and in particular the digital internal market, and, commissioner, i heard you this morning - live from brussels in luxembourg - strongly advocating this digital internal market, so i believe we are on the right track and of course for the digital attractiveness of europe. and that is the fundamental issue. in particular, we are advancing very high-speed infrastructure. the more this infrastructure is available and accessible, the less attractive zero-rate practices will be. finally, with the end of roaming, we have created additional opportunities for competition between operators at european level. i believe that this increased competition should also help to reduce the risk of zero rate policy. in conclusion, i would like to stress the great step forward we have taken together. with our definition of the open internet, we are putting an end to practices that have been harmful to consumers for too long.
member of the commission. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. there is no contradiction between the council and the commission. the tsm regulation aims to ensure a coherent approach to open internet access in the internal market. national regulators will be responsible for ensuring the effective implementation of the net neutrality rules. the tsm regulation, which was adopted by the parliament in its plenary session on 27 october, is the first time that binding net neutrality rules have been incorporated into european law. these rules are genuine common rules on the basis of full harmonization. and since it is a regulation, the rules are directly enforceable both by national courts at the request of citizens or other end-users and by regulators. until now, most europeans have had no comparable legal protection for their right to access or distribute information, content and services of their choice over the internet. the regulation also lays down the principle of non-discriminatory data traffic management for the first time in the eu. it contains a clear anti-discrimination clause which must be observed. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the regulation is clear on commercial agreements and practices such as zero-rating, where the use of certain services is not counted against the end-user's data volume. it is neither a blanket ban nor a zero-rating exemption. such practices are only permitted if they are compatible with the rules of net neutrality. our tsm regulation includes three safeguards to protect end-users from any adverse effects of business agreements and practices, including zero-rating. and these safeguards are designed, can and will ensure that the right of all end-users to access and distribute information, content and services of their choice over the internet - the cornerstone of the net neutrality provisions in the tsm regulation - can be effectively applied and enforced. those safeguards ensure that regulators and courts examine the advantages and disadvantages of zero-rating and other practices on a case-by-case basis to ensure that the objective of effective choice for end-users is not undermined. the first safeguard is that commercial agreements and practices are incompatible with the regulation if they restrict end-users from exercising their right to access or distribute information, content, applications and services of their choice over the internet. this applies to all possible situations where end-users' choice is significantly restricted in practice. the second safeguard relates to the fact that all business agreements and practices, including zero-rating, must comply with the principle of equal and non-discriminatory treatment of all traffic, from which no unilateral or contractual deviation is permitted. this means that internet access providers are not allowed to use discriminatory traffic control measures to comply with their contractual agreements or business practices. the third safeguard concerns the role of national regulatory and other competent authorities. the tsm regulation gives national regulatory authorities the task to empower them, to oblige them to ensure that end-users' rights, including those of content, services and applications providers, are not affected by monitoring and enforcement measures. in particular, national regulators should be empowered to address agreements and business practices, including zero-rating, that could lead to situations where end-users' choice would be significantly restricted in practice. let me be clear: i have confidence in the national regulators. they are independent and will continue to develop their independence. they are democratically elected and they do a good job. a basic trust, not a basic distrust, is my position. together, these three safeguards provide a future-proof approach which allows us to respond not only to current practices but also to future ones. these provisions allow both independent regulators and courts to weigh up the concrete effects of business practices. they should examine whether a particular practice circumvents the guarantees of an open internet and whether it significantly reduces end-user choice in practice, taking into account specific national circumstances. in addition, the competition law enshrined in the treaty is directly applicable and can also be enforced. furthermore, the tsm regulation requires the body of european regulators for electronic communications berec and gerek, in close cooperation with the commission and after consulting stakeholders, to issue guidelines for the implementation of the obligation of national regulators in order to contribute to its consistent application. the commission will ensure, in close cooperation with berec, that end-user choice is ensured, thereby ensuring competition, pluralism and cultural diversity. berec and the commission have already started work on these guidelines. berec is expected to adopt it within nine months with our participation. the guidelines will provide national regulatory authorities with a common benchmark for the examination of agreements and business practices, so that they can make and enforce consistent, coherent decisions. let me add that we are monitoring the market developments and if there is any abuse in the market we will react, we will amend our legislative text. that means that it is up to us and you to observe the market developments, the practice and then to see in a year or two: has it worked? i expect yes. if there are gaps, then it will be possible to make improvements, to make amendments.
on behalf of the ppe group mr president, commissioner, president-in-office of the council, zero rating is a commercial practice whose beneficiaries are consumers, and to prohibit commercial practices without having demonstrated - i insist: without having demonstrated - that they are harming competition is to have a very interventionist view of the market, is not to believe, at bottom, in one of the founding principles of the european union: that the market must be free and competitive. in this case, the single market regulation for telecommunications could not be clearer: internet access providers must guarantee the right of any user to access the content of his choice, without suffering any discrimination and without reducing his possibilities of choice as a result of commercial practices, whether zero rating or any other practice. national regulators now have the power to assess any practice and can intervene in the event of abuse by applying appropriate sanctions. but it is also a regulation and therefore these rules are directly enforceable by the national courts. the commission and berec will work on a guide for complementary action. i call on the commission to speed up this work so that it can help to implement the directive in order to ensure that it is better applied in each member state. (the speaker agrees to answer a question put under the 'blue card' procedure (rule 162 (8) of the rules of procedure))
the answer is 'blue card'. i have just explained, mr president, that it is necessary to show that commercial practices are being abused and that they are harming competition in order to intervene. in a free and competitive market, entry is not banned, but problems of this nature are shown to exist and then action is taken. there must be bodies involved, as in this case the national regulators, and there must be evidence of this. all this is guaranteed by the single market regulation for telecommunications.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, many citizens are grateful to be able to connect to a platform without having to pay a huge discount on their data rate. the issue, however, is the threat this practice poses to fair and honest competition on the internet. there is a broad consensus in this parliament and on the street about the need to ensure net neutrality, and providing access to a certain platform or service at no charge is a way to target and prioritize traffic to those particular platforms or services over their competitors. in my view, this poses a major risk to net neutrality itself and to fair and honest competition, and it also opens the door for the economically strongest - and not necessarily the most innovative - to emerge victorious, all while putting at risk the diversity of the offer for citizens. the development of the digital single market is therefore a priority. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect.
i believe that there are no longer any qualifications to define the refugee crisis we are experiencing and the challenge it poses to the european union: legal challenge, social challenge, humanitarian challenge and also budgetary challenge, and i shall concentrate on the latter. when the european commission presented the european agenda on migration, it included the necessary funds - almost 10 billion euros, including the 2 300 for the trust funds for syria and for africa - and i sincerely believe that the european union is making a commendable effort, through the budget, to deal with this crisis. but the needs and commitments do not end there, because that is the part that goes to the european budget, but what about the part that goes to the member states? at both the informal council of 23 september and the european council of october - and minister schmit has recalled this - the member states committed themselves, together with unhcr, the world food programme and other agencies, to contributing eur 1 billion, as well as matching european contributions to the trust funds. and unfortunately, despite the efforts of some member states, we are still more than 2 billion euros short. but it is not all bad news, and the european commission recently informed us that the member states will receive 9.4 billion euros from the european budget for various adjustments, but also for extraordinary revenue from fines and duties. we have already informed the council: this parliament has no doubt about the amount or legality of this reimbursement, but we would certainly consider it a commendable political gesture if the 28 committed themselves to using part of this extra revenue from the european budget to finance their share of the trust funds. making our actions match our commitments is the greatest test we face and it's a test we can't afford to fail. this is the conclusion of the letter to the 28 from president tusk, prime minister bettel and president juncker. let's see if it's true!
madam president, i can only share the intention and the objectives which have led to the creation of these funds. we have more and more crises that last longer, we have more and more needs, more and more displaced people, but we do not have more funding according to these needs. that funding is becoming less predictable and therefore we are not able to serve the people who need it. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. but we cannot deceive ourselves or others: most of these funds come from other funds which were already earmarked for similar actions. the commission has also responded, but if we look at the list of contributions from the member states - i will not say which ones - in many cases they do not correspond at all to the values of the european union, which advocates serving the people who need it. we must therefore ensure that these funds are additional and not simply a substitute for other efforts. if we are honest in preaching that we have to serve people fleeing from hunger and war, we have to be responsible in putting the means in place to make our preaching a reality.
vice-president of the commission. – madam president, two general points. firstly, this is a global crisis and it requires a global response. we in the european union are 20% of the world economy but 50% or more of development and humanitarian aid. we are doing our part, and it is important that everybody who has the means to contribute should do so. more wealth means more responsibility, and i share the comments that have been made that we need to call for mobilisation so we can help people and help people help themselves. my second general observation is that, in the same way that the financial and economic crisis has pointed out to us that we have work to do in terms of building the institutions and capabilities to deal collectively with this crisis, the refugee crisis is also exposing some of the deficiencies of the european union in terms of collective action. i hope that we will see proposals ranging from border control, common defence and security, to rethinking dublin but, most importantly, more coordinated and coherent medium- to long-term engagement with the countries that need our assistance to continue to build their own capacity to cope with their development challenges. it goes without saying that the best way to deal with the humanitarian crisis is not to have it in the first place. in other words, we have to invest more in conflict prevention, conflict resolution and disaster risk reduction – in things that help fewer people to be affected in the future by what, inevitably, climate change is going to cause – more disasters – and what, unfortunately, violent extremism is producing – more conflicts and more severe dramas. this goes without saying. i do not think that the european union has been perfect, but yes, we are more engaged and we are contributing more than many others around us. i would like to make some specific comments. it has been pointed out, and rightly so, that we have to reach out to other key development partners, and we are doing so. i myself was in the united states last week to meet with the world bank, the imf and the us authorities. the us is our most important partner and the most aligned in terms of how we approach this kind of crisis, and we need to expand beyond an immediate urgent response to creating fiscal capacity for countries to have a buffer against crises, to get the development community more aligned in how we deal with fragility. i am very pleased to see the imf building a much stronger capacity to address fragility in the world, and rightly so. there has been a very clear call that this money should not be a fragmented little island, and that is my fault, as i should have started by saying we are placing this 2.3 billion in the context of what is now 10 billion from the commission to address the refugee crisis inside and also outside. the specificity of these trust funds is that they are a new way for us to better organise and deploy our resources in a more agile manner, but it does not diminish accountability, and we are of course going to have the reporting to, and engagement with, the european parliament. i hope this will be more substantive, because it would be a well thought-out, longer-term programme. there was a question on whether this money is only revamping what already exists in our budget. the answer is that a big chunk of it is fresh money. we have taken a billion from the edf reserve. this is money that is now added specifically to deal with this crisis. we have also found and relocated funds from lower-priority activities to what we believe is right now our top priority, and i think this is right to be done. we have been criticised, and unfortunately those who made this criticism were here to speak but not to listen – if you ask a question it is a good thing to actually wait for the answer. we have a very good track record in the european union in development programmes, and in particular in humanitarian aid. the uk government has ranked us – my former service that is, and i am very proud for the people there – as a top performer for a good reason, because we have eyes and ears on the ground and we are very connected to what the priorities are. we have been deploying our resources to aid people in syria. the point was made that we only help the neighbourhood but not inside syria. that is not correct. half of our humanitarian aid goes inside syria and about half of that goes to rebel-controlled areas. no, we are not going to disclose with whom we work there, because that would put people at risk – but we have a very strong presence there. we are one of the very few funders that have never given up on the most affected parts of syria where bombs fall and people are living in tragic circumstances. the point was made a couple of times that we are wasteful and that our accounts have not been signed off for 20 years in a row. wrong. our accounts have been signed off for eight years in a row; the last signing came yesterday. we should not mix up errors, which are undesirable but are what they are, with waste or fraud, which they are not. errors such as people incorrectly filing documents on how money is being used are errors, not fraud. i think we have to be clear that yes, we are facing an enormous challenge. this is hugely important for europe’s own standing, and we will face this much more effectively working together. i hope we will see that these trust funds – which are, by the way, a new platform for action – will gain more traction and that we will see more contributions from our member states and, i would also say, from others. there have been some encouraging signals, for example from the us, that they may now join us in the syria trust fund; whether directly or through parallel financing remains to be seen. finally, i want to thank parliament very much for engaging in this topic, for its call for more joined-up action and for member states to join us. i will finish with special thanks to luxembourg, and to minister schmit. if only all were like you!
president of the council. madam president, i have little to add to what the vice-president has just said. i believe that we are in an absolute emergency and that we must now actually mobilize the resources we need. it is true that some member states may not have responded sufficiently and that not all commitments have been met. i will convey the strong message of parliament that the commitments are absolutely respected and fulfilled. it must also be said openly that there are no two absolutely separate entities: there is no union with its budget on one side and the member states on the other. what we do, we do as the european union. while some contributions come from the union budget, and therefore from the member states, and other resources come from the member states, they must be combined. i believe what you just said about the trust fund, which we should also open. i think you have pointed out a crucial point, as have others among you: this issue concerns europe first and foremost, because it is taking place in its neighbourhood, and it affects us because people are coming to europe. but in reality, this is not just a european problem, it is an international crisis. it is therefore quite clear that if we are to act, we must also involve the entire international community and in particular a number of states which have a vested interest in our successfully managing this crisis. the second point is of course the longer term. i think that's the whole point of development. perhaps we should also rethink our development policies a little, because we cannot conclude that they have been a success. should we look at where the money goes? how efficiently are we spending it? how can we engage the countries in question - insofar as we can engage them since, as has been raised, we are sometimes in situations where there is no state, there is no beginning of the rule of law, etc.? so there is also a major problem, because when we talk about eritrea, for example, we know very well that there is a regime somewhere that is making people flee, young people because eventually, they are forced to spend their lives in an army that they reject. so i think that there is a difficult point to be solved here and, of course, action must be taken in the long term. i conclude from this extremely rich debate that a clear message must be given, that the only solution to overcome these problems is a solution of solidarity, there are no others. it is not by betting on one or the other, by carrying out an action separate from the overall action that we will achieve results. that is the conclusion i draw from the speeches made by your parliament.
in writing. the commission has set up two trust funds as part of the package of measures adopted to deal with the refugee crisis: the eu regional trust fund in response to the syrian crisis (the madad fund) and the emergency trust fund for stability and addressing the root causes of irregular migration and displaced persons movements in africa. through them, the eu is stepping up its response to today's challenges, as a complementary tool to the development cooperation already in place in the region to help the most fragile and vulnerable countries in africa. the eu budget financing for both funds amounts to eur 500 million for the madad fund and eur 1.8 billion for the trust fund for africa. while member states have committed to making voluntary contributions to reach the amount equivalent to eu funding, to date this contribution only amounts to eur 78.2 million. we therefore call on the member states to honour the commitments made by their heads of state or government at the september, october and november summits.

the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. so perhaps we should refer this to the bureau of parliament so that it can study and see how many times the last debates in the house have dealt with issues relating to equality between men and women. for those of us here, it is not something that is on the back burner, it is an absolute priority for the european institutions. i now turn to the question of the daphne programme to combat gender-based violence. i wanted to start by giving you some statistics. in march 2014, the european union agency for fundamental rights produced a report on gender-based violence with some truly chilling data: 33 percent of european women, according to a survey, had been victims of physical, sexual, occupational violence of various types throughout their lives. 33% of women! an estimated nine million european women have been victims of violence. these data became an alarm and indicate the need for action in this matter. i'll give you more details. so far this year, in spain, in my country, 44 women have been killed as victims of gender-based violence. and i can say the figures because a law we have in our country, a comprehensive law on gender violence, makes it possible to have real data on the situation, which at european level does not happen. today in europe we have no uniform criteria for determining the scale of what we are talking about when we refer to a reality which we know to be a social scourge and on which action is necessary, essential and urgent. today we're talking about the daphne program. the overall objective of the daphne programme is to prevent and combat all forms of violence, whether they occur in the private or public sphere. it also aims to achieve a high level of protection of health, well-being and cohesion, and is open to ngos, public institutions and associations. it was set up in 1997 as an initiative to promote the action of non-governmental organisations and to establish better cooperation. the european commission has decided to include the daphne programme in the general programme on rights, equality and citizenship for the period 2014-2020. at the time when this decision was taken, this parliament, civil society organisations and women's organisations were opposed to it, because it was essential for us that there should be a specific european programme to combat gender-based violence, because the visibility of this reality is essential to raise the awareness of those of us who have the obligation and responsibility to act in this area. finally it could not remain as a specific programme and remained in the rights, equality and citizenship programme. the programme aims to prevent and combat all forms of violence against children, young people and women, as well as violence against other groups at risk. the financial allocation for the implementation of this programme, in the period 2014-2020, amounts to eur 439 million; 43% of the funds correspond to group 2, which is the fight against violence against children, young people and women. and we want to bring this up for debate and we want to ask the european commission how these objectives are going to be pursued in the context of the new rights, equality and citizenship programme, and we also want clarification on the amount of specific funding for the fight against and prevention of gender-based violence. since we have not been able to maintain a specific programme and it has been generalized into a global programme, we want to know what the european commission's intentions are on what specific funding will be available in this area, what programmes will be able to be financed in cooperation with the member states, with social organisations, with civil society, because we are talking about an urgency, and it is therefore necessary that, from the member states and from the european commission, we get down to work to end, as i say, the greatest social lacracy europe currently has.
member of the commission.– madam president, yes, the statistical figures are shocking. the latest figures which were delivered by the fundamental rights agency and from other surveys really show that there is a huge instance of violence against women – and the numbers are not decreasing. we are fully aware of the need for better collection of data to address this problem properly and also the need for effective campaigning against violence against women. another of the means which we traditionally use is funding grassroots activities and supporting member states’ activities. there is continuity: we have funded activities contributing to fighting violence against women under the daphne programme, and we continue to do so also within the 2014-2020 multiannual financial framework, under the rights, equality and citizenship programme. it is our priority, and the objective must remain highly visible. this is why we have kept referring to ‘daphne’ activities in the annual work programmes of the rights, equality and citizenship programme for 2014 and 2015. we want to make clear that, although the name of the programme from which the relevant funding is made has changed, the objective of fighting violence against women remains high on the agenda. this is also the reason why relevant calls for proposals published on the dg justice website always contain a specific reference to the daphne objective, both in their title and in their text. a filtering mechanism has been set up which allows searching per programme and per priority. this means it is possible for interested ngos to have an overview on one page of all upcoming, open and closed daphne calls. a reference to daphne is also included on the website presenting the rights, equality and citizenship programme. we follow the same approach in all communication activities relating to funding opportunities under the rights, equality and citizenship programme. in particular, in order to raise awareness about the funding possibilities under the new programme, reference to daphne is always made when the commission holds information events. the commission has so far organised eight such information events in cooperation with member states. the commission also participated in several meetings of stakeholders, where we were invited to present the funding opportunities under the new programmes. in their relations with member states and in the relevant conferences, the commission representatives will continue to refer to daphne funding and to highlight its essential role in combating violence against women. before going into the details of the specific amounts to be spent and the actions to be funded, i would like to stress that clarity and transparency – allowing parliament and citizens to scrutinise the use made of public funding – are a must. in this respect, dg justice publishes the award decision of each of its calls for proposals and the summaries of the projects selected for funding, including amounts and partners involved, on the website. in addition, a first monitoring report on the programme’s implementation for the budgetary year 2014 will be transmitted to parliament and the council at the beginning of 2016. it will contain information on the use of funds per specific objective, thus also including daphne and gender equality. now to the details. the whole amount reserved for the daphne specific objective in the 2015 annual work programme is eur 14 million. the main part of it will be spent on concrete, tangible projects, awarded through five different calls for proposals. i insist that they must make a real difference to the lives of women and children in the eu. the first of these calls is already under evaluation. with an amount of eur 3 million, it targets women and girls and addresses sexual harassment and sexual violence against women and girls. two other calls, for a total amount of eur 3.4 million, will specifically target children: one on the elimination of corporal punishment, to be launched in november, and one dedicated to support the already existing european hotlines for missing children under the phone number 116, which is currently open. in this case, the aim is to support the integration of hotlines into child protection systems rather than have them as stand-alone services, and to put in place structures and measures to ensure their sustainability after the end of the union funding. the fourth call aims at supporting victims. also to be published in november, it will tap funds from both the rights, equality and citizenship programme under the daphne objective, and from the justice programme. eur 3 million will stem from the rights, equality and citizenship programme, plus eur 2 million from the justice programme, amounting to eur 5 million in total. this call will address, in a comprehensive way, victims of violence and crime and will contribute to the implementation of the victims’ directive. the deadline for member states to transpose the directive is 16 november this year – in a few days. the funding will help women and children who are victims of violence to benefit from the rights deriving from the directive, such as the right to specialised support services. a fifth call for a total amount of eur 3 million will encourage multi-agency and multi-disciplinary cooperation to respond to violence against women and/or children, and encourage victims and witnesses to report incidents of violence. in addition, about eur 1.1 million of the 2015 budget will be spent on supporting european organisations and networks that work to combat violence against women and children. about eur 370 000 will be spent on procurement activities, for example for carrying out a necessary study on migrants’ attitudes towards female genital mutilation. the same general approach applies to the specific objective of the promotion of equality between women and men. i want policies with a tangible impact and a focus on implementing existing legislation. the whole amount reserved for this specific objective in the 2015 annual work programme is around eur 7 million. under the 2015 annual work programme, a call for an amount of eur 3.4 million will be launched in the coming months to finance projects presenting innovative answers to educational and occupational labour-market segregation. the aim is to promote good practices on gender roles and to overcome gender stereotypes in education and training and in the workplace. finally, for 2016, nearly eur 1 million has been reserved to support the work of the european women’s lobby as well as around eur 1 million funding for gender equality-related research. let me also add from my side the comment that for me also the timing for the discussions on gender topics is rather problematic because they are held every time very late at night. it also gives me the impression that this topic is a secondary-level one.

polčák’s questions: yes, we of course cooperate with the relevant bodies, and not only with ngos but with governmental bodies – with the relevant ministries – and we try to plan together with them the will come back to this topic later in november and, as i said before, i am ready to put the issue into the wider context of the gender policy which we are planning for the next three years.
in writing. the fight against gender-based violence is the most widespread human rights violation in europe and the rest of the world, and affects all strata of society. the general objective of the daphne programme is to prevent and combat all forms of violence, whether in the public or private sphere, affecting children, young people and women, including sexual exploitation and trafficking in human beings, by taking preventive measures and offering support and protection to victims and groups at risk. the projects funded have been a real success in popularity and effectiveness. the commission decided, despite opposition from parliament and civil society, to include daphne in the new rights, equality and citizenship programme 2014-2020. it is essential that the name 'daphne' be retained within the framework of that programme in order to ensure the visibility of the objectives of combating violence and to achieve a wider dissemination of funding opportunities. it is also important that the commission ensures the transparency of information on actions selected for funding and their contribution to the achievement of the set objectives.

in writing. gender-based violence in all its forms affects more than nine million women, but the commission does not seem to be aware of the seriousness of the situation. we are still waiting for the future strategy on gender policies (2016-2019), but the signals are not good. the daphne programme on gender-based violence has been diluted in the multiannual framework on rights and citizenship, reducing the visibility and relevance of an essential programme, while doubts exist about its budget allocation. i am of course concerned about the uncertainties in funding - as my colleagues have pointed out - but this invisibility is no less serious because, increasingly, it seems as if gender-based violence and the murder of women have acquired a certain air of inevitability, an element of banality. we must fight this situation with active mobilization and education, because social condemnation of violence is one of the most effective measures to denounce these facts. it is this ideological and cultural battle that we must wage.

madam president, a ghost is haunting europe, a ghost called democracy. the european union has a problem of coherence and respect for its own democratic principles, especially today in the field of economic governance, with the euro area and greece as the most visible examples. but let us look at three illustrations which are very different from each other, but which have the same effect on the idea and reality of europe. first, this afternoon, in voting on the electoral law, we deny proportionality, we dare not speak of a "european list" - we say a "transnational list" - and we pass the real decision to the states. even in the seat of the democratic representation of the 500 million europeans we are not able to act as such: we resign. secondly, the action plan which the union is proposing to turkey. we close our eyes to the lack of respect for the rule of law and freedom of expression and we are prepared to compensate for this with a containment and surveillance service. thirdly, the case of the state against catalonia. here we have the opposite abuse: the law was used against democracy. the reason for the state is invoked against the democratic will of the majority in a parliament as legitimate as this one and, incidentally, very explicitly pro-european.
madam president, this very evening the regional government of catalonia has declared itself in rebellion before the constitutional court and has decided to sabotage democracy and to act directly against the fundamental rights of more than half of catalans and most of the spanish people. in the last legislature, that regional government began to implement an illegal secession strategy with respect to the rest of the spanish nation. it affects the sovereignty of all of us - the spanish people - and it substantially affects the rule of law and democracy. in the heart of europe, the most corrupt political class in our nation is running forwards and, to hide the operation, they behave like populists who play on the noble identity feelings of many good people. it is an unusual case that looks practically like a coup d'état to democracy in catalonia, without weapons and by chapters. the european union must know, and must explore, how to support the fundamental rights to democracy of so many european spaniards affected.
madam president, the situation of employment in europe cannot be separated from the absence of a strong public sector, which guarantees fair distribution and democratic control of production. this underdevelopment of the public sector, which particularly affects countries such as spain, is based on two pillars. the first is europe's obsession with deficits, which is being used to implement the harsh neoliberal measures. the second is structural tax avoidance, which is encouraged by the governments themselves and the commission through the opacity of tax agreements and tax competition between the states. we are watching closely the commission's new proposals on corporate taxation. we are pleased that work is being done towards harmonizing corporation tax and linking it to the real economy, but we lack confidence, political confidence. the european institutions are complicit with the multinationals in their strategy of circumvention, as demonstrated by the false closure of the luxleaks investigation committee. so we have to end this situation now.
madam president, the day before yesterday, 9 november, the parliament of catalonia adopted by an absolute majority a declaration which marked the beginning of the construction of the catalan republic. this is the mandate given to the democratically elected members of parliament in the recent catalan elections. the spanish state has offered no alternative and has repeatedly refused to allow a referendum on catalan independence. three days after that declaration, the state bodies have put in place mechanisms of prohibition and punishment, that is, exclusively of repression. it is difficult to understand why the spanish government and political forces have not had the democratic capacity to initiate any kind of dialogue or rapprochement to address the majority wish of the citizens of catalonia. democracy in catalonia will continue its journey, despite the sanctions and repression, because the democratic will of the people always comes first. we have said this many times in this house.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it is an initiative aimed at improving european citizens' access to public services and their rights. this report proposes a programme on interoperability solutions for public administrations in the eu; these solutions at european level are aimed at being compatible across the 28 member states. this reduces compatibility costs and facilitates mobility and access to public services for citizens moving from one member state to another within the eu. the report also stresses the need to tackle the digital divide and ensure that smes have access to such solutions. electronic interoperability represents an opportunity to improve the functioning of the public sector by increasing the services it can offer to citizens. i therefore decided to vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report on interoperability solutions as a means of modernising the public sector because of its importance after the agreement with the council. interoperability increasingly promotes the potential quality of public services and creates a context of increased competitiveness for businesses and greater satisfaction for citizens. it is also the achievement of the digital market. in addition, the exploitation of the potential of the decision in question implies a greater emphasis on the economic and social appropriation of the programme.
in writing. ‒ parliament supports the launch of the isa2 programme, which is needed to provide technological solutions to facilitate interoperability in electronic communications both cross-border and cross-sectoral, in areas such as e-government, health, invoicing or public procurement. the programme is intended to modernise public administrations and to make further progress in the implementation of transnational services in europe. the commission shall be assisted by the european parliament and the council. thanks to the contributions made by parliament, interoperability efforts between the different levels of public administrations - local, national, european - as well as with various eu agencies have been strengthened, and regional and local administrations have been included among the beneficiaries of structural funds for the development of interoperable solutions. in addition, as the spanish socialists demand, parliament has succeeded in introducing the principle of combating digital exclusion, so that the development of interoperable public services takes account of the most disadvantaged citizens as well as the least populated areas in order to combat the digital divide. i have therefore voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ this new programme, isa2, will ensure better interoperability of online administrative services across europe, with solutions made available to administrations, whether national or local. it will contribute to the modernisation of public services and the realisation of the european digital market and will enable citizens and businesses to benefit from better quality online services across europe, while respecting the existing rules on private data. that is why i supported this report.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this agreement because, although the text of the european parliament's report was watered down during the negotiations with the council, the main points are mainly mentioned in the recitals, or there is a reference to the legislation in force: the issue of net neutrality (paragraph 32 and reference to the tsm proposal) or data protection (article 16, paragraph 43). we also believe that the modernisation of the increasingly interconnected public sector is essential to meet the demands of individuals, who are used to the continuous modernisation of the private sector.

in writing. ‒ i strongly support interoperability in the eu in all possible fields. interoperability is a fundamental element of the connecting europe facility (cef) in order to complete the single market in the railways sector, for example removing regulatory and physical barriers. but interoperability is also essential in the public administrations and digital world. common solutions, promotion of good practices, technological neutrality and adaptability should be a key priority. principles of security, privacy and protection of personal data should always be applied. in this respect, net neutrality is of the uttermost importance to ensure that there is no discrimination between internet services and competition is fully guaranteed.

in writing. ‒ we are discussing a report on the proposal for a decision of the european parliament and of the council establishing a programme on interoperability solutions for european public administrations, businesses and citizens (isa2). in this way, it is intended to continue the effort of the isa programme, supporting cooperation between public administrations in the service of community acts and policies on the basis of an effective and efficient use of information technologies for the establishment of cross-border public services, and contributing to the removal of barriers to cross-border interactions due to the lack of interoperability and common solutions. i therefore consider it necessary to vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it is an initiative aimed at improving european citizens' access to public services and their rights. this report proposes a programme on interoperability solutions for public administrations in the eu; these solutions at european level are aimed at being compatible across the 28 member states. this reduces compatibility costs and facilitates mobility and access to public services for citizens moving from one member state to another within the eu. the report also stresses the need to tackle the digital divide and ensure that smes have access to such solutions. electronic interoperability represents an opportunity to improve the functioning of the public sector by increasing the services it can offer to citizens. i therefore decided to vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ the report on interoperability solutions as a means of modernising the public sector is absolutely necessary. this new package will enable a programme to be established on interoperability solutions for european public administrations, businesses and citizens. there is no doubt that improvements to existing cross-border and cross-sector interoperability solutions are needed. the eu must develop and exploit new interoperability solutions and be able to analyse and evaluate future solutions at european level. this is good news for businesses, especially smes. it is also for public administration; interoperability is a means of modernising the public sector. finally, and most importantly, it is good news for the citizens of europe.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it is a reform which will help, among other things, to strengthen the democratic dimension of european elections, to give greater legitimacy to the work of the european parliament and to guarantee greater electoral equality for citizens. in particular, i welcome the fact that it has been agreed that the political groups should nominate formal candidates for the presidency of the commission at least 12 weeks before the european elections and that all countries should set a minimum threshold of votes (between 3% and 5%) for parliamentary representation. i also welcome the adoption of the following measures: - creation of ballot papers with greater visibility of the name and logo of the european parties; - creation of a european electoral constituency with lists headed by the candidate nominated by each political family for the post of president of the commission; - study of the harmonisation of the minimum voting age at 16 years; - possibility of allowing voting by mail, e-mail and internet. finally, i regret that the use of instruments such as the rack lists or other equivalent methods to ensure gender equality has been rejected.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because there are several points in it with which i cannot agree in any way. the report does not contemplate the possibility of the president of the european commission being democratically elected by direct suffrage among the european citizens. i refuse to give the democratic character of the present method of electing the president of the commission after the adoption of the treaty of lisbon, as described in the report. i am also against the idea of a european constituency where 26 meps are directly elected from lists of european parties. i am also not in favour of requiring national parties to include the logo of the european party on the ballot. this should be left to the choice of each national party. i have therefore not voted in favour of the own-initiative report.
in writing. ‒ through the reform of the european electoral law we had a unique opportunity to make european elections more than an evaluation of national politics, to bring an institution like the european parliament closer to the citizens and to make parliamentarians, their representatives, subject to the scrutiny of the people. although some improvements have been made, such as the establishment of joint lists or transnational lists to encourage citizen participation, progress has been limited on most issues. the result has been a very unambitious text. moreover, the establishment of a mandatory electoral threshold only puts obstacles in the way of representative democracy, since it does not take into account the particularities of each state. this law is a clear example that doing things quickly doesn't mean doing them better.
in writing. ‒ i appreciate the work done on the report by the rapporteurs and the alternative rapporteurs but i had to vote against the report because there was no possibility of not setting a threshold for the european elections. my party, being a regional party, has to run in coalition with others in order to get representation in the house; if there were constituencies, we would have got two mps. at present there is no threshold in the spanish state for these elections and therefore i cannot vote in favour of their inclusion.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because it includes among its main amendments the introduction of a mandatory threshold in european elections for countries with a single electoral constituency (this type of constituency is the one that exists in spain). the introduction of a mandatory threshold makes it impossible for certain political parties or platforms to be represented in the european parliament and undermines citizens' equal voting rights. supporters of this option say it will avoid fragmentation in the european parliament and the arrival of eurosceptics. in my view, these fears must be allayed by conveying to our citizens pride in the project we are defending. during the preparation of this report, amendments were tabled which directly contradict my view of representation in the european parliament. just as i am critical of the introduction of a mandatory threshold limiting the representation of the will of the citizens, i am critical of my own group for trying to introduce a nuance favouring fragmenting regional parties; the proposal has been to reduce the mandatory threshold required, in order to favour their representation over others at national level. this is only taking us further away from the building of a people's europe.

in writing. ‒ the european elections are of particular importance because they involve the european citizen in the process of european construction, allowing him to elect the representatives he considers most suited to shape the european policies from which he will then benefit. however, so far, more than elections with a european dimension, they have been a sum of national elections. it was therefore time to vote in favour of the standardisation of the rules governing these elections. i think it is particularly necessary to set thresholds to prevent members representing only the interests of very small communities from being represented in the european parliament. it is precisely the european project that is moving away from particular interests to defend common interests. however, because of the existence of zoning lists and positive quotas, i have had to vote against this resolution. i am in favour of achieving a greater and more balanced representation of women in political life, but i believe in the principle of merit and not in that of discrimination, even if it is positive.
in writing. ‒ we voted against the report on the reform of eu electoral law. in principle, we believe that a reform of the legislation is necessary, which focuses on the need for eu parties to modernise and to make proposals, for example on candidates, which are accompanied by the necessary principles of transparency. we believe that the report and some of the amendments, which focus on transparency, the primaries, gender equality, the possibility of using zip-lines, are the first necessary steps towards modernising the eu, towards access to the european parliament and towards making it truly representative of the society it represents. we believe that the necessary plurality of this parliament must be a red line and that the proposals on thresholds may force us to vote against them, because they undermine the foundations on which the electoral system and the eu itself are built.

in writing. ‒ i voted with regret against this resolution. i am completely in favour of a greater degree of europeanisation of the european elections, but for me it is unacceptable that with the new rules, regional parties like mine can become excluded from the european parliament due to high thresholds. if this is the way to go, the motto of the eu should become ‘united in uniformity’.
in writing. ‒ we voted against the report on the reform of eu electoral law. in principle, we believe that a reform of the legislation is necessary, which focuses on the need for eu parties to modernise and to make proposals, for example on candidates, which are accompanied by the necessary principles of transparency. we believe that the report and some of the amendments, which focus on transparency, the primaries, gender equality, the possibility of using zip-lines, are the first necessary steps towards modernising the eu, towards access to the european parliament and towards making it truly representative of the society it represents. we believe that the necessary plurality of this parliament must be a red line and that the proposals on thresholds may force us to vote against them, because they undermine the foundations on which the electoral system and the eu itself are built.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it is a reform which will help, among other things, to strengthen the democratic dimension of european elections, to give greater legitimacy to the work of the european parliament and to guarantee greater electoral equality for citizens. in particular, i welcome the fact that it has been agreed that the political groups should nominate formal candidates for the presidency of the commission at least 12 weeks before the european elections and that all countries should set a minimum threshold of votes (between 3% and 5%) for parliamentary representation. i also welcome the adoption of the following measures: - creation of ballot papers with greater visibility of the name and logo of the european parties; - creation of a european electoral constituency with lists headed by the candidate nominated by each political family for the post of president of the commission; - study of the harmonisation of the minimum voting age at 16 years; - possibility of allowing voting by mail, e-mail and internet. finally, i regret that the use of instruments such as the rack lists or other equivalent methods to ensure gender equality has been rejected.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because there are several points in it with which i cannot agree in any way. the report does not contemplate the possibility of the president of the european commission being democratically elected by direct suffrage among the european citizens. i refuse to give the democratic character of the present method of electing the president of the commission after the adoption of the treaty of lisbon, as described in the report. i am also against the idea of a european constituency where 26 meps are directly elected from lists of european parties. i am also not in favour of requiring national parties to include the logo of the european party on the ballot. this should be left to the choice of each national party. i have therefore not voted in favour of the own-initiative report.
in writing. ‒ i do agree with the reform of eu electoral legislation, as i believe it has very positive consequences for the european union as a whole. on the one hand, it aims to enhance the participation of european union citizens in decision-making and to facilitate the means through which they can express their vote. it also helps all europeans to become more aware of the way the european institutions work and therefore feel more involved when they vote. the aim is to increase the popularity of european parties in each member state and to create a level playing field for the various participants in european elections. i believe that this is a major step towards the integration and cohesion of the eu. however, i do not agree with the lowering of the minimum voting age to 16 years, as i consider it to be a measure contrary to the spanish constitution and the definition of 'age of majority', with all the responsibilities that this entails.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this resolution because it sets out a privatisation agenda and does not offer solutions to the main problems facing the sector. with an exclusive focus on competitiveness and the internationalisation of the sector, this resolution continues the drive towards the development of the single european airspace, which implies a liberalisation and privatisation of the operation of the different national airspaces. the privatisation of air services only creates problems for users, public coffers and even safety standards. the commission is nevertheless pursuing its neoliberal agenda, which is limited to competitiveness and the internationalisation of the sector. nor does this resolution address the more serious problems of social dumping and the lowering of safety standards in the sector. it is for all these reasons that i have decided to vote against this resolution.
in writing. ‒ the resolution we have just adopted is the european parliament's contribution to the package on the aviation sector which the european commission will present before the end of the year. this package will be essential to create the conditions that will make this sector one of the most competitive and sustainable, while improving the rules that guarantee the highest level of safety in our airspace, for which we call for the definitive implementation of the so-called single european sky. the text also points out the clear link between working conditions in the aviation sector and flight safety. we therefore call on the commission to put an end to harmful business practices such as fake freelancers, zero-hour contracts or pay-to-fly programmes. we are voting in favour of a resolution which deals with the regulatory requirements for improving competitiveness as well as with the social and labour standards in the sector.
in writing. ‒ the loss of competitiveness of certain european airlines in relation to companies from third countries that receive subsidies and compete on unequal terms requires measures to enable eu airlines and airports to compete: introducing reciprocity clauses, requiring greater control by states, eliminating unfair commercial practices and abusing some of the loopholes in european legislation or signing agreements with third countries to regulate access to control of companies. in addition, the conditions of workers in the sector are deteriorating, which may also have an impact on aviation safety. it is important that workers in this sector remain highly qualified professionals whose working conditions cannot be further degraded. the definition of the place of establishment of the company and its employees must be clarified, since there are abuses by certain airlines, such as some low-cost airlines. as this resolution calls for, these issues must be included in the package of measures on aviation which the commission will adopt in december, and i have therefore voted in favour of it.

in writing. ‒ in view of the adoption by the european commission of an aviation package in december, i supported today this resolution which underlines the need to support the competitiveness of the european airlines, airports and the aeronautic industry to better face international competition in the sector. the resolution also encourages innovation, for instance in the fields of digitalisation, to improve air traffic management and to ensure the security of passengers.
in writing. ‒ on 2 december, the commission presented a set of documents called the aviation package, which aimed to define the future strategy for the eu's aviation sector. the joint resolution by the epp, s&d and alde groups follows this line and insists on strengthening the competitiveness of the sector as a matter of priority, barely mentioning the social aspects. in these circumstances, it could be that such competitiveness vis-à-vis third countries was achieved by dumping. in an attempt to avoid this possibility, if the amendments tabled by the gue/ngl group, which reject privatisation and stress the need to preserve and strengthen jobs and working conditions in the sector, as well as the protection of workers and users in the event of the bankruptcy of airlines, had been accepted in this vote, we would have voted in favour of the resolution. but since they were rejected, we voted against.

in writing. ‒ i strongly support the resolution we are putting forward today. in particular i support paragraphs 6 and 7, which are a clear message to commissioner bulc. on fair competition, dg move and dg comp have to become more closely involved, especially regarding state aid. it is quite evident that regulation 868/2004 on protection against unfair pricing practice in the air transport sector has proven ineffective or at least inadequate as regards the kind of competition coming from gulf carriers. the commission knows very well that such amount of subsidies would clearly be considered illegal state aid if applied to any eu companies. the status quo is not an option. eu airlines must continue to restructure and become more efficient. however, the eu must act fast with regard to unfair competition, ensure reciprocity and eliminate unfair practices, including subsidies and state aid to airlines from third countries that clearly distort the market. the ec should include and insert a binding and transparent fair competition clause in eu external aviation relations regarding the eu rules on the ownership and control of eu airlines, the ec should propose changes in the aviation package with regard to the vague concept of effective control. regarding airports, i call on the commission to establish a public list of ‘ghost’ and inefficient airports.
