member of the commission.– mr president, there are now only three weeks left until the 10th wto ministerial conference in nairobi. this will mark the wto’s 20th anniversary and it is the first such conference taking place in africa. this is a conference that is taking place at a critical moment for the wto. following the success of the last such conference in bali and the adoption of the trade facilitation agreement, there were high hopes that we would advance towards a comprehensive agreement on the doha development agenda, and the eu worked really hard to achieve this. unfortunately, many countries have not been able or willing to look for a compromise on cutting the trade-distorting subsidies they provide to their farmers. in nairobi we need to free the machinery of the wto from the constraints that have been holding it back for so many years. we need to move ahead. the ministerial conference needs to take decisions on parts of the doha round and agree on what to do next. we are now working in geneva intensively to create convergence around three main outcomes that are attainable and where we all see that there are development credentials. the first one is to aim for an agreement to discipline the use of all forms of agricultural export support, which is an important long-standing and pro-development issue that needs a coherent, balanced and multilateral solution. together with the government of brazil and a few other wto members, the european union has tabled a formal proposal for a comprehensive solution addressing agricultural export subsidies, but also export credits and other similar measures. i am convinced that this is a good basis for discussion and a compromise, and it also showcases the positive effects of the major agricultural reforms that we have been conducting here in the eu. without them, it would have been impossible to achieve a situation where we table a joint agricultural proposal with brazil. so we are now working on this in geneva to gather support. secondly, we also need to make sure that we can deliver for the benefit of the poorest and most vulnerable wto members: the least-developed countries. here we are looking at, for instance, duty-free; quota-free; cotton; rules of origin. the third item where we need to deliver is an outcome strengthening notification and transparency requirements in the wto. achieving consensus on these issues will be linked to the need for an agreement on the path forward for the wto after the ministerial conference. this is going to be challenging. our interests here are very clear. the wto needs to continue the work on unresolved issues. they can only be effectively addressed by multilateral solutions – trade-distorting domestic support in agriculture, rules or regulatory issues, for instance – but we need to approach these issues with fresh ideas, as the old approaches have clearly not delivered the result, and in this connection large emerging countries must assume greater responsibilities. similarly, we need to aim to ensure that the ministerial conference begins the process of opening the organization to considering new issues and acknowledges the possibilities for wto members to negotiate issues within smaller groups of interested members. this is really important if the wto is to remain relevant and at the centre of global rule—making. the upcoming ministerial conference will be a very important event. it will have a strong bearing on the future of the multilateral trading system. i appreciate very much the cooperation we have had so far and the interest that this parliament has taken, and i am looking forward to parliament’s delegation being there so we can have close cooperation at the ministerial conference.
on behalf of the ppe group mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, let me first of all congratulate the co-author of this resolution, mr lange, on the fruitful cooperation we have had. i also wish to thank the commissioner and her team, whose fruitful work - as she has stressed - has resulted in this resolution. in the european union, in the european people's party, we have always been firmly committed to multilateralism and obviously the appropriate framework for taking it forward is, without a doubt, the world trade organisation. this approach, as shown by agreements such as the trade facilitation agreement, is aimed in particular at improving the economic situation of all its member countries. because let there be no doubt: greater trade openness, greater economic development. there are many examples to prove this. i think it is worth pointing out that the ministerial conference to be held in nairobi, as the commissioner has rightly pointed out, will be a turning point that we all want and we will all contribute to making it a success, because we need economic growth, we need job creation, now more than ever. and we must not forget that multilateralism must not only coexist with, but also be complemented by, the bilateral agreements, regional agreements and plurilateral agreements through which trade is being liberalized around the world. agreements such as the acp, the atc and the mercosur agreement are now more than ever vital to the union's trade agenda, because they can complement and also promote the work of the world trade organisation in those areas where multilateralism fails to reach.
mr president, commissioner, i fully support the resolution and the excellent work of its rapporteurs, bernd lange and pablo zalba. i want to say loud and clear that the european union remains and must remain strongly committed to multilateralism, playing a leading role and acting as a bridge between the different wto partners in all negotiations. this is no time for regrets. it is time to demand that all members of the organization immediately ratify and implement the trade facilitation agreement and it is also time to demand that they get involved and commit themselves to the conclusion of a long, too long, doha round and to the road map to be followed after the nairobi conference. i won't accept defeat. to do this, i believe and share the commissioner's view that some partners need to come together to reduce distortions in trade in agricultural products and export subsidies; that emerging economies effectively exercise their respective share of responsibility in accordance with their level of development and their involvement in international trade; and that there should be greater flexibility from the advanced countries in favour of the less advanced countries. finally, a reform of the wto is needed: it must strengthen its parliamentary dimension and strengthen its governance so that there can be no doubt about its usefulness and necessity.
mr president, the doha round has faced great challenges. the multilateral approach is not easy because the interests of rich and poor countries are in conflict and the interests of the great economic powers - those of the north - always prevail. this makes it impossible to reach consensus that benefits everyone and especially the most disadvantaged: those in the south. we must not fall into the so-called pragmatism of the easy way represented by the atci, the acs, the ceta or the atp, because these paths are nothing but the imposition of the hegemony of the rich through an agreement between giants, between arrogant. in nairobi, it is crucial to redouble efforts to find a democratic framework for trade where all voices are represented; for international trade to become, once and for all, a tool to overcome inequality, poverty and climate change; and for it to be a driver of well-being for people and not a suppressor of rights and the environment, which is what these 'macro-treatments' are.
mr president, commissioner, i would first of all like to congratulate mr bernd lange and mr pablo zalba on this important resolution, which reflects the european parliament's priorities for the 10th wto ministerial conference to be held in kenya in december. the creation of the wto was a fundamental step towards a more integrated and dynamic trading system. the wto has also assumed that developing countries, countries with economies in transition and least developed countries can take advantage of trade to boost their development. through the wto, the european union has demonstrated its interest in fostering a multilateral framework for trade negotiations that is compatible with bilateral, regional and plurilateral agreements. our environment is changing; the international trading system has changed and will continue to do so in the coming years. we are in a more open system, with new countries in transition that are part of a reality that must be taken into account. we therefore need to maximise the opportunities that trade offers, and that includes supporting structural reform of the wto to ensure a more open and fair trade system that takes into account the interests of smes, micro-enterprises and innovative start-ups. it would also be important to remove trade barriers in highly innovative sectors such as renewable energy, and thus give a strong boost to a fast-growing and job-creating sector.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, you know very well that the success of bali and the success of the wto will only be at the expense of the most disadvantaged and weakest people on the planet: the peasantry and the working classes. because, despite what some of you have said here and some of you have said here, the reality is that the more international trade, the more free trade, the poorer people there are in the world and the more wealth is concentrated in a few hands. and let me remind you that at the 2003 ministerial conference in cancun, mr lee kyung hae, a farmer who was denied a decent life by the world trade organization, took his own life at the gates of this conference to denounce the tragedy of the disappearance of the world's farming economies. it is not time to move forward with the wto, it is time to end it. you also say in the motion for a resolution that the reform of the cap meets the expectations of the wto. the destruction of the livelihoods of thousands of farmers in the european union shows that the wto is a failure for europe and for the world.
member of the commission.– mr president, thank you for this debate, and thank you also to the two rapporteurs, mr zalba and mr lange, for the work that you have been doing. even though there are some dissenting voices, there seems to be a great deal of support for your resolution, so congratulations on that. like most of you, the commission and myself are very committed to the multilateral system. we need to do everything we can to vitalise the wto because, yes, we do need an international forum in which we can split up international rules and to which almost all the countries of the world now belong: 161 and growing. there are so many issues that we need to discuss at global level, so we need to free energy for that in the future. but first, of course, we need to deliver in nairobi. the process is called the doha development round, so we should not forget development: that is the reason for all the efforts made by the commission so far. and yes, mr pereira, we have been working very hard to ally ourselves with other countries – like-minded acp countries that have met many times – in an attempt to see how we can push forward a joint agenda. we need to make sure that the poorest and most vulnerable countries in the world become the beneficiaries of this agreement. and that is why we are looking at export competition. we have tabled proposals to address agricultural export subsidies because they are indeed very damaging to the poor world. we are looking at different development-related issues such as duty-free quotas, free rules of origin, cotton, services, etc. and we are also looking at increasing the transparency of the system. this is not easy. there are many different voices in there, so we are working very hard in geneva. and i would like to say, for the benefit of the colleagues from ukip (who have now all left), that when 28 countries speak unanimously with one voice, as we do in the wto, then of course we have quite a lot of leverage. but that is not enough; there are 161 countries, so we need to move forward. it is possible to have different views on how far we have reformed the cap, but it is true that we, the european union, are the world’s biggest importer of food from the world’s poorest countries. we do not use export subsidies for our food today, and that is why we are pushing for their abolition in nairobi, together with brazil and many others. we are working hard. there are three more weeks. we need to make sure that there is an outcome, but it is not certain yet. we will do whatever we can until the very last moment in nairobi to achieve an agreement on the way forward. and yes, mr. fjellner, i hope that we can also include trade facilitation and push for aid for trade and green goods if that is possible. we are also making progress on the trade in services agreement (tisa), but that would have a parallel track rather than being dealt with in nairobi. and i will be looking forward to regularly meeting the delegation from the european parliament, who i know will be in nairobi. hopefully, when we next discuss this after christmas, we can at least be happy that some conclusions were reached there. if all this fails, it will not be because of the european union.
member of the commission.– madam president, the commission is, as you know, committed to promoting and protecting human rights in all our engagement with third partners, including, of course, with vietnam, which we are discussing tonight. with this aim, we organised a stakeholders’ consultation in may, and the summary paper of the discussion published thereafter highlights the stakeholders’ suggestions for improving the situation of human rights issues and underlines our commitment to transparency and to regular and continued engagement with civil society. i can confirm that issues relating to human rights have been addressed in the context of the eu-vietnam free trade agreement negotiations, with the aim of embedding respect for human rights in the agreement, and also with a view to enhancing its positive impact and minimising the risk of adverse impacts. i have also personally discussed matters with the minister. the preamble of the agreement reaffirms the eu’s and vietnam’s commitment to key international human rights principles and instruments. there is also an institutional and legal link between the free trade agreement and the partnership and cooperation agreement with vietnam. these links ensure that respect for human rights underpins eu-vietnam bilateral relations, including the fta, and enable us to take measures considered appropriate in the event of a breach of the agreement. the fta also contains provisions ensuring the transparency and inclusiveness of the decision-making process and any legal proceedings, thereby strengthening the enabling environment for the respect of human rights, democracy and the rule of law in vietnam. with regard to labour rights, the fta includes an ambitious chapter on trade and sustainable development, and that includes not only respect for all core labour standards and ratification of fundamental ilo conventions and their implementation, but it also pays special attention to corporate social responsibility and fair and ethical trade schemes. the monitoring of human rights development in vietnam is, of course, very important. this will continue to be done primarily through the institutions and structures set up in the pca framework, including the human rights dialogue – and there will be a meeting in a couple of weeks again. we also have a dedicated instrument, the european instrument for democracy and human rights, as you all know. the implementation of the commitments undertaken will be followed up in both the eu and vietnam through the mechanisms and institutions established therein, as well as through the existing eu civil society dialogue and with ex-post evaluations of the fta. i strongly believe – and i think mr lange said the same – that trade liberalisation and human rights can and must go hand in hand. the new communication on trade and investment that the commission published a couple of weeks ago makes it clear that eu trade policy must be for all: citizens; consumers; workers; the self-employed; small, big and medium-sized companies; and the poorest people in the developing countries. it must deliver growth, jobs and innovation, but it has to be responsible, and that means that eu trade policy must defend european values. it has to be effective at delivering economic opportunities and it has to be transparent and open to public scrutiny. human rights are therefore a very important part of this trade strategy. the commission wants to ensure that trade policy contributes to the advancement of human rights in the eu and in third countries, in conjunction with our other policies – foreign policy and development cooperation. let me assure you of the importance of finding this balance between engagement and conditionality. the commission is, as you know, convinced that the policy of engagement is more effective than a policy exclusively based on conditionality, even if that can also play a role. engagement allows us to engage and to create channels for dialogue, keeping them open with a lot of stakeholders involved. we intend to make full use of those channels to promote change on the ground in vietnam. thank you very much for your contribution to this, and you can be sure that we will keep you informed very closely about the development once the agreement is finally concluded.
on behalf of the ppe group madam president, madam commissioner, three years after the signing of the comprehensive framework agreement on partnership and cooperation between the european union and vietnam in 2012, an understanding was reached last august on the free trade agreement - with a communist country, by the way. for the european union, this agreement is of great economic importance, as it is expected to increase and facilitate access to a market with a gdp growth forecast of 6% in 2015 and will also create new investment opportunities. the free trade agreement has a binding relationship with the comprehensive framework agreement on partnership and cooperation, which includes human rights clauses. this link ensures that these principles should govern relations between the european union and vietnam, including trade relations. twenty-five years have passed since the establishment of diplomatic relations and in this period we have seen a progressive improvement in the human rights situation in vietnam. it is true that there are still shortcomings, in particular the continued application of the death penalty and harassment of civil society activists, restrictions on the media and limitations on religious freedom. we must condemn these practices and press for their rapid eradication, but we must not forget that vietnam is taking steps in the right direction. vietnam is currently a member of the united nations human rights council and in 2014 ratified the convention against torture and the convention on the rights of persons with disabilities. we must continue to monitor the human rights situation in vietnam, while not forgetting that the eu's so-called best friend in asean remains a promising ally for the eu in asia.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. madam president, the commission has reached agreement in principle on a free trade agreement with vietnam, and this is a great surprise to us, because the suggestions of this parliament and the recommendations of the european ombudsman himself have not been followed at all. an agreement has been reached without even having carried out a human rights impact assessment in line with the un recommendation, which both the ombudsman and this house were calling for. it is true that the agreement includes the traditional chapter on sustainable development, but we all know that it is insufficient. they are just pretty words with no real framework for their implementation. what guarantees do you have that the parties will meet their obligations? we also consider it essential that attention be paid to the potential impact of the agreement on gender issues. it is essential that the european union's trade policy does not run counter to our gender equality objectives. it is also crucial that the issue of corporate responsibility for violations of human rights and social and environmental standards is addressed. we cannot continue to allow total impunity for big corporations at the expense of the rights of people and the planet. without these elements, the agreement with vietnam will be a new failure of european policy, with dramatic consequences, as always, for the people.
member of the commission.– madam president, of course, trade alone cannot solve all of the world’s human rights problems, but it can make a contribution by enhancing respect for human rights and fostering sustainable development. that is what we are committed to doing in our agreements, especially the one that we are discussing tonight – the agreement with vietnam. nobody denies that there are severe problems relating to human rights in vietnam. you have listed many of them, and i could add a few more. they are there and they are serious. that is why we need to address them and why we are engaging with the vietnamese authorities. there have been some improvements – far from enough – but the vietnamese authorities seem to be willing to engage with us. that is why we have developed tools for doing this. we have the legal link between the fda and the partnership agreement. we will make evaluations, especially looking at the human rights situation. we do have the human rights dialogue that the eeas is conducting. there will be another meeting in a couple of weeks, and we will set up advisory groups with civil society in order to monitor this on the ground with people who are there and are familiar with the daily situation. to explain all this, we will by the end of this year – in a couple of weeks – publish an ad hoc commission paper explaining how the existing measures of the partnership agreement and the negotiated measures of the free trade agreement will contribute to human rights empowerment with the flanking measures that we will put in place and how the human rights i mentioned will be assessed once the latter agreement has entered into force. all this will, of course, be public and transparent so that you can follow and contribute to the dialogue. there is a conditionality clause in all of our agreements to cover very serious breaches, but we prefer whenever possible to work on engagement and to try to establish forums for dialogue to see if we can make improvements. if we have no agreement with vietnam, we will, of course, say no to all such forums. i am not sure whether that would contribute to empowering the people of vietnam. this agreement will be finally concluded next week. very shortly after that it will be published so that you can read it and make your own assessment. then, during the whole translation and legal procedure, there will be plenty of time for discussion, and the commission is ready to enter into that dialogue with you. i can assure you once again that we will keep you informed at all stages and are always ready to take your input, ideas and views into account and to have a dialogue with you on this.
member of the commission.– madam president, we welcome the resolution by parliament on the eu-peru and colombia trade agreement and the accession of ecuador. the accession of ecuador has been agreed between the eu and its member states and peru and colombia and is another step forward in our effort to engage with latin america and consolidate our position in the region. that is important for us. the commission considers that this agreement will be beneficial for both sides. it will enable us to consolidate traditional trade flows while also boosting and diversifying trade and investment on mr president, commissioner, i listened to you carefully and i share the commission's concern about the possibility of reaching the 20% target for renewable energy generation. you have said that we will have to implement and explain this strategy in our countries, but the truth is that, in the case of spain, this is going to be very difficult when we have a government that has stood out for its retroactive cuts in the financing of renewables or for applying a tax on the sun; a government that works in favour of the big oligopolies, the same ones that the european union ignores in its analysis of the market, especially the spanish one: it would seem that the commission sees a pond but not the piranhas that are swimming in it. new interconnectors or price liberalisation are counterproductive when four companies are still allowed to manipulate their marginal costs or force the state to subsidize their notional costs, from nuclear to combined cycle. we need a different energy model: a commitment to saving energy and local generation, from renewable energy to improved coal technology. only then will we have an efficient and sovereign energy system.
mr president, mr vice-president, consumers are a key player in the single energy market or the energy union. i will refer to three key areas where you can actively contribute. first, price and cost transparency, because more information allows for better decision-making. secondly, interoperability, for which standards are essential, and portability, because choosing or changing suppliers strengthens competition in the energy market, without the not insignificant obstacles that still exist for that to happen. and thirdly, digitisation: firstly, to develop intelligent networks that facilitate more efficient connections and distribution; and secondly, to incorporate digital technologies that enable efficient management of individual consumption. in short, a more competitive market, enhancing information, interoperability and portability, together with digitalisation, will determine the better participation of consumers in the european energy market. without consumers, the development of the energy union will be much more difficult and will lack a key player.
mr president, spain's national reform plan announced 17.1% compliance with the 20% renewable energy target for 2020, but both eurostat and the european commission consider that the real figure is 15.8%, i.e. 1.3% lower than the one announced by the government. however, the worrying thing is that, having recognised the need to install 8 537 megawatts of renewable energy to meet the 20% target, the spanish government has only planned an auction of 700 megawatts. in these conditions, there is no time for renewable energy to meet the targets set. the commission notes that the commission has not provided any evidence that the aid granted to the beneficiary was granted in breach of the state aid rules. commissioner, the report on the state of the energy union presented today warns spain that it is worthwhile assessing its policies, whether they are sufficient and effective to meet the renewable energy targets. so i ask you this question: are you planning to wait until 2019 to warn about an announced non-compliance or are you going to take some preventive measure to ensure that spain meets the 20% renewable energy target by 2020?

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the finding that these instruments are no longer applicable to any member state, have lost their relevance in union law and should be repealed.

in writing. ‒ this derogation is devoid of political content and simply concerns the supersession, by means of successive acts, of certain rules which are therefore superseded or contained in other rules. that is why we voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it strengthens scientific cooperation in relation to the conservation of southern bluefin tuna. the world's population of different types of tuna has been at risk, but there are signs of recovery, at least in some of its varieties. scientific cooperation is therefore needed to improve the global information on this resource. the survival of this important species and of the communities that have historically been engaged in its artisanal exploitation depend on well-founded and sustainable fisheries policies. this is the case for atlantic bluefin tuna and almadraba, which is an important indicator of their population; sharing this information should be fundamental to developing sustainable fisheries policies. i therefore decided to vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because the proposal is to authorize the exchange of notes between the eu and the enlarged commission of the convention for the conservation of southern bluefin tuna. the signature of this international legal instrument will enable the eu to move from being a non-cooperating party to the enlarged commission of the btwc to becoming a full member of the btwc.
in writing. ‒ from the perspective of global fisheries governance, it is important that the european union takes the lead in promoting and implementing sustainable fisheries management. the present proposal to include the eu as a full member of the commission for the conservation of southern bluefin tuna (ccsbt), thus abandoning the status of 'non-cooperating party' that it has maintained until now, is in line with this. that is why i support it as rapporteur for the s&d group. this new framework will serve to promote coherence in the eu's approaches across the oceans, for example between the management of southern bluefin tuna (sbct) and that of atlantic bluefin tuna (acaa), while reinforcing its commitment to the long-term conservation and sustainable use of fisheries resources worldwide.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of accession so that the eu can move from being a non-cooperating party to the enlarged commission of the ccsbt to being a full member of it, with the aim of contributing to the rational and sustainable management of marine resources and the fight against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing.
in writing. ‒ i chose to support this proposal, as accession to the extended commission of the convention for the conservation of southern bluefin tuna is a positive step in encouraging a rational and responsible marine conservation. we need to ensure the responsible management and conservation of marine resources, including blue fin tuna, and this proposal encourages their sustainable and responsible harvesting. therefore, i voted in favour of it.
in writing. ‒ this report concerns the accession of the european union to the enlarged commission of the convention for the conservation of southern bluefin tuna (ccsbt). this convention is a regional fisheries organization (rfo). the aim is to have the union accede to the convention in order to have the right to join and vote in the ccsbt, with the aim of strengthening the union's action in the protection of bluefin tuna, given the similarities between the management of southern (indian ocean) bluefin tuna and that of the atlantic. while the intention is commendable, it does raise two problems: on the one hand, once this accession is effective, the member states will be asked to align their positions with that of the union. this is a transfer of sovereignty "underground". on the other hand, the annual fee, estimated at eur 70 000, is not justified by the southern bluefin tuna quotas allocated to europe, which are reduced to 10 tonnes and cover only the incidental catches of our vessels. i therefore abstained, because it is not relevant for the european union to join all the world's rfmos, even for the stated purpose of monitoring stock trends.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour, as the proposal is to authorize the exchange of notes between the eu and the enlarged commission of the convention for the conservation of southern bluefin tuna (ccsbt). the signature of this international legal instrument will allow the eu, which has been a non-party cooperator of the enlarged commission of the btwc since 2006, to become a full member of the commission. the ccsbt convention was open only to states, thus excluding regional economic integration organisations (reois) such as the eu. the tcctb amended the resolution governing the enlarged commission at its 20th meeting in october 2013 to allow ories that so wish to become members of the enlarged commission (the only status they could have been granted until then was that of non-party cooperators) through an exchange of notes procedure in which the applicant body expresses to the tcctb its firm commitment to respect the terms of the convention and to comply with the decisions of the enlarged commission of the tcctb.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this proposal for a directive which aims to increase transparency and consumer rights in the insurance market. in particular, it seeks to avoid that financial service users are obliged to accept the purchase of insurance when they contract with financial institutions. such rules help to ensure strict regulation of financial markets and products, which is especially necessary after the crisis that started in the summer of 2007, which highlighted the very negative consequences of deregulation promoted by neoliberal policies. the agenda for financial regulation is a priority for the european socialists and social democrats, and we will therefore continue to work along these lines throughout this legislature.
in writing. ‒ i could not vote in favour of this report because, although it contains positive elements on consumer protection, the result of the tripartite dialogue will not contribute to improving the transparency of the sector. the directive provides for greater consumer protection and improved information and transparency on certain products. however, it excludes the insurance of investments and financial products, which is a complex network that can sometimes conceal speculative operations based on risk management. in order to avoid impacts that may even reach the sovereign debt, as happened during 2012, full transparency in relation to these activities is necessary, something that this directive does not propose. i could not therefore vote in favour.

in writing. ‒ this directive amends the previous legislation on the sale of insurance by insurance intermediaries (or brokers). the legislation aims to increase transparency in the market by ensuring a level playing field for the various players. however, the directive has not gone as far as it could: brokers are still not obliged to inform customers of the commissions they charge and the transparency requirements will not apply to the whole insurance market. we have therefore decided to abstain.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour because i consider it unacceptable that today in europe one in four children is at risk of poverty and social exclusion and 20 million do not have access to a hot meal a day. it is imperative that we ensure that all children have access to health, education, decent housing and adequate food. the socialists have therefore proposed the establishment of a child guarantee as part of an integrated european plan to combat child poverty, which also includes programmes to provide help and opportunities for parents to get out of situations of social exclusion and to integrate into the labour market. in this connection, we deeply regret that the proposal is not accompanied by a specific guarantee fund, since the european right as a whole has not supported its creation. the report also calls on the commission to make the fight against child poverty a central priority of the new annual growth survey 2016, because investing in children is not just investing in the future of the eu, but is a matter of social justice.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it situates the causes of child poverty in its true structural framework and not in the family context, as is often the case in neoliberal proposals. the fundamental role of the right to health, education and social protection, in addition to the right to decent work, is recognised in the fight against child poverty. this highlights the need to build a different society, and not just adopt other policies, to put an end to this serious social problem.

in writing. ‒ more than one in four children in the eu is at risk of poverty and social exclusion. this figure has risen alarmingly as a result of the economic crisis and the continuing social cuts by some european governments, such as the popular party government in spain. a unicef report on childhood in spain revealed that investment in childhood fell by 14.6% between 2010 and 2013, that is, 775 euros per child were cut, thus returning to figures before 2007. this report shows once again the commitment of this parliament to the fight against child poverty, in accordance with the commitments it has made in the framework of the united nations convention on the rights of the child and the 2030 agenda for sustainable development. we therefore voted in favour, although we deeply regret that no agreement was reached on the creation of a specific fund to combat child poverty, which would have allowed for more investment, more efficient use of the funds and better monitoring of their use.

in writing. - poverty is not just a question of money. in addition to the inability to access children's basic needs such as food, clothing and housing, poverty is also linked to social exclusion and lack of access to quality health and education. the eu and the un convention on the rights of the child must therefore continue to work to ensure that children have access to these rights. this week meps overwhelmingly adopted a resolution calling on eu countries to redouble their efforts to combat child poverty and social inequalities. and this draft report proposes a series of measures to eliminate poverty and social exclusion among children, and is therefore on the right track to make further progress in reducing child poverty and its consequences.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour because i am convinced that, as stated in the united nations convention on the rights of the child, all children should be guaranteed the right to education, health services, housing, protection, participation in decisions affecting them, leisure and free time, a balanced diet and care in the family environment. the eu must therefore legislate to comply with the provisions of the convention. we cannot allow child poverty to grow in europe, as all the reports indicate. social inequalities reproduce disadvantages across generations, and the negative effects of poverty and social exclusion on children can last a lifetime. the eu must therefore do more and better to eradicate the scourge of child poverty and inequalities.

in writing. ‒ this report received my support today. indeed, a special focus should be placed on child poverty and i commend the rapporteur for bringing this to the floor in today’s vote. how is it possible in today’s day and age that one in four of europe’s children live below the poverty line? we have to do more, much more and invest further in education. in addition, i voted in favour of the introduction of a child guarantee with its specific fund which could have clear objectives at european level. furthermore, i supported a specific indicator on children at risk of poverty or social exclusion in the economic and monetary union.
in writing. ‒ the report is a progressive text, with a multidimensional approach to child poverty, for which comprehensive solutions are also called for. among others, it proposes that member states adopt policies that promote access to universal, public, free and quality health care, social services and education for both children and families, while ensuring cultural inclusion, democratic participation, balanced nutrition and adequate housing. the report links the poverty and social exclusion of children to that of their parents and stresses that for children to be well-behaved and their childhood rights to be safeguarded, measures must be taken to address unemployment, job security, family support or the public development of socio-educational networks. it is important to mention that the text includes gender aspects. the report does not reflect our rejection of the european semester or the country-specific recommendations, but in any case its content is positive for the reduction of inequalities, with particular attention to child poverty, which is why we voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ more than one in four children in the eu is at risk of poverty and social exclusion. this figure has risen alarmingly as a result of the economic crisis and the continuing social cuts by some european governments, such as the popular party government in spain. a unicef report on childhood in spain revealed that investment in childhood fell by 14.6% between 2010 and 2013, that is, 775 euros per child were cut, thus returning to figures before 2007. this report shows once again the commitment of this parliament to the fight against child poverty, in accordance with the commitments it has made in the framework of the united nations convention on the rights of the child and the 2030 agenda for sustainable development. we therefore voted in favour, although we deeply regret that no agreement was reached on the creation of a specific fund to combat child poverty, which would have allowed for more investment, more efficient use of the funds and better monitoring of their use.

in writing. ‒ as a result of events such as the economic crisis and, more recently, the migration crisis, large inequalities are being created in the population. i am certainly in favour of taking steps to reduce this situation. in spain, equality has always been a priority, so we have focused on providing a social welfare system that guarantees education and healthcare for all children under 18, as well as a guarantee of income. after the economic crisis we approved the 2013-2016 napin, mainly focused on the fight against child poverty and its guarantee of welfare. my position in favour of this vote is therefore clear. i certainly support these measures.
in writing. ‒ the legislative framework for cohesion policy ensures funding opportunities for marginalised communities in urban and rural areas. the 2014-2020 programming period focuses on the implementation of participatory local development and integrated territorial investments (iti) targeting marginalised communities. in voting in favour of the report, the socialists are calling on the european commission to adopt a definition of 'marginalized communities', which does not yet exist, with the aim of enabling these eu citizens to benefit even more from the european structural and investment funds. the vote against paragraph 11 of the report is because it assumes, through a wrong and generalized approach, that the eu does not have structures for fighting corruption and the fraudulent use of funds (and the existing ones are not accountable, transparent and democratic), and that marginalised communities are excluded from eu funds, which is a wrong assumption. the socialists have always advocated maximum transparency in the existing fund management structures and that marginalised communities continue to benefit from cohesion policy.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it contains positive elements for the effective application, through cohesion policy, of the principle of non-discrimination enshrined in the treaties. the resolution calls on the commission to clarify the concept of marginalised communities; stresses that cuts in public services further complicate the situation of vulnerable groups; highlights existing racism and institutional discrimination against communities such as the roma; calls on the member states to ensure the participation of associations working with marginalised communities; denounces the multiple discrimination against women, people with disabilities and migrants in marginalised communities, among other groups. i therefore voted in favour of the report, even though it is purely propositional.

in writing. ‒ this own-initiative report is important as it provides solutions and insights into the role that cohesion policies can play in contributing to the inclusion of marginalised communities. inclusion policies are largely dependent on national, regional and local governments and are therefore at the mercy of the political interest they arouse in the government in office. moreover, experience shows that aid is not always directed at meeting the real needs of these communities. cohesion policy therefore remains one of the strongest instruments with which the eu can combat marginalisation while supporting territorial and social cohesion in the eu.

in writing. ‒ cohesion policy is one of the strongest eu instruments to fight inequality and support economic, social and territorial cohesion in its regions. i supported today this report that sets up recommendations on how to use eu structural funds for a better inclusion of marginalised communities in view of the future cohesion policy programming period, while taking into account the specific national and regional needs and solutions that vary across europe.
in writing. ‒ this report illustrates a constant drift of the european union's cohesion policy. initially designed to improve economic, social and territorial cohesion within the union, cohesion policy tends to divert the european regional development fund (erdf) and the european social fund (esf) from their objectives. increasingly, these funds are being used to meet the needs of so-called marginalised communities, although not all of them actually fit this definition. the rapporteur mentions mainly roma and migrants as marginalised communities. once again, therefore, public money is being spent without any reciprocity being asked of the people who are being helped. assimilation and respect for the law are not among the eu's priorities vis-à-vis roma as migrants. finally, the most deplorable aspect of this report is that the truly marginalised communities, such as the disabled, the homeless and the unemployed, are the victims of the priority given by the european union and the member states to roma and migrants.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this report on increasing the social protection of minorities in europe because we believe that all policies aimed at increasing social cohesion, recognising the very existence of minorities and implementing measures to improve the living conditions of the millions of people who are currently at risk of social exclusion, are positive.

in writing. - i am in full agreement with these policies. in particular, i would like to highlight the european fund for aid to the most deprived (fead), which is part of the eu's cohesion policy and involves the purchase, management and free delivery of basic consumer goods to the most deprived. the fead partly replaces the food aid fund and refocuses it on social support, so that food aid is linked to social support to help marginalised communities overcome their situation. i also believe that the roma community should not be forgotten, as discrimination against them is a reality in the eu and must be tackled from all angles. i therefore support these policies which focus on promoting cohesion and social inclusion in order to achieve the eu poverty eradication target, which seeks to reduce by at least 20 million the number of people in the eu at risk of poverty and social exclusion.
in writing. ‒ in the face of the increase in wars and armed conflicts, i am fully convinced that it is now more urgent than ever to lay the foundations of a new international order through a reform of the un, so that it has effective mechanisms to defend international law, human rights and multilateralism on a global scale. while i agree with the report that the un needs to be reformed to strengthen its legitimacy and make it more transparent and democratic, i do not share the rapporteur's approach to reform. it proposes to strengthen cooperation between the united nations, the world bank and the international monetary fund in order to increase the submission of states to the organizations of the capitalist system at the international level. the report also argues that the eu currently plays a role in promoting peace and conflict prevention and crisis management in the world and should therefore have a permanent seat on the security council. this would certainly undermine the sovereignty of the eu member states. for these reasons i voted against.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because of the urgent need to strengthen the role of the european union in the un, with the aim of achieving our foreign policy objectives in a more satisfactory way. the most important reform, which i have advocated in my work in the committee on development, is the development of the current economic and social council into a council for sustainable development. this council will ensure that the un bodies have a more political approach and that coordination between them is improved. finally, i would like to emphasize my positive vote on amendment no 1, which calls on the eu to support the strengthening of the coherence, synergies and complementarities between the peacekeeping monitoring, the un peacebuilding structure and un security council resolution 1325 on women, peace and security. the amendment also includes the revision of the humanitarian aid policy, which now states that international humanitarian law and human rights legislation could justify offering women victims of war rape the possibility of safe abortion.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report to make better use of existing cooperation mechanisms, to ensure that member states in the un security council defend the eu's common positions. within this strategy to improve the eu's presence in the un system there are also other proposals, such as revitalizing the work of the general assembly and reforming the economic and social council. i thank my group mate for the effort made.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report on the eu's position on possible reforms of the united nations to strengthen the organisation and better achieve the eu's foreign policy objectives. i support the reform of the un system as a means of strengthening the efficiency of the organisation and better promoting the eu's foreign policy objectives. the eu must play an active role within the organisation, project its values, and contribute to effective multilateralism to provide global solutions to global problems. in this respect, we support the call for the eu to have a permanent seat on the security council. the socialist amendments have enriched the report with references to human rights, gender equality, lgbtqi rights, non-proliferation, the responsibility to protect and the moratorium on the death penalty. we also call on the eu to play an active role in the debate on the legal definition of the term 'climate refugee' and express our wish that the next person elected to the post of un secretary-general will be a woman.

madam president, last year we discovered that about 340 multinationals secured privileged deals with luxembourg in order to avoid paying taxes on their activities in europe. other member states have done similar deals. our committee has made several proposals to fight the situation, taking into account the weak state of our finances. dear colleagues, what multinationals do not pay, smes should not compensate with a higher tax burden. simplification of tax systems, a common corporate tax base to ensure fair competition and much higher transparency are all fundamental reforms we need. it is disappointing that some member states like spain have been so reluctant to make public tax rulings and multinational privileges. we catalans also want a new state to lead in this fight for a more fair and reformed tax system that does not give privileges to multinationals against smes and citizens, putting at risk our welfare state.
madam president, we welcome the fact that this report takes a clear stand against tax evasion and its devastating effects. it is the working men and women who suffer the cuts, despite paying the taxes that the big fortunes and multinationals avoid. but a clearer position on the political responsibilities of the commission and the council is needed, which amply justifies the extension of the mandate of the taxe committee, as this parliament publicly committed itself to on monday. we now know that mr juncker and mr dijsselbloem had to learn about and protect fraudulent practices from their governments. we therefore feel that their tax proposals are aimed at silencing the scandal and not really correcting the accounting loopholes and regulatory loopholes through which taxpayers' money is being drained. we already have examples of the counterproductive attitude of some governments - like mine, the spanish one - and european institutions in hindering greater transparency and better protection of whistleblowers, the cuts imposed on tax inspections or their taste for tax amnesties. it is therefore necessary to broaden and extend its approaches to building a fair system.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the main conclusions of the taxe committee are that many companies in europe pay little and badly, and that there is also competition between the states. a number of very important conclusions have been drawn, i would say a long-term roadmap. now, the question is, who's going to get it started? when? how? and i would like to warn this parliament, ladies and gentlemen, that there will very likely be great difficulties in putting into practice the measures contained in this road map, in this extraordinary report drawn up by the rapporteurs, because the member states do not accept the work of the commission and they do not accept the work of this parliament either, because they claim that this is a matter of national sovereignty, they claim that this is a matter for the states and that it is legitimate to compete among themselves. i think that is what we have to avoid and this parliament has to be very aware of what is happening in order to put these measures into practice.
mr president, the ferreira-theurer report by the taxe committee is the best argument for what can result from a committee of inquiry, as proposed by the green group: an experience full of positive lessons and disappointing findings. the surprising thing is not to see how multinationals divert their profits to places where they can pay less tax, but to discover the necessary complicity of some member states and to see how the commission protects both of them by preventing this parliament from having access to documents which compromise them. we were talking about the fact that the amount that multinationals no longer contribute to the public purse is close to the union's own budget, an absurdity which we can only tackle if the member states of the union stop competing unfairly with each other, that is, if we make progress in the harmonization of our tax systems; in fact, if we convert into european taxation the tax on the profits of those companies which precisely benefit the most from the single market, that is, those which operate in all the member states: to begin with, the taxation of digital business, a case in which the concept of paying taxes where the profits are generated only corresponds to the whole of the union.
president of the council. mr president, honourable members of the european parliament, madam vice-president of the commission, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honour for me to represent the luxembourg presidency of the council here today in the european parliament's assembly for this discussion on the 2016 budget. the agreement which the two arms of the budgetary authority, the european parliament and the presidency, have managed to reach, also with the help of the european commission, which has played an excellent role as an honest broker, is a very good end result for everyone, for all the institutions and, above all, a very good result for europe. i shall never forget the conciliation session on the evening of 13 november when we were, thanks to the openness of each other, in the process of reaching a compromise, of finalising the final texts, when we received the tragic news of the terrorist attacks and the barbaric acts that had been committed in paris. we have decided to observe a minute's silence and i remember the words i have spoken and the words spoken by the president, jean arthuis, in this moment of great sadness and mourning. the minute of silence we shared together reinforced our determination to achieve, which was already very strong, and i believe that we have, by the agreement we have managed to reach, proved the unity, solidarity and efficiency of the european union. let me emphasize efficiency since we managed to finish four days before the end of the period. i think that the credit for this goes to president arthuis, who, like myself and the committee, wanted to put the final proposals on the table as quickly as possible. it saved us time and money. i would like to draw a few figures from this budget: 155 billion in commitment appropriations, 153.89 billion in payment appropriations and then four other figures which seem to me to be fundamental and which are the cardinal points of this year. first, we have doubled the amount available to refugees, from two billion in the initial budget to four billion for actions both internally for refugees and at borders, border posts or even in the countries of origin. secondly, we have spent 19 billion on growth and jobs, 18 billion on the things i have just mentioned and then one billion in particular on the youth employment action which is so important to all those around these benches. thirdly, we have provided the necessary funds to reduce delays, backlogs and arrears of payments, which will increase from 17 billion to 2 billion next year, a figure which is extremely low indeed. the fourth amount i would like to mention is the 800 million budgetary margin which prudence has led us to provide. i would like to conclude by saying that we have also been wise in increasing the appropriations for the internal security fund; what had just happened in paris, at the same time, proved to us that this was the right direction. i shall stop there, mr president, and i shall thank you in my second speech. i would simply like to conclude by saying that this budget was concerned with balancing three constraints: the first, of course, is growth and investment on the one hand; the second is the emergencies and priorities around refugees, what you might call solidarity. the third is the budgetary constraints we have both in the european parliament and in most of the member states of the european union. there is a consistency here that i would like to stress.
vice-president of the commission.– mr president, on behalf of the commission i very much welcome the successful conclusion of the work of the conciliation committee for the 2016 budget and would like very sincerely to thank parliament’s delegation led by the chair, mr arthuis, as well as mr fernandes and mr deprez, but also ms gardiazabal rubial for the work on amending budget 2015, and mr geier for what he has done to have a very good decision in the end on agencies. it has been a privilege to work with the luxembourg presidency, with minister gramegna, who has contributed enormously to a spirit of conciliation rather than confrontation. we have finished with a very strong sense of unity. minister gramegna reminded us of the sober setting in which negotiations were completed. but it was not only the fact that we faced the security concerns stemming from the paris terror attack that was a determinant of how we worked. we face unprecedented humanitarian and refugee crises; the necessity – and, i would add, urgency – of supporting a fragile economic recovery in the european union. we face market difficulties for many of our farmers and the debt crisis in greece, and in that context we have come to a decision on the 2016 budget that is sound, focused on priorities and also makes use of the flexibility that has been built into the new multiannual financial framework (mff), to a great degree thanks to parliament. let me very quickly give a presentation of the key points of this budget. with regard to commitments: with the eur 155 billion we are some eur 101 million above what we had proposed from the commission. i am stressing this fact: that we actually went slightly above the proposal. this is a 3.2 increase compared to 2015. the two main blocs in commitments are support for investment growth in jobs, including for youth employment, and addressing the refugee crisis, where we have tripled funds for the asylum migration and integration fund, increased by 15% funds for the internal security fund and increased significantly, by 20%, humanitarian aid as well as funds for the neighbourhood instrument. with regard to payments, it is very important to stress that we are working on implementing the payment plan agreed by the institutions and at the same time, directing the limited capacity for increase to where it matters the most. in terms of amounts, we have eur 143.9 billion. this is an increase of 1.8% compared to the 2015 budget, and there we have an 11% increase for heading 1a - competitiveness for growth and jobs; a 57% increase for heading 3 – security and citizenship; and a 36% increase for heading 4 – global europe. in other words, this is a budget where we walk our talk when we address priorities. let me stress that there is a very strong commitment on the side of the commission to monitor implementation, use money wisely and any possibility that might arise during the year to direct to priorities as they emerge. finally, a word on margins. we have retained in this tight budget eur 2.3 billion in commitments and eur 1.9 billion in payments. facing the uncertainties of tomorrow, we ought to have space to act. finally, i want to recognise the staff of the directorate-general for the budget (dg budg) and other commission services, parliament’s staff who work on budgetary affairs, and also those who work on the budget in the council. thank you for all your hard work.
i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in the budgetary procedure, but that it should be involved in the budgetary procedure. but i must say that these negotiations have been exemplary and that is why i would like to join in the thanks that have been paid here today to the commission, to the presidency and, of course, to the other members of the european parliament, because i think we have reached a good agreement which puts extraordinary resources into addressing extraordinary situations - such as the refugee crisis - but which also continues to invest in research and development policies and which, moreover, serves our agricultural and livestock sector, which has been so badly affected by the russian veto or the milk crisis. and in addition to this, we have achieved a commitment to evaluate the youth employment initiative and decide together what we need to do in the coming months, although it is also true - and it is a pity - that we have not been able to include a major increase in payments for 2016 nor a political commitment by the member states to use the extraordinary revenue and finance their share of the european agenda on migration. although - as i said - it is a good agreement, i do not think we can fall into complacency, because in the future we have to deal with the structural problems that the budget has. and, if i may, one last thought because, as minister gramegna said, i cannot help thinking that, during the meeting last friday the 13th, while we were negotiating, 130 people were killed by terrorists in paris. it was not easy to continue working under those conditions, but we did it because neither your bombs nor your guns will ever destroy our ideas.
on behalf of the green group, i am sure that the commission will be able to give its opinion on this matter in due course, and i hope that the council will be able to give its opinion on this matter in due course. why, then, did i ask for a yes vote in our group? because all of you - mrs georgieva, mr gramegna - have done a good job; because it reflects some of the main demands of this parliament; because it tightens up almost all the margins available; because it is the first budget of the new commission, and neither the commission nor parliament are responsible for the narrow margin allowed by the current financial framework. we have some good news: the recovery of funds for h2020, cosme and erasmus; the contribution to international cooperation under heading 4; the visible but, i fear, still insufficient effort in the programmes for the refugee question; with two unknowns that we must follow closely: the political commitment to give maximum attention to the youth employment initiative and the commitment to avoid the reproduction of the huge volume of overdue payments. this budget allows us to get closer to the two horizons we have set out to work in depth on a new budgetary logic for the european union: the revision of the multiannual financial framework and the report of the working group which will give us results on the concept of 'own resources', a concept which today still appears as a sarcasm if we consider it from a european point of view. we must approach these scenarios with three objectives: to have revenues coming mostly from genuine own resources no taxation without representation; to move from programmes to policies with a spending budget in which the general interest predominates over distribution; and to approach an overall amount commensurate with the challenges we really face: open conflicts, migration, climate change, ageing, social inequalities and a democracy increasingly in danger.
