kill. i also welcome the inclusion of minors in this new directive.
on behalf of the green group, mr president, commissioner, we have spent more than three hours this morning on a priority debate on the paris attacks and the terrible terrorist threats that are coming our way, and now we are going to have less than one to talk about the biggest cause of violent deaths in europe as a whole: violence against women, which hits us every day and with far greater intensity than any terrorist threat. the figures have already been mentioned, but i will repeat them because they are terribly monstrous: one in three european women has suffered some form of violence and one in four has been sexually assaulted. will europe recognize it once and for all? this is our first security problem. and how do we deal with it? some member states of the european union still have legislation that conceals, protects or conceals this violence. in this question we put to you, madam commissioner, we are asking for solutions, urgent solutions, because every day women are killed by someone who thinks he is their master and lord, to the point of taking their lives, and every day many women have to flee and leave their homes, even though they are the victims, to seek some safe refuge. we can't wait. we need to put strong pressure on those governments which are not doing what they should, because they are accomplices of murderers, and we need a european directive against gender-based violence. we need the maximum involvement of the european institutions. mrs jourová, i see you are resigned. you complain about the problems of competence, but - as our colleague maria arena has already said - all the treaties of the european union say that we are the guarantors of equality, and what greater attack on equality than this sexist violence, than this violence against women. you have us on your side, you have parliament on your side, but please act quickly.
member of the commission.– mr president, ladies and gentlemen, thank you very much for this discussion. yes, we all have to do more; not only the european commission, we must act at all levels. you mentioned that the commission is the guardian of the treaties and especially article 8, which is the equality article. i am very much concerned about equality and i want to bring about effective actions using effective instruments. you call for new legislation. i said clearly that we are going to accede to the istanbul convention. as regards a possible new directive on combating violence against women, i myself do not think that a new directive is something that will solve the problem quickly. just look at the process of preparing european legislation. i am not criticising it, but even if we find a legal basis for this, it would take several years to bring it into force in the member states and to allow it to do its work. so i am talking about other instruments. i am declaring here that there is a problem with the legal basis for legislation, because violence against women is a criminal wrongdoing. so it is up to the member states to use their competences in criminal law. we can, and we must do what we can. we will do it through accession to the istanbul convention, which gives us the competences to act also in the legislative sphere. what i see as the more efficient instrument is to invest the available funding into efficient awareness-raising, into campaigning, into support for grassroots organisations and civil society and into the training of experts and professionals in order to further help the victims of violence. as regards other actors who the commission is prepared to support, we must first of all talk about the member states that we are supporting, but at the same time who we are pushing to enforce legislation which must improve the situation. we must speak openly about society as such, because violence against women in many member states is happening with silent acceptance within society as if it is something normal. in some member states this is even silently accepted by the media. so we should look in this direction and together try to improve the situation. local communities must not be blind and deaf. they must understand that something is happening around them. let us speak about the victims themselves. ladies and gentlemen, i have the recent statistics and the research saying that only 15% of violence against women has been reported to the relevant authorities. yes, the victims remain silent, and that is also because they do not have enough trust in the authorities that they will act to help them. this is what the victims directive is about: that victims should not fear reporting violence and that they could expect efficient support from the relevant authorities. and finally – and mr verhofstadt mentioned this – we should consider men themselves. yes, they must also do something to improve the situation. i was in sweden recently where they have very good programmes specifically focused on men, who have an essential role to play in combating violence against women because, without their understanding that the situation must improve, we cannot change anything. this is a complex issue. this requires a list of many measures done by many different actors on many levels. so let us do it. i am committed to going into more detail about the commission’s concrete plans when discussing the gender strategy in mid-december at the committee on women’s rights and gender equality.
in writing. violence against women is the most widespread human rights violation in the world, and affects all strata of society. in the eu, 9 million women have been victims of gender-based violence. while we must raise our voices and fight these crimes every day and from all walks of life, november 25, the international day for the elimination of violence against women, should serve to raise awareness and raise awareness. the institutions should act to defend women's equality and eradicate gender-based violence by adopting legislative measures, activating the 'parallel clause' to include gender-based violence among the criminal areas listed in article 83 (1) tfeu. we need to have comparable studies and statistics and a european strategy. it is also important that all states and the eu itself ratify the council of europe convention on preventing and combating violence against women. the commission should present without delay a new equality strategy including specific measures against gender-based violence and follow up the ep's call for a european year against gender-based violence.

president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the valletta summit on migration gave us the opportunity to give concrete expression to the union's commitments. strengthen our political cooperation with african partners at all levels, in order to address the root causes of illegal migration and to combat migrant smuggling and trafficking in human beings. the final declaration and action plan agreed in valletta reflect the success of this approach to advancing dialogue and cooperation with african countries. let me first of all emphasize the high level of participation from european and african countries. a large majority were represented at the level of heads of state or government. this shows the political importance that all of us in europe and africa attach to the challenges we are facing today. now it is a question of ensuring that these political commitments are also translated into equally firm commitments in the implementation of the action plan. i would like to highlight the most innovative aspects of the documents adopted. firstly, the main pragmatic and operational nature of these texts, which are based on a number of well-identified actions in each area of intervention. these actions are intended to promote sustainable economic, social and environmental development. the summit agreed to implement 16 priority initiatives by the end of 2016 as a first response. secondly, the action plan must be read in the context of the whole. the implementation of the various measures must therefore take place in parallel. the five chapters of the action plan are root causes, irregular migration, legal migration and mobility, protection and asylum, prevention of irregular migration and trafficking in migrants, return, readmission and reintegration. these chapters form a whole that corresponds to our shared priorities. progress in one area will allow simultaneous progress in other areas. thirdly, the content of the action plan is fully in line with the conclusions of the european council and the council on the importance of the return and readmission of irregular migrants. for the first time in the euro-african dialogue on migration, there is a clear and joint commitment to implement specific measures to facilitate the return and sustainable reintegration of irregular migrants. as stated in the final declaration of the summit, cooperation on return and reintegration can only strengthen the european migration and mobility policy, making it more effective and comprehensive. finally, we have committed ourselves to allocating appropriate resources to the implementation of these measures using all available financial instruments and the new eu emergency fund. we also decided to use the existing dialogue structures, the rabat and khartoum processes, as well as the eu-africa dialogue on migration and mobility, for the follow-up of the operational aspects of the action plan. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, on the g20 summit, i should now like to report on the results of the antalya summit, at which the union was represented by the president of the european council and the president of the commission. the g20 results are positive for europeans. there are many points of convergence between the g20 and the european union in the assessment of the current situation and the priorities identified. in its statement on terrorism, the g20 condemned the cowardly attacks in paris and ankara. he noted that terrorism cannot and should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilization or ethnic origin. in fact, this was also amply expressed this morning in the debate. the g20 also stressed its determination to work together to prevent terrorism by enhancing cooperation in full respect of the central role of the united nations and in accordance with security council resolutions and the united nations global counter-terrorism strategy. the g20 leaders also focused on terrorist financing and called for the swift implementation of the financial action task force standards in all jurisdictions. they also stressed the importance of a comprehensive approach based on the will to tackle the factors that foster terrorism. i shall not dwell on the migration aspect, which i have just mentioned in connection with valletta, so i shall concentrate on the economic issues that were discussed at the g20, or at least some of them. in antalya, the leaders focused on the g20's priority objective of achieving strong, sustainable and balanced growth. they reaffirmed their commitment, expressed in brisbane last year, to increase the g20's aggregate gdp by a further 2% by 2018. the underlying ambition is that global growth is uneven and still falls short of expectations, despite positive prospects in some major economies, including the european union. at this stage, half of the commitments in the g20 growth strategies, which include both demand-sustaining measures and structural reforms, have already been implemented, achieving more than one third of the 2% target. in addition to the commitments made in the national growth strategies, i would like to emphasise the g20's focus on investment, particularly in the case of the country-specific strategies for this year. these strategies include concrete measures to improve the investment environment. i am particularly pleased to note that in antalya particular attention was paid to private sector involvement in small and mediumsized enterprises and financial intermediation and that the antalya action plan contains a direct reference to the investment plan for europe. the investment is indeed our main concern. in this respect, i would like to welcome the fact that the european parliament has approved the candidates for the posts of executive director and deputy executive director of the european fund for strategic investments. we can now look forward to seeing it fully operational. in the field of international taxation, which was also on the agenda, the leaders endorsed the package of measures on base erosion and profit transfers. they recognised that broad and consistent implementation would be essential to ensure the effectiveness of this project, in particular as regards the exchange of information on advance cross-border rulings. an inclusive framework for the implementation of the beps project will be developed by the oecd in early 2016. taxation is another major priority shared by the union and the g20 and the presidency is actively pursuing its work to combat tax fraud and evasion and aggressive tax optimisation. in particular, the council recently reached agreement on the automatic exchange of information on advance tax rulings and this directive will be adopted in december. in this context, the report of the taxe special committee will certainly be a valuable contribution to the continuation of the debate in this field. let me end by briefly mentioning the progress, or rather the lack of progress, in implementing the quota and governance reforms at the imf that were agreed in 2010. the g20 and the european union have given top priority to the implementation of reforms in this area, but the united states has again been asked to ratify them as soon as possible, which it has of course not yet done. in this area, as in the other areas of g20 work, the presidency will continue its efforts to ensure that europeans take a common line within the g20 on the issues under discussion and thus best protect and promote our common interests. the union's work for the g20 finance ministers' meeting in hainan in december is already under way. this will be the first meeting held under the chinese g20 presidency.
vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs. – mr president, this is not the first time we have met here to discuss the refugee crisis, but at the valletta summit we focused mainly on saving lives and fighting the smuggling of human beings, something we have discussed in this very hemicycle several times, and we did so with our african partners, as there is no other way to effectively manage the current and future migrant and refugee flows. the issue of migration is here to stay. demography and economy tell us so. the first message that we shared in malta was this: migration and refugee flows are a phenomenon that concerns both europe and africa, as we are all at the same time countries of origin, countries of transit and countries of destination, in europe and in africa. there are more migrants and refugees on the move within africa itself than from africa to europe, and we are together in this: in africa and in europe. this is the basis of our partnership. building walls on our frontiers is no solution, and it definitely is not an option in the middle of the sea. that is evident to everybody. it will not stop migration; it will only weaken our international standing and our credibility. the current migratory and refugee crisis has sparked strong emotions in recent months, including in europe: good ones and bad ones, compassion as well as fear. but our duty as politicians is to act rationally. we must finally put in place a mechanism for human mobility fit for the 21st century, a mechanism that stems irregular migration and the exploitation of human suffering, including through return and readmission agreements, but also a mechanism that allows effective legal mobility to the benefit of both countries of origin and countries of destination, and their societies. mobility can benefit both europe and africa. it must happen legally and safely, not by turning the mediterranean and the sahara into mass graves. this is the core message of valletta and the basis of our partnership, of our common work, with our african friends. to do so, as the presidency just reminded us, we focused on five clusters of actions in malta. one: addressing root causes of irregular migration and forced displacement; two: legal migration and mobility; three: protection and asylum; four: the fight against irregular migration; and five: return, readmission and reintegration. we identified within those clusters nearly 90 individual broad actions that we will implement before the end of 2016. let me be completely sincere with you today; you know me by now, i always tend to be so. the conversation – especially the preparation of the summit – has not been easy at times. it has been tense at times, not only between the europeans and the africans but also within the two different groups – among europeans and among african countries. but i think our discussion has helped us a lot, as we managed to find common ground and an understanding on all the most relevant issues. as happens quite often in our work with our african friends, the preparation was sometimes tense, but the summit itself and the beginning of the follow-up on implementation were extremely positive and fruitful. our approach to our african partners is not about putting money on the table and asking for readmission in exchange. i am also very clear on this here, just as i was with our african friends. it is not about using development aid as a bargaining chip in our negotiations on migration management. that would not only be against all our values but also against our own interests, because it would not work. the right approach – the approach we suggested to our african friends – is to develop common instruments and the related means, including financial ones, to effectively manage together a complex phenomenon that concerns both europeans and africans. we have a common issue to deal with. we have to develop useful and effective tools, and we have to allocate resources to have those tools effectively implemented. it is a partnership. yes, there is a strong link between how we invest our development money and how we manage migration. that is clear. in the long run, migration will only be manageable if we favour africa’s growth and stability. this is why in malta we signed the constitutive agreement of a trust fund for africa. as president juncker mentioned this morning, this has already been on the table as a commission proposal for some months. but in malta we actually signed the starting point of this trust fund, which is an additional tool to tackle the root causes of poverty and irregular migration. the commission is putting eur 1.8 billion into it and member states have started to top up that figure, and i encourage them to continue to do so consistently – and i underline consistently. it will finance job opportunities, especially for young people and women. it will prop up projects focused on addressing the root causes of forced displacement. it will reinforce the resilience of communities touched by the transit of migratory flows, build capacity in management of refugee flows and migration flows (which are in nature quite different one from the other) and focus too on support to internally displaced people, which are all things that our african friends tell us they need support on, because they themselves are hosting on their territory hundreds of thousands of refugees and migrants, something that as europeans we hardly realise. at the same time, we have started to draw up a new system to discourage irregular flows and develop dialogues on legal mobility. this includes more cooperation from our african friends on readmissions as well as on the capacity of host countries and host communities to reintegrate returnees. i myself have been in ethiopia to a project that we finance on facilitating the reintegration of returnees, not in that case from the european union but from a different region, and i have seen with my own eyes that young women and girls especially – but also young boys, very young ones – if supported, and if their communities are supported in offering them a decent and an open perspective for the future, are not only glad to be back but are also passing on a message to their fellows citizens that embarking on dangerous trips across the desert or across the mediterranean is not necessarily a good idea. again, i stress in parallel that we have to strengthen the legal and regular channels for migration, because that is the safe way of tackling mobility among us. the fight against the smuggling and the trafficking and the work to strengthen resilience must go hand in hand. this is the reason why we agreed to implement in parallel the actions of all five clusters; together, not one before the other. the next steps will build on the rabat and khartoum processes – we do not need to reinvent mechanisms, we have to use correctly the existing mechanisms – through a number of meetings at senior official level but also by identifying already now, together with our african partners – not only national governments but also local authorities and ngos – concrete projects to be financed by the trust fund in partnership with all our african friends. in this respect i have engaged in these months in high-level meetings with african partners, from countries of origin and transit, and also themselves of destination. i can quote some numbers that are really impressive. i have done so in ethiopia, in niger, in north africa – all of their countries – and last week again in chad, where, let me say with a certain pride, for the first time the european union was invited to the g5 sahel summit – just one week after the malta summit – which is, i believe, testimony to the fact that the political partnership among us is strong and is getting stronger. we are trying to build a stronger partnership with africa, a partnership that is fit for the huge challenges ahead. let me be very clear on this: while we focus on the challenge of migration, we have to keep in mind that we have plenty of other common issues. we need to build a partnership with africa, because our partnership with africa is not limited to migration or the management of refugee flows. it is part of a much bigger picture. in the current crisis, governing migration is among the interests we share, europeans and africans alike. but again, we have security on our table, we have climate change on our table; we have development, energy, counter-radicalisation and job opportunities for our youth, in europe and in africa. we have a proper political – and not only political – partnership that includes plenty of other issues, one in which migration management is one of the pieces of the puzzle that brings us together with them. on all of these issues – and especially on security, but mainly on migration, which is the issue of today’s debate – we can only deal with these different challenges together. valletta was a first step. we have started building trust between us and also rational solutions that can stand the test of time. this is the challenge of our generation, and the cooperation of this parliament and of europe as a whole will be crucial to its success. also because again, and i stress this, our partnership president of the court of auditors.– madam president, i am honoured to present the court’s annual report to this plenary session of the european parliament. this year it comes at a particularly difficult time. on behalf of all of us at the court, i would like to express our deepest condolences to the french people and to the families of the victims of the recent terrorist attacks in paris. those who attack european values are actually attacking our democracy. we must all stand firm against them. this is a time for european solidarity, to defend the fundamental values in our treaty. it is a time when the european union and member states must also address other major challenges: generating jobs and growth; meeting energy needs while achieving climate goals; and managing asylum and migration flows. in our view, the european budget could be invested better and more quickly to meet the many challenges europe faces. taken together, our audit results over recent years point to a need for a wholly new approach: decision-makers must align the budget better with the european union’s long-term strategic priorities and make it more capable of responding in a crisis; legislators need to ensure that spending schemes are clear about the results to be achieved and the risk it is acceptable to take; financial managers have to ensure that the money spent complies with the rules and achieves the intended results. next year’s mid-term review of the multiannual financial framework provides a crucial opportunity to rethink our priorities and the design of some spending schemes. in the meantime, more must be done with the tools already in place. our report identifies long-standing financial management issues that need to be addressed. but before i go through them, i would like to be absolutely clear that the 2014 european union accounts have been signed off. they are reliable and we have issued a clean audit opinion to that effect. that said, let me highlight four areas of european union financial management requiring attention. first, too much money is still not spent in accordance with the european union’s financial rules. there is a persistently high level of payment errors. the overall estimated error rate for payments in 2014 was 4.4%, and it has been stable for the last three years. the commission and member states have made progress in recent years in preventing and correcting errors, but more errors could have been corrected if all the available information had been used. our analysis shows that there is scope to design spending schemes that are less error—prone, in particular by simplifying payment conditions and procedures. second, the performance of the budget. the european union must invest the budget better. we found that the multiannual financial framework could be better aligned with the eu’s strategy, both in terms of periods and priorities. we also highlight the fact that the high level of european union targets and political aims is not translated into clear operational objectives, which is fundamental for effective management and reporting on performance. third, the european union needs to deal with a number of financial backlogs that have built up, not least to free up funds so that they can be used where they are needed most. in particular, some member states are struggling to absorb the eu funds they have been allocated, and there continues to be a high level of unused funds in financial instruments. finally, european union financial management would strongly benefit from improved transparency, because this is crucial to ensuring citizens’ trust. we have recommended the action the commission should take to improve transparency about long—term cash flow needs, payment errors and corrections made, as well as the results of spending the european union budget. but it is equally important to ensure transparency for european union policies not directly funded from the european union budget. new ways of funding european union policies should not put financial risks beyond public scrutiny and audit. to conclude, the european union must invest its money better. it must act to ensure that its investments better match the european union’s priorities; that simpler rules are framed to achieve results; and that financial resources are managed more efficiently. taken together, all this would indeed represent a wholly new approach. the court of auditors stands alongside parliament and the other european institutions at this very difficult time. defending our democracy and ensuring the well—being of our citizens will place a great burden on our common resources. helping to ensure that those resources are used to their best effect will continue to be the principal task of the european court of auditors. (applause)
vice-president of the commission.– madam president, honourable members, president caldeira, members of the court, on behalf of the commission i would like to express our deepest gratitude to the court for the work you do. it helps us to use our taxpayers’ money better. i fully agree with the call by president caldeira for a new approach, and it is what we have embraced in the commission with our strategy on a results-focused budget. we have made progress on financial management, and the court has recognised that our accounts are in order by signing them for an eighth year in a row. they are modern, they are up to standard, and we thank the court for the work it has done that helped us to stabilise the error rate and, indeed, to reduce it slightly. that is a trend that we must pursue in the future. however, we also recognise there is more work to be done, and i would like to focus my response on the four points that president caldeira made. firstly, we have work to do on bringing the error rate down further by improving the quality of first-level checks, by continuing our simplification efforts – simpler rules mean fewer errors – and by further deepening work on the cost-effectiveness of checks. the court tells us that we have a higher level in respect of schemes that reimburse costs, and a lower level in respect of entitlement programmes. we have to take this into account. secondly, we fully agree with the court about the importance of focusing on performance. we are in a very difficult time for the european union, and every single euro matters. the union has to work better for our people, and this is at the heart of the work we are doing on a results-focused budget. we will also continue combining performance and compliance. we believe that work we have started already on preventive and corrective action in relation to errors is bringing positive results: eur 3.5 billion has been returned to the budget thanks to corrective action and preventive action that we have taken. we believe that, if we take into account the calculated residual error rate, we would be very close to the 2% that we strive to achieve. thirdly, on financial backlogs. this was a priority issue in the discussion on the 2016 budget, and we are committed to bringing the backlog down to eur 2 billion by the end of 2016 – to a sustainable level. and of course, work has to concentrate on the new programmes so we do not end up with the same problem three years down the road. last but definitely not least: transparency is our taxpayers’ best friend, and we are committed to continuing to improve it. we are grateful to parliament for recognising that we have made progress over this last year in terms of the transparency of our work, and we absolutely commit here to continuing that effort in the future. in conclusion, president caldeira said we must invest money better. we agree.
i would like to thank the president of the court of auditors, mr caldeira, and all the members of the court for the report they have presented to us for this year. the diagnosis is still a serious one, because the sick person, which is our budget, has been and is still subject to great difficulties: ever smaller; increasingly financed, through financial instruments which, as we see, have a problem of implementation and also of control; subject to great tensions because they do not come from own resources, properly european, but from intergovernmental resources, which means that those who consider themselves to be the owners of the resources can decide in a short-term way on their fate; and also subject to delays and serious risks of non-payment, as the court tells us. but the court also tells us that there is hope, that is to say, it tells parliament, the institutions - and the commission, of course - that we need a new approach and that in 2017, in that review of the financial perspectives, we will be able to improve, with all that we have learned in recent years, and to ensure that the european budget is no longer subject to totally cyclical changes. in a few months we have come to want to cure with it the economic crisis, youth unemployment, the refugee crisis and now the security crisis, and that series of elements cannot be financed suddenly with the european budget, which was in principle intended to recover the europe 2020 strategy. however, there are new elements in the report which will help us: everything about the change in trend; the mistakes in shared management and direct management have become more equal - then, mrs georgieva, madam vice-president, we will have to help ourselves to improve the commission's direct management - and we also thank the court of auditors for having indicated the nature of the mistakes. i believe that with all this information we will be able to improve not only the configuration of the 2016 budget, which has just been adopted, and its control, but also the revision next year.

madam president, the european budget is a complex and constantly evolving instrument, and 2014 - the first year of the current financial framework - is proof of this: new rules, a new spending orientation towards the objectives of the 2020 strategy and performance-oriented budgeting. the budget must be geared to generating added value from expenditure, and for this reason we must have clear objectives and appropriate indicators which take account of the specific features of the european funds, since infrastructure is not the same as aid to combat poverty, the results of which are very difficult to measure. we therefore need to simplify the main spending policies, in particular those for smes and individuals, which are more prone to error, and to encourage close collaboration between the actors involved in management and control, mainly the european commission and the member states.
in writing. i consider the presentation of this report to be a very important opportunity to examine in depth the weaknesses in the definition and implementation of european policies. i will dwell on two points which are strongly interrelated. firstly, the eu has often favoured the development of gigantic infrastructures of dubious utility. the case of airports is notable, but the same lack of planning and coordination is found in other areas of transport and energy policy, under the dubious approach that infrastructure will eventually create its own market. the second is the difficulties of public administrations, especially local administrations, which really want to implement alternative public policies, because of the administrative obstacles and financial needs involved in the adoption of european projects. there is a need to rethink european funds to ensure their efficient use and their real contribution to improving social and regional cohesion through the transformation of the production model. finally, i would like to mention the importance of identifying not only management but also legislative failures. the case of grassland, for example, shows the need for reform of agricultural policy to make it truly adapted to the environmental conditions on the ground.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. madam president, the other day we talked about how to tackle destabilisation, and afghanistan is a very clear example. mr brzezinski reminded us how the taliban were financed to make a vietnam for the soviet union and now we see, 15 years later - almost 15 years after - the new occupation, the failure: there is no more democracy, there are no more human rights; women are still being suffocated, killed and confined in their homes; there is more violence and there is a strengthening of the taliban. i think we have to turn around; we have to think about things in a different way. and we would have to do so by withdrawing and, above all, by returning to the united nations: to a transition under the auspices of the united nations. we must also give confidence: the us drone strikes in afghanistan and pakistan must stop. an international investigation into the attack on the doctors without borders hospital is needed. let's not be afraid. let's change and try other things, especially international legality.
madam president, first of all let me say that i am very happy that the cambodian opposition leader sam rainsy is here today, together with tioulong saumura, who is also a member of the cambodian national assembly. i welcome you both to this chamber today. the message once again is clear: the hun sen government has to stop the political repression of political opposition and come back to respect for the rule of law and democracy. it is not the first time this parliament has condemned such behaviour. we also call on the eu to stop ‘business as usual’ with cambodia. let me remind you that the eu is the largest foreign donor to cambodia. we call on hun sen and the national assembly to reinstate sam rainsy immediately and to restore his parliamentary immunity. this is why i am so delighted that we are adopting this resolution today. thank you very much, sam rainsy. you are an example to all of us. democracy and non-violence will always win.
author. madam president, human rights are inalienable, indivisible and interdependent and interrelated. freedom of expression is a right necessary to achieve a democratic society, as are political or social rights. bangladesh is a leading trade partner of the european union, but it is not a model in terms of human rights. five bloggers and independent journalists have been killed this year, and trade unions and anyone opposed to the regime are also persecuted. and what about labor rights? two years after the rana plaza tragedy, bangladeshi workers are still in conditions akin to slavery. in bangladesh, disappearances and extrajudicial killings are common. violence against women and lgbt groups is on the agenda. in bangladesh, there is still, to this day, the death penalty. enough of the cynicism! we cannot continue to be partners with states whose authorities systematically violate human rights. the dignity of the individual must always be put before the economic benefits of a few. always, you know?
on behalf of the alde group. madam president, madam commissioner, under the cooperation agreement on partnership and development with bangladesh, we, the european union, have increased funding for the period 2014-2020 by 70% compared to the previous period. article 1 of the agreement states that respect for human rights and democratic principles is an essential element. yes, in article 1. freedom of the press and media is an indispensable pillar of a democratic, pluralistic and open society. the continued murder of bloggers and editors, the implementation of policies that curtail media freedom of expression, the banning of 'anti-state' language or the closure of social media - such as facebook, whatsapp or messenger - are clear signs that democracy in bangladesh is deteriorating too fast. at this point i would like to ask you these questions: do we think bangladesh is respecting the agreement? do we think we have to keep the same conditions? in this connection, i would like to call on the european external action service to demand that the bangladeshi government immediately return to the path of democracy.

in writing. ‒ i could not vote in favour although i welcome the call in this resolution for the european commission to increase the level of humanitarian aid funds to support the education of children affected by humanitarian emergencies and protracted crises, while asking host countries to make an effort for better integration into their education systems. the final text of the resolution gives a 'crucial' role to the private sector in education systems. the right to quality education and universal access for all is unacceptable and incompatible with the private business of a few. that is why, throughout the whole process of adopting this resolution, we have advocated the need to make this resolution a clear call for and commitment to public, free and universal educational systems for both basic, secondary and university education, which has been rejected by a majority made up mainly of conservatives and liberals. since i am opposed to the european commission financing private enterprises in the education sector and i am in favour of public education, i have abstained from voting on this resolution.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution because of the importance of education in emergency situations. if we are to achieve the ambitious global goal 4 of the 2030 agenda - inclusive and quality education for all - we not only need to increase its funding, it is also absolutely crucial to coordinate emergency response programming with the long-term programming required for sustainable development. i would also like to explain my abstention on amendment no 1 proposed by the gue/ngl group. the opening text of paragraph 25 underlines the importance of the private sector as a potential source of innovative funding for education. this does not mean that the text is committed to privatised education, as the gue/ngl group's amendment would suggest. the document emphasises in paragraph 1 the importance of quality public universal education as a catalyst for development. i have always advocated quality public education as the most effective instrument for moving towards real equality of opportunity.
in writing. ‒ i abstained from voting on this motion for a resolution on education for children in situations of emergency and protracted crisis. the motion for a resolution makes a very positive call for increased funding for education in emergency situations, considering education as a fundamental, transversal and necessary element in all humanitarian action. the report also stresses the importance of universal, quality public education - both primary, secondary and higher education - for overcoming crises and achieving sustainable development. however, the report includes a paragraph which opens the door to the privatisation of education, which we consider unacceptable.
in writing. ‒ i supported the motion for a resolution on education for children in emergencies and protracted crises and i welcome the work done to reach this text, which highlights the importance of quality public universal education as a catalyst for development that increases the chances for other interventions in the areas of health, sanitation, disaster risk reduction, job creation, etc. in addition, it must be borne in mind that there should never be any discrimination against disadvantaged children, in particular those with disabilities, in access to education in emergency situations.
‒ 65 million children aged three to 15 are trapped in some kind of crisis, usually of long duration, without access to education. we're talking about more than one lost generation globally. the resolution calls for an increase in humanitarian aid for education in crisis situations from 1.9% to 4%, and for an increase in the humanitarian aid budget for 2016 by 26 million to ensure access to education in emergencies. it also called on the member states to support the commission's objective of increasing the proportion of humanitarian funds allocated to education and to promote the creation of a global fund. we socialists stress the importance of education as a key factor in development, in job creation and poverty reduction, as well as a powerful tool to help children overcome the traumas caused by conflict or other emergencies. i therefore voted in favour of this motion for a resolution.
in writing. ‒ i could not vote in favour although i welcome the call in this resolution for the european commission to increase the level of humanitarian aid funds to support the education of children affected by humanitarian emergencies and protracted crises, while asking host countries to make an effort for better integration into their education systems. the final text of the resolution gives a 'crucial' role to the private sector in education systems. the right to quality education and universal access for all is unacceptable and incompatible with the private business of a few. that is why, throughout the whole process of adopting this resolution, we have advocated the need to make this resolution a clear call for and commitment to public, free and universal educational systems for both basic, secondary and university education, which has been rejected by a majority made up mainly of conservatives and liberals. since i am opposed to the european commission financing private enterprises in the education sector and i am in favour of public education, i have abstained from voting on this resolution.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour, bearing in mind that the united nations estimates that one billion children live in conflict-affected areas. the eu and its humanitarian organisations should therefore systematically include the education and protection of children throughout the whole cycle of emergency response and ensure that there is flexible multiannual funding for protracted crises.
in writing. ‒ further to being a catalyst for development and poverty reduction, education plays a crucial role, especially in a protracted crisis or in the reconstruction of post-conflict societies. evidence shows that children with access to school and education are less likely to be exposed to forced marriage, radicalisation or human trafficking. i therefore supported this resolution that calls on the eu to work with partner countries, civil society and other relevant partners to improve educational opportunities for young people in conflict situations but that also urges the member states and the commission to support refugee students in transit.
in writing. ‒ i abstained from voting on this motion for a resolution on education for children in situations of emergency and protracted crisis. the motion for a resolution makes a very positive call for increased funding for education in emergency situations, considering education as a fundamental, transversal and necessary element in all humanitarian action. the report also stresses the importance of universal, quality public education - both primary, secondary and higher education - for overcoming crises and achieving sustainable development. however, the report includes a paragraph which opens the door to the privatisation of education, which we consider unacceptable.

in writing. i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution because it is an official position of the european parliament to ask the commission and the member states to cooperate in the task of lightening the administrative burden and simplifying the rules on cohesion policy funds. the concern expressed by parliament relates, among other things, to the relatively high percentage of programmes which are not finally implemented, due not only to budgetary constraints linked to the impact of the crisis and austerity policies, but also to delays in payments, bureaucratic burden or contradiction of rules. however, this simplification of the rules should not be used as an excuse either to relax the control of accounts and the use of the budgetary appropriations allocated or to leave the door open to financing instruments which are already beginning to participate actively in operational programmes, such as private credit institutions or venture capital funds.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this simplification. the general cohesion policy has, at the moment, many overlapping areas and areas where it is difficult to decide which would be the best fit. we believe that a simplification of the policy would make it easier to understand its usefulness and make it easier for the public to be aware of its existence.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on simplification and results orientation of cohesion policy for the period 2014-2020 to ask the commission to introduce detailed guidelines on simplification to inform member states and their regions about its role in eliminating or at least reducing the administrative burden and over-regulation observed at national and local level in public procurement processes, selection of project proposals and monitoring and control activities. in addition, the commission should provide a sheet to streamline and simplify control, monitoring and reporting activities for beneficiaries in order to eliminate current bottlenecks.
in writing. ‒ the eu institutions have taken important steps to address the issue of simplification. despite the efforts made, excessive formalities continue to be an obstacle to the efficient management of the esi funds. this motion for a resolution calls on the commission, inter alia, to share the simplification initiatives and guidelines, to strike an optimal balance between accountability and simplification, to fully implement e-cohesion in the management of the esi funds, to adopt and implement a flexible approach with regard to the obligations of beneficiaries to provide data and information, and to engage in a structured and ongoing dialogue with the european parliament and other stakeholders. i therefore voted in favour of this motion for a resolution.

i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. madam president, mr timmermans, mr katainen, your proposal is far from that of parliament. i think that lack of ambition and concreteness in measures and in implementation, and that holds back their potential to drive systemic change, and we really need that to create a circular economy that, among other things, virtually eliminates waste. the commission does make it very clear in relation to the financial framework for waste management that any investment in this area must meet the recycling objectives. for example, it confirms that there will be no investment in incinerators that is not absolutely justified, i.e. only in exceptional cases. i ask for more ambition in prevention and reuse, in selective collection of bio-waste and in recycling targets. it is perfectly possible and beneficial in every respect to move forward more and more quickly, and cities and territories such as ljubljana, gipuzkoa and contarina have already demonstrated this.
madam president, commissioner, a strong commitment in europe to the circular economy is, together with equality, one of our main competitive advantages in a union that depends, like no other region in the world, on imports of raw materials. the principle of treating waste as a resource is one of the keys to the future. supporting research and working on technologies and processes that allow us to reuse at least 70% of waste is key to developing new forms of production, nearly two million jobs and a source of sustainable, smart and innovative growth. that is why i share the principle of setting binding recycling targets, eliminating landfills, making energy use of only what cannot be reused, promoting innovation in this sector and making this principle a hallmark of 'made in europe'. i also propose a common european fiscal policy that supports the circular economy and trade rules that protect sustainable production from non-sustainable production. but it must also incorporate the key to reuse into the intelligence of tax systems.
member of the commission.– madam president, i wish to thank the honourable members very much for their comments and advice. let me start by saying that commissioner vella will be present in the committee on the environment, public health and food safety on 21 december. that committee will have the opportunity to look at the package in a very in-depth manner. first, what is different with this package compared to the previous one, which was withdrawn by the commission? first of all, the previous legislative proposal on waste was partially based on humble aspirations. for instance, if you look at the landfill target, it was not legally binding. i do hope that there is no political group – even the greens – who would put their political weight behind changing our proposal to the one we withdrew, because it would be weaker than the current proposal. this proposal is now legally binding, whereas the former was not – it was aspirational; it was a kind of hope that somebody would do something. now it is legally binding. also, it is not 25%: it is 10% by 2030. furthermore, what is different is that we are not only talking about how to deal with the waste, but about how to reduce the amount of waste. that is important and it is one of the reasons why we wanted to withdraw the package, make it more realistic and make it more ambitious, and also to look at how we could reduce the amount of waste and create incentives to use so-called waste, which provides valuable raw materials for industry if dealt with properly. i very much liked mr tajani’s use of the word ‘reindustrialisation’. this is very important, because if we manage to get our incentives right – and mr telička mentioned economic incentives also – it really encourages the private sector, entrepreneurs, innovators and also industry, to transform the current business model into a more circular business model. also, if you compare the circular recycling target and look at the landfill target, they are one entity. by 2030, recycling levels should be up to 65%. this is legally binding. we also have a review clause which means that by 2025 we have to look at whether we should raise the target above 65%. also, when we change the landfill target to be more ambitious, it will strengthen achievement of the recycling target. how many jobs will this create? well, nobody really knows. our assessment is that just looking at the landfill target and recycling target, one could imagine some 170 000 new direct jobs. but i would not stare at those figures, because nobody really knows how business will change in the meantime. if you look, for instance, at the eco-design directive or eco—design practices and energy labelling practices – without any widening of the scope which we are about to propose – just current practices, our assessment is that, by 2020, the amount of energy we will have saved is approximately the same as the annual primary energy consumption of italy. so basically it will save money and increase the purchasing power of the average consumer in europe by a little under eur 500 per year. nobody can really assess what kind of impact this will have on job creation. even if we add our proposal to widen the scope of eco-design, nobody knows exactly what its impact will be, but it is positive anyway; it is significant. i want to thank members for this discussion and have one last point on food waste because it was clearly mentioned. member states are committed to sustainable development goals, and this is mentioned very clearly in the waste legislative package, so member states must take measures to reduce food waste at each stage of the food supply chain, monitor food waste levels and report back, recording the progress made. the commission will also elaborate a common methodology to measure food waste. in addition to this, we will clarify legislation relating to waste food and feed in order to facilitate redistribution of safe, edible food to people in need, where it is safe to do so. we will also look at what we could do in order to guide member states in food donations. this is a big issue. this is a big part of the european investment package, and there is plenty of room for a pragmatic approach with moderate result-minded thinking. let us try to find new tools in order to empower consumers and businesses to change the business model.
in writing. spanish socialists believe that the paradigm shift from a linear to a circular economy is an urgent necessity. we therefore support the need to promote new business and consumption models that promote sustainable economic growth at the time of cop21. we will monitor compliance with the established binding targets covering the entire product life cycle, from design to procurement and resource management, by scrutinizing projects funded by eur 650 million under h2020 and more than eur 5.5 billion under the structural funds. during the parliamentary procedure now under way, we reiterated our highest ambition to reduce municipal waste by 70%, not 65% as proposed by the ec, and the need to set binding targets for food waste.

in writing. first of all, i would like to welcome the proposal put forward by the european commission, as i consider it crucial to advance the circular economy model. the current linear economic model of 'take, make, throw away' is based on having large amounts of energy and other cheap and easily accessible resources, but it is already reaching the limit of its physical capacity. the circular economy is an attractive and viable alternative that we must encourage together with the private sector. the circular economy is restorative and regenerative, and through this circular model we can get products, components and resources in general to maintain their usefulness and value at all times. this model would lead us to a continuous cycle of positive development that conserves and enhances natural capital, optimizes resource use, and minimizes systemic risk by managing a finite amount of stocks and renewable flows.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. madam president, first of all i want to make it clear that frontex is designed to protect the borders. frontex is an instrument of a europe without solidarity, of a europe of walls and fences, of a europe complicit in the mediterranean becoming a great mass grave. the very activity of the frontex agency is therefore in itself a violation of human rights. frontex is synonymous with mass deportations, violations of fundamental rights at the borders, racist raids and military operations in the mediterranean to prevent the arrival of immigrants. because of this border control, thousands of people have no choice but to put their lives in the hands of the mafia in order to reach europe. 'frontex staff watched from the deck of their boat as turkish, greek and ngo fishermen saved lives' said a volunteer who helped rescue a boat carrying 300 people bound for lesbos a few weeks ago. frontex and respect for fundamental rights are a contradiction, and this is not resolved by a complaints mechanism. to guarantee fundamental rights at the borders, we must dismantle frontex, put an end to the defence of borders and tear down the walls of this fortress europe.
madam president, first of all i would like to congratulate the co-authors, my colleague mrs metsola and mrs keller, on agreeing to produce this report and accepting the complaint made by the european ombudsman in his day, in which he asked for a mechanism to deal with possible violations of fundamental rights. europe is the benchmark in the field of fundamental rights, and this is another step in the european union's commitment to respect the rights of all these groups. the borders belong to all europeans and their control is the responsibility of the european union as a whole. frontex's main task is the integrated management of the union's external borders, but it also cooperates with all national authorities in the management of these borders. there is no doubt that being able to accept these individual complaints, discarding those that do not take place, will strengthen this mechanism, offering special protection to vulnerable groups such as immigrants, women, children, the disabled and lgtbi groups.
madam president, this report is not a report on the nature of frontex or on its justification as an agency in the constellation of the area of freedom, justice and security, but on what parliament can do to reinforce the commitment of frontex which explained the last reform of its rules of procedure. a commitment to fundamental rights and therefore to frontex agents having specialised training, identifying themselves as such by emblems and, in addition, having a specific commitment to particularly vulnerable groups, especially in the field of gender and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. but above all, allow the executive director of frontex to exclude staff who do not strictly comply with the protocols and the regulation binding the agency to respect the fundamental rights enshrined in a charter of fundamental rights of the european union which does not discriminate between europeans and non-europeans in order to affirm the commitment of the european union to fundamental rights.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, commissioner, i would not dare to take a positive or negative view of the european year of development, it is still too early. it's true that 2015 is being a very important year. since july we have had a new framework for financing development; since september we have had a new regulatory agenda under the united nations sustainable development goals; and in the coming days, in paris, i hope that an ambitious plan against climate change will also be adopted. however, we can't put on medals, because the complicated part starts now. we have all the work to do. it is up to us to ensure that the good intentions of 2015 do not remain on wet paper, but are transformed into truly effective actions. we wish it so. the new 2030 agenda for sustainable development is universal in nature, which means that we share the responsibility for making it a reality. part of our work is to ensure that the principle of policy coherence for development is effectively implemented, and only then will we achieve our goals. we must stop giving with one hand what we take away with the other, as is the case, for example, with our trade policy, which cannot continue to impoverish the people of the south and undermine the objectives of development policy. only if we have achieved all the targets proposed this year by 2030 will the success of 2015 as the european year of development be a reality, as the year of change.
mr president, we are coming to the end of a year in which there has been a little more coherence, a lot of interinstitutional dialogue and cooperation with the social partners. this year parliament has taken a consistent stance on international summits. but in december we have more problems than in january; we have more crises, development crises, humanitarian crises, conflicts that require an even more ambitious response than at the beginning of the year. we would not be generous with what we have done this year if we did not take the momentum to respond to these challenges with determination and the first of these challenges is to meet our commitment to dedicate 0.7 percent of our wealth to supporting those who barely reach 0.7 percent of our well-being. that is the future to which we must dedicate this year's legacy.
president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mrs regner, mrs gabriel, i welcome the opportunity to address parliament and to inform you of the progress of the work on the commission's proposal for a directive on improving the gender balance in boards. on this issue, parliament has already adopted - as you have just mentioned - its position at first reading, in which it broadly supports the commission's approach. in october, the commission published new figures on the gender balance in the boards of publicly listed companies. these figures show that, in the european union as a whole, only one fifth of the members of the boards of directors are women. although ridiculously low, this figure indicates some progress. i agree that it would take a lot of patience to actually achieve equality or balance in this respect. it is therefore necessary to do something different and to speed up the process a little. it should be remembered that in 2010, when these debates began at eu level, only one in ten of the boards was female. so we must continue to tackle this problem. there is simply no reason for the 21st century to be a century of male-dominated boards. greater equality in management positions is a positive signal to society as a whole. the balance between women and men in decision-making bodies is of course a matter of practical equality. it is also a symbol, but i would add that diversity is very often - as you said, mrs gabriel - positive from the point of view of good corporate governance. the luxembourg presidency has made this issue one of its main priorities. we have put forward several new drafting proposals with a view to finding a compromise within the council. the proposal was examined and discussed at length in the council's various bodies. we have now, after all these discussions, put the matter on the agenda of the epsco council, which will meet next monday, to take stock and see whether a qualified majority in favour of the proposal could actually be obtained. i do not want to prejudge the outcome of these discussions in the council, but i can unfortunately tell you in advance that the recent discussions in coreper have not been very encouraging. today i received very good news, as i learned that a country - which you know well, madam commissioner - has indeed announced that it has changed its position from a negative to a positive one. that is a good signal, i think, and a very positive one. so, as you know, this proposal contains binding procedural rules which are aimed at achieving quantitative objectives. it requires that the procedure for selecting members of the boards of directors be fair and based on merit and transparency. the main difficulties arise from the fact that member states have different approaches to the subject. some member states are more advanced than others in terms of the level of equality between women and men in this area. but overall i would say there is a consensus in favour of the aim of this proposal. however, while a large number of member states are in favour of legislation at union level, others - and unfortunately, for the time being, they are still a blocking minority - maintain a preference for national measures (also arguing for subsidiarity) or advocate non-binding measures at european union level. the presidency has also drawn up council conclusions on the subject of equality between women and men, which will also be adopted on this point, and i believe that we will succeed in having them adopted at the epsco council on 7 december. our work was based on a report by the european institute for gender equality, which gave an update on the current situation in the european union. in conclusion, we need to ensure that our largest companies can benefit from the talent and dynamism of both women and men. europe has a wealth of untapped talent and, above all, today we see that 60% of university graduates in europe are women. so there is no reason why in the twenty-first century governments, corporations, banks or other institutions should still be run primarily by men. let me thank the european parliament for keeping the issue of equality between women and men on the agenda. i hope that this debate will inspire some of you at our council meeting on 7 december.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, today in europe, six out of every ten students or graduates are women. however, eight out of ten directors of european companies are men. this is unequal, unfair, costs us money and harms the union's competitiveness. and it's easy to work out. quotas have proved effective in correcting these types of problems: all that is needed is a political decision to facilitate and promote the incorporation of female talent into the management of the european economy. there are good reasons for doing so. there are plenty of studies - like the one presented here last month by fiona jurdant of the oecd - showing that companies with balanced boards are more competitive, have fewer governance problems, more return on capital and better economic results. that's why they work better and generate more trust with customers and investors; that's why bringing that value into our economy is strategic and innovative; that's why betting on public programs and legislation to achieve it is an investment; that's why it's a competitive advantage in which we need to be world leaders; and that's why we need transparency and fairness in the selection of the people who make up the boards of directors. i thank the luxembourg presidency and the commissioner for their willingness, work and interest and for all their efforts to bring this initiative forward. i encourage the countries that are blocking it to reconsider their positions and i hope they understand that as long as these things continue to happen, the great proclamations about equality will be wet paper.

mr president, mr orbán's government in hungary is systematically violating human rights. the proposal to introduce the death penalty, the inhumane treatment of refugees at the borders, the constant violence against migrants. and there has not yet been any serious sanction against this member state of the european union. why would you do that? well, because he's one of yours. because he's from the european people's party. because a few weeks ago he was at the european people's party congress in madrid with mr mariano rajoy, mrs merkel and even mr berlusconi. and there you applauded his xenophobic speech. they support him, they pat him on the back, because they protect their friends and because, deep down, in fact, many, deep down, share his programme.
mr. president, what is this? a debate about hungary? i'm not sure. it is a debate on the situation in hungary at the hands of the government of viktor orbán of the family of the european people's party, installed in an extreme nationalist rhetoric and, moreover, aggressively anti-european rayano in europhobia, which speaks of the death penalty, raises walls. and so it is a debate that reaches across europe and affects the whole of europe in the worst crisis in its history. it defies the copenhagen criteria, which are not only required when you join the club, but when you stay in the club. and they are therefore calling for european action by this european parliament and the european commission. and the european commission is unable even to put in place the rule of law mechanism to assess the lack of democratic quality, respect for minority rights, judicial independence and the right to a judge pre-determined by law in hungary, as is clearly shown by a citizens' initiative registered on 30 november calling for the application of article 7. commissioner, convince the college of commissioners, mrs jourová, that the commission should do something to defend european values, which are being put in the most serious crisis by the government of viktor orbán in hungary. the answer is 'blue card'. mr president, of course i have not heard any questions because there have been none. i have heard mention of an article in the treaty on european union which should be read with all the others, particularly in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. tell the government of viktor orbán - in case it has not heard - that being part of the european union means being part of a space without the death penalty and therefore anyone who brings this issue into the debate will have to answer to the whole of europe. this is a conquest of the civilization of law and freedom which must be actively preserved by the guardian of the treaties, which is the commission. that's why we're arguing. when a european union leader dares to talk about the reintroduction of the death penalty as a subject of debate, he is disrespecting the contract he signed when he became a member of the european union.

mr president, in my short speech i wanted to address the issue of the digital single market. i wanted to take advantage of the fact that the commissioner is sitting here, when this agenda falls partly within her portfolio in some legal aspects. i have held several meetings with various business groups in the czech republic and attended various conferences, and i was pleasantly surprised by the way in which this topic is perceived by czech businessmen. for the sake of completeness, i shall provide at least one statistic. in the czech republic, 26 smes sell goods online, the highest number of smes in europe. so i wanted to use this short speech to call on the european commission to speed up the preparation, especially at the legal level, of online sales contracts and the movement of goods across europe, so that entrepreneurs can make their businesses and their profits more efficient.
mr president, the european ceramic industry employs more than 200 000 people in europe, 30 000 in spain and more than half, 17 000, in my region, the valencian community. it is a competitive, innovative, export-oriented and high value-added industry. an industry which is, however, suffering from social and environmental dumping, subsidised prices and higher energy costs than its competitors, and which, moreover, now has to deal with global overproduction and the possible granting of market economy status to china. it is obvious that china is not a market economy, and the european union should not grant it such status in advance if it does not meet the conditions laid down. to preserve a competitive and job-creating european ceramic industry we need new and effective trade defence instruments. we need to make importers subject to the same requirements as european producers and reciprocity in market access. i have just been appointed chairman of the european parliament's ceramics forum and i will work with my colleagues in this parliament to ensure that the ceramic industry can continue to set an example.
mr president, i would like to use this european platform to talk about the almadraba, a thousand-year-old art of tuna fishing. an art that creates employment and is strongly linked to the territory, capable of producing, but with absolute care and respect for the species. i would ask my colleagues to support the written declaration on the working class and the demands it contains. i would like to stress in particular the need to provide an additional quota for bluefin tuna in order to improve scientific observation of tuna, as a recent study by the committee on fisheries has pointed out. i also ask the commission to implement measures at european level to support the cod, measures which must necessarily include requiring member states, such as spain, to respect environmental criteria in allocating quotas to sustainable gear such as this model of fishing. this fishing art contains the seed of a new production model, an economy model at the service of work and the environment. that is why it is important that this parliament should support the life of an entire people, the life of an entire region.
mr president, the paris summit raises the very serious problem of global warming. indeed, control of the weather and the man-made elements that alter it are of vital importance to life on earth. but this problem has not only technical solutions, because it is a political and civilization problem. if the developed countries in particular continue to pursue industrial and economic growth without respite, we shall also be heading for collective disaster. soon, very soon, we will have to set our development ideal. if the well-being of humanity is to be sustainable, we cannot base it on constant growth but on development, global for each and sustainable for all, which does not seek only to increase wealth but wants to keep us all in well-being, that is, in knowledge, beauty and goodness. because the big change on the planet is in attitudes, values and goals.

in writing. ‒ the eu and liechtenstein signed an agreement on the automatic exchange of bank account information on 28 october 2015, an important step in efforts to crack down on tax fraud and tax evasion, updating the 2004 agreement, which ensured that liechtenstein complied with measures equivalent to those of the eu directive on taxation of savings income. under the agreement, as of 2017, the eu and liechtenstein will automatically exchange information on the bank accounts of their respective residents. the aim is to deal with situations where the taxpayer intends to conceal capital on which he has not paid taxes. it will be ensured that liechtenstein applies measures equivalent to the new legal framework that the eu has adopted in this area and in particular to those of the administrative cooperation directive. i note as key issues that the tax administrations of the member states and liechtenstein will be able to correctly and unequivocally identify the taxpayers concerned, administer and enforce their tax laws in cross-border situations, assess the likelihood of tax evasion and increase effectiveness in the prosecution of these offences. i have therefore voted in favour of this agreement.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this scandalous report which provides that frontex, the european border management agency, facilitates complaints from migrants about possible violations of their rights, while they themselves are present on our territory illegally. the procedure allows third parties, such as heavily subsidised ngos, to lodge complaints on behalf of migrants. in addition, information campaigns will be organised among migrants to ensure that they use this remedy and the various documents relating to the procedure will be available in their languages. all of this, of course, has one goal: to reduce the number of evictions even further, which is already almost zero. a few days after the paris attacks, this report shows that the speeches made by the socialists and the republicans, who have recently shown their firmness on immigration and security, are nothing but dust in the eyes. the members of the national front and their allies, true to their commitments, voted against this text and tabled an alternative resolution, in order to really oppose mass immigration. this proposal was rejected by the french and european immigration deputies...
in writing. ‒ we abstained from voting on the special report of the european ombudsman on his own-initiative inquiry into frontex because, on the one hand, we are against the role currently played by frontex and believe that this agency should be rethought and eventually dismantled. we have also not voted against the report because it does not include any aspects that could strengthen frontex's operations, but it does contain the european ombudsman's conclusions on the agency's human rights obligations, including aspects which we consider to be fundamental, but not sufficient. the report also deals with individual complaint and denunciation mechanisms for cases of violation of human rights and fundamental rights, which have not been accepted until now. at the same time, it calls for measures to improve human rights safeguards and guarantees in the agency's operations and recommends that gender training be made compulsory before joining a frontex operation, in particular to raise awareness of gender-based violence and the vulnerability of migrant women.
